It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Specific, internally consistent claims attributed to data; not confirmable here.

text: I have asked Oranga Tamariki about the serious allegation in the member's question of kids being housed in motels with untrained staff, and they've been unable to identify what the member is referring to. If the member has evidence of this occurring, I would strongly encourage her to provide this information so it can be addressed... yes, I am aware that motels are being used as an emergency option, as a last resort where no other safe option is available. This practice even pre-dates Oranga Tamariki as an organisation.
explanation: Claims OT could not identify the untrained-staff allegation and that motel use predates OT; plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Specific statistical claim about typical stay lengths; plausible from monitoring data but not independently confirmable here, and it omits the long-stay outliers.

text: I have read the ICM report very closely, and there is no mention in that report of untrained staff being used to look after children in motels.
explanation: Factual claim about the contents of the ICM report; checkable against the report but not verifiable from the text here.

text: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
explanation: Specific, checkable spending and harm-reduction figures presented as fact.

text: When Māori thrive, all New Zealanders will thrive.
explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism, measure, or policy detail.

text: Why has the Government prioritised an almost 80 percent pay rise for the directors of Fire and Emergency New Zealand, while front-line firefighters are getting no pay rise and have to continue to work in unsafe conditions with equipment that keeps breaking down?
explanation: Quantifies the director rise and names concrete frontline concerns.

text: How does a 49 percent increase in hospitality businesses going into liquidation in just the last year indicate that his economic plan is working?
explanation: Precise figure and timeframe.

text: we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders
explanation: Names the policy and a quantified result (3 million prescriptions).

text: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
explanation: Names a precise rate (69.8%) and a job figure (281,000).

text: We support the addition to the motion made by Chris Hipkins and we absolutely—absolutely—call for peace on this particular issue. We want to ensure that our people understand the impacts that it will have on our people living here in Aotearoa.
explanation: General call for peace with no concrete proposal or detail.

text: We have been really proud of the fact that we’ve been able to hear more te reo Māori in the House. We’ve been proud to be able to hear more waiata in the House and to hear a wairua Māori in this House.
explanation: Conveys a real trend but with no figures, mechanism, or timeframe — a general statement of pride.

text: Te Pāti Māori's support for changes to section 4 is conditional on broad support by te iwi Māori on proposed changes made with iwi Māori, while acknowledging the independent voices of whānau, hapū, and iwi, who may take different positions.
explanation: Defines the condition (broad iwi support, made with iwi) precisely.

text: The electricity costs are up more than 20 percent. Rates are up nearly 22 percent. Health costs continue to rise, food prices continue to climb
explanation: Gives concrete percentage rises for electricity and rates.

text: The top 10 percent now own nearly half the wealth in Aotearoa, while the bottom 50 percent share just 6.7 percent between them. The bottom 20 percent now hold negative wealth.
explanation: Several precise wealth-distribution figures.

text: Democracy is, in truth, a very fragile institution. It lives or dies on the basis of trust, and really, transparency is the mechanism through which that trust can thrive or that it doesn't.
explanation: General rhetorical framing about democracy and trust with no concrete detail.

text: should that secondary piece of legislation fall off a website, it would still be law, regardless of people not being able to access it.
explanation: Concrete scenario tied to her proposed amendment, though no precise drafting offered here.

text: the Minister of Justice has asked officials to examine the costs associated with the OIA request... he wants to know what revisions could be made to make the Act more efficient and practical.
explanation: Names the actor (Minister of Justice) and the specific action (examining OIA costs and possible revisions).

text: it can result in an overhung Parliament, as it did in 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and, of course, this one as well.
explanation: Lists the precise election years to support the point about overhang.

text: if you are able to download secondary legislation, then you may well have the tools to be able to apply a voice system or to increase the size of the print, etc., and so that could be quite an effective way of addressing the accessibility issue by simply changing the word “or” in that paragraph, to the word “and”.
explanation: Precise textual amendment ('or' to 'and') tied to replacement section 75(2)(a).

text: Others may talk big about splashing the cash. We are taking a responsible approach.
explanation: Slogan-like; 'responsible approach' commits to nothing concrete.

text: The conflict will have a negative impact on the economy, through prices, but also, potentially, through other channels like shipping disruptions, freight costs, reduced demand for New Zealand exports, financial markets disruption, and greater uncertainty. The Government can take the sharpest edges off for vulnerable New Zealanders, and you've seen that with the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit, but there is a real cost from this conflict: New Zealand is poorer because of these global events.
explanation: Names concrete channels and the $50 in-work tax credit, but no magnitudes on the GDP impact.

text: Treasury emphasised that that maximum prudent level of debt for New Zealand in normal times must be 50 percent of GDP... we faced ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years.
explanation: Concrete threshold (50% of GDP), probability (75%), and timeframe (50 years).

text: Stats New Zealand points out that rents rose only 1.2 percent in the year—the smallest annual increase in 16 years.
explanation: Names a precise figure (1.2%), a timeframe (the year), and a comparator (smallest in 16 years).

text: Yesterday, Ministers signed off on a proposal through the Regional Infrastructure Fund to increase New Zealand's diesel storage capacity through a commercial arrangement with Channel Infrastructure at Marsden Point. This will provide up to an additional 93 million litres of diesel storage, which is around a 20 percent increase in current capacity…
explanation: Names the fund, the partner, the site, the volume (93m litres) and the percentage increase.

text: Labour’s plan is built on long-term investment, shared prosperity, and good jobs that keep young people building their futures here in New Zealand.
explanation: Slogan-level framing—‘long-term investment, shared prosperity, good jobs’—with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

text: access to capital is one of the reasons why New Zealand’s productivity is lagging. What is Labour’s solution to that? The New Zealand future fund—that’s what it’s about. If you look at Ireland, they have a very simple sovereign wealth fund; Mark Carney and Canada just released their own sovereign wealth fund.
explanation: Names a concrete policy (NZ future fund) and comparators, but no figures or mechanism detail.

text: At a time when unemployment is at an all-time high and we have high business liquidations—a 15-year record in high business liquidations—what does this Government do? ... more business liquidations and more unemployment, with the loss of 8,700 public sector roles.
explanation: Cites a '15-year record' and the 8,700 figure.

text: I was actually quoting from a transcript of the Hon Nicola Willis' press conference on 27 August 2025, where she said, "The purpose of this briefing is to update you on the Government's next steps to increase grocery competition and reduce food prices for Kiwis."
explanation: Exact date and verbatim quotation.

text: in this Budget alone, 86,000 households will have their rent increased by $30, and 30,000 of those households are pensioners; the 8,700 public servants losing their jobs
explanation: Multiple precise figures for households, pensioners, dollar amounts and job losses.

text: we've achieved a path back to surplus, so we're not adding to our debt.
explanation: Names the goal (surplus, no added debt) but without figures or date.

text: that Labour Government that was hopeless and that had overcooked the stimulus and driven up $100 billion of extra debt, driven up inflation, including 30 percent house price inflation in one year
explanation: Names dollar and percentage figures.

text: The Government has no policy to criminalise homelessness. What we do have is a policy to give the police the power to issue move-on orders to people displaying disorderly behaviour in public places, and only people who refuse to follow those orders will face prosecution.
explanation: Clearly states the mechanism and the prosecution threshold (refusal to comply).

text: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
explanation: Names the survey, the figure (49,000), and the period.

text: Well, the Act creates a new offence of stalking and harassment, punishable by imprisonment for up to five years, where an offender undertakes a pattern of behaviour which the offender knew was likely to cause the victim fear or distress. The pattern of behaviour is defined as two specified acts within a two-year period. It includes activities such as following, loitering near, obstructing a person, recording or tracking, or other specified acts.
explanation: Precise legal detail: offence elements, penalty, the 'two acts within two years' threshold and enumerated behaviours.

text: We are a party and a Government of fiscal discipline. We think about where we spend taxpayer money—because it's not our money; it's taxpayer money
explanation: Slogan-level claim of fiscal discipline with no concrete measure.

text: In regard to the corporate tax rate, yes, we did consider, as part of the assessment when we put in place Investment Boost, whether we would be better to reduce the corporate tax rate or do another alternative. We selected to do Investment Boost, because Investment Boost is a targeted mechanism in order to ensure that the benefit goes to those who most need it.
explanation: Names the actual policy choice (Investment Boost vs rate cut) but gives no figures or detail on the assessment.

text: this Government isn't intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy that we inherited and which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.
explanation: Cites the >$800/MWh 2024 figure and the backup-only role.

text: One-third of Kiwis live in Auckland, 40 percent of GDP
explanation: Concrete proportions, though stated without source.

text: I move, That this House congratulate Auckland Football Club on becoming the first New Zealand club to win the A-League championship with their 1-0 victory over Sydney FC in the 2026 Isuzu UTE A-League Grand Final last weekend
explanation: Names club, exact score, opponent, named competition and timeframe.

text: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Quantifies the trend (third drop, 20%+ in 8 of 12 districts).

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Names the funding ($30.6m), the budget year, age range, and cities.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Gives concrete stay-length figures (one night, fewer than three nights) and reasons.

text: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
explanation: Exact figure (all 72) and the start date.

text: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
explanation: Multiple precise figures with budget years and an outcome metric.

text: My understanding is that the current website won't require retrospectivity... They're expensive to create and they're expensive to maintain, and I'd be surprised if we go for a whole new one again.
explanation: Gives a clear answer plus practical rationale (cost), but no concrete figures.

text: the fact that the secondary legislation doesn't come into force until it's published kind of takes care of that. If the regulator wants the rule to be enforced or regulatable, they should publish it and bring it into force.
explanation: Names the specific clause and the operative mechanism (no force until published), though no figures or dates.

text: If we are sensible with the rules and the regulations that we put in place about who can work in our education and health systems, for example, by allowing those who train in CANZUK countries—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to work here as a right, we will save millions in costs associated with burnout and the constant under-resourcing of those sectors.
explanation: Names a concrete policy (automatic work rights for CANZUK-trained staff) and the sectors affected, though no dollar figures or timeline.

text: You've got, essentially, a default provision in clause 2(1), which is the "Act comes into force on a date or dates set by Order in Council."... except for, in subclause (2), the specific sections... they'll come into force on the day after Royal assent.
explanation: Detailed walk-through of the commencement scheme with clause numbers, the 6-month and 5-year fallbacks, and the Order in Council mechanism.

text: most light vehicles under 14 years old will move to two-yearly WOF inspections, up from yearly, and new vehicles will go to four years before needing their WOF. Older vehicles, motorcycles, and light rental vehicles will move from six-monthly to yearly inspections.
explanation: Precise inspection intervals by vehicle category.

text: We are focused on three things: rebuilding the economy, restoring law and order, and delivering better outcomes for New Zealanders.
explanation: Stated aspirations of a brand-new government with no delivery yet to point to.

text: I can. I'm very proud to say we'll have a national flood plan by the end of this year. We are the first Government to do so, and we are taking action and putting investment into climate change, not just words and bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
explanation: Concrete commitment with a deadline (national flood plan by year-end), but it is a forward promise not yet delivered — credit pending follow-through.

text: Well, as I've said to the member before, I'm very proud that we've made house purchasing more affordable. Rents have come down, I think 6,000 or 7,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list, and, when I last looked, 2,100 children have been moved out of emergency housing into proper, dry homes, and there's big investment going in and support happening in homeless situations as well.
explanation: Claims concrete delivered outcomes on housing, but figures are approximate and unverified here.

text: Just last week, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced further measures against 40 members of the Iranian regime implicated in the recent brutal killing of tens of thousands of protesters.
explanation: Describes a concrete delivered government action (targeted measures), though enforcement impact unclear.

text: Well, the good news is that we abolished the ute tax. Remember that one? ... We abolished the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax ... We've actually cancelled Labour's fuel excise hikes that were planned. We've kept that in place frozen, but we're progressing a rates cap—get on board with that.
explanation: Claims credit for delivered actions (abolishing the ute tax and Auckland fuel tax, cancelling excise hikes) that were in fact enacted.

text: This Government’s fiscal strategy is about returning to surplus and bending the debt curve over, from going up to going down.
explanation: Stated fiscal intent rather than demonstrated delivery.

text: They are health, where we have committed increases in funding for front-line health services above and beyond population and inflationary pressures.
explanation: Asserts committed and delivered funding increases for front-line health, partial delivery claim.

text: In February, I commissioned an independent review of the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The review will focus on decisions by the monetary policy committee... I will consider the findings of the review when it is completed later this year.
explanation: A concrete action already taken, with follow-through pending the report.

text: The committee’s charter has been amended to ease restrictions on members speaking publicly... committee members who wish to publicly communicate their individual views... are now encouraged to do so.
explanation: An enacted change ('has been amended') rather than a promise.

text: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
explanation: Not merely an announcement — the bill is being progressed under urgency in the House, demonstrating follow-through on the stated commitment.

text: First, we expect to generate savings of $2.4 billion over the Budget period, which can be deployed to other areas, such as delivering more services in our health system, increasing educational resources for schools, building infrastructure, or strengthening our defence.
explanation: A projected/expected saving, not yet delivered; an announced target rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: We said we'd reduce the number of victims of crime by 20,000 by 2029 because we wanted to have fewer victims of serious, violent, and sexual offending in this country.
explanation: A concrete commitment with a target, but as a goal it is yet to be delivered.

text: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
explanation: Claims measurable progress toward a stated target attributed to government action.

text: We've changed the rule so that permanent name suppression can only be granted if the victim agrees.
explanation: Describes an enacted rule change attributable to the government.

text: As of today, the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Act has commenced into law. Stalking is now a criminal offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment... The previous Government had different priorities; this Government has focused on actually delivering.
explanation: Names a specific commitment now enacted and in force; concrete delivery, not just announcement.

text: But look, at the end of the day, delivery is happening on this side.
explanation: Asserts delivery in general terms without naming what was delivered.

text: Yes, I have received advice on the impacts of high levels of rooftop solar and household batteries on wholesale markets and distribution costs. It identified potential benefits to household bills, while also requiring significant investment in the grid. That is why the Government is making a number of regulatory changes to make it easier to install rooftop solar and batteries—this includes removing building consent requirements for installing rooftop solar and batteries, mandating retailers to pay a fair price for electricity sold back into the grid from 1 July, along with a number of other regulatory changes.
explanation: Describes regulatory changes underway rather than fully implemented outcomes.

text: To name just a few of the commitments in the deal, we're unlocking Eden Park's ownership and operating model, and recognising Eden Park as New Zealand's national stadium. We have agreed to work together on key transport projects to unlock growth, including the second harbour crossing, the Northwest Rapid Transit, and City Rail Link level crossings.
explanation: Describes agreed commitments and intentions; delivery is prospective ('agreed to work together'), not yet realised.

text: We’re delivering for Auckland, including through projects like the Port of Auckland wharf expansion, which was first approved under the Government’s fast-track approvals process... We’ve also signed the landmark Auckland city deal, the first of its kind in New Zealand... That deal includes specific outcomes, including a new Crown uplift funding tool and a coordinated 30-year transport strategy.
explanation: Cites a signed deal and approved projects (some delivery) but mostly recent agreements rather than completed outcomes.

text: We are very proud of the work that we’re doing... around the introduction of a national adaptation framework and, importantly, New Zealand’s first national flood map. This is tangible delivery and action to help New Zealanders who are dealing with the impacts of climate change... that is action over and above words—and that is pretty much all we heard from the last Government.
explanation: Points to delivered products (framework, flood map) over rhetoric.

text: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Points to measured progress against a target.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Describes a concretely funded and expanded programme.

text: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
explanation: Claims concrete personal follow-through (visiting every site) rather than aspiration.

text: This Government has invested $41 million in their professionalisation through Budget 2025... Harm within youth justice and care and protection residences has seen a 14 percent decrease since 2024... with $22 million for repairs and upgrades to Oranga Tamariki residences and $33 million in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences.
explanation: Names funded actions and a measured improvement (14% harm decrease), indicating delivery rather than promise.

text: Much faith has been placed in me by many people. I intend to work hard to repay that faith—flaws and all.
explanation: A sincere statement of intent at the outset of a term, but purely aspirational with no concrete commitment or record to point to yet.

text: last year we announced a $3.35 million investment for Whanganui Airport to complete construction of the new sealed parallel taxiway. This will address longstanding safety issues by reducing the need for aircraft to backtrack on the active runway before take-off and after landing.
explanation: An announced/funded investment; delivery framed as future completion.

text: the Rangitata vessel will receive $3 million from the fund to improve its ability to carry different types of cargo across a wider range of ports nationwide... This investment will fund a deck-mounted crane capable of loading and unloading bulk cargo to be operating by the year’s end.
explanation: A committed, funded investment with a delivery date by year's end.

text: In addition to our Ōhakea investment, we are also investing $1.1 million from the regional connectivity package to the first concessionary loan to Golden Bay Air. This loan will ensure that the regional airline can refinance existing aircraft debt and fund essential ongoing major maintenance checks.
explanation: A concrete funded measure, though described as ensuring future outcomes.

text: I have recently confirmed the Government's move to make RNZAF Base Ōhakea available 24/7 as an alternative runway for wide-body aircraft, resolving a longstanding constraint for airlines... To fix this, we have approved funding for Airways New Zealand to provide round-the-clock air traffic control services. Opening up Ōhakea 24/7 was one of the key actions within the aviation action plan. I am proud to see it delivered.
explanation: Describes a concrete, funded, delivered action against a stated plan item.

text: Yes, he was, because, actually, we have taken a policy in our Government that we table the advice, and then we make some decisions. What we don't do is create an $800 megawatt per hour cost that ends up shutting down mills, and low and middle income working New Zealanders lose their jobs. That's exactly what that member did—economic vandal, arsonist, now complaining about the fire that we're putting out that you created.
explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing; no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

text: No. The New Zealand people voted to put the adults in charge and to turf the teenagers out.
explanation: Divisive applause line aimed at his own side.

text: we're in the process of approving a project in Southland that will deliver renewable energy to 100,000 homes, which the Labour-Greens Government didn't approve.
explanation: Frames an achievement against the opposition rather than building common ground.

text: I agree Christopher Luxon is a very smart man.
explanation: Witty, crowd-pleasing deflection—rhetorically effective but not substantive or bridge-building.

text: I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel. I respect those views and the vigour with which they have been offered.
explanation: Acknowledges opposing views respectfully, an attempt to bring others along.

text: I don’t think I have ever seen anything quite as pathetic as the incoming Prime Minister literally sprinting out the door of Parliament to fly back to Auckland because he had been summoned by Winston Peters
explanation: A combative applause line for his own side; mocks an opponent rather than persuading the undecided.

text: The clear question every Kiwi family is asking themselves is: are they better off than they were three years ago? And the answer is no.
explanation: Rhetorically effective framing but appeals to his own side rather than persuading the undecided.

text: One of the most important roles of the Speaker is to protect the rights of the minority, and we find ourselves now in the minority in this House.
explanation: Constructive, acknowledges the Speaker's duty to both Government and Opposition without rancour.

text: When Māori thrive, all New Zealanders will thrive.
explanation: Inclusive, unity-seeking framing that invites a shared interest rather than dividing along ethnic lines.

text: I do want to welcome one change, and I want to congratulate New Zealand First for the change, and that is the reversal of National’s policy to allow foreign homebuyers back into the New Zealand housing market.
explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit a coalition party for a policy reversal — genuine cross-party acknowledgement of a point on which they agree.

text: this is no longer the story of the haves and the have-nots; this is the story of the have-nots and the have-yachts.
explanation: Memorable wordplay, but a divisive us-vs-them frame rather than consensus-building.

text: the voices of kaumātua choosing between power and prescriptions, the voices of parents skipping meals so their babies can eat, and the voices of rangatahi packing their bags for Melbourne, Perth, and London
explanation: Evocative, empathetic imagery that rallies; effective but directed at his own constituency's grievance.

text: Te Pāti Māori believes Aotearoa should be run like a marae. On a marae, we welcome you, we house you, we feed you, and we care for you. On a marae, you do not leave people standing out in the cold while a few sit comfortably inside.
explanation: An inclusive, values-based vision invoking shared cultural practice; warm but tied to the party's frame.

text: Te Pāti Māori offers our congratulations to you, Mr Speaker-Elect, on your new role.
explanation: Warm, goodwill-building opener that extends an olive branch across the House.

text: We will welcome you. We will feed you. We will house you. We will connect you. We will educate you. We will care for you. We will hear you. We will love you.
explanation: Inclusive, welcoming vision extended even to opponents ('you'), invitational rather than combative.

text: We respect international law because the alternative is worse. The alternative is a world where only force dictates outcomes.
explanation: Values-based appeal for upholding law over force.

text: we are absolutely going into this, examining the questions, being open to supporting the bill, and we’d gently encourage Government members to be open to, at some stage, exploring other reserved provisions
explanation: Constructive, cross-party tone — signals openness to support and invites the Government to collaborate on further reserved provisions.

text: New section 76(b)—I think this is a brilliant new section of the bill—requires the administering agency to publish details as to the availability of anything that has been exempt.
explanation: Opposition member openly praising a provision of the Government's bill — collegial, bridge-building tone.

text: Democracy is, in truth, a very fragile institution. It lives or dies on the basis of trust, and really, transparency is the mechanism through which that trust can thrive or that it doesn't.
explanation: Appeals to a shared value (trust in democracy) in a way that could reach across the aisle, but remains abstract.

text: Absolutely not. Just because we have achieved the target well ahead of expectations doesn't mean we stop now. Every young person deserves the opportunity to be the best version of themselves.
explanation: Aspirational, inclusive note about young people.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement builds goodwill rather than partisan point-scoring.

text: I think she might be having a few issues; she may need some medical help
explanation: Personal aspersion on the Minister's mental health; he later withdrew it.

text: But what I think New Zealanders will be shocked by is what they have replaced it with: the idea that more young New Zealanders should take up smoking in order to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible.
explanation: Casts the policy as deliberately wanting youth to smoke — a heightened, motive-imputing characterisation that strawmans the Government's stated fiscal rationale.

text: Does the Government believe that low-income New Zealanders with children and who are working part-time are less deserving of additional support than low-income New Zealanders with children and who are getting the support?
explanation: Pointed but substantive question about eligibility design; the 'less deserving' framing is mildly loaded but engages the policy.

text: She did not name the individual; she described a job, and there is a difference here. Somebody occupying a very senior position within the Prime Minister's Office having their position named is totally consistent with the practices of this House.
explanation: Procedural argument made without personal attack.

text: I do want to welcome one change, and I want to congratulate New Zealand First for the change, and that is the reversal of National’s policy to allow foreign homebuyers back into the New Zealand housing market.
explanation: Gracious, substance-focused, congratulates an opponent rather than attacking.

text: The Government’s actions have been irresponsible, unprincipled, and do a disservice to New Zealand’s independent approach to foreign affairs.
explanation: Strong condemnatory language but directed at the Government's conduct and foreign-policy stance, not personal insult.

text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would first say, then, that we do condemn Iran’s attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf, but the Government have made a clear promise in this statement that puts New Zealand at risk in expressing New Zealand’s readiness to assist in opening the Strait of Hormuz.
explanation: Criticises the Government's foreign-policy decision while explicitly condemning Iran's attacks; engages substance, not persons.

text: we are absolutely going into this, examining the questions, being open to supporting the bill, and we’d gently encourage Government members to be open to, at some stage, exploring other reserved provisions
explanation: Respectful and collegial ('gently encourage'), focused on the substance of the legislation.

text: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
explanation: Constructive, policy-focused engagement with the Minister's amendment.

text: New section 76(b)—I think this is a brilliant new section of the bill—requires the administering agency to publish details as to the availability of anything that has been exempt.
explanation: Respectful, substance-focused, generous to the drafters.

text: I'd suggest the person doing the most damage to themselves today is Mr Hipkins, who seems to be in a state of fervent denial.
explanation: Personal characterisation of an opponent rather than engagement with substance.

text: What I’m simply saying is that the Indian side are using a different turn of phrase to describe that aspiration—just as that member’s colleague uses a different turn of phrase of refer to Indian New Zealanders than I would ever use.
explanation: Inserts a pointed dig at a NZ First member's language about Indian New Zealanders, a character-adjacent attack rather than engaging the question's substance.

text: I will seek to ensure that the Budget delivers the public services that New Zealanders of all walks of life rely on... That’s called good priorities—not a wasteful scheme that missed every target it ever set for itself.
explanation: 'Wasteful scheme that missed every target' is harsh but directed at the policy's performance rather than a person.

text: The video which Mr Hipkins has referred to previously, in which he said that I made the statement that "National would make groceries cheaper"—that statement is not included in that video at any stage. I have provided the full transcript to Mr Hipkins; he has chosen not to correct his statement.
explanation: Accuses the opponent of failing to correct the record, but grounded in a factual dispute.

text: what that clause is essentially doing is legislative repair, updating a reference to a definition in another piece of legislation that’s since been repealed and replaced. It replaces the reference to the term defined by reference to the now out of date Securities Market Act 1988, i.e. “registered market”, to the relevant term in the New Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, which is “licensed market” and that replaced the Securities Market Act in 1988.
explanation: Patient, substantive explanation engaging directly with the member's question.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Generously credits the previous Government for starting a programme that is working.

text: he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn't just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he's caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn't actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people
explanation: Argument by emotive analogy/ad hominem rather than evidence.

text: If the member actually cared about working New Zealanders, he’d support Resource Management Act reforms, support job-rich fast-track projects, support the repeal of the oil and gas ban, support council rate caps, support the income-tax thresholds, and I could go on and on and on.
explanation: Implies disagreement equals not caring — a false dichotomy.

text: Well, I reject the characterisation of the way the member is presenting that question. This is an issue that was well understood and socialised before even the election in 2023.
explanation: Asserts the issue was 'well understood and socialised' without evidence.

text: having an 84 percent increase in spending drove a 32-year high of inflation, rapidly high interest rates, and, actually, really put massive pressure on low and middle income working New Zealanders.
explanation: Asserts a single-cause story linking spending to inflation and rates without supporting the magnitude.

text: New Zealand is far from the Middle East, and I do not overestimate our influence over events there. We are not central to this region or this conflict.
explanation: Measured, realistic appraisal of NZ's limited influence rather than overclaiming.

text: this Government doesn’t like to talk about family violence, because they think if the victimisation happens in someone’s own home, then it’s not something the Government should care about at all.
explanation: Builds on a fabricated characterisation of opponents' beliefs rather than any evidence of their position.

text: Why should the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who have lost jobs under his leadership have confidence in him when the job that he seems most committed to fighting for is his own?
explanation: Juxtaposes job losses with the leadership-vote story rhetorically rather than establishing any causal link.

text: International law applies to everyone, including our friends and allies. No country should place itself above international law.
explanation: Coherent principle of even-handed application, stated without supporting detail.

text: The Labour Government did not approve the winding down of Marsden Point; it was a private business.
explanation: Draws the relevant distinction between a private decision and government approval.

text: I'll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission's report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.”
explanation: Cites the report by paragraph and quotes it directly to rebut the Minister's characterisation — evidence-anchored argument.

text: this suggests, in my view, that the Government may be looking at limiting the information that's available to the media, the information that's available to the public.
explanation: Reasoned inference from 'dots' she lays out, but hedged ('may be') and not a tight entailment.

text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would first say, then, that we do condemn Iran’s attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf, but the Government have made a clear promise in this statement that puts New Zealand at risk in expressing New Zealand’s readiness to assist in opening the Strait of Hormuz.
explanation: Builds an argued case that a public commitment creates risk/expectation; reasoned, though the 'puts NZ at risk' inference is asserted.

text: should that secondary piece of legislation fall off a website, it would still be law, regardless of people not being able to access it.
explanation: Identifies a genuine logical gap — accessibility failure vs legal validity — to justify her amendment.

text: In October 2025, there was a paper produced that, essentially, looked at how well the administrative data does against the census data. It was a bit of an experimental test to see how well it compares, and the results were not too bad. However, they did point to second-layer data as being a potential issue. When people respond to the higher-level categories, that was fairly accurate, but those second-level categories are quite difficult to get right.
explanation: Grounds her caution in a specific October 2025 comparison study and draws a nuanced distinction between accurate high-level and unreliable second-layer data.

text: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
explanation: Identifies a concrete failure mode (law in force but inaccessible) and proposes a targeted fix; conclusion follows from premise.

text: What the member is actually saying is that, in her book, the way to grow an economy is to suck more money out of the pockets of working people.
explanation: Strawman: recasts the opponent's argument about Government spending as a claim about taxing workers more.

text: No, not at all. I think they’re living in the real world, where there’s a huge conflict in the Middle East and where we are experiencing the largest oil shock in history.
explanation: Attributes domestic pessimism to external shocks plausibly, but the superlative claim is an unsupported exaggeration.

text: if that had not been offset by savings, which it was, this year’s deficit track would be $25 billion and net core Crown debt would be on track to reach 59 percent of GDP by the end of the forecast.
explanation: Structured counterfactual argument with figures, though the assumptions behind it are stated only briefly.

text: While the impacts of the conflict are still very uncertain, I would observe that oil prices are currently around 35 percent higher than they were before the conflict began—so, well south of some of the IMF's more dire predictions.
explanation: Reasons from current data against the modelled adverse scenarios with stated uncertainty.

text: The latest update shows that around 59 days of petrol, 54 days of diesel, and 50 days of jet fuel are in country, within our exclusive economic zone, or on the water heading here. That data is updated twice weekly. Importantly, we use maritime tracking, including the Starboard software system, to cross-check against the shipping information that fuel companies share with us.
explanation: Describes cross-checking shipping data against independent maritime tracking — evidence-based.

text: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
explanation: Relies on a strawman of the opponent's position rather than engaging her actual argument.

text: On this side of the House, surprisingly, we don’t believe that the only way in which we can help New Zealanders is by writing blank cheques and spraying money everywhere and, hopefully, it hits a target. On this side of the House, we apply a little bit of substance, which is called fiscal discipline.
explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy (blank cheques vs discipline) and caricatures the opposing approach.

text: The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.
explanation: Causal claim is plausible but compressed and overstated.

text: in practice, Auckland Council will support the Auckland Regional Transport Committee to engage with Māori, using Auckland Council’s well-established processes, staff resources, and existing engagement forums. The reality is that Auckland Council already has existing mechanisms by which to undertake that task, and this legislation is simply replicating that existing mechanism and not looking to introduce a new mechanism or a new definition
explanation: Argues the provision is not novel because it mirrors existing practice; supported by the cited section comparisons, though it sidesteps the definitional point itself.

text: The 4 December 2025 application date is the date on which the consultation paper was released, and, therefore, in effect, by applying that date, it mitigates any structuring opportunities or people looking to make changes to take advantage of the fact that as of that date, it was made public.
explanation: Clear logical rationale: aligning the date with public release prevents structuring.

text: The Bioeconomy Science Institute performs an important role in supporting the growth and development of New Zealand's biological sector, but it will only be effective if it's operating on a financially sustainable footing... The Bioeconomy Science Institute brought together four Crown Research Institutes with subsequently identified areas of overlap and duplication. I note this has been a voluntary redundancy round and operational decisions about staffing sit with the Bioeconomy Science Institute Board.
explanation: Offers an overlap/duplication rationale, though doesn't address the growth question directly.

text: there’s three arguments that concern us. One, there’s already distinct commercial legislation: the Port Companies Act 1988; two, the acts that that Act describes required governance structures, and what’s being proposed here would duplicate these; and thirdly, the different focus of ports to be highly competitive compared to the focus that the OIA for local government is.
explanation: Clearly enumerated, structured reasoning citing specific legislation and a duplication argument.

text: The target itself, through all the documents I’ve seen, was unlikely to be achieved even with that Government’s proposed policies.
explanation: Appeals to 'all the documents I've seen' without citing them; reasonable but unsubstantiated in the text.

text: I think he’s probably on a few things, actually!
explanation: Ad hominem insinuation with no relevance to the argument.

text: an institution that has worked better to allow people to flourish in self-chosen ways up and down our country than perhaps any other institution imaginable
explanation: Grand claim resting on rhetorical superlative with no supporting evidence.

text: A former Prime Minister said that we were removing interest deductibility from residential property to tilt the market towards first-home buyers. You know what happened? Rents went through the roof and first-home buyers had less to save a deposit. We actually have helped first-home buyers, who are now buying homes at record levels—I think at 28 percent of new purchases
explanation: Constructs a cause-and-effect story (policy → rents up → reversal → record first-home buying) but asserts the causal links rather than isolating them from other market factors.

text: This should finally put to bed the incessant but incorrect claims that charter schools somehow cost more to the taxpayer than State schools. They cost less, and the students who choose to attend them are just as worthy of a State-funded education as any other student in New Zealand.
explanation: Conclusion rests on the preceding figures; some overreach in 'finally put to bed'.

text: a natural monopoly is a service that has constantly increasing returns to scale, so one provider is the most efficient way to provide. And, as it happens, roads and sewer networks and water pipes and public transport networks and a whole lot of things that cities rely on are natural monopolies. That's why you can't have a competitive market, and that is the public policy case for zoning
explanation: A clearly structured argument from a definition to a conclusion (the case for zoning), with the steps spelled out.

text: They will know in due course, and I’m sorry to say it, but I doubt that the member will be the first to know.
explanation: Asked on what date New Zealanders will know how the tax cuts are funded; gives no date, deflects with a jab.

text: It is also the case that there has been opportunity created in the manufacturing sector as a direct result of the Investment Boost policy, which has reduced the tax paid by those firms who have invested in new machinery. I challenge the member to commit to the Investment Boost policy if she wants to stay on the right side of manufacturers.
explanation: Asked about 10,000 fewer manufacturing jobs; partly addresses sector challenges but pivots to advocating her policy and challenging the questioner.

text: I will absolutely present the forecasts in May, and I expect that they will be significantly worse than the forecasts previously presented. I'm not going to give a running commentary on all the discussions Treasury has with me as they develop their understanding of how the conflict will impact the economy.
explanation: Asked why she can't share the latest scenarios now; declines to release them but explains why and commits to a date.

text: Yes, in the context in which they were given, including my statement yesterday that the member "wishes to return to the monetary policy framework that resulted in New Zealand's highest period of inflation in recent history". At a time of heightened global instability, proposing to dilute the Reserve Bank's focus on inflation is the last thing New Zealand needs.
explanation: Directly answers 'yes' she stands by her statements and reaffirms the contested one.

text: Because it starts from 1 April—that is, from next Wednesday. Families already receiving the in-work tax credit won’t have to do anything. Inland Revenue will automatically deliver the increase. Families paid weekly will see the increase from 7 April 2026, and those paid fortnightly will see it from 14 April 2026.
explanation: Answers Brewer's 'How is this support timely?' directly with start dates and delivery mechanism.

text: We have a range of advice regarding solar and batteries that is under active consideration, and when it is no longer under active consideration, then that will be released.
explanation: Asked plainly whether advice was shared with the National Party, he gives a non-answer about release timing.

text: Yeah, a lot of consideration in regards to revenue methods. The primary method that we're focused on is growing our economy so that we can grow the revenue of every business and every household in this country. That's been a major focus of this Government, and one of the ways we achieve that is through a broad based - low rate tax system. I receive a wide range of advice from Treasury as part of my role.
explanation: Woods asked specifically what consideration he gave to broadening the base / taxing things other than income; he pivots to economic growth and offers no substance on base-broadening.

text: Has the Government considered a land value tax? No. Has the Government considered a capital gains tax? No. Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No.
explanation: Gives clear, unambiguous 'No' answers to Russell's questions about whether specific taxes were considered, though he avoids the corporate-rate/2022-briefing question.

text: Auckland Council will define the Eden Park precinct area when it develops the Auckland roading classification framework. I'm advised that this work is currently under way and that the local boards are being consulted with on the framework.
explanation: Directly answers White's question about who defines the precinct and how, including the ministerial-agreement safeguard.

text: The question from Dr Deborah Russell on clause 5 in regards to the money involved—$146 million over the forecast period.
explanation: Answers Russell's direct question about revenue with a precise figure.

text: I think that, because the first question was incorrect, I would have to take away and verify what that member is saying before I can answer it.
explanation: Asked what she would say to a quoted caregiver, she declines to answer and defers to verification, citing an alleged earlier inaccuracy.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Carter asked her to justify a 25%-plus increase under her watch; she offers context on stay lengths and reasons but does not directly address or justify the increase.

text: I have read the ICM report very closely, and there is no mention in that report of untrained staff being used to look after children in motels.
explanation: Asked how placing complex-needs children with untrained caregivers fits her priorities, she rebuts the premise (the report doesn't mention untrained staff) rather than addressing the priorities question.

text: I have asked Oranga Tamariki about the serious allegation in the member's question of kids being housed in motels with untrained staff, and they've been unable to identify what the member is referring to. If the member has evidence of this occurring, I would strongly encourage her to provide this information so it can be addressed... yes, I am aware that motels are being used as an emergency option, as a last resort where no other safe option is available. This practice even pre-dates Oranga Tamariki as an organisation.
explanation: Directly engages the 'were you aware' question: challenges the untrained-staff premise as unverified, then answers yes on motel use as a last resort.

text: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
explanation: Directly answers 'how many sites have you visited' with a precise count.

text: I'll seek some advice on that.
explanation: Asked a specific question about whether infringement-fee powers can be conferred on local boards, he provides no substantive answer.

text: decisions by officials and elected representatives are always subject to judicial review—so if there's anything that the local boards, councils are doing which would fall foul of natural justice, for example, or the empowering provisions of statute under which they are enabled to make those decisions, those decisions are reviewable through judicial review.
explanation: Asked where accountability lies, he gives a direct (judicial review) answer, but addresses only the legal-challenge avenue rather than the everyday accountability the question pressed on.

text: section 48 is the section which says that the council must develop Auckland roading classification framework. Within that framework will be the roads and areas that local boards will or will not be responsible for. The bill doesn't set those decisions; that's up to the council when they develop the roading classification framework.
explanation: Responds to White's question about which streets local boards control by pointing to the mechanism (s48 framework), though it defers the specifics to the council.

text: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
explanation: Gives Xu-Nan a clear 'no' to bilingual drafting in this bill, with a stated reason.

text: From 1 November, most light vehicle users will benefit from these changes, but it is important to note that the ongoing obligation to keep your vehicle roadworthy—including your tyres—in tip-top shape, continues.
explanation: Directly answers when the changes come into effect (1 November) and adds the relevant caveat.

text: We are determined to make sure we deliver on our climate change commitments—that means net zero 2050; that means doing everything we can to deliver on our Paris agreements... We have reversed the oil and gas ban so we don't create an energy dry-year risk and high power bills for New Zealanders.
explanation: Asserts commitment to net zero 2050 and Paris in the same breath as boasting of reversing the oil-and-gas exploration ban — a visible tension between the climate goal and the action taken.

text: In answer to the first part, absolutely, but as I have just explained to the member, we don't have the information or intelligence by which these independent actions by the US and Israel were launched, and the member doesn't, either.
explanation: Affirms standing by his pledge to 'call out' threats to the rules-based order, yet refuses to apply that standard to the US/Israel strikes — tension between stated value and conduct.

text: Yes, and the way trust is built is by delivering improved outcomes for Māori.
explanation: Reaffirms a commitment to building trust with Māori while his Government weakens Treaty clauses—words in tension with actions raised in the follow-ups.

text: what we’re not interested in doing is running up the Public Service from 47,000 to 65,000, with, I think, a 46 percent increase in support and admin roles, and only an 18 percent increase in front-line roles.
explanation: Claims to prioritise front-line delivery while the same exercise cuts services Davidson identifies as front-line; tension between stated value and the cuts.

text: The Minister explained his comments well, and, actually, I'm quite confident that he did not at any time direct RNZ or TVNZ.
explanation: Defends a colleague; consistency with prior standards not verifiable from the text.

text: New Zealand opposed the US invasion of Iraq and history proved that was the correct decision.
explanation: Invokes a consistent NZ tradition of independent foreign policy to back his current stance.

text: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we called that out as a breach of the international rules-based order, and we were right to do that. When Vladimir Putin invades his next country of choice, what moral authority will we have as a country to call on him to obey the international rules-based order if we are not willing to ask the same standard of countries that we have a closer relationship with?
explanation: Demands consistency between NZ's Ukraine stance and its response to allies' actions.

text: Speaking in the House recently, I alluded to a Facebook post of Nicola Willis where she was unpacking some groceries. I said in that Facebook post that she had committed to lowering grocery prices—I was mistaken. I should have referred to her press statements of 14 June 2023, 13 July 2023, 12 October 2023, her press conference on 27 August 2025, her Facebook video in September 2025—all of which committed her to lowering grocery prices.
explanation: Openly corrects his own earlier error on the record, consistent with owning mistakes.

text: as an Opposition and as a future Government, we will seek to bring New Zealanders together, not drive a wedge between Kiwis.
explanation: Tension between the stated unity pledge and the highly combative, attack-heavy speech in which it is delivered.

text: Well, because this Government is determined to ensure that the prices Kiwis pay will be lower than they would have otherwise been without the policy decisions that we are taking. The issue that the member continues to forget is that the period of the highest increases in food prices happened under a previous administration's policies.
explanation: Defends a commitment ('get food prices under control') against a record of rising food prices by reframing it as 'lower than otherwise'—a shift from the original pledge.

text: What we can control is our own spending, and this Government is determined to take a responsible course in which we do not add fuel to the inflation fire, as was not the case in recent history under previous Governments.
explanation: States a fiscal-restraint value consistent with the Government's stated stance, but no delivered action is verifiable from the text.

text: I can confirm that unemployment is higher now than we would both wish it to be and than it has been in the past. That is why our Government is so focused on growing the economy, creating the conditions in which businesses and firms can hire more people.
explanation: Acknowledging an unfavourable fact about her own Government's record is consistent and non-evasive.

text: This Government, on the other hand, considers the operating allowance to be a ceiling, not a floor, and has committed to keeping new Budget spending below it. We did so in Budget 2024, in Budget 2025, and we will do so again in Budget 2026.
explanation: Frames a consistent stated principle backed by claimed repeated practice across three budgets.

text: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
explanation: Matches the National/ACT campaign commitment to remove the dual mandate; words align with the action being taken in the same sitting.

text: How pro-farmer are they going to be when foot-and-mouth arrives in New Zealand because of the cuts they are making to our biosecurity?
explanation: Treats a low-probability, high-impact event (foot-and-mouth arriving) as a near-certain consequence of biosecurity cuts; no timeframe and implausible as stated.

text: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we called that out as a breach of the international rules-based order, and we were right to do that. When Vladimir Putin invades his next country of choice, what moral authority will we have as a country to call on him to obey the international rules-based order if we are not willing to ask the same standard of countries that we have a closer relationship with?
explanation: Presumes Putin 'invades his next country of choice'; plausible concern but speculative and undated.

text: enjoy the leather benches for 163 days more, because your time is done.
explanation: Predicts the Government will lose office at the election; uncertain and partisan-optimistic.

text: It didn't work in Iraq, it didn't work in Afghanistan, and it won't work in Iran.
explanation: Prediction that the intervention will fail; directionally plausible by historical analogy but uncertain and unfalsifiable in the near term.

text: by this time next year, inflation will be back to the 1 to 3 percent target range.
explanation: A one-year forecast consistent with RBNZ projections at the time; inflation did in fact return to the 1–3% band by late 2024, so a well-founded prediction.

text: The modelling showed that the key benefit of LNG is to provide the market with certainty to access fuel during a dry year. That will reduce the risk premium and provide downward pressure on electricity prices... that is why we expect to see a reduction in consumer bills by at least $50 per household.
explanation: Prediction that bills will fall by at least $50 per household; optimistic and dependent on volatile global LNG prices, so uncertain.

text: I reject the premise in that question because that is factually not correct. Kiwi power bills for both households and businesses will reduce as a result of the LNG importation terminal because the simple reality is that when you don't have fuel to make electricity, our prices spike.
explanation: Predicts household and business bills will fall as a result of the terminal; uncertain and contested.

text: The Port of Auckland project alone delivers $5.4 billion to the Auckland economy and sustains nearly 160,000 jobs by 2053.
explanation: A long-range (2053) economic and jobs projection; highly uncertain and optimistic.

text: we are supporting urban growth across the Eastern, Western and Northern Corridors—this is expected to deliver around 12,000 greenfield homes and 3,000 infilled and intensified homes over the next decade; we’ve identified Takitimu North Link stage two and the Tauriko West roads of national significance as a priority project—this will be reflected in the next Government policy statement on land transport in 2027
explanation: Predicts ~12,000 greenfield and 3,000 intensified homes over the next decade; ambitious target dependent on delivery, so plausible but uncertain.

text: For those that are accepted, the Government then intends to pass bespoke legislation in 2027 giving effect to those proposals. For the remaining councils, they will fall into a slower backstop pathway. This will take effect following the 2028 local government elections and will replace regional councils.
explanation: Forecasts a legislative timetable and outcome; plausible plan but contingent on future decisions.

text: currently, our tax base does not cover certain revenue-generation methods when it comes to things like capital gains and additional assets like private jets, superyachts, etc.
explanation: Identifies the gap (capital gains, certain assets) with concrete examples, though without figures or a defined mechanism.

text: the insertion of the definition around stored value instruments is a really important one, because... we do see more money-laundering happening by other avenues... It's really important in light of a drastic increase over the last decade of the use of cryptocurrency.
explanation: Names concrete instruments (stored value, gold, precious metals, crypto, NFTs) but no figures.

text: One of the really important exercises that Auckland Council and Auckland Transport did a little while ago, under the advice of the seniors community group, was to get policymakers to, essentially, go from the Ferry Building in Britomart to, I believe, the Auckland War Memorial Museum without their smartphone and have to navigate public transport without that.
explanation: Concrete, detailed example with named locations to illustrate accessibility for seniors.

text: Noting that the dissolution of Parliament is on 1 October, I want to be balanced to say that even if we see a report-back date on 22 September, which grants an additional 2½ weeks on top of that... it still gives the current Government full ability to read this bill through all stages before the dissolution of Parliament.
explanation: Names exact dates and the precise extension being proposed.

text: I move, That the motion be amended to replace the words "20 August 2026" with "20 September 2026".
explanation: Precise, actionable amendment with exact dates.

text: Yeah, I’m not surprised to hear that sort of speech coming from Ryan Hamilton, the MP up in Hamilton, given his personal views in 2021, which are well reported in the media, in relation to COVID. I’m going to leave it there lest I embarrass that member with a number of quotes that he has in relation to vaccinations and mandates.
explanation: An insinuating personal attack on a member's past views with a threat to 'embarrass' him, rather than engaging his argument.

text: Why did she promise Kiwis to "help bring down food prices", "get food prices under control", and that they would "pay less for home-grown food at the checkout" when she had no intention of keeping those promises?
explanation: Quotes the Minister's own pledges but the 'no intention of keeping' framing imputes bad faith rather than just challenging the record.

text: The National Government has had three years to come up with a plan, and what have we seen instead? Tax breaks for tobacco companies and property speculators, and cuts to services that our families and every community depend on.
explanation: Sharp partisan framing, but aimed at policy choices rather than personal attack.

text: What about the smoke-free generation rules that your Government revoked and repealed? What was the economic impact on the health system as a result of the repealing of that particular piece of legislation, given the Minister's last comments?
explanation: Challenges a specific government action and its fiscal consequences on substance rather than attacking the person.

text: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.
explanation: Constructive, acknowledges cross-party committee work and public submitters with respect.

text: When we have a higher tax rate, and also particularly when we’re punishing those who cannot already afford it in a cost of living crisis, plus not expanding the scope of the tax base, we wonder why we are in this fiscal black hole that we are seeing right now.
explanation: Critique aimed at policy settings rather than individuals, though 'punishing those who cannot afford it' is emotive.

text: how would the Minister ensure, or what confidence does the Minister have, that since not only has the person responsible changed but that entire role has also moved from the Ministry of Education under the Education Review Office, that they’re going to uphold the same level of standards and scrutiny when it comes to registration of hostels as well as non-compliance?
explanation: Constructive, respectful accountability question.

text: if you’re looking at the subheading, am I correct to assume that it can’t incur expenses that’re not within the appropriation, but in clause 6(1A) it seems to imply that it can’t occur expenses that it already has authorised.
explanation: A genuine request for clarification framed respectfully, engaging only with the text.

text: I do want to thank the Minister for her engagement throughout this committee stage, particularly her due diligence and her transparency, and also the fact that she made what for many may sound like two very technical and potentially boring bills really interesting and exciting.
explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of a Minister from another party.

text: Thank you, Minister. That’s very sensible. I think that’s a really sensible reason for a date, then.
explanation: Graciously concedes the Minister gave a good answer.

text: When National’s answer to every fiscal challenge has been the same—and that’s been to sell off or to hand stuff overseas or to keep cutting public services, while at the same time investing in other parts of the economy like property speculation, those are the types of choices as to why they’re so unpopular and so out of touch with everyday New Zealanders.
explanation: Relies on a strawman generalisation rather than evidenced analysis.

text: Again, for the third week in a row—the third week in a row—the night before your Budget—all the National Party has been talking about is the Labour Party... the National Party, who are in Government, who are the Crown, are obsessed with the Labour Party, and that's because they've got no good news for New Zealand.
explanation: Infers 'no good news' from the focus on Labour — a plausible but unsupported leap.

text: access to capital is one of the reasons why New Zealand’s productivity is lagging. What is Labour’s solution to that? The New Zealand future fund—that’s what it’s about. If you look at Ireland, they have a very simple sovereign wealth fund; Mark Carney and Canada just released their own sovereign wealth fund.
explanation: Offers a diagnosis (capital access) and a policy, but supports it mainly by analogy to Ireland and Canada rather than evidence.

text: There’s a reason why Florida is not covered by reinsurance but New Zealand continues to be, despite us being the second-highest amount of spending for natural disaster risks throughout the world.
explanation: Uses a comparative example to argue reinsurers price NZ's climate risk seriously — a reasoned point.

text: the New Zealand Law Society suggested there should be proportionality or necessity tests as part of this... there is no mandatory privacy impact assessments, there's short review cycles for these agreements, there's no requirement for independent audits, and stronger transparency was needed.
explanation: Grounds the objection in authoritative submissions (Law Society, Privacy Commissioner) with specific deficiencies.

text: When we have a higher tax rate, and also particularly when we’re punishing those who cannot already afford it in a cost of living crisis, plus not expanding the scope of the tax base, we wonder why we are in this fiscal black hole that we are seeing right now.
explanation: Rhetorically implies the bill's approach causes the 'fiscal black hole' but asserts the causal link rather than demonstrating it; loaded framing ('punishing').

text: Would that be an appropriate time to consider more broadly... and to be able to consider some of those changes and allow for the public to actually hear or for us to get public submissions on the other changes that haven't had time to consult?
explanation: Reasoned point that changes lacking consultation risk unintended consequences and should get a submissions process.

text: I'm always surprised at why Standing Order 195 needs to actually be waived, because Standing Order 195 is about meeting outside of the Wellington area during a sitting... By waiving that, there must be some form of indication by the Government that that is a possibility.
explanation: Reasonable inference that waiving SO 195 implies the Government anticipates out-of-Wellington sittings, though the conclusion is presented as a question.

text: the committee that this is going to—the Social Services and Community Committee—although it may not have all that many bills going through it, it has the most number of agencies when you are looking at scrutiny week.
explanation: Uses the committee's workload as evidence for why the truncated timeline is impractical—relevant evidence supporting the conclusion.

text: the date that the regulatory impact statement was finalised was 27 November 2025. This Government could absolutely give the people of New Zealand more than enough time to submit on this bill. If they introduce something like this early on in the year, they could in fact allow for a full six-month select committee without having to have a truncated process.
explanation: Uses a concrete date to show the Government had ample lead time, supporting the conclusion that the truncation was a choice rather than a necessity.

text: Get a hearing aid!
explanation: A dismissive personal jab at another member during debate, not engagement with substance.

text: David Seymour thinks that we don't need public services to look after those in need and we don't need the Government to look after the environment, because in his mind these are all issues of personal responsibility.
explanation: Characterises an opponent's views in an unflattering way rather than quoting or engaging his actual position.
