text: Instead of fixing the economy, they have been fixated on overseas culture wars, importing division, stirring up fear, and trying to start their own thriller here at home.
explanation: Attributes bad motives ('importing division, stirring up fear') to the Government rather than engaging its policy.

text: But just to say you and I have had a good relationship over the last three years, and I hope to maintain that, because my first experience of a Speaker here had me kicked out several times. The last Speaker had me suspended.
explanation: Acknowledges a constructive past relationship and expresses hope to maintain it; the references to being ejected are stated matter-of-factly, not as an attack.

text: Te Pāti Māori offers our congratulations to you, Mr Speaker-Elect, on your new role.
explanation: A gracious, respectful congratulation to the incoming Speaker; pure courtesy with no attack.

text: This is like a cross-party regulatory systems bill, and you guys are sitting there being political and trying to shit on us all day.
explanation: Crude language ('shit on us') and an accusation that opponents are merely 'being political' rather than engaging the substance.

text: I think that it's a great occasion when we can come together to support the long and arduous process that many hapū and iwi go through to have their claims settled. … I hope that we can progress at pace together, unanimously.
explanation: Respectful, focused on the shared task of settling claims.

text: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
explanation: Disagrees respectfully and defers a broader discussion to 'another day'.

text: This is a special place, one which bestows upon us the power to make the laws of our land and exert great control over the people. Please use that power lightly and infrequently.
explanation: Respectful, institution-focused, no personal attack.

text: This is why we are all here: to debate freely; to have an open, robust contest of ideas; to challenge one another in an environment where disputes are resolved by the showing of hands and not by the throwing of fists.
explanation: Explicitly elevates reasoned disagreement over conflict; respectful of opponents and institution.

text: That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters, and that is to make sure that Māori are not deciding who the next Prime Minister is come 7 November
explanation: Asserts the boundary/census changes are intended to suppress Māori voters; this imputed intent is contested and unsupported by the bill's stated purpose.

text: That is why Te Pāti Māori will implement a wealth tax. Under our policy, 98 percent of Aotearoa will pay less tax.
explanation: The '98 percent will pay less' figure is a party modelling claim presented as fact.

text: We all know that this illegal invasion has directly led to fuel prices reaching over $4 in some parts of Aotearoa, yet the Prime Minister has refused to condemn the aggressors in this conflict.
explanation: Fuel price spikes are plausible given the Strait disruption, but 'directly led' is a simplified single-cause attribution.

text: Over 160,000 people wrote submissions on the bill; 99 percent opposed it.
explanation: Submission counts and overwhelming opposition to the Regulatory Standards Bill are broadly consistent with the public record, though the exact figures are approximate.

text: may I remind Winston: you only won five seats; we won six.
explanation: A checkable factual claim about seat counts, consistent with the 2023 result.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Mix of contestable framing; ‘millions for tobacco companies’ references the smokefree repeal but is presented in a misleading light.

text: the Public Transport Operating Model, introduced by Steven Joyce under the National Government—which was the privatisation of the public transport system—enabled a contracting race to the bottom that meant lower wages and lower working conditions. Fair pay agreements would enable a standardised wage and a standardised set of conditions that would have meant that we did not have bus drivers leaving to become truck drivers.
explanation: Wellington's 'bustastrophe' and driver shortages were real; attributing them squarely to PTOM and labelling it 'privatisation' is a contestable simplification.

text: Is it a sign of growth when 17,000 people attend a jobs fair in Auckland, when only 100 employers were looking for workers?
explanation: Embedded figures (17,000 attendees vs 100 employers) used to dramatise the imbalance; the ratio framing may strip context.

text: The fact that we introduced a new public holiday—Matariki—that was the first of our own public holidays here in New Zealand—I’m proud of that fact. When my kids came home and taught me about Matariki; told me about the names of the stars in the sky, I could see the pride in their faces when they talked about it.
explanation: Accurate — Matariki, established 2022, is NZ's first public holiday recognising a uniquely Māori/NZ tradition.

text: Both of those are reserved for provisions that require a 75 percent majority of all members in this House to pass.
explanation: Accurate statement of the entrenched-provision threshold in the Electoral Act.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: The self-serving claim that the new area is 'very supportive of the current coalition Government' is an unverifiable partisan assertion.

text: the inflation expectations in this document are wildly different to the inflation expectations that New Zealand faces today because of external events—nothing to do with this Government.
explanation: Largely fair that external events shifted expectations, though the categorical disclaimer of any government role is overstated.

text: If you look at why we are low income, low productivity relative to the rest of the world—and I’ve lived all over the world and seen that actually we are well overregulated.
explanation: NZ does have comparatively low labour productivity and income vs other OECD nations (broadly true), but the regulation-as-cause framing is contestable.

text: It is second highest, as a net proportion of the economy, in New Zealand’s history. The first highest was in the 1990s under the previous National Government of that time. It grew 2.5 times under the previous Labour Government—2.5 times that debt increase.
explanation: Acknowledges the 1990s National peak and gives a quantified Labour-era increase; broadly consistent with the COVID debt surge, though ‘2.5x’ needs the baseline specified.

text: Don’t believe we’re going to get there? Well, Japan’s debt is 230 percent of gross domestic product.
explanation: Japan’s gross government debt-to-GDP is indeed around 230–250 percent.

text: I have done a bit of work in the past on the Incorporated Societies Act when that came into force. From memory, that's the Incorporated Societies Act 2020, and I think there was sort of a fallback provision of being five years or six years after Royal assent for some of those provisions.
explanation: Offers a precedent from memory with explicit hedging; the cited statute's year and detail are uncertain (the Incorporated Societies Act was 2022), but he flags he has to check.

text: local boards make decisions as though they are the local authority. They act as Auckland Council. That is outlined in clause 7, replacement section 12(4)
explanation: Consistent with the statutory framework, though Williams contests its application to nationally-set rules.

text: in October 2025, the High Court found that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) was operating outside of existing legislative authority when reassessing a person’s entitlement to supplementary assistance after they receive a backdated ACC payment for a past period.
explanation: A specific, checkable account of a High Court finding presented to justify the bill.

text: The term "official versions" means that a printout of the website is taken to state the law. That makes it easier to use in court proceedings. If you are presenting the court with a printout of the website, that will be accepted as what is the law.
explanation: Accurate account of the evidentiary status of official legislative versions.

text: decisions by officials and elected representatives are always subject to judicial review—so if there's anything that the local boards, councils are doing which would fall foul of natural justice, for example, or the empowering provisions of statute under which they are enabled to make those decisions, those decisions are reviewable through judicial review.
explanation: Accurate statement of administrative law — such decisions are indeed amenable to judicial review.

text: That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters, and that is to make sure that Māori are not deciding who the next Prime Minister is come 7 November
explanation: Claims a hidden coordinated 'agenda' across bills with no evidence offered — bare assertion of motive.

text: Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
explanation: Appeals to the authority of a journal but the cited statistic is contested and the causal link asserted, not shown.

text: How can Aotearoa trust that this Government will stick to their word and keep Aotearoa out of this invasion when it was the National Party who advocated for New Zealand to support the invasion of Iraq in 2003?
explanation: Argues distrust by reference to a 2003 position; a guilt-by-history inference rather than evidence about current intentions.

text: A nurse should not pay proportionally more tax than a millionaire hiding wealth in trusts. A cleaner should not have to carry more of the load than someone whose wealth grows while they sleep.
explanation: A reasonable fairness point, but rests on a vivid contrast rather than data.

text: The top 10 percent now own nearly half the wealth in Aotearoa, while the bottom 50 percent share just 6.7 percent between them. The bottom 20 percent now hold negative wealth.
explanation: Uses distributional data to support the inequality argument.

text: the problem that the Opposition has is that they can't do basic arithmetic: one plus one doesn't equal four.
explanation: Ad hominem dressed as a quip; no engagement with the opposition's actual argument.

text: let’s actually do the work that helps, and not create unnecessary scaremongering about what this bill does.
explanation: Asserts the opposition is scaremongering without offering evidence of what the bill actually does to counter their reading.

text: When we think about new people moving boundaries, moving electorates, needing to understand what electorate they are part of, and connecting with it, having two terms in an electorate before there’s another boundary change and anything there happens makes sense.
explanation: Gives a reasoned rationale (voters need time to understand and connect with a new electorate) that supports the two-term interval, though no evidence is cited.

text: Where's there's not an appropriate product approved for a dog or a cat, we use the equivalent human medicine. These are available internationally, but they're not used here because we haven't been able to get them approved. This bill will enable us to use the right products for the right animals here in New Zealand.
explanation: Grounds the argument in concrete first-hand sector experience and a specific practical problem, though it relies on his own and a vet's testimony rather than data.

text: having sat on the board of a company in Australia that was required by the Australian legislation to report under their version of what will soon be law here in New Zealand. It is a conversation that occurs around that table, of “Have we gone far enough visiting the factory in Vietnam? Do we actually know X, Y, or Z from that part of our supply chain in Europe?”
explanation: Draws on direct boardroom experience under Australia's comparable regime to inform the practical implementation questions — grounded, relevant firsthand evidence.

text: it couldn’t get any more vivid as a picture to be cancelling a national resilience fund and handing out buckets of KFC. I mean, how short term can you get it?
explanation: Rhetorical ridicule and juxtaposition stand in for an argument; no evidence linking the two.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Cites a specific figure ($2.9b) but strings claims together as a caricature of National’s plan without substantiation.

text: the official advice was ignored by the Minister that Pasifika women, Māori, young people, disabled would all be adversely affected by the fact that fair pay agreements will be repealed.
explanation: Appeals to 'official advice' to support the claim — reasonable evidence use, though the 'ignored' charge is asserted.

text: It’s really interesting to note that the OECD has put out a good report available online—if anyone would like to check it out—showing that productivity actually increases under fair pay agreements. Not only did the OECD agree but also so does the Treasury.
explanation: Cites named authorities (OECD, Treasury) to support the productivity claim — evidence-based, though leaning on appeal to authority and a contested reading.

text: it means that representation reviews, when they occur, and various dates associated with them will be set at regular and predictable interval periods—and that’s really important—rather than depending on where a five-year census is and where the three-year electoral cycle is.
explanation: Clear logical case for aligning the cycles: predictable intervals beat dates that float on the mismatch between a five-year census and three-year electoral cycle.

text: The purpose of this bill is to align the policy setting in the Electoral Act with the Government’s work to modernise the census... It makes the logical link between the boundary reviews and the electoral cycle.
explanation: States a coherent purpose and the logical link being made, but the reasoning is brief and assertive rather than evidenced.

text: despite escalating costs, we have been getting data that is getting poorer and poorer.
explanation: States a plausible problem (rising cost, falling quality) as the rationale for change, but offers it as assertion without supporting data.

text: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
explanation: Uses comparative practice to support reform, though leaning partly on an appeal to international norms.

text: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
explanation: Marshals a chronology to argue the reform is overdue and cross-partisan in origin.

text: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
explanation: Counters critics by pointing to genuine tightening provisions; a fair point, though 'common-sense' substitutes for detailed justification.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: Infers broad constituent support from his own doorknocking — an appeal to personal anecdote rather than data.

text: We already had a downgrade by Moody's, who have put our economy and Government on negative watch as a result, so there is no alternative to our approach.
explanation: Concludes 'there is no alternative' — a false dichotomy that closes off other policy options without argument.

text: The current situation, as interpreted by the courts, is those who receive lump-sum payments are treated more generously than the former, which are those on ACC and welfare. So the Government has a duty to fix this.
explanation: States a fairness-between-cohorts argument, but doesn't engage the rebuttal that the comparison is itself disputed.

text: It is so important for the functioning of a free and liberal democratic society that we enable these satirists to contribute to the public discourse in a way that connects with the public.
explanation: Reasonable principle but asserted rather than evidenced; leans on the value of free speech.

text: I actually had a professor in the United States, Ricardo Hausmann was his name, and he used to say two things: he would say, for Government policy, you want to look at whether there is a problem to be solved first. Then, the second thing is: is there a role for Government in solving the problem?
explanation: Applies an explicit analytical framework (is there a problem; is there a role for government) to structure his case; appeals to an authority but uses it to organise reasoning rather than substitute for it.

text: all Māori will start to migrate on to that Māori roll and they will be making the decisions come 7 November
explanation: Prediction tied to the 7 November election that ALL Māori will move to the Māori roll and prove decisive; the sweeping magnitude makes it implausible.

text: That is why Te Pāti Māori will implement a wealth tax. Under our policy, 98 percent of Aotearoa will pay less tax.
explanation: Predicts a distributional outcome of an as-yet-unimplemented policy.

text: Repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act will undo all the progress that has been made to try and fix a systemically racist organisation that, over generations, has stolen our kids.
explanation: Predicts repeal will 'undo all the progress'; directionally arguable but the absolute 'all' is uncertain and unproven.

text: Scrapping Aotearoa's world-leading smokefree laws will sacrifice Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy.
explanation: Predicts harm to Māori health from repeal; plausible given higher Māori smoking rates but magnitude uncertain.

text: We will ensure this Government's reign is short.
explanation: Predicts a one-term government; the coalition in fact governed a full term, and at the time this was an optimistic forecast against incumbency.

text: I’d like to take the opportunity to welcome the 5,200-odd voters that will be joining the wonderful Whanganui electorate at this year’s election.
explanation: Warm, inclusive welcome to incoming constituents, non-partisan in tone.

text: I just want to take the opportunity to acknowledge the trainers, the industry players, and, particularly, those from Whanganui who are affected by the closure of this industry.
explanation: Empathetic acknowledgement of those harmed by the policy, including his own constituents—inclusive in tone.

text: I cannot sit here and not note that it is my colleague Greg Fleming, a member of the National-led Government, the National Party, that has actually got this to the House during our Government. Labour had the opportunity in 2021; they didn’t get it there, so well done Greg and well done to Camilla.
explanation: Converts a 'Kumbaya' moment into partisan credit-claiming, which cuts against the cross-party tone others built.

text: Tomorrow morning, you come down to the City Mission with me and actually do some mahi and help raise the money from the people who pay the taxes to make this country work and provide the support that we need to be able to deliver the social services we need to deliver in this country.
explanation: Combative challenge directed at opponents rather than an attempt to persuade or build common ground.

text: the problem that the Opposition has is that they can't do basic arithmetic: one plus one doesn't equal four.
explanation: Belittling rather than persuasive or unifying.

text: The choice at this year's election is clear: a strong and stable coalition or a tax, spend, and borrow Labour - Greens - Te Pāti Māori coalition
explanation: Binary us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than persuading the undecided.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: Warm welcome to constituents, but blends into a partisan boast that appeals to his own side.

text: I know that the next few months will be extremely tough for this country... but this too shall pass and I remain optimistic in this country. Brighter days will return, because this Government has a good plan.
explanation: Optimistic, steadying message, but credits 'this Government' and so appeals mainly to his own side.

text: It is so important for the functioning of a free and liberal democratic society that we enable these satirists to contribute to the public discourse in a way that connects with the public.
explanation: Appeals to a widely shared democratic value to build cross-bench support for the copyright bill.

text: There are bills in this House that are game-changing—consequential pieces of legislation that give members of Parliament a sense of purpose about why we are here—and then there are regulatory systems bills. No offence to the Minister; he’s done a great job. I commend this select committee process, and I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Disarming, good-humoured tone that compliments the Minister and commends a cross-party process — bridge-building rather than combative.

text: This is like a cross-party regulatory systems bill, and you guys are sitting there being political and trying to shit on us all day.
explanation: Appeals to the cross-party nature of the bill but frames the other side as bad-faith, undercutting any consensus-building.

text: the better way to look at what the intention of Parliament is when it passes a statute is to look at the words in the purpose in the context of the statute.
explanation: Engaging, candid framing ('lengthy ramblings of a junior Minister') that brings the committee along.

text: Just to be clear, for those who made submissions, this bill does not set up digital drivers' licences; it just provides the framework … I want to acknowledge the submitters who raised concerns about whether or not digital drivers' licences would become compulsory. That is not the Government's intention. … this is a voluntary step that people can take up if they wish to do so.
explanation: Reassures and brings submitters along rather than dismissing them.

text: It’s been an excellent debate with support across the House, no sniping, no politics. I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Celebrates cross-party cooperation and a non-partisan spirit.

text: This is why we are all here: to debate freely; to have an open, robust contest of ideas; to challenge one another in an environment where disputes are resolved by the showing of hands and not by the throwing of fists.
explanation: Inclusive ('we are all here'), celebrates contest of ideas across the House, and frames Parliament as common ground — bridge-building.

text: I’d like to take the opportunity to welcome the 5,200-odd voters that will be joining the wonderful Whanganui electorate at this year’s election.
explanation: Names a concrete figure (5,200 voters) and the affected electorate.

text: I want to acknowledge those that were involved in building the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse for its positive impact on the health of greyhounds since that has been opened.
explanation: Names a concrete facility (the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse) and its claimed effect, though without measures.

text: having sat on the board of a company in Australia that was required by the Australian legislation to report under their version of what will soon be law here in New Zealand. It is a conversation that occurs around that table, of “Have we gone far enough visiting the factory in Vietnam? Do we actually know X, Y, or Z from that part of our supply chain in Europe?”
explanation: Concrete illustration of the real compliance questions directors face, with named supply-chain locations.

text: Every cost that is incurred increases the cost of the supply chain, and ultimately of the products that New Zealanders are buying. There is a way to do this and make it practical and ensure that cost is minimised but the outcome is achieved.
explanation: Identifies the cost-pass-through concern but offers no concrete figure or mechanism for keeping it 'realistic'.

text: Where's there's not an appropriate product approved for a dog or a cat, we use the equivalent human medicine. These are available internationally, but they're not used here because we haven't been able to get them approved. This bill will enable us to use the right products for the right animals here in New Zealand.
explanation: Identifies a concrete scenario (no approved product for a dog/cat, human medicine substituted) but no figures or named products.

text: Under this Government, debt is higher than Treasury has predicted, prices are rising, and productivity has stalled.
explanation: Names three concrete metrics but gives no figures or magnitudes.

text: We were in the Chamber last night, debating this stage in the committee of the whole House, and that would have been an opportunity for these amendments to be made at that stage. I'm unclear as to why the bill has had to be recommitted to the committee of the whole House and for these amendments to be made now.
explanation: Pinpoints the timing issue and the specific procedural step in question.

text: why Amendment Paper 583 has made changes to home schooling without consultation with any of the community affected and why it wasn’t sent to select committee.
explanation: Names the specific amendment paper and the precise process failures alleged (no consultation, no select committee).

text: We know that there are 32,000 fewer jobs under this Government... Kinleith Mill lost 150 jobs, Kinleith plywood 119, and Winstone Pulp's Ruapehu mills—230 there... Toi Ohomai in Tokoroa had 60 job losses in and around the same time that we've seen three closures of wood manufacturing.
explanation: Itemised job-loss figures by named employer and location, plus an aggregate figure.

text: in Northland there are 2,200 fewer jobs there now; the Hawke’s Bay, 9,400 fewer jobs; Taranaki, 6,300 fewer jobs; Tasman, Nelson, Marlborough, 2,600 fewer jobs; Southland, 4,200 fewer jobs.
explanation: Region-by-region job-loss figures.

text: despite escalating costs, we have been getting data that is getting poorer and poorer.
explanation: Asserts a cost/quality trend for the census but gives no figures or evidence.

text: The purpose of this bill is to align the policy setting in the Electoral Act with the Government’s work to modernise the census... It makes the logical link between the boundary reviews and the electoral cycle.
explanation: Identifies the alignment goal but stays at a high level with little concrete detail.

text: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
explanation: Identifies a specific provision (rapid delivery responsibilities) but stays general on how the risk reduction is achieved.

text: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
explanation: Names specific comparator countries and the statute, grounding the comparative claim.

text: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
explanation: Names specific years, actors, and prior bills — a detailed legislative history.

text: This is a good bill. I commend it to the House.
explanation: A routine endorsement that commits to no detail, figure, or reasoning.

text: To the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Megan Woods, who just sat down: it’s coming; the fringe benefit tax legislation is coming later this year. Watch this space.
explanation: Indicates 'later this year' but no precise timing or detail.

text: I say this because New Zealand has near on $200 billion of nominal debt and that has an interest attachment to that... Over the last few weeks that risk premium has gone up and we should expect it is going to make a difference to the Budget that is going to be announced in May.
explanation: Gives a debt figure and a concrete near-term consequence for the May Budget.

text: There will be two, I guess, Amendment Papers, one pertaining to the temporary tax changes for the in-work tax credit, and, also, the amendment to change the thin capitalisation rules, which I look forward to thoroughly debating in the committee stage.
explanation: Names two concrete forthcoming amendments (in-work tax credit changes; thin capitalisation rules) and the stage at which they arise.

text: The first is the Conduct of Financial Institutions regime, which we brought into place in March 2025. That requires, of course, all financial institutions to operate fairly and transparently towards consumers in the products they offer. Next, we do have the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, which is before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment.
explanation: Names specific regimes and bills with a date and the committee handling them, to substantiate that existing instruments cover the issue.

text: I reflect on 2020, when New Zealand saw its first slavery conviction in New Zealand and we were appalled. We found it abhorrent and we couldn’t believe that it happened on our shores. Moving on from that, over the past six years, we have seen a growing trend.
explanation: References a landmark NZ conviction and a rising trend; the specific date and 'first conviction' framing are debatable (earlier human-trafficking convictions exist), so the claim is directionally true but imprecise.

text: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
explanation: Cites specific compliance statistics presented favourably; plausible but self-reported.

text: The latest validated data shows the number of people waiting for a first specialist assessment has reduced by more than 4,500 since January last year, following an 81 percent blowout between 2017 and 2023.
explanation: Specific figures, but selectively framed (a reduction in those waiting alongside the separate issue of rising declined referrals being raised) and unverifiable here.

text: Budget 2026 will provide $35 million over four years to strengthen road ambulance services... This is on top of an additional $77.7 million that has been invested since 2023, which brought total funding for road ambulance services to $452 million for this financial year.
explanation: Specific funding figures presented as fact; plausible and checkable against Budget documents.

text: most importantly, $20 billion a year is the value of the unpaid work contribution that our seniors make to this economy.
explanation: Attributed to the NZIER Business of Ageing report; a sourced figure, though such valuations are estimates.

text: it was actually only a week ago that Christopher Luxon, under huge pressure, put up a confidence vote in caucus and almost lost to an empty chair. ... double digits of his caucus voted no.
explanation: Asserts internal caucus vote details ('double digits voted no', 'almost lost to an empty chair') hedged with 'from what I've been hearing'—unverifiable and likely exaggerated.

text: They know that when New Zealanders see that there are 32,000 thousand fewer jobs in this country ... when there are 2,000 people leaving the country every week ... 15 percent—that's ... business liquidations, that's what it's increased by. ... the 18 percent increase in power prices. There are people in this country that are paying 100 bucks to visit the doctor.
explanation: The figures are presented assertively without sources; several are plausible but rounded and selectively framed for impact.

text: We have been asking Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon every week for two years to show us the numbers of people who have received $250. Do they answer? No, because the answer is zero. It is yet another broken promise.
explanation: Asserts zero recipients of a promised $250; the rhetorical 'zero' is likely an overstatement of a contested delivery record.

text: the Department of Corrections have flagged that this bill has the capacity to increase the cost to Corrections by $300 million.
explanation: Specific sourced claim about a departmental cost flag; plausible but unverifiable from the text and characterised as 'capacity to' rather than a firm estimate.

text: They're crowing about making it easier to access prescriptions, but let's not forget they used to be free. They put the charges back on them, make it slightly easier, and say, "Aren't we great?"
explanation: Prescription co-payments were removed and then reinstated, so the underlying sequence is broadly accurate.

text: The numbers tell the story: 235 education workers, 240 police, 850 defence staff.
explanation: Specific official-sounding figures, plausible but not independently verified here.

text: In 2024, a Federated Farmers survey said that about 73 percent of dairy farmers, 66 percent of sheep and beef, and 51 percent of arable had farm workers who lived on their farm.
explanation: Attributed survey statistics; plausible and sourced, though unverified in text.

text: What began in 1901 as the Carter Home for aged poor men, housing around 20 residents, has grown into significant community asset that now supports more than 100 people aged 65 and over.
explanation: Specific historical and current figures about Carter Court; plausible and consistent with the bill's background.

text: the promise of this Government to help the squeezed middle has been an absolute lie
explanation: Characterises an opponent's promise as an 'absolute lie' — hyperbolic framing of a contested outcome.

text: At a time when we know the number one issue in Aotearoa is the cost of living, this Government is choosing to retrospectively burden people.
explanation: Cost of living being a top public concern is broadly supportable; 'number one' is an assertion.

text: Do you know where else Gisborne takes us, Mr Speaker? State Highway 35—State Highway 35 that was not mentioned in today’s Budget. We talked about resilience. We talked about connectivity.
explanation: Claim that SH35 was not mentioned in the Budget; plausible and checkable.

text: The Māori economy grew from $69 billion in 2018 to $126 billion in 2023.
explanation: Specific figures broadly consistent with published Māori economy asset-base estimates.

text: Working for Families aspect of this bill—for those who don’t know, an amazing initiative introduced by the Labour Government under Helen Clark.
explanation: Accurate: Working for Families was introduced under the Clark-led Labour Government.

text: It is a fact that the function of the Ministry for the Environment continues exactly as it is in the new form of the ministry there, but it's under a different form of MCERT.
explanation: Asserts as 'fact' that functions continue 'exactly as is'; this is the contested government claim that submitters and the PCE disputed, so the certainty is overstated.

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: A forward projection presented as near-fact; magnitude is contestable.

text: when that policy was announced in 2018, no officials and no industry knew anything about it
explanation: Claim that no officials or industry were consulted on the 2018 oil/gas decision — directionally argued but an absolute that's hard to confirm.

text: In fact, it’s mentioned that 50 percent of all international visitors will visit the conservation estate, and what’s wrong with charging them a reasonable amount to they can contribute to the conservation that we wish to deploy on to that land.
explanation: Roughly half of international visitors engaging with the conservation estate is broadly consistent with tourism/DOC figures.

text: One of the amendments that came from that was to strengthen the feedback from the Secretary for the Environment, who will hand the ultimate responsibility for this new ministry back to Parliament. We have inserted a new clause, and it’s requiring the secretary to report annually to ensure that he’s reporting on the performance of their function, as is required under the Environment Act.
explanation: Consistent with the annual-reporting amendment also referenced by Cameron Luxton.

text: many families around this country are better off as a result of the Government's tax-setting changes and the FamilyBoost scheme that is providing much relief to hard-working Kiwi families at a time of hardship for many.
explanation: 'Many families better off' is an unquantified, unverifiable assertion.

text: In fact, tenancy satisfaction is up since the changes, and build costs are coming down and savings have been made.
explanation: Several positive claims asserted without figures; directionally plausible but unsupported here.

text: Eligibility for the social housing register is unchanged from the previous Government to today, which allows for comparisons. Is the measure perfect? No, it is not... Is the register going down? Yes, it is.
explanation: Claim that register eligibility is unchanged is a checkable factual assertion stated firmly to rebut an allegation of manipulation.

text: Revenue into the National Land Transport Fund is actually forecast to decline because people are driving less … We are also facing rising costs because 80 percent of our buses are diesel buses, and the price of diesel in particular is rising quickly…
explanation: Claims about diesel bus share and NLTF revenue dynamics are broadly plausible but unverified here.

text: she’s now been here for nine years, entering her fourth term as the member of Parliament for Taranaki-King Country.
explanation: Kuriger entered Parliament in 2014, making 2023 her fourth term (2014, 2017, 2020, 2023) and roughly nine years — accurate.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Broad unsupported claim that the whole Public Service lacked basic financial management; overgeneralised and not evidenced.

text: Meta is not as transparent, although they will tell us, and they did tell us, that they are the most transparent. If you go to the transparency centre for Meta, however, what you will find is a step process that they go through and it gets to a point where it says, basically, in not so many words, “and then the algorithm does its magic”.
explanation: Characterises Meta's transparency centre critically; broadly fair but a paraphrase ('in not so many words') that simplifies.

text: I wish to correct a statement that I made during the second reading of the Anzac commemoration bill.
explanation: Proactively fixing an inaccurate earlier claim improves the truthfulness of the record.

text: Adolescents are neurologically, psychologically more vulnerable to these feedback systems because of their brain development and the point of development they’re at. They’re also wired for social reward, for peer approval, for novelty, for identity information and formation.
explanation: Consistent with developmental neuroscience on adolescent sensitivity to social reward; broadly supported.

text: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
explanation: Accurate description of how engagement-based recommender systems and ad-funded business models work.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Absolute 'nobody' is hyperbole — some support exists for the project.

text: More than the last 40 years combined.
explanation: Striking quantified claim about urgency use; plausible but unverified and likely an upper-bound framing.

text: This is also a project with a potential negative cost-benefit ratio. It could have a cost-benefit ration of 0.75. That means, for every dollar we put into it, we are losing out on the benefits.
explanation: Presents a hedged ('potential', 'could') BCR figure; plausible but unsourced.

text: There is no consensus in the planning world as to what character actually refers to, but there is a whole lot of literature that argues that character is a way of protecting the status quo and making sure that people of the same economic class, the same race, and the same background remain
explanation: Broadly reflects critiques in urban-planning scholarship of 'character' protections, stated without specifics.

text: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
explanation: A concrete, checkable figure consistent with public-housing waitlist data for Auckland.

text: We spend a greater share of our GDP on infrastructure than many compatible countries, but we achieve less.
explanation: Aligns with the report's finding on spend-vs-outcomes; broadly supportable.

text: This is why we decided to make a change in this bill to reduce the minimum housing capacity in plan change 120 from 2 million homes to 1.4 million. This is a more realistic approach, focusing growth in the city centre, around town centres, and along major transport routes.
explanation: Accurately states the bill's change; 'more realistic' is the contested editorial framing.

text: A lot of submitters mentioned that the current legislation is fragmented and inconsistent and there is no single national regulator with clear responsibility for online safety. Stronger coordination and leadership are needed to better protect our communities.
explanation: Accurate characterisation of NZ's fragmented online-safety regulatory landscape with no single dedicated regulator.

text: Nicola Willis tells people it’s bad luck, basically, if they lose their job—“Oh, well.”
explanation: Presented as a factual characterisation of Willis's view but is an unsupported, hostile paraphrase likely to mislead.

text: Budget 2024 cut $178 million from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority’s budget. This was money that was largely to reduce household electricity bills... In a year when the Government had $790 million - odd in tax cuts for landlords, $178 million was sliced from initiatives that could have directly helped families with the cost of living.
explanation: Specific fiscal claims stated as fact; plausible but unverified and the juxtaposition is framed for contrast.

text: The regulatory impact statement shows that the only consultation undertaken in respect of this measure was with the Privacy Commissioner, and one of the concerns that we had that was that there needed to be a broader look taken at this.
explanation: Specific, checkable claim citing the regulatory impact statement about the scope of consultation; plausible and concrete.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Accurate that Treasury's Living Standards Framework originated under Bill English's tenure around 2011.

text: for the income tax year ended 31 March 2024, 119,000 companies were owed nearly $29 billion by shareholders who were natural persons or trustees.
explanation: Specific figures cited from the regulatory impact statement / IRD data.

text: there’s nothing to show for it but just unprecedented Government debt and a huge $8.9 billion interest bill, and growing. No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing.
explanation: 'No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing' is hyperbole that ignores any infrastructure delivered in the period.

text: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
explanation: There were real disputes over time-limited funding for these programmes, but 'hidden fiscal cliffs' is contested — the prior Government argued the funding was openly time-limited.

text: food prices increased by over 12 percent in the year to March 2023. In the year to March 2026, food prices increased by 3.4 percent. It’s a much better improvement than that Government, when they sat on their hands.
explanation: Two specific year-to-March food-inflation figures; the 12% comparison is broadly grounded though the framing is selective.

text: what they’ve outlaid is nearly 12,000 projects that are at a value of $275 billion, with most of those projects unfunded.
explanation: Concrete figures attributed to the report; checkable and presented straightforwardly.

text: This bill, of course, locks in the Government's decision this week to reduce the minimum housing capacity required by Plan Change 120 from 2 million to 1.4 million.
explanation: Accurate description of what the bill does, consistent with the bill text and other speakers.

text: If you lose the Waikare Gorge, which we did, the time it takes to get to Wairoa from Napier is 10 hours, as opposed to one and a half.
explanation: Concrete travel-time contrast; plausible given Cyclone Gabrielle disruption, presented as fact.

text: I was very much there in 2017, when we talked about, as the last National Government, the Hawke’s Bay Expressway. It was almost all but there. Then what happened? We didn’t get in to Government that time. It got cancelled, and there goes another six years of that project.
explanation: Account of the Expressway being shelved after 2017; broadly plausible but a partisan framing of the project's history.

text: Unfortunately, the more involved a Government becomes in people’s business, and businesses, for that matter, the worse things seem to get.
explanation: Broad, unfalsifiable-as-stated generalisation ('the worse things seem to get') that overstates a contested correlation as a rule.

text: It is unjust to prioritise the niceties of urban Wellington and Auckland when the locals of Tiniroto and Ruakituri are still taking a two-hour detour because the roads have been closed for nearly 10 months.
explanation: The Cyclone Gabrielle road closures (from mid-February 2023) leaving rural detours by December is broadly accurate; specific locality detail supports it, though 'nearly 10 months' and exact detour length are not independently verified here.

text: We have every confidence in Police management and capability to plan. This is why the police Minister does not need to speculate about that level of detail, because we have full confidence in the Police executive management to deal with these issues.
explanation: A general expression of confidence with no detail, figures or mechanism.

text: putting a single supervisor in charge will ensure that we have great clarity and that, therefore, we can respond where risk exists, rather than a blanket response across all activity
explanation: Names the structural change and its intended risk-based effect, but no detail on how clarity is achieved.

text: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
explanation: Concrete measures and figures: doubled store visits, 90%+ compliance, doubled infringement notices, 18 extra compliance officers.

text: The funding, announced last week, will provide for the establishment of two ambulance hubs in Auckland, with one already confirmed for South Auckland; deployment of an electronic patient clinical record system... additional training and support for ambulance communications centre staff; and additional clinical welfare checks for patients.
explanation: Itemised, concrete uses of the funding (two hubs, named location, IT system, training).

text: We invested $221.3 million into alcohol and drug treatment services in 2024-25, and we have a good handle on the coverage and outputs of those services, which support over 46,895 people per year.
explanation: Exact dollar figure, fiscal year, and an oddly precise client count.

text: They don’t want to talk about the fact that the minimum wage has not kept up with the cost of living.
explanation: General assertion with no figures or period.

text: We've come up with a solution to that. We're going to use a capital gains tax to pay for three free GP visits for everyone in the country.
explanation: A concrete policy (CGT funding three free GP visits) though without rates or thresholds.

text: they are saving money by keeping people on the street, and they are putting a fraction into new houses—211 this Government have funded that have led to a new house from the 2024 allocation, and 228 from the 2025 allocation.
explanation: Cites exact house counts against budget allocations.

text: They know that when New Zealanders see that there are 32,000 thousand fewer jobs in this country ... when there are 2,000 people leaving the country every week ... 15 percent—that's ... business liquidations, that's what it's increased by. ... the 18 percent increase in power prices. There are people in this country that are paying 100 bucks to visit the doctor.
explanation: A battery of concrete figures (jobs, emigration, liquidations, power prices, GP cost).

text: How can he expect to house the growing number of homeless when the pipeline of houses contracted or under construction has dropped from 8,863 in 2023 to just 1,513 today, a drop of 83 percent in just two years?
explanation: Precise figures: pipeline from 8,863 to 1,513, an 83% drop over two years.

text: National backs recreational fishers, and I'm proud to say I'm one of them.
explanation: Slogan-like affirmation with no policy detail, mechanism, or measure.

text: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
explanation: Names the concrete action — removing the minimum-size-limit sections — though not the mechanism or timing.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Names dates and the exact bill title.

text: What began in 1901 as the Carter Home for aged poor men, housing around 20 residents, has grown into significant community asset that now supports more than 100 people aged 65 and over.
explanation: Names dates and resident numbers then and now.

text: In 2024, a Federated Farmers survey said that about 73 percent of dairy farmers, 66 percent of sheep and beef, and 51 percent of arable had farm workers who lived on their farm.
explanation: Named source, year, and three percentage figures.

text: Labour is ready with a plan and ready to work with hapū, iwi, and whānau Māori.
explanation: States readiness and a 'plan' but gives no content of it.

text: something I think we could move forward as a Parliament, if we really want to have some benefit for Māori, is, perhaps, start looking closely at lending on things like multiply owned Māori land, especially when people have the means to service the mortgages and the loans for that.
explanation: Identifies a concrete policy area (lending on multiply owned Māori land) but hedged as 'perhaps, start looking closely' with no mechanism or measure.

text: Currently, we have whānau in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti who are using Afterpay to buy groceries. They're using Afterpay, so they're borrowing to buy the essentials just to get by.
explanation: Names a concrete region (Ikaroa-Rāwhiti), a named mechanism (Afterpay) and a concrete use (groceries/essentials), but no figures or scale.

text: no blanket legislation would ever have known the peculiarities to the Waiapu River and to the Motu Awa in Rangitukia.
explanation: Names specific places and customary practices rather than speaking only in generalities.

text: The Māori economy grew from $69 billion in 2018 to $126 billion in 2023.
explanation: Exact dollar figures with years.

text: These amendments here, there are a lot of technical amendments, but there are a lot of improvements in gaining greater transparency, improving the fiscal responsibility, and improving the practical outcomes of the Act itself.
explanation: Lists aims (transparency, fiscal responsibility, outcomes) but no concrete detail of what the amendments do.

text: This bill is actually a very small bill... that's the only entity—the Ministry for the Environment—that needs an Act for it to be disestablished. That's what the primary reason for this bill is all about.
explanation: Explains concretely why an Act is required (the Ministry is the only statutory entity among those merging).

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: Names a precise number of jobs.

text: One of the amendments that came from that was to strengthen the feedback from the Secretary for the Environment, who will hand the ultimate responsibility for this new ministry back to Parliament. We have inserted a new clause, and it’s requiring the secretary to report annually to ensure that he’s reporting on the performance of their function, as is required under the Environment Act.
explanation: Describes a concrete amendment—an annual reporting requirement on the Secretary.

text: This bill is actually quite a small bill—it’s only eight pages long—it has the intention of facilitating the Government’s plan to combine the functions of a number of entities, with those entities being the Ministry for the Environment, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, the Ministry of Transport, and also the local government functions within the Department of Internal Affairs.
explanation: Names the page count and the precise entities being merged.

text: New Zealanders deserve treatments not based on identity or politics or what box they have to tick.
explanation: Values statement with no mechanism or measure.

text: I can indicate, straight up, ACT will be supporting this through the first reading because we actually do believe in free speech.
explanation: States position and reason but at the level of principle rather than detail.

text: In just a few weeks' time, we're actually going to have expedited access to medicines—the accelerated pathway... Where overseas regulators have already approved a medicine, there's going to be an expedited pathway so we can get those treatments to Kiwis faster.
explanation: Describes the mechanism (recognising overseas approvals) and rough timing, though no exact date.

text: we got rid of the Therapeutic Products Act, a really bad piece of legislation... We got rid of the Māori Health Authority... We actually got the second phase of the commission of inquiry into COVID up and going
explanation: Names the specific legislation, body and inquiry.

text: We know that $135 million is going to go into supporting our ambulance services across the country. We had the excellent announcement of around $15.5 million for specialist palliative care for children
explanation: Names dollar amounts tied to specific health services.

text: As I often say to the Greens: there is no magic money tree, and to the extent that there is one, the leaves just got clipped off.
explanation: A slogan committing to nothing concrete.

text: Revenue into the National Land Transport Fund is actually forecast to decline because people are driving less … We are also facing rising costs because 80 percent of our buses are diesel buses, and the price of diesel in particular is rising quickly…
explanation: Cites a concrete figure (80% diesel buses) and named mechanisms, though no dollar amounts.

text: the capacity that will be unlocked as a result of this will be, roughly, around 1.6 million homes. That is a substantial advance on the status quo, which is in the Auckland Unitary Plan—which hasn't been updated for years—which is around 1.2 million homes.
explanation: Gives concrete capacity figures and the comparison baseline.

text: New Zealand currently has over 1,800 public charge points. Combined with the investment we announced yesterday, the national total will be around 4,500. We’re well on our way to the target of 10,000 by 2030.
explanation: Cites current count (1,800+), projected total (~4,500), and a dated target (10,000 by 2030).

text: The Ashbourne project was approved on 21 April: hundreds of news homes and two solar farms in the Waikato. On 1 May, the Pound Road Industrial Development was approved in Canterbury... Over $450 million is expected to be contributed to the economy. Then, on 7 May, also in Canterbury, the Ryans Road Industrial Development was also approved, enabling the development and subdivision of 126 industrial lots.
explanation: Names projects, dates, locations and lot/dollar figures.

text: Auckland is a city where hundreds of Kāinga Ora public homes have been delayed or cancelled as a result of this Government.
explanation: Rough magnitude only (“hundreds”), no exact figure or location.

text: Auckland is a city—let’s contextualise it—where rough-sleeping homelessness has doubled in the last few years because of the choices of this Government to restrict access to emergency housing.
explanation: Quantified direction (“doubled”) and a named cause, but no figures or timeframe.

text: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
explanation: Names a specific number and location.

text: This is also a project with a potential negative cost-benefit ratio. It could have a cost-benefit ration of 0.75. That means, for every dollar we put into it, we are losing out on the benefits.
explanation: Cites a concrete ratio (0.75).

text: bus fares in the Wellington region are set to go up by 3.1 percent from May this year. If you live in the west of Wellington, in Karori, or the east of Wellington, in Miramar, it’s going to cost you $5 per trip to get into the city centre.
explanation: Exact percentage, month, named suburbs, and per-trip cost.

text: The Labour Party is completely out of touch.
explanation: Vague slogan; commits to nothing.

text: Maybe it is time for all of us to reflect on our own habits. Maybe it is time for us to put down our cell phones a little bit more often, spend more time with our children, listen to them... no technology will replace the guidance, love, and people of our family.
explanation: Sentimental exhortation with no concrete measure.

text: The National Infrastructure Plan provides a 30-year road map to address these challenges, and it has four basic principles. One, plan what we can afford; second, look after what we’ve got; third, prioritise the right projects; and fourth, make it easier to build better.
explanation: Enumerates four named principles but they remain high-level directions without mechanisms or figures.

text: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
explanation: Names the residents' group and the concrete concern (development outpacing confirmed infrastructure).

text: This is why we decided to make a change in this bill to reduce the minimum housing capacity in plan change 120 from 2 million homes to 1.4 million. This is a more realistic approach, focusing growth in the city centre, around town centres, and along major transport routes.
explanation: Gives the figures and where growth is to be focused (city centre, town centres, transport routes).

text: For us, it is imperative that we do have a long-term plan, we do invest in our future, and we set up a reason for our young people to stay—not something we have seen from this Government.
explanation: Pure aspiration — 'long-term plan' and 'invest in our future' with no policy, figure, or mechanism.

text: In the 2024 International Monetary Fund (IMF) report on the New Zealand economy, one of the things they talk about is that to achieve objectives, reform could combine comprehensive capital gains, land value tax, and changes to corporate income tax.
explanation: Names the source and the three specific reform components, though without figures.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Names the originator (Bill English), the body (Treasury), and a date (2011).

text: I’d like to hear from the Minister, given we don’t have a chance to really get into this at a select committee, some of the thought processes that he and his officials went through on landing on that option out of six, and what it was that made that option the one that they went with.
explanation: References the specific option (five) and the evaluation criteria.

text: for the income tax year ended 31 March 2024, 119,000 companies were owed nearly $29 billion by shareholders who were natural persons or trustees.
explanation: Precise count, dollar figure, and tax year.

text: It’s a great day in the reform of Auckland Transport. I commend the bill.
explanation: Celebratory endorsement with no substantive content.

text: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
explanation: Names concrete examples (Pharmac, school lunch programme) of the time-limited funding the bill targets.

text: That was a provision within this bill that encourages residential solar uptake, ensuring residents up and down this country who export excess power back to the grid... won't face income tax, recognising that the compliance burden would outweigh any benefit and it will encourage solar and battery uptake.
explanation: Clearly describes the mechanism (no income tax on exported residential solar) and its rationale.

text: With tariffs eliminated or reduced on 95 percent of New Zealand’s exports, and duty-free access on almost 57 percent of New Zealand exports from day one, more of our value-added goods can reach Indian customers.
explanation: Precise tariff figures (95 percent reduced, 57 percent duty-free from day one).

text: At present, the steepest penalty for breaches is capped at $600,000. The new framework, inspired by approaches used in Australia and the United Kingdom, introduces a flexible upper limit. The maximum fine will now be the highest of three times the value gained from the offending conduct, the total value of the transactions involved, or a flat $5 million.
explanation: Precise current cap ($600k), the three-limb new maximum, and the $5m flat figure.

text: You can’t spend your way out of every problem, nor can you regulate your way out of it. All you get is debt and dependency.
explanation: Slogan-level statement of principle; no figures, policies, or mechanisms.

text: The world wants me to think it’s a toy so that I play with it all the time, so it makes me more accessible, and they make it look fun and all colourful and there are things to do and interesting things to see. But it’s a trap.
explanation: Evocative framing but no concrete mechanism, figure, or policy detail.

text: for those people that cannot find jobs and cannot get into education... there is still a safety net for them to be supported financially. But those people who are financially able to be supported by their families should be, and they should actually be encouraged into work and training
explanation: Describes the intended structure but without the test's thresholds or how 'financially able' is determined.

text: when I was managing a school bus company, I observed students in some remote communities, and some not so remote communities, who were kept out of school for various reasons, not travelling on the school bus when they should’ve been, who were then being, in some cases, used by their parents to work in spaces, whether they were illegal or not, for no employment.
explanation: Concrete lived example with a specific setting, though the scale and prevalence are left vague.

text: It is unjust to prioritise the niceties of urban Wellington and Auckland when the locals of Tiniroto and Ruakituri are still taking a two-hour detour because the roads have been closed for nearly 10 months.
explanation: Names specific settlements, the detour length, and the duration of closure.

text: That is why in November last year, this Government released a comprehensive methamphetamine action plan. Part of that package saw $30 million over four years invested to increase the services available to communities hardest hit by meth, with almost $4 million going to local providers in Northland.
explanation: A funded, launched plan in implementation, though outcomes not yet demonstrated.

text: Today I announced a major increase in compliance activity which supports the law changes we made last year to ban disposable vapes and increase penalties for sales to under-18-year-olds. Health New Zealand more than doubled store visits and controlled purchase operations, targeting illegal sales to minors in the last year. Compliance is strong with upwards of 90 percent of retailers doing the right thing … infringement notices more than double over the last year. The infringement efforts have been boosted with the recruitment of an additional 18 compliance officers.
explanation: Points to enacted law changes and delivered enforcement increases, not just intentions.

text: I'm pleased that this increased investment means there are now record ambulance staffing levels and faster response times for the most serious emergencies, and that it contributes to the New Zealand First - National coalition commitment.
explanation: Claims delivered outcomes (staffing, response times) tied to prior investment.

text: Over the last two years, this Government has invested an extra $343 million into the aged-care sector to provide stability while we work on changes to the system. Health New Zealand has introduced a new Casemix funding model and framework across the South Island…
explanation: Describes concrete delivered investment and a rolled-out funding model.

text: New Zealand First stood in our coalition agreement to defend the superannuation age of entitlement at 65, and we will continue to protect that position.
explanation: The commitment was secured in the coalition agreement, i.e. backed by a concrete negotiated outcome, not just rhetoric.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Carried the issue from campaign promise to a member's bill picked up as a Government bill — demonstrated follow-through.

text: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
explanation: Clear commitment to remove specific clauses, but delivery depends on the select committee process and is not yet enacted.

text: We’re very proud of the changes we’ve made with Pharmac and actually changing that organisation to make sure it’s delivering for New Zealanders who need important medicines.
explanation: Claims credit for delivered Pharmac changes/new fundings referenced earlier; partly substantiated but framed broadly.

text: We know that $135 million is going to go into supporting our ambulance services across the country. We had the excellent announcement of around $15.5 million for specialist palliative care for children
explanation: Funding commitments announced, not yet delivered/spent, so partial follow-through.

text: Down my way, in Central Otago, we also had the excellent announcement of $180 million to go into the Southern Lakes area—some of it for operational funding over four years, and some of it for capital funding.
explanation: Announced investment he advocated for; delivery still pending.

text: That’s why we have reintroduced things like three strikes, the gang patch ban, etc.
explanation: Claims credit for delivered measures (three strikes reintroduction and the gang patch ban) that the coalition has in fact enacted, not merely announced.

text: we got rid of the Therapeutic Products Act, a really bad piece of legislation... We got rid of the Māori Health Authority... We actually got the second phase of the commission of inquiry into COVID up and going
explanation: Lists enacted changes (repeal of the Act, disestablishment, inquiry phase) — concrete, delivered actions.

text: over the next four years, these initiatives will deliver savings of $2.4 billion, which will be redeployed to deliver more health services, lift education outcomes, build job-rich public infrastructure, and strengthen the defence force and police.
explanation: An announced future saving, not yet delivered; intent rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: I direct the member to the work the Transport Agency is doing on the Brynderwyns and the Mangamukas, for example, where we have seen real progress, and on the East Coast post - Cyclone Gabrielle.
explanation: Points to concrete, partly-delivered resilience work, while conceding more remains.

text: The reality is that Kāinga Ora's debt track is now $10 billion less than what it was three years ago. That's $10 billion less that the taxpayer has to fund or borrow.
explanation: Claims credit for a delivered fiscal outcome under his stewardship.

text: Parliament, last year, passed time of use pricing legislation unanimously, and I was really pleased by that, and I was really pleased to engage with the Opposition around finding a framework that we can all accept.
explanation: Points to enacted legislation, not just intent.

text: Yesterday, we announced that recovery work on the Napier to Wairoa corridor following Cyclone Gabrielle has been completed. The final asphalting is now done, meaning the 4-kilometre road rebuild at State Highway 2—known as "Devil's Elbow"—is once again open to traffic. It's a major milestone in recovery works in Hawke's Bay and will mean a more efficient connection between Wairoa and Napier.
explanation: Describes a concrete project actually completed and reopened, not merely announced.

text: which Government has given the green light to the Waikare Gorge realignment? It’s ours.
explanation: Claims credit for greenlighting a concrete project; approval is action, though delivery is still pending.

text: While I have spent the last 15 minutes talking, I will spend the rest of my career listening, advocating, and delivering, because the Nimon family motto states “I show, not boast”.
explanation: Commitment to 'delivering' but entirely forward-looking and aspirational, with no record yet — announcement of intent, not demonstrated follow-through.

text: In part of that lesson, I will take her through the history, which is that under her Government, inflation was higher and, Lord alive, if another Labour-led Government was elected, you betcha, inflation will be higher again, borrowing will be higher again, and taxes will be higher again, too.
explanation: Predicts higher inflation/borrowing/tax under a future Labour government; partisan and not well-evidenced.

text: Our goal is to avoid ever getting to response phase 3 or 4. These are envisaged in the National Fuel Plan as the point at which prioritisation of fuel would be required... But in direct answer to the member’s question, I would not expect us to be skipping through the response phases.
explanation: Predicts NZ will avoid phases 3/4 and not skip levels; plausible but contingent on fuel supply, provisional.

text: Yes, I can assure this House that our Budget will forecast more jobs and income opportunities for Kiwis to get ahead in the years ahead, and I want to acknowledge the role that food distribution entities take.
explanation: Prediction that the Budget will produce more jobs and income; plausible but unquantified and optimistic.

text: I will absolutely present the forecasts in May, and I expect that they will be significantly worse than the forecasts previously presented. I'm not going to give a running commentary on all the discussions Treasury has with me as they develop their understanding of how the conflict will impact the economy.
explanation: Predicts the May forecasts will be 'significantly worse'; plausible given the fuel shock, but unquantified.

text: It's not my responsibility to agree or disagree with a particular forecast. As I just noted in my earlier answer, there are a range of forecasts from bank economists and others that predict a higher rate of inflation this year than would have been the case without the Middle East conflict. It is my view that I concur that inflation will go higher this year as a result of the Middle East conflict.
explanation: Predicts higher inflation this year due to the conflict; well-grounded directional call, magnitude left open.

text: New Zealanders will go, “No, you’ve had your chance”, and they’ll give them the flick.
explanation: Predicts the Government loses the coming election; partisan and uncertain.

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: Forecasts 3,300 job losses; specific but an optimistic-of-doom projection with uncertain timing.

text: When it’s eventually done, by the end of 2027, New Zealand will have a world-leading national ticketing system.
explanation: Prediction that the system will be world-leading and complete by end-2027; IT rollouts frequently slip, and 'world-leading' is hard to verify.

text: over the next four years alone, over 200,000 jobs will be created in this economy—tens of thousands of jobs. In the private sector—which, by the way, makes up the vast bulk of the number of people employed in New Zealand.
explanation: Forecasts 200,000+ private-sector jobs over four years; plausible directionally but uncertain in magnitude.

text: Yes. In the round, the new ministry, I believe, will lead to improvements of our natural environment over time.
explanation: Prediction that the restructure will improve the environment 'over time' — plausible directionally but no mechanism quantified or timeframe; outcome uncertain.

text: Westpower estimates the scheme will generate enough electricity for 12,000 homes and prevent—Chlöe Swarbrick—129,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. I'm told this is equivalent to taking 69,000 cars off the road annually.
explanation: Forecast of future annual generation/emissions savings from a scheme not yet built; plausible but contingent on completion and output.

text: Quite to the contrary of mutterings from the other side that these projects are a "waste of money"—the local residents of Napier and Wairoa and the Napier electorate will be interested to discover that members opposite consider these projects a waste of money—we are, in fact, making good progress. The final repairs are under way on Rail Bridge 217, the rail line between Hastings and Napier, expected to be completed by the middle of the year.
explanation: Predicts Rail Bridge 217 and TREC works complete by mid-year; plausible for works already under way.
