text: bus fares in the Wellington region are set to go up by 3.1 percent from May this year. If you live in the west of Wellington, in Karori, or the east of Wellington, in Miramar, it’s going to cost you $5 per trip to get into the city centre.
explanation: Near-term scheduled fare rise; high confidence as it is an announced change.

text: you'll have an AI system on the other end of the phone who won't understand anything you say, over and over again. Our public services will get worse without the people and the workers who are the backbone of our Public Service.
explanation: Predicts degraded public services from automation/cuts; directionally arguable but uncertain in magnitude.

text: long-term transport planning for our biggest city, Auckland, which of course will be 2 million people by 2033.
explanation: Population forecast (2 million by 2033); consistent with projections but inherently uncertain.

text: In 2025, New Zealand businesses exported over $80 million worth of iron and steel into India, where tariffs are currently as high as 22 percent. Under this agreement, these tariffs will be phased out over the next 10 years.
explanation: Forecasts a 10-year tariff phase-out; reflects agreed schedule but a decade-long commitment carries uncertainty.

text: That is why businesses and manufacturers are going to back this Government for its re-election, and it’s exactly why they will not return the last lot
explanation: Predicts businesses will back the Government at re-election; partisan and unfounded.

text: The Prime Minister is a dud, the finance Minister has no credibility, and they are lashing around for relevance.
explanation: Direct personal attacks on competence and character ('a dud', 'no credibility').

text: You’ve sat there and listened to Shane Jones lie to this House on repeated occasions. All I’m doing is pointing that out.
explanation: Direct accusation that a member is lying (unparliamentary); aimed at conduct on a contested factual matter rather than personal traits.

text: they want to pretend that the homelessness that their policies have created doesn’t exist by shifting it out of the centre city. In the Prime Minister’s own words, he doesn’t want tourists to come in and see homeless people on the streets.
explanation: Imputes bad faith ('want to pretend') though it does cite a paraphrased quote and a policy concern.

text: they are saving money by keeping people on the street, and they are putting a fraction into new houses—211 this Government have funded that have led to a new house from the 2024 allocation, and 228 from the 2025 allocation.
explanation: 'Saving money by keeping people on the street' imputes a callous motive to the Government.

text: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
explanation: A measured procedural objection focused on accuracy, distinguishing legitimate political answers from false assertions.

text: If this guy opened a funeral parlour, nobody would die. He can screw up anything—
explanation: Pure personal mockery, no policy content.

text: He says I’m not even on TikTok. I am, and I’m sorry that you haven’t found my account yet! I’ll put some economics up there, and maybe some advice for public speaking. You might learn something, buddy.
explanation: Condescending personal jab ('you might learn something, buddy') aimed at the speaker rather than his argument.

text: We've seen other initiatives—such as unions, who are supposed to represent workers, actually campaigning for workers not to go to work and even taking legal action to avoid going into work.
explanation: Characterises unions in a derisive 'supposed to' framing rather than engaging the substance of their position.

text: we don’t generally think of ourselves as penalising other countries. None the less, where we believe there has been a breach of our understandings between countries, we ensure that we are doing the best to represent New Zealand’s position on the world stage, behind closed doors and openly, and I think our Minister of Foreign Affairs has had a good couple of years of doing that, after we were nearly invisible on the world stage under his predecessor.
explanation: ‘Nearly invisible on the world stage under his predecessor’ is a swipe at the prior government rather than substance.

text: I move, That this House condemn all incidents of antisemitism in New Zealand and affirm that antisemitism has no place here.
explanation: Respectful, value-based motion with no personal attack; standard consensus-seeking House condemnation.

text: the promise of this Government to help the squeezed middle has been an absolute lie
explanation: 'Absolute lie' is an accusation of bad faith rather than substantive policy critique.

text: One billion dollars of targeted Māori funding was cut—that is what responsible budgeting looks like under this National-led Government.
explanation: Sarcastic framing of 'responsible budgeting' but tied to a substantive claim about cuts.

text: It appears that no real thought has gone into how a revised tax system can actually have material impact on Māori businesses, Māori-owned corporations, and Māori land trusts.
explanation: Criticises the design of the bill rather than any person, though 'no real thought' is a fairly sweeping dismissal of the work done.

text: Do you know where else Gisborne takes us, Mr Speaker? State Highway 35—State Highway 35 that was not mentioned in today’s Budget. We talked about resilience. We talked about connectivity.
explanation: Substantive regional-equity critique, policy-focused.

text: While we support the increase of the minimum payments you can earn outside your benefit, the reality is, if you’re looking at this bill and the overall impact it’s going to have on the quality of life of people throughout Aotearoa—who are still, with this increase of $3,000 a year, going to be struggling to afford the very basics.
explanation: Supports the measure while raising a substantive adequacy concern.

text: when that policy was announced in 2018, no officials and no industry knew anything about it
explanation: Criticises the process of a past Government's policy rather than attacking individuals.

text: I respect the fact that Governments of the day have the right to be able to create policy, but I do not respect policies that have been derived with no quality process to back it up.
explanation: Concedes the opponent's legitimacy before criticising the process — measured tone.

text: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
explanation: Critical of the previous government's budgeting practices, not of individuals.

text: I can’t help but admire the passion that Cushla Tangaere-Manuel has for her province.
explanation: Generous acknowledgement of a political opponent across the aisle.

text: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Respectful, credits the select committee process, no personal attacks.

text: let's enter an alternative universe in which the Labour Party actually has some policies. I realise that's a big ask, but let's enter a fantasy world in which Labour gets it together and actually gets some policies; let's enter the twilight zone and pretend.
explanation: Sustained mockery of the opposition party rather than any engagement with substance.

text: I suggest the member, at the end of the night, goes back and reads the Hansard, because if she was listening, she would find out that that's not what I'm doing.
explanation: Dismissive and condescending ('if she was listening') rather than engaging the concern.

text: there are three facile and fallacious statements and assertions in that member’s statement. Dealing with the last point, as has been extensively litigated, there are no tax breaks for tobacco companies advanced by the Budget... I note that members opposite were arguing on the weekend that bringing back the interest deductibility rules was not a tax increase, which is a little bit inconsistent with their argument today that that is a tax break for landlords.
explanation: 'Facile and fallacious' is dismissive, but the rebuttal then engages the substance.

text: there's been decades of under-investment largely because local body politicians have prioritised building convention centres and half-billion - dollar town hall upgrades on the ground of heritage and not focused on the basics.
explanation: Critical of local politicians' choices but focused on spending priorities rather than personal abuse.

text: You will not find harder-working public servants than the Ministry for the Environment. They have done that, as the spokesperson says, with declining baselines and reducing staff numbers... I'm very, very proud of the officials. I take this opportunity to say thank you to them for their exceptional work in difficult circumstances.
explanation: Respectful and generous toward officials, even acknowledging a point made by the opposition spokesperson.

text: there are more of us in this generation that deserve to live close to the places where we work our asses off than the people who sit there, have no job, own multiple properties, and do nothing to earn their wealth.
explanation: A sweeping class-based attack characterising property owners as idle and undeserving.

text: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
explanation: Imputes selfish, class-based motives to residents rather than engaging their stated concerns.

text: the ACT Party are hypocrites. They say, “All hail property rights.”, but I wonder whether they know that property rights don’t only apply to oneself; they apply to your neighbour, as well.
explanation: Labels opponents “hypocrites,” but the criticism is tied to a substantive point about their stated principles.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Dismissive overstatement, though aimed at the project not a person.

text: I just wanted to ask the Minister what he's seen from that programme, whether he thinks it's been successful, whether it's something that they might be looking into rolling out across the country, and what he is hearing from youth transitional housing providers across the country
explanation: Calm, constructive, substance-focused questioning with no attack.

text: One of the most often-made comments I get from international visitors who come and visit me is that they can’t believe how much free stuff there is in New Zealand, and this is one of them here.
explanation: Appeal to anecdote—personal impressions from visitors offered as support for the charging policy.

text: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
explanation: Identifies a real budgeting issue but offers no figures or examples, and 'left, right, and centre' is rhetorical.

text: This bill is actually a very small bill... that's the only entity—the Ministry for the Environment—that needs an Act for it to be disestablished. That's what the primary reason for this bill is all about.
explanation: Coherent procedural explanation; correctly narrow but downplays substantive concerns.

text: I respect the fact that Governments of the day have the right to be able to create policy, but I do not respect policies that have been derived with no quality process to back it up.
explanation: Argues from process quality rather than mere partisanship; a principled criterion, though the premise is asserted.

text: In fact, it’s mentioned that 50 percent of all international visitors will visit the conservation estate, and what’s wrong with charging them a reasonable amount to they can contribute to the conservation that we wish to deploy on to that land.
explanation: Uses a relevant statistic to support a user-pays argument; conclusion follows reasonably.

text: Oh, do you want us to waste money now, do you? Oh, actually, you do—I forgot about that. You're from those guys.
explanation: False dichotomy (disclose costs = waste money) plus an ad hominem by association.

text: Some applicants have said to me that fast track is driving competition in the consenting system... in some cases, this is leading to more reasonable behaviour by councils, acting in a more proportionate way. Isn't competition a wonderful thing?
explanation: Relies on anecdotal applicant feedback ('have said to me') rather than evidence; rhetorical flourish at the end.

text: tens of hundreds of millions of dollars have been wasted on business cases designed for phantom projects. It's clear that the system has been underperforming for all Ministers and Governments of all stripes.
explanation: Reasoned diagnosis (Ministers lack expertise to vet large investments) but the loss figure is asserted, not sourced.

text: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
explanation: Uses named project examples to support the time-saving claim.

text: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are not magic. PPPs are a procurement tool; they are not a funding tool.
explanation: Clear conceptual distinction that corrects a common misconception; reasoning is tight.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Sweeping appeal-to-popularity assertion without evidence.

text: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
explanation: Asserts motive without evidence.

text: you'll have an AI system on the other end of the phone who won't understand anything you say, over and over again. Our public services will get worse without the people and the workers who are the backbone of our Public Service.
explanation: Plausible inference but leans on a worst-case AI image rather than evidence.

text: it's not just nurses or doctors or health professionals working in our hospitals; it's also people who work on the front line in the Ministry of Social Development (MSD), and in the back rooms in MSD, who go in and spend time in our hospitals supporting whaiora or patients in those hospitals.
explanation: A reasoned argument that ring-fencing health from cuts ignores cross-agency interdependence; a genuine logical point.

text: zoning is actually about sending a signal to the market that this is the kind of growth that we are planning for.
explanation: Clear, reasoned explanation of zoning's function that follows logically.

text: We spend a greater share of our GDP on infrastructure than many compatible countries, but we achieve less.
explanation: Frames the problem as efficiency not just spend; reasonable, though the comparator is unspecified.

text: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
explanation: Grounds the position in stated constituent engagement and a coherent infrastructure-sequencing concern.

text: this is something that was quickly thrown together because someone in the Prime Minister’s office panicked and said, “Oh my God, we’ve got no legislation to bring on Budget day. There’s nothing there. ... Someone, quick, find some legislation.”
explanation: Invented quote and motive imputation with no evidence.

text: The only difference is that in Government, when we saw something shutting down, as a Cabinet, we discussed it; we took a paper to Cabinet, and we said, “What are the implications for New Zealand? We need to put a plan in place to respond to that.” Have we seen this Government do that? No, we have not.
explanation: Draws a clear distinction but the contrast claim is asserted, not evidenced.

text: it is the asymmetrical treatment of people and information and disclosure that resides in this bill that means that Labour cannot support it.
explanation: Concludes by tying the opposition to a named principle (asymmetrical treatment of information) drawn from the three changes she enumerated.

text: On one hand, we give Ministers complete discretion to decide about information sharing, including how that information can be used in policing, but we say that when it comes to trusts, we’re actually bringing down the shade.
explanation: Builds a structured asymmetry argument—broad ministerial information-sharing power vs reduced transparency for trusts—to support the conclusion that the bill is inconsistent.

text: I’d like to hear from the Minister, given we don’t have a chance to really get into this at a select committee, some of the thought processes that he and his officials went through on landing on that option out of six, and what it was that made that option the one that they went with.
explanation: Engages the regulatory impact statement's six options and scoring criteria to press a substantive question.

text: there’s nothing to show for it but just unprecedented Government debt and a huge $8.9 billion interest bill, and growing. No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing.
explanation: Absolute 'nothing' claim is rhetorical exaggeration unsupported by the nuance in the reports.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: Cites report figures but layers a partisan 'non-core/wastage' interpretation onto them.

text: these liquidations are a direct result of an overcooked economy where we saw inflation up to 7.3 percent, food inflation up to over 12 percent, where we saw interest rates up—12 consecutive official cash rate increases.
explanation: Attributes liquidations directly to past conditions via correlation; cites figures but asserts the causation.

text: In 2007, a management company signed a 40-year deal, a leasehold with Ngāti Whātua. Council chipped in some money, the build was $94 million, and they’ve got it for 40 years. In 2047, that’ll be handed back to the ratepayers of Auckland for zero.
explanation: Uses a concrete worked example to support the PPP/BOOT argument.

text: That was a provision within this bill that encourages residential solar uptake, ensuring residents up and down this country who export excess power back to the grid... won't face income tax, recognising that the compliance burden would outweigh any benefit and it will encourage solar and battery uptake.
explanation: Gives a coherent compliance-cost justification linking the measure to its intended effect.

text: to say that there is no plan for energy security other than hoping that it rains
explanation: Mocking, us-vs-them rallying line, not consensus-building.

text: Because politics is about a choice, and the choice that that member’s party is offering is more tax, more borrowing, more red tape, fewer fast-tracked projects, less focus on improving the conditions for businesses, and more taxes swallowing those businesses.
explanation: An us-vs-them choice framing that rallies her side and caricatures the opponent rather than persuading the undecided.

text: No. Attempts to divide Chris Bishop and I will always fail.
explanation: A loyal, deflecting one-liner; rhetorically tidy but appeals only to her own side.

text: I want to acknowledge that making those savings is challenging, and it has involved difficult trade-offs from every Minister in our Government.
explanation: Reasonable, measured tone but ultimately defends her own side's choices.

text: I can confirm that 87,444 unique families have received the FamilyBoost childcare tax credit so far, and I do want to thank the member and her party for supporting the most recent legislation, which expanded that scheme and which has seen that, in the December quarter, at least 11,068 families received at least $150 a fortnight—
explanation: Cross-party thanks to Labour for supporting the expansion is a genuine bridge-building note.

text: The Prime Minister is a dud, the finance Minister has no credibility, and they are lashing around for relevance.
explanation: Purely combative, alienating, no attempt to persuade the undecided.

text: he has shamelessly indicated that he will move an instruction to the committee to limit the public’s ability to do that. That is shameful. It is shameful because it is yet another example of this Government wanting to bypass proper parliamentary process.
explanation: Combative, us-vs-them framing of 'this Government'; rallies rather than builds bridges.

text: Some people are so blinded by their hatred of Israel, and perhaps the type of people that live there, and their hatred of America that they can't see the moral dimension of this conflict.
explanation: Sharply us-vs-them; alienates rather than persuades the unconvinced.

text: Does he also anticipate taking responsibility for far more development opportunity created for Māori than the Māori Party could ever dream of creating?
explanation: Us-versus-them framing that scores points against opponents rather than persuading.

text: Would the Minister anticipate severe scrutiny from the Opposition if a Government was to start interfering in Police independence, right down to the level of detail of when they fill up their petrol tanks?
explanation: A supportive set-up question framing the Opposition's line as over-reach; rhetorically effective but appeals to its own side.

text: On this side of the House, and particularly in the ACT Party, we stand for that simple idea that the creative powers of a free society are the only true resource that we have. If we unleash them under the rule of law, with respect for the equal dignity of each and every one of us who inhabits this free society, then you just don’t know what we can achieve, but maybe we will show that Kiwis really can fly.
explanation: Aspirational, rhetorically effective vision but framed around 'this side of the House', appealing mainly to his own side.

text: It’s not about Labour or National or ACT or the Greens; whoever’s in power is going to have to grapple with this for all New Zealand.
explanation: Explicitly non-partisan framing inviting all parties to share the problem — consensus-building.

text: I can’t help but admire the passion that Cushla Tangaere-Manuel has for her province.
explanation: Builds a bridge by recognising shared regional passion before making his own case.

text: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Positive and constructive about the cross-party committee, though ultimately a partisan endorsement.

text: New Zealanders deserve treatments not based on identity or politics or what box they have to tick.
explanation: Appeals to fairness, but framed as a swipe at 'identity' politics rather than bridge-building.

text: So, look, I’m very happy to unite with other people across the House in favour of this. It really is increasing people’s freedom in New Zealand, and that’s the reason I’ll be supporting it and also other ACT MPs will be supporting it.
explanation: Frames the vote as cross-House unity around a shared value of freedom.

text: We absolutely are going to support it in ACT, and I want to acknowledge Labour for supporting it as well.
explanation: Acknowledges an opposition party's support, a small cross-party gesture.

text: let's actually just engage in this debate in good faith, actually recognise that the Government is actually trying to do something to actually provide certainty to the disability sector and community.
explanation: Calls for good-faith debate, but the framing assumes the Government's good intent and appeals mainly to his own side.

text: I think we actually have a responsibility in this House to debate and discuss these issues with respect, with facts, and actually not with rhetoric and create scaremongering or other things that could cause distress.
explanation: Appeals to a shared standard of conduct across the House, though framed partly as a rebuke.

text: let's enter an alternative universe in which the Labour Party actually has some policies. I realise that's a big ask, but let's enter a fantasy world in which Labour gets it together and actually gets some policies; let's enter the twilight zone and pretend.
explanation: Purely divisive ridicule that alienates rather than persuades.

text: What is important is that the Government has a plan to build the productive capacity of this economy, and what is definitely true is that the Government's plan for growth and prosperity can be contrasted against the Opposition's plan, which so far consists of 16 pages released publicly—much of which just contain graphics and photos.
explanation: Us-vs-them contrast that rallies his side rather than building consensus.

text: The idea that Wellington is a Public Service town and only that is wrong and offensive.
explanation: Mounts a positive, somewhat inclusive defence of Wellington (Wētā, Xero, Sharesies) though framed combatively.

text: Well, I'm proud of the record of past National Governments in electrifying the rail network in Auckland, for example, so the member's general point that electrification at the moment is lowering costs is, of course, correct. We have to weigh up funding those sort of things…
explanation: Concedes the opponent's point as correct and frames a genuine trade-off rather than dismissing her — bridge-building tone.

text: Can I also say, in reflecting on the last few weeks, isn’t it fantastic that we had a peaceful transfer of power in New Zealand?... I do want to take this moment to acknowledge the former Government for the very good way they allowed the new Government to take office in a very sensible way.
explanation: Generously acknowledges opponents and the value of peaceful transition — bridge-building, across-the-aisle tone.

text: Nothing says centrepiece Budget legislation more than the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, Ryan Hamilton, taking a two-second call on the first piece of legislation that has come to the House.
explanation: Rallying mockery of the other side, not consensus-building.

text: We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year's Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
explanation: Effective for her own side but framed as an indictment, not bridge-building.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Reframes a partisan dispute by crediting a National finance minister, an attempt to find cross-party common ground.

text: we think opening up that window and getting that information out there for a longer time is good for our democracy and we can support that.
explanation: Credits a specific measure in the Government's bill (longer PREFU window) despite opposing the bill overall — a fair-minded, bridging note.

text: genuine collaborations, genuine multipartisanship, whoever is in Government, is actually about coming together to form enduring plans that can cross Governments, that can endure
explanation: Explicitly inclusive, cross-government framing aimed at durable consensus.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Position held consistently from 2023 campaign through a 2024 bill to the Government bill announced — words match a sustained record.

text: We’re very proud of the changes we’ve made with Pharmac and actually changing that organisation to make sure it’s delivering for New Zealanders who need important medicines.
explanation: Aligns ACT's stated medicines focus with named recent Pharmac announcements — some consistency shown.

text: So, look, I’m very happy to unite with other people across the House in favour of this. It really is increasing people’s freedom in New Zealand, and that’s the reason I’ll be supporting it and also other ACT MPs will be supporting it.
explanation: Voting to liberalise alcohol law on freedom grounds is consistent with ACT's stated deregulatory, liberty-focused positioning.

text: I can indicate, straight up, ACT will be supporting this through the first reading because we actually do believe in free speech.
explanation: Support for a free-speech-oriented parody/satire bill is consistent with ACT's long-standing free-speech advocacy.

text: we got rid of the Therapeutic Products Act, a really bad piece of legislation... We got rid of the Māori Health Authority... We actually got the second phase of the commission of inquiry into COVID up and going
explanation: Presents these as ticking off ACT's coalition-agreement priorities, matching stated commitments to action.

text: I wish to correct a statement that I made during the second reading of the Anzac commemoration bill.
explanation: Voluntarily correcting her own prior statement on the record shows words-and-actions consistency.

text: I lived through the 1990s National Party “mother of all Budgets” welfare reform, and I don’t think any of us have got an appetite to be doing major reform on the welfare system, just carte blanche cutting benefits.
explanation: A current National MP distancing herself from her own party’s historic welfare-cutting record; a candid, self-aware stance rather than defending the prior position.

text: As other members have said, they’re addicted to social media, well, I admit that I have suffered that addiction, as well.
explanation: Self-implicating admission that aligns her with the very behaviour she critiques rather than exempting herself.

text: I get sick and tired when I hear members of the Opposition stand up and say, "Oh, they've U-turned; oh, they've changed their mind." You know what? Isn't that amazing leadership. To listen to the people and adjust our response to make sure that we are delivering for Kiwis and what they want.
explanation: Reframes policy reversals as responsive listening — a defensible reinterpretation of shifting positions rather than denial of them.

text: We don't believe in extra Government; we believe in limited Government. It is one of our values.
explanation: States a party value consistent with the bill's deregulatory aim; no contradiction visible in the text, but unverified against the wider record.

text: I started the way I wished to continue, being positive, approachable, connected, and always taking the high road.
explanation: Self-description of a consistent approach; plausible and matches her conciliatory 'bridge' framing, but a self-claim with no external record yet to verify.

text: when I was managing a school bus company, I observed students in some remote communities, and some not so remote communities, who were kept out of school for various reasons, not travelling on the school bus when they should’ve been, who were then being, in some cases, used by their parents to work in spaces, whether they were illegal or not, for no employment.
explanation: Grounds her support in her own prior work experience, consistent with the position she is advocating.

text: I grew up in a time when we were not prepared for the impacts of social media, and my entire mental health as a young person has been affected by that.
explanation: Personal disclosure that grounds her stance; her advocacy is consistent with the stated experience, though unverifiable.

text: …New Zealand's situation has, I understand, been mentioned at the OECD, I think it was, just recently in Paris as the exemplar of how a country should manage this fuel situation and, at the same time, keep their economy going. … The Government's doing well. The Public Service is doing well. The public is doing very well.
explanation: Heavily hedged ('I understand', 'I think it was') claim of being an OECD 'exemplar'; vague sourcing and self-congratulatory, hard to verify.

text: I’m sorry, but that doesn’t concur with the figures I have been given by Stats NZ, which show there are now 7,000 more people of Pasifika ethnicity who are employed in Auckland, from December 2024 to December 2025.
explanation: Counters with an employment count that doesn't directly rebut the unemployment claim — different measures, mildly misleading juxtaposition.

text: We have not received any request to contribute to the US and Israel's military action. New Zealand is not central to the issues in the Middle East. Any decision would be one for joint Ministers or Cabinet.
explanation: Factual claim about no request having been received; plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: I’m advised by Stats NZ that the number of unemployed Pacific people in New Zealand rose by 13,000 people compared with December 2023, but the positive news is that from December 2024 to December 2025, in Auckland alone, Pasifika employment rose by 7,000 people.
explanation: Attributed to Stats NZ; the contrast pairs a since-2023 rise with a one-year Auckland gain, selectively favourable but stated as data.

text: We finally got the second frigate on the water a week ago. We haven't had two frigates on the water since 2019.
explanation: Specific, checkable claim about frigate availability; plausible and consistent with NZDF capacity issues.

text: Cameron Luxton, I think it’s probably true, has built more houses personally than the Government built in the six years that it had!
explanation: Hyperbole — KiwiBuild and state-build delivered thousands of homes; the claim is plainly false even hedged with 'probably'.

text: A former Prime Minister said that we were removing interest deductibility from residential property to tilt the market towards first-home buyers. You know what happened? Rents went through the roof and first-home buyers had less to save a deposit. We actually have helped first-home buyers, who are now buying homes at record levels—I think at 28 percent of new purchases
explanation: Mixes a checkable statistic (28% of purchases, hedged with 'I think') with contestable causal claims about rents and deposits.

text: We’re seeing $1.5 billion on naval capacity... We were spending only 0.9 percent of GDP on defence. That’s heading quickly towards 2 percent.
explanation: 0.9% of GDP is roughly accurate; 'heading quickly towards 2 percent' overstates the near-term trajectory.

text: Per person, after inflation, he increased expenditure by 30 percent.
explanation: Real per-capita core Crown spending rose substantially 2017–2023; the ~30% figure is broadly defensible but depends on the measure used.

text: a natural monopoly is a service that has constantly increasing returns to scale, so one provider is the most efficient way to provide. And, as it happens, roads and sewer networks and water pipes and public transport networks and a whole lot of things that cities rely on are natural monopolies. That's why you can't have a competitive market, and that is the public policy case for zoning
explanation: Accurate economics: the natural-monopoly characterisation of network infrastructure is sound.

text: when we came into Government, only 75 percent of Kiwis could access their GP. That's now gone up to 79.5 percent. Things are trending in the right direction.
explanation: Specific percentages presented without a defined measure or source; directional claim plausible but not verifiable here.

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Cited as latest quarterly data; precise and plausible though unverified here.

text: The latest quarterly data shows we’ve exceeded our target for training 500 mental health and addiction workers a year, with 514 in training over the past year, up from 457 in the previous year... we’ve grown the front-line workforce by over 11 percent since coming to office.
explanation: Quantified claims attributed to quarterly data; plausible and internally consistent.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Precise official figures attributed to advice; plausible and not contradicted, but unverifiable here.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Specific performance figures presented as fact; plausible but unverified from the text.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Specific figures presented as fact; the juxtaposition of a long-run doubling with a single recent week's sub-1% growth risks overstating a turnaround.

text: Does she agree that 246 tamariki and rangatahi in care spending over 4,000 nights in motels, with the longest stay being nearly a year, is inconsistent with motels being used as a last resort?
explanation: Cites concrete figures: 246 children, over 4,000 nights, longest stay nearly a year.

text: This Green Party bill is a narrow, carefully considered change to the Copyright Act 1994. It provides certainty for our creative sector, aligns us with international best practices, and strengthens the foundational principles of democracy and freedom of expression.
explanation: Names the statute (Copyright Act 1994) and the intended effects, though the claimed benefits stay fairly general.

text: It is also important that we uphold protection for Māori intellectual and cultural property. This bill offers an opportunity to reinforce protections and include the Wai 262 recommendations through the select committee process, ensuring that tikanga Māori remains central to how we approach copyright and artistic expression in Aotearoa.
explanation: Points to a concrete vehicle (Wai 262 recommendations via select committee) but without detailing what provisions would be added.

text: The reporting is talking about the number of applicants, and the number of applicants declined, but that doesn't really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied.
explanation: Pins the concern to particular reporting contents (applicant counts, declines) and the clause 22 transparency objective.

text: It was introduced on Monday night with no consultation with disabled people, and about 30 minutes before it was announced, there was a briefing for some disability groups. Now, just three days later, we are at the first reading
explanation: Concrete timeline details about the bill's process.

text: Report the news; don’t be the news. And, for the avoidance of doubt, the news should be the truth—the facts, not someone’s reckons. Everyone has an opinion; don’t mistake it for news.
explanation: A clear principle but a general exhortation rather than a concrete proposal.

text: we had a situation, that we inherited, of massive inflation, up to over 7 percent. Debt—just the interest rates alone that the Minister of Finance is having to find money for—of $11 billion a year extra every single year; basically, borrowed money paying for borrowed money.
explanation: Cites concrete inflation and debt-servicing figures.

text: With over 3,000 New Zealanders already registered in the region and potentially thousands more unregistered, the ability to move many people quickly to safety relies on having aircraft like the C130J and skilled personnel ready to deploy.
explanation: Gives a registration figure (over 3,000) and links it to a specific capability requirement.

text: I give you, then, international law on the law of the sea and the rights for this country and other countries to be able to have commercial shipping, and we call on Iran to comply with the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2817.
explanation: Names a specific legal basis (law of the sea) and a specific Security Council resolution.

text: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations.
explanation: Concrete action: pre-deploying consular staff and two named aircraft (C130J) to the region for evacuations.

text: It’s got to be a good deal, and it’s free to vote. It’s the sale of the century, actually!
explanation: Rhetorical sales-pitch flourish with no content.

text: Just in the last few hours, it has announced that those who face the greatest and most acute challenges with the cost of living are going to get an extra $50 a week to help absorb the pressure of this crisis, and we’re doing it in a way that is targeted, that is temporary, and that is timely.
explanation: Names the $50/week measure but reverts to the 'targeted, temporary, timely' slogan.

text: that’s about 20 percent of people who can’t, but, of course, when she was the Minister, it was 25 percent who can’t. So we acknowledge that there is a problem, but we’re actually fixing it and making it better and we’ve taken real initiative. We put another—if I recall—$160 million into GPs last year.
explanation: Cites percentages and a dollar figure for GP investment.

text: I’m pleased to see $40 million in uplift for early childhood centres. We’re deregulating, we’re cutting the red tape, but they face cost pressures and they’re getting a 1.5 percent uplift, which, critically, will begin on 1 July.
explanation: Names dollar figure, percentage uplift, and a start date (1 July).

text: If a council consents a building, then they will get a quarter of a percent of the value of that building. But if they do more than 1 percent of their existing housing stock, it goes up to half a percent. If they do more than 2 percent of their existing housing stock, if they consent that many houses in one year, then they will get 1.25 percent.
explanation: Precise tiered mechanism with exact percentages and thresholds.

text: For the first time, the Government’s target of 25 percent of the ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding has been invested in prevention and early intervention.
explanation: Names a 25% ring-fenced funding target for prevention, though without dollar amounts.

text: I recently announced that Whangārei, Hutt Valley, and Hawke’s Bay are the latest hospitals to get peer support workers in their emergency department. They will join the roll-out of peer support specialists already working in eight emergency departments around the country since coming into office.
explanation: Names specific new sites and a concrete count (eight existing EDs with peer support).

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Precise percentages against named wait-time targets.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Precise percentages tied to defined access windows.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Exact counts (70,754 consultations; 56,498 users) and a date.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Gives pool size (~25,000), historical growth (doubled, >14%) and current growth (below 1%).

text: In the recent letter of expectation sent to ACC, I set out three priorities: (1) putting clients first by providing care that supports lasting recovery; (2) helping New Zealanders return to work and independence... and (3) resetting ACC by getting the organisation back to basics, with a clear focus on delivery and outcomes.
explanation: Lists three named priorities, though they remain fairly high-level objectives without metrics.

text: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
explanation: Names a concrete action (letter to the Commission) and what it covers, though no thresholds.

text: I have seen nothing new from the National Party in this incoming Government.
explanation: Sweeping characterisation with no detail on its own, though he goes on to support it with examples afterwards.

text: The member for Banks Peninsula, Vanessa Weenink, GP, would have had people come into her practice with emphysema caused by smoking addiction. Will she vote for it or will she uphold her Hippocratic Oath that says “Do no harm.”?
explanation: Names a specific member and her profession and a concrete clinical scenario, though it ends in a rhetorical question.

text: if we were to half that, it would be a three-week period, which is actually a very short time. The bill may not be a large bill but it’s a complicated bill because of what it’s doing and because the benefits framework and the accommodation supplement framework is a network.
explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe (three-week submission period) and identifies the structural reason for concern.

text: what we are providing is not a handy reference, it is the definitive source of what the law is in New Zealand. If that’s the case, saying, “It wasn’t practicable for me to provide the law. The website’s down for a week and we can’t actually get it back up because it’s tricky.”—that’s actually not good enough.
explanation: Anchored to clause 17 / replacement section 72(2) and the exact words 'as far as practicable'.

text: Standing Order 46 is very clear that the House on a Thursday rises at 6 p.m. except when Standing Order 53 applies when you may interrupt the business up to five minutes before to avoid interrupting a speaker. To allow the speeches to continue now would be to not be consistent with Standing Orders.
explanation: Cites exact Standing Orders, the day, the time, and the precise procedural condition.

text: I'm really excited about the future ahead with the changes that we're going to be making under this bill... When quality data is collected more regularly, essentially what it means is that we can provide better outcomes with more knowledge.
explanation: General enthusiasm and a vague 'better outcomes with more knowledge'; no mechanisms, figures, or concrete detail.

text: I want to reassure members of the public that the National Party values families. Indeed, one of our 10 values is strong families and caring communities, and notwithstanding this bill perhaps going through today, our party values strong families and caring communities.
explanation: Cites a named party value ('strong families and caring communities') but offers no policy detail or measure.

text: there's a situation where in two groups of people, one group is being treated more generously than the other. Is that fair? When they want to talk about fairness... what about those that are not being treated as generously as the other group?
explanation: Frames the two-cohort comparison without figures or mechanism.

text: I’ve worked in our family business that deals with people that are either homeless or borderline homeless, an emergency and transitional housing facility, so I’ve seen over the years what causes homelessness: unaddressed mental health issues.
explanation: Identifies a specific claimed cause (mental health) and her own relevant experience, but no figures or mechanisms.

text: A few years ago, $2.75 million of public funds were given to an organisation linked to the gang named the Mongrel Mob.
explanation: Precise dollar figure and named gang.

text: Well, that is our goal in Government over the next three years, if we're fortunate to be returned by the people of New Zealand to achieve that goal, and the good news is the many goals we have achieved. This is going to be another one.
explanation: Asked how he will know the budgeted savings are actually achieved; offers reassurance about track record rather than any verification mechanism.

text: it would be wrong to make any predictions, but what we had dealt with is a historic rise in the number of public servants over the six years of the previous administration... One element would be a greater use of technology, and the specific roles is something that will emerge over time.
explanation: Asked which specific roles he expects AI to replace; explicitly declines to specify, saying it will 'emerge over time'.

text: I haven't seen that particular analysis, just as I didn't see any analysis about increasing the size of the Public Service by 18,000, which the previous administration undertook, but I'm pretty sure—I don't know; I could be wrong—that that costs a lot more.
explanation: Candidly admits there is no cost-benefit analysis for the 55,000 cap, but deflects rather than justifying the absence.

text: What we grumbled about was the fact that on the day that we had announced that there were 49,000 fewer victims of crime in this country, there was a story that ignored that entirely and talked about something else. We weren't happy about it—that's life.
explanation: Asked whether Mitchell raised the coverage with him; he confirms it and candidly explains the grievance.

text: I’m not aware of current plans to invest in the development of silicon chips, and my suggestion is that we focus on the things that we do well and sell them to the world, and then we purchase the things that other people in the world do better than us
explanation: Asked (by Seymour) whether the Public Service will make its own silicon chips; answers directly that there are no such plans and gives a clear rationale.

text: My experience of the Minister is that he always keeps his promises. He’s a very a decent human being, and frankly, I only wish that everyone would recognise that instead of asking such stupidly loaded questions.
explanation: Asked about beef mince up 23% and bread up 57%, she addresses neither figure.

text: there was the same issue prior to this Government, except that it was worse because, under the extensive and overdone lockdowns in Auckland, the home of most Pasifika people in New Zealand, many young people were denied their education... attendance rates were a mere 17 percent.
explanation: Asked about 21% of young Pasifika not in employment/education/training now, she deflects to past lockdowns.

text: I’m sorry, but that doesn’t concur with the figures I have been given by Stats NZ, which show there are now 7,000 more people of Pasifika ethnicity who are employed in Auckland, from December 2024 to December 2025.
explanation: Disputes the questioner's figure but answers with an employment-gain stat rather than the unemployment figure asked about.

text: We have not received any request to contribute to the US and Israel's military action. New Zealand is not central to the issues in the Middle East. Any decision would be one for joint Ministers or Cabinet.
explanation: Directly states no request has been received and clarifies the decision process, addressing the underlying concern.

text: No. The Public Service already has a clear and flexible policy that allows agencies to manage working from home arrangements as required. … While we acknowledge the increase in fuel prices, we do not currently face a fuel shortage. If that situation were to change, then we would consider whether further measures were required.
explanation: Answers the question with a clear 'No' and gives the reasoning.

text: I refute that question. It was never—promised. This was a service that was always about complementing GP practices.
explanation: Verrall asked whether the service would be at a tenth of promised volumes; he rejects the premise that anything was promised rather than engaging the volume comparison.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Leary asked about unaffordable counselling costs and six-month waits; he answers with access stats, prompting a point of order that he didn't address costs.

text: It was never meant to be a silver bullet. It was to complement our primary care services. We announced it six months ago, and we're looking to scale it up.
explanation: Asked how the usage compares to the original 1-million-a-year claim, he reframes the service's purpose rather than addressing the gap to that target.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Verrall asked how many had a consult since launch; he gives precise figures directly.

text: I recently announced at the inaugural World Rural Health Conference in New Zealand that the Government would invest $1 million to train rural GPs to deliver planned-care services locally. This will increase access to support for people living in rural areas and reduce the need for hospital visits.
explanation: Directly answers the (friendly) question about his recent rural-care announcement.

text: Well, I don't know what the member means by fossil fuel crisis. That member's on the record saying that in 2008 we'd run out of oil by 2015, and last time I looked, we've got plenty of it.
explanation: Asked how fuel costs affect highway costs, road demand and PPP repayment; he answers none of it and instead mocks the questioner's past statements.

text: the Government is focused on growing front-line roles in the Public Service to deliver better services for New Zealand taxpayers.
explanation: Asked whether the no-front-line-cuts promise applies to the 8,700 reduction; restates the front-line commitment without confirming whether it holds against the cut.

text: I’m not going to accept the programme’s perfect; we inherited a dog. I have taken action as Minister to fix the programme and we are now making good progress on it.
explanation: Candidly admits the programme is not perfect rather than spinning it as flawless.

text: Yes. In the round, the new ministry, I believe, will lead to improvements of our natural environment over time.
explanation: Answers Brooking's direct challenge with an unambiguous 'Yes', then qualifies it modestly.

text: The answer is: no, I didn't; it was an operational decision made by Kāinga Ora and the board.
explanation: Directly answers the question 'Did the Minister sign off on it?' with a clear no and an explanation of who decided.

text: In the recent letter of expectation sent to ACC, I set out three priorities: (1) putting clients first by providing care that supports lasting recovery; (2) helping New Zealanders return to work and independence... and (3) resetting ACC by getting the organisation back to basics, with a clear focus on delivery and outcomes.
explanation: Asked what direction he gave ACC; he enumerates the three priorities directly.

text: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
explanation: Directly answers what actions he has taken on fuel markets.

text: Does she agree that 246 tamariki and rangatahi in care spending over 4,000 nights in motels, with the longest stay being nearly a year, is inconsistent with motels being used as a last resort?
explanation: Uses the long-stay data to challenge the 'last resort' characterisation; a reasonable evidence-based contradiction, though it sets aside the median-stay context.

text: Overall, this bill will increase the availability of alcohol in our communities, including at off-licences, which cause the most alcohol-related harm. We should be reducing harm from alcohol, not promoting it to obtain economic growth, which is stated is also the point of this law.
explanation: Connects availability to harm using a public-health premise, though the 'off-licences cause the most harm' and net-availability claims are asserted rather than demonstrated here.

text: The reporting is talking about the number of applicants, and the number of applicants declined, but that doesn't really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied.
explanation: Identifies a specific gap between aggregate reporting and the transparency goal of explaining individual decisions; reasoned critique.

text: There is a pattern that has emerged from the current Government: when working New Zealanders win workers' rights cases through the courts, like pay equity, like Uber drivers, and like this case where parents who became full-time carers for their disabled children have been awarded by the court that they are employees of the Government... the Government's response... is to change the law. That is a political choice.
explanation: Builds a pattern argument from three concrete examples (pay equity, Uber drivers, carers) to support the conclusion; some generalisation but evidence-grounded.

text: This Minister has been consistent in targeting disabled people and the systemic erosion of disabled people's rights.
explanation: Strong causal/intent claim asserted without the supporting evidence given for the preceding pattern argument.

text: There will be taxing the feijoas that fall off your tree, because they're so desperate.
explanation: Hyperbolic invention with no evidentiary basis.

text: Our main streets and public places have been blighted by disruption and disturbance, leading to our communities becoming places of intimidation and dysfunction. Now, that has been obvious to anybody that's visited our main streets in recent times.
explanation: Leans on an appeal to common sense ('obvious to anybody') rather than evidence for the scale of the problem.

text: It's a fair criticism to be made of Grant Robertson, the former finance Minister, who was stoking the fires of inflation
explanation: Asserts a causal link (spending stoking inflation) that is arguable but stated without specific evidence here.

text: New Zealand has 39 departments and ministries administering budget lines. That compares with 16 in Australia, 24 in the UK, and 12 in Finland. More departments equal more management and administration functions that are duplicated across the Public Service
explanation: Uses cross-country benchmarking to support the duplication argument; reasonable, though it assumes comparability of structures.

text: Less than a quarter of 1 percent of adult New Zealanders are a member of a gang, but they're associated with 20 to 25 percent of the violent crime.
explanation: Uses a statistic to justify targeting gangs; the conclusion follows from the premise.

text: he has shamelessly indicated that he will move an instruction to the committee to limit the public’s ability to do that. That is shameful. It is shameful because it is yet another example of this Government wanting to bypass proper parliamentary process.
explanation: Leans on repetition and an appeal to emotion ('shameful') more than evidence.

text: I found it extraordinary that Tama Potaka is trying to convince us that there's only 24 homeless people in Auckland. ... he doesn't care because that number suits his narrative.
explanation: Cites front-line provider feedback against the figure, but partly characterises rather than evidences.

text: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
explanation: Clearly articulates the inconsistency between a conceded point and the Minister's repeated claim.

text: Jill Hawkey from the Christchurch Methodist Mission specifically said that Chris Bishop's claim that those in need can access emergency housing “simply isn't true.”
explanation: Cites a specific expert source to support the argument rather than mere assertion.

text: They cannot have it both ways. They can't, on one hand, say there's only 24 people that are rough sleeping in Auckland, but also there are so many that we need to bring on the move-on orders—because it's such an issue.
explanation: Identifies a genuine internal tension between two government positions; logically pointed.

text: It’s a neoliberal straight-jacket and it’s been roundly criticised by anyone who knows anything about it.
explanation: 'Anyone who knows anything about it' is an unsupported overgeneralisation and appeal to consensus, with no evidence cited here.

text: there is a reason why six months is the default period and why many times there's a request for extensions of time on that six months. That's because it's an important deliberative part of our democracy that this Government is time and again ignoring, which means we're having lower quality legislation, less trust in our Government, and less trust in this democracy, and that is a real worry.
explanation: Argues from the existence of the six-month default to a conclusion about quality and trust; reasonable but the causal chain to 'less trust in democracy' is asserted rather than evidenced.

text: We know, as Robert Kennedy said, GDP goes up when there's a war. GDP goes up when there's an earthquake. GDP goes up when there's a car accident and the car has to be repaired. Those are not good outcomes.
explanation: A sound, well-known argument that GDP captures destructive activity, illustrated with valid examples; conclusion follows, though it leans on an authority/quotation.

text: I’d be curious if the Minister could explain to this committee why we didn’t simply put the relevant definitions and provisions in the Legislation Act for all of the legislation, rather than having general provisions in a specific Act, and having essentially a big red legislative hand going, “And if you want to know about this, you’ve got to go all the way over there”, which is strikes me as kind of poor drafting and just, frankly, hard to read.
explanation: Coherent argument that cross-cutting definitions belong in the Legislation Act rather than a specific Act; conclusion follows from the premise.

text: In Standing Order 295(1)(b), it says that “if it is proposed to move any special powers or instruction in respect of the committee’s consideration of the bill, [it must] indicate the terms of that proposed motion.” ... So she can only move a motion that refers to the special powers that she has referred to, and the only special power she referred to was the truncated report-back time.
explanation: Tightly reasoned procedural argument citing specific Standing Orders (295, 298) and applying them to the facts; premises lead clearly to the conclusion.

text: The reason why we don't have enough gas today is the previous Government banned oil and gas, and that's why our energy prices are high. Thank you, Labour.
explanation: Sarcastic 'Thank you, Labour' is a partisan jab, though aimed at a policy decision rather than a person.

text: The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.
explanation: Criticism of a prior policy decision, not a personal attack.

text: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
explanation: Misrepresents Russell's position ('keen to do all that', '66 percent... on the agenda') when she raised 66% only as historical context; a strawman attributing intentions she did not state.

text: But look, at the end of the day, delivery is happening on this side.
explanation: Partisan 'this side' framing, said while dismissing an interjector, rather than engaging substance.

text: As I’ve outlined, the key deliverable—which, on this side of House, is what we’re focused on: deliverables and outcomes, not slogans. The last side of the House had six years to deliver for Auckland, which it didn’t
explanation: Dismissive of the opposition's record but aimed at performance, not persons.

text: Nicola Willis tells people it’s bad luck, basically, if they lose their job—“Oh, well.”
explanation: Caricatures the Finance Minister's position with a mocking paraphrase ('Oh, well') rather than engaging her actual stance.

text: Is it because it got caught up in such coalition friction that ACT stopped anything meaningful happening with it?
explanation: Pointed jab at a coalition partner, but couched as a question about process.

text: Already, we have seen, at the current climate talks, that New Zealand received the "Fossil of the Day" award... This was the very first country to be singled out, and it is because of this Government's winding back the clock to bring back oil and gas exploration.
explanation: Pointed criticism of government policy and its international standing, but substantive rather than a personal attack.

text: On one hand, we give Ministers complete discretion to decide about information sharing, including how that information can be used in policing, but we say that when it comes to trusts, we’re actually bringing down the shade.
explanation: Engages the substance of the legislation's design; criticism of policy choices, not of persons.

text: I’d like to hear from the Minister, given we don’t have a chance to really get into this at a select committee, some of the thought processes that he and his officials went through on landing on that option out of six, and what it was that made that option the one that they went with.
explanation: Substantive, respectful scrutiny focused on the policy detail.

text: Ginny Andersen used to be so much nicer when she'd turn up in my office trying to be nice to me. I don't know what's happened to her since then, but anyway, if she doesn't want an answer, she won't get one.
explanation: A personal, belittling remark about a named colleague that engages no substance.

text: My experience of the Minister is that he always keeps his promises. He’s a very a decent human being, and frankly, I only wish that everyone would recognise that instead of asking such stupidly loaded questions.
explanation: Dismisses the question as 'stupidly loaded' — disparaging the questioner rather than the substance.

text: Because we're a really sensible Government and not stupid.
explanation: Flippant and self-congratulatory but not a personal attack on the questioner.

text: Report the news; don’t be the news. And, for the avoidance of doubt, the news should be the truth—the facts, not someone’s reckons. Everyone has an opinion; don’t mistake it for news.
explanation: Pointed advice to media framed generally and good-naturedly ('love you as I do'), not a personal attack.

text: I think it is important to have some semblance of respect in this House towards each other. Every member is supposed to be an honourable member.
explanation: An explicit call for mutual respect and decorum in debate.

text: The fact that Nicola Willis and her peers can't open a Budget and say, "This funding ends in 2023 or 2024 or 2025." is a reflection not on the budgeting of the Labour Government but on the innumeracy of the National Party.
explanation: Direct personal attack ('innumeracy') on Nicola Willis and the National Party rather than the policy.

text: The member for Banks Peninsula, Vanessa Weenink, GP, would have had people come into her practice with emphysema caused by smoking addiction. Will she vote for it or will she uphold her Hippocratic Oath that says “Do no harm.”?
explanation: Singles out a named member and pressures her personally, implying she would betray her medical ethics.

text: here’s one of the things that this Speech from the Throne says: “for the past several years the number of people employed in the public service has grown at a rate that has not been matched by a commensurate increase in the level of services provided to the public.” Does that sound like Christopher Luxon to you? No, that’s the 2008 Speech from the Throne.
explanation: Pointed and mocking in tone but engages the substance of the policy content rather than attacking a person.

text: We know, as Robert Kennedy said, GDP goes up when there's a war. GDP goes up when there's an earthquake. GDP goes up when there's a car accident and the car has to be repaired. Those are not good outcomes.
explanation: Substantive, idea-focused point with no personal attack.

text: I know that in his inimitable way, Mr Xu-Nan is going very methodically through the legislation
explanation: Gracious and respectful.

text: I've often made the observation that a politician complaining about the media is like a farmer complaining about the weather: you may be right, but it makes no difference, and so you've got to figure out how to succeed in any respect.
explanation: Disarming, self-deprecating turn of phrase that deflects tension, though it does not build cross-party consensus.

text: Yes, including my statement at the Media Awards on Friday where I referred to the member as “my very good friend Carmel Sepuloni”, and I hope she won’t contradict me on that point.
explanation: Friendly, disarming, builds rapport across party lines.

text: we also want to make much better progress in rehabilitating prisoners. So an important part of our overall justice priority is to deal with those... making sure that all prisoners are eligible for those rehabilitation programmes
explanation: Balances a tough-on-crime message with a constructive rehabilitation aim, broadening appeal.

text: Recognising that we as a country are trying to do something that is quite unique around the world and it is a challenging prospect of how a country recognises the Treaty of Waitangi and honours that Treaty, while also stands for those core human rights of equal citizenship and equality before the law. And that I don't for a moment think is an easy discussion
explanation: Measured, good-faith framing that invites a careful national conversation rather than polarising.

text: This is a broad church, this Parliament, but we all desire to improve the lot of our fellow New Zealanders.
explanation: Explicitly unifying, attributing good intent across the House.

text: In fact, a lot of what the Key Government did was more progressive than what that Government’s proposing, so you should be utterly and totally ashamed of yourself.
explanation: Alienating, shaming framing that shuts down dialogue.

text: Let’s get people into work in nursing and doctors by helping them pay off their student loans. It might not be a bad idea, because in 2008 John Key said, “We’re going to introduce voluntary bonding schemes based on student loan write-offs.”
explanation: Concedes a point to the opposing side ('It might not be a bad idea'), a small bridge-building acknowledgement amid the attack.

text: We need to hear from people who are directly affected, the people who might be asked to move on. We need their views, and they’re not views that are got quickly or easily; in fact, they might not even be in writing.
explanation: Argues inclusively for hearing from marginalised affected people; widens rather than narrows the conversation.

text: congratulations to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for the new website, which I hope we’ve all gone and had a good look at. Good work there. It actually does seem to work quite well. It’s a great example of technical modernisation by this Parliament, in fact.
explanation: Positive, non-partisan tone crediting a shared parliamentary achievement.

text: We're not going to agree on everything all the time, but I do think, on something as important as statistics and how we approach the census question, it's really good that we try to get as much agreement as we can.
explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-party common ground and acknowledges shared importance of the issue — consensus-building.

text: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations.
explanation: Describes a concrete decision being acted on, though it is a pre-deployment readiness measure rather than a completed evacuation.

text: We finally got the second frigate on the water a week ago. We haven't had two frigates on the water since 2019.
explanation: Claims a delivered capability (second frigate operational) as her government's doing, though follow-through detail is thin.

text: they understand there's been neglect for years of their fire trucks, and this Government, under Brooke van Velden, is finally fixing it.
explanation: Claims credit for 'fixing' neglected equipment but describes work in progress rather than a verified delivered outcome.

text: Speaking as the leader of the ACT Party, I’m immensely proud of the savings and the improvements that we’ve managed to drive: Karen Chhour, in youth crime; the attendance that I’ve been responsible for; the improvements in medicine funding
explanation: Claims credit for specific delivered areas (attendance, medicine funding, youth crime), though delivery extent is asserted not demonstrated.

text: the number of Māori new entrants who are at or above expectations was 25 percent... In the couple of years we've been in, we've got it up to 43 percent. We've nearly doubled the number of young Māori new entrants who are meeting expectations for critical skills.
explanation: Claims a measurable delivered improvement and credit for it, though attribution to the policy is unverified.

text: Tomorrow, legislation will come into force that will allow most overseas investments to be consented in just 15 days by introducing a new two-track system that puts the emphasis on risky investment
explanation: Legislation imminently in force represents follow-through, though the operational outcome is yet to be delivered.

text: I announced this policy as ACT’s housing policy in 2016, much closer to when I was visiting Whangārei Hospital... Back then, we called it GST sharing. The spirit of that is here.
explanation: A long-stated policy now turned into an actual Budget measure with him as a driver.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Claims a delivered improvement (growth reduced) attributable to his direction, but it is an early/partial trend rather than a settled result.

text: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
explanation: A concrete step taken, but it is setting expectations rather than a delivered outcome.

text: I refute that question. It was never—promised. This was a service that was always about complementing GP practices.
explanation: Denies a target was ever promised, which sits in tension with the original publicly stated 1-million-a-year ambition Verrall is quoting.

text: I'd just like to say I admire the thought and consideration of all parties on this bill. It's a shame that we were not able to reach consensus.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of all parties' contributions.

text: I’ll start off by saying that the Commerce Commission do a very good job.
explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of an institution before critiquing the reform.

text: like the previous Labour Government’s long, largescale asset purchasing programme, COVID spending, half of which was helicopter money creating inflation, debt, and asset hikes, with real house prices having left the room.
explanation: Critiques the previous government's programme rather than attacking individuals.

text: those that believe in climate change have told us that the science is settled, but anyone that understands science will know that science is never settled and there are disagreements about what is the truth in this whole climate cult.
explanation: 'Climate cult' derides those who disagree rather than engaging their arguments.

text: Look, we know there were many submitters who were fearful and worried about the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, and fair enough—it is what we know. This is a bold change, and so we hear them.
explanation: Respectful recognition of opposing concerns.

text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in total opposition to this bill, a bill that will just cause more harm coming from a Government that clearly does not care about the most vulnerable in our society. This bill is absolutely a disgrace.
