explanation: Attributes bad faith ('clearly does not care') and uses charged language ('disgrace').

text: It's going bankrupt the country for the price of a Mount Vic extra tunnel. It's crazy, what's happening with this Government, fixated on their roads.
explanation: 'Crazy' and 'fixated on their roads' are dismissive of the Government's approach.

text: I haven't heard the same angst from over on the other side of the House about the fact that the Minister gets to appoint three voting members... Clearly, their issue with co-governance just belongs with mana whenua, and so it's a shame, really.
explanation: Legitimate point about inconsistency but framed as an accusation of bad faith against ACT.

text: I was very pleased when I heard the Associate Minister of Transport saying earlier that … they'd picked that up and that issue's going to be addressed. … I acknowledge that, because I think it's really important that when people come to talk to select committees and they actually come with a genuine concern that needs fixing, we don't just let it fall off the radar.
explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of an opponent's action on submitters' concerns.

text: I'd like to acknowledge Mike Butterick and the work he's done to progress this, and I also acknowledge the promotion that he's recently had.
explanation: Generous, respectful recognition of an opponent's work.

text: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
explanation: Dismissive ad hominem about a party's temperament rather than its argument.

text: Virtue signalling over wellbeing doesn’t help pay the bills.
explanation: Dismisses the wellbeing framework as 'virtue signalling' — a belittling characterisation, though aimed at the policy approach.

text: There is no public transport in Levin.
explanation: A factual heckle aimed at the question rather than a person; minor.

text: We saw back in 2024 in the first round where there was bad lending and the old rules where you had to go, "Oh, I bought McDonalds this week and I got Netflix. Can I have a loan now?", and it was just ridiculous.
explanation: Mocking in tone but directed at a past policy rather than a person; legitimate if overstated criticism of the old rules.

text: next time someone from the Government gets up and tells us that they care about workers, I urge the public to think, "How much do they care about workers in this country? How much do they care about people?—full stop."
explanation: Questions opponents' sincerity about caring for people rather than their policy.

text: Twenty-five percent unemployment, and it’s all the parents’ fault!
explanation: Sarcastic framing ('all the parents’ fault') mocks the government's stance; aimed at the policy logic but hyperbolic.

text: There is absolutely no way that I can do the job I want to do for my constituents and go through this in the thorough way that they deserve, when it is their neighbourhood that's being affected ... I do not accept that there is any reason why this has to happen so urgently.
explanation: Earnest objection to the urgency process focused on constituents' right to participate, not personal attack.

text: I thank the technical people behind this piece of legislation, because there will have been some really hard discussions and some very disciplined, bright people making this happen, and I'm grateful that they have.
explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of officials' work; constructive and non-partisan.

text: I love the idea of local boards having more control over roads. I think it's a really sound one.
explanation: Warm, constructive framing of an opponent's policy.

text: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
explanation: Ad hominem plus a strawman of the Greens' actual argument.

text: This bill can seem dry to the average listener—like the Green Party members that voted against it—but, in fact, it's actually transformative in the milieu of legislation. I am very happy to commend it to the House.
explanation: Slips in a cheap shot equating Green Party members with 'dry' rather than engaging their reasons for voting against.

text: Some members of the House that had six years to do something about it didn't do something about it.
explanation: A jab at the previous Labour Government's record, but a fair line of attack on performance.

text: I’m talking about the parents in South Auckland that don’t have a lot of self-control because of their unfortunate addiction to alcohol.
explanation: Raises a genuine social concern about vulnerable families without personal attack, though generalising about a community.

text: I do oppose this bill and I continue to oppose this bill, notwithstanding the fact that I respect the views—particularly from my colleagues in the National Party and Government and also across the House—on this.
explanation: Explicitly respects opposing colleagues while stating her own disagreement — disagreement framed without disparagement.

text: they are secretly looking through every other piece of legislation in this country with a Treaty clause to see how they can weaken that provision.
explanation: Accusation of covert intent, though aimed at process rather than personal insult.

text: This is a terrible bill. It goes much too far in addressing what everyone would acknowledge is sometimes a problem, which is, obviously, something that is very difficult within our cities, which is when we see antisocial behaviour.
explanation: Strong condemnation of the bill but acknowledges the underlying problem (antisocial behaviour) is real — criticism of policy, not personal attack.

text: The issue here is that it was not recorded, and the transparent processes that we have associated with the Official Information Act (OIA) have clearly, in this instance, been breached. It has left the Government open to questions about their transparency and their accountability.
explanation: Focuses on process and accountability; explicitly concedes that conversations with Ministers are a normal part of democracy.

text: Now, it has taken until May—this very month—for the court to order that these briefing documents be made available. Now, that is an extraordinary thing to happen in a transparent democracy, for us to have to wait for a court to order that something be released that should have properly been released under the Official Information Act.
explanation: Critical of process and transparency without descending into personal attack.

text: the specific question I have in relation to clause 48 and 49, which is a consequential amendment to the Child Poverty Reduction Act, is will this particular clause and the change of section 52 to new section 11A maintain the same independence that is currently in section 52?
explanation: Measured, substance-focused questioning of the Minister.

text: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we've just heard and the scaremongering that's going on.
explanation: Labels the opposition's case 'scaremongering' rather than rebutting its substance.

text: I actually thought it was already the law—if you see some of the Green Party’s social media—however, it turns out that’s not parody or satire; they’re actually being serious.
explanation: A joke at the Green Party's expense implying their genuine posts read as parody; humorous but a dig at opponents rather than substance.

text: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
explanation: Calm, policy-focused contribution engaging the substance raised by other speakers.

text: When I was younger, we had a global ice age coming at us. Oh, a few years later, actually, we were wrong.
explanation: Invokes the 1970s 'coming ice age' myth as an anecdotal analogy to discredit current climate science — appeal to anecdote/false analogy.

text: the famous Thomas Sowell quote that in the 1920s in the US they taxed the rich people at 76 percent and wondered why they weren’t getting much income. When they reduced it to 24 percent, the income skyrocketed.
explanation: Appeal to authority (Sowell) and a contested historical anecdote presented as a general law of taxation; ignores confounders.

text: like the previous Labour Government’s long, largescale asset purchasing programme, COVID spending, half of which was helicopter money creating inflation, debt, and asset hikes, with real house prices having left the room.
explanation: Asserts a causal chain to inflation and asset hikes without supporting evidence.

text: the top 70 percent of income revenue in New Zealand comes from the 20 percent of those in the higher income brackets.
explanation: Uses a statistic to rebut the 'tax the rich' framing, though the figure alone doesn't establish his broader conclusion.

text: The member from the member ACT Party was talking about how markets will take care of this; sometimes markets are not enough. Sometimes there is market failure, which is why we absolutely need a strong Commerce Commission and we absolutely need good governance in that respect as well.
explanation: Sound economic point (market failure justifies regulation) directly rebutting a coalition partner's claim.

text: We hear that they will vote against this, preaching personal liberty. But Te Pāti Māori, in this House, we ask, “Whose liberty—the liberty of a business to ignore blood in its supply chain, or the liberty of human beings to live without chains?”
explanation: Frames the choice as a false dichotomy between corporate paperwork freedom and human freedom, ignoring ACT's stated efficacy argument.

text: By failing to cross-reference the Waitakere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008 in the new Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, this Government renders these protections toothless. They invite a death by a thousand cuts upon our most sacred taonga.
explanation: Identifies a concrete legislative gap, but the conclusion is delivered through emotive metaphor rather than demonstrated effect.

text: Māori are underrepresented among homeowners precisely because of land loss, precisely because of discriminatory policy and economic exclusion.
explanation: Provides causal grounding (land loss, discriminatory policy) for the homeownership disparity; a reasoned point, though asserted rather than cited.

text: It assumes that if you threaten people with $2,000 fines and the rest—ha!—they'll simply disappear. But people don't disappear because Parliament tells them to; they move because they have somewhere safe to go.
explanation: Coherent argument that punitive measures don't resolve the underlying lack of housing; reasoning follows from the premise.

text: Introducing a parental assistance test for 16- to 19-year-olds seeking jobseeker support assumes that all rangatahi have parents who can support them, that every home is safe, and that every whānau has spare money. Well, that’s not the reality
explanation: Identifies the unstated assumptions in the policy design and rebuts them with concrete conditions (unsafe homes, no spare money); structured critique.

text: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
explanation: Rhetorical dismissal with no engagement of the substantive claims.

text: I have visited the schools that were told they were going to get new classrooms, except there was never any money put aside for it.
explanation: Uses personal observation as evidence for the unfunded-commitments argument — an appeal to anecdote, but tied to a concrete claim.

text: you go to the supermarket, everything’s on your phone; you go to a sports game, everything’s on your phone; checking in for a flight, everything’s on your phone—whatever we’re doing—so why couldn’t we have our driver’s licence on our phone? It’s a great step forward. A progressive step from a progressive Government. I commend the bill.
explanation: Argument by analogy/everyday convenience (everything else is on the phone) rather than evidence; a reasonable but light case for digital licences.

text: Auckland's just sold a number of shares in Auckland Airport and transferred them into their future fund—a future fund that actually has detail available to the public. You don't have to wait until after the election to see how it's going to work... They had a plan, and they were transparent about it.
explanation: Uses the Auckland example as evidence for a transparency standard, with a partisan jab attached.

text: It's actually a publicly listed company that, if you're watching at home today, you could go and buy shares in... At what point do we say it's OK for publicly listed companies to then be subject to official information? ... Does that extend to power companies? I think of Genesis, Meridian, Mercury—they are, appropriately, not subject to the Official Information Act for those reasons.
explanation: Builds a structured consistency argument from the Port's listed status to comparable entities, well reasoned.

text: How absolutely 1984 can we get? ... a statement that was made by George Orwell ... which was that "Some animals are more equal than others."
explanation: Literary analogy used in place of argument (and misattributed — the line is from Animal Farm).

text: There is absolutely no way that I can do the job I want to do for my constituents and go through this in the thorough way that they deserve, when it is their neighbourhood that's being affected ... I do not accept that there is any reason why this has to happen so urgently.
explanation: Argues that urgency denies proper scrutiny of changes affecting specific communities.

text: this legislation is something we live and breathe, but it is extremely disempowering when you don't know what the law is. It's incredibly important that we see the wood for the trees in this House, but we also allow people access to the branches of that tree, to the little things, because that's power in the hands of the people.
explanation: Makes a reasoned access-to-justice argument, but leans on metaphor ('wood for the trees', 'power in the hands of the people') rather than evidence.

text: what happens when you have people with a conflict of interest in terms of determining what happens to a local street? For example, the local board member themselves might live in that street.
explanation: Identifies a genuine structural risk (proximity-based conflicts inherent in localised decision-making) with a concrete illustration.

text: Do you know what that RIS says? ... "The proposals in this RIS have been developed at pace. This time frame necessarily limits the identification of options, level of analysis and the collation and review of evidence. There has been very little engagement with stakeholders on these proposals by officials."
explanation: Backs her process critique by quoting the official regulatory impact statement directly.

text: So here they were paying off their late-model vehicle, had the means to do that, lo and behold, just when they thought it was going to be the last instalment, they were hit with a massive final payment, effectively paying for the vehicle, probably, thrice at that point.
explanation: Uses a single second-hand anecdote ('a professional couple that I know') to argue that lending risk affects everyone, not just the poor — an appeal to anecdote rather than evidence, though it does illustrate the balloon-payment mechanism.

text: The member opposite just talked about fairness, and we all know fairness is too subjective of a term. This is not about fairness; this is about justice.
explanation: Reframes the debate from fairness to justice, a conceptual move rather than an evidenced one.

text: at a time when we’ve had cuts to Kāinga Ora; at a time when we have had cuts to Māori-specific education initiatives; at a time when we’ve had cuts to Te Puni Kōkiri; and cuts to services that directly impact Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and communities around Aotearoa, this Government is choosing for their first matter of business, post an underwhelming Budget, to discuss a taxation bill that will have very little real impact on the lives of the majority of Aotearoa.
explanation: Builds a case from a list of named cuts, though 'very little real impact' is asserted.

text: no blanket legislation would ever have known the peculiarities to the Waiapu River and to the Motu Awa in Rangitukia.
explanation: Argument grounded in a concrete local example (named net/haka tradition) to show one-size-fits-all law misses local detail, though stated as a sweeping generalisation.

text: iwi may benefit from the Investment Boost as they have the capacity, they’ve got the asset base, they’ve got the capital; however, a lot of Māori businesses are actually small, independent, family owned, so they won’t have the opportunity to take advantage of Investment Boost.
explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion reasoning: capital-intensive entities benefit from Investment Boost while small family businesses cannot, so the benefit is unevenly distributed.

text: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
explanation: Misrepresents the opponent's position (which was that legal ≠ right) and substitutes a smear.

text: I would like to ask the House to imagine for a moment that—in a different country, in a different world—someone sold a teenager a lolly filled with poison. The teenager in this distant world reacts violently to the poison. The Government of this imaginary country pays the person—who sold the poisonous lolly to the youth—money to give the youth the antidote.
explanation: An emotive analogy that frames the issue rather than evidencing it; appeal to emotion and a loaded analogy that assumes the conclusion (sellers = providers).

text: there's a situation where in two groups of people, one group is being treated more generously than the other. Is that fair? When they want to talk about fairness... what about those that are not being treated as generously as the other group?
explanation: Restates the equal-treatment argument but doesn't address the contested premise that the cohorts are comparable.

text: It’s not intended to solve homelessness, but I’ll tell you what will solve homelessness: addressing mental health issues in our country; addressing a lack of proper education, which we are doing; going after gangs for the brokenness that they cause amongst families; and, yes, growing our country so that we can give people a hand up, not a hand down.
explanation: Asserts multiple causes and remedies without evidence linking them; ends on a slogan ('hand up, not a hand down').

text: Detective Sergeant Mark Moorhouse publicly rejected claims—and he’s based in Hawke’s Bay, where this programme was being run—that local police broadly supported the programme. He said, “the bulk of us do not support it.” He also said that he had seen no evidence that the gang wanted to move away from profits generated through methamphetamine dealing.
explanation: Supports her case with a named front-line source rather than pure assertion, though it is a single appeal-to-authority data point.

text: And what is the Government's answer to this problem? Their answer is to sack almost 9,000 public servants. Now, this makes no sense.
explanation: Asserts the policy 'makes no sense' as a conclusion before the supporting argument.

text: Where is the funding for this AI transformation that will allow us to lose almost 9,000 public servants? We haven't seen any of that information. We haven't seen any detail on how this is actually going to work.
explanation: Presses a concrete gap—missing funding and implementation detail behind the AI/savings claim.

text: The issue here is that it was not recorded, and the transparent processes that we have associated with the Official Information Act (OIA) have clearly, in this instance, been breached. It has left the Government open to questions about their transparency and their accountability.
explanation: Identifies the precise problem (lack of record-keeping breaching OIA processes) rather than relying on innuendo.

text: We have the Government’s own Attorney-General stating that this bill is inconsistent with two important rights under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act: the freedom of expression and the freedom of movement.
explanation: Cites an authoritative legal source against the Government's own bill; legitimate appeal to authority backed by an official report.

text: We had the Ministry of Justice saying there is no evidence that move-on orders would reduce crime. We had the Treasury saying the costs of implementing move-on orders would outweigh the benefits. We had the Ministry of Urban Development stating the bill has the potential to cause further harm to people experiencing homelessness.
explanation: Marshals multiple independent official sources (Justice, Treasury, Urban Development) to support the conclusion.

text: as human beings we don't tend to continue to do things that don't function. We don't go out of our way to ensure that those mechanisms or those practices endure if they don't serve that function.
explanation: Uses a general appeal to human nature to argue existing Māori engagement mechanisms work, rather than citing evidence of their performance.

text: It explicitly adds an objective to work with private providers. It allows the Minister to hand-pick board members. It allows the director-general to actually sit in on board meetings... It scraps the audit requirements for the health plan, and it downgrades Māori leadership to advisory roles only.
explanation: Builds the centralisation/privatisation case from named provisions.

text: These were changes that were made by a previous National-Act Government in establishing Auckland Transport, but bringing these functions back now under elected members feels like the right thing to do. It strengthens, we believe, both voice and responsibility.
explanation: Ties support to a clear rationale (democratic accountability, clearer responsibility).

text: They're under pressure because there's not enough staff: there's not enough doctors, there's not enough nurses, there's not enough allied professionals—there's not enough staff in general, and there's certainly not enough primary care upstream.
explanation: Identifies workforce shortage as the causal driver of ED pressure rather than the absence of legal targets.

text: Submitters did also raise some concerns, though, that there was the potential that some of that decision making could become fragmented across, I think there’s 21, local boards. There will be some work needed in that sphere
explanation: Acknowledges a genuine trade-off and risk in the bill rather than overselling it.

text: the number of these catastrophic burning events have dropped in the last hundred years, as have all of the areas burnt.
explanation: Presented as settled fact from 'a little graph'; global burned-area trends are contested and recent extreme fire seasons contradict the sweeping claim — misleading.

text: the famous Thomas Sowell quote that in the 1920s in the US they taxed the rich people at 76 percent and wondered why they weren’t getting much income. When they reduced it to 24 percent, the income skyrocketed.
explanation: 1920s US top rates did fall sharply and revenue from the wealthy rose, but the causal 'skyrocketed because of the cut' framing is a selective, much-disputed reading.

text: Data shows that nine times more people die from the cold as opposed to the heat.
explanation: Some studies do find cold-related deaths exceed heat-related ones, but the ratio and its use to dismiss warming risk is selective and context-dependent.

text: the top 70 percent of income revenue in New Zealand comes from the 20 percent of those in the higher income brackets.
explanation: Directionally consistent with NZ income-tax concentration data, though the exact 70/20 split is a rounded, debatable figure.

text: I also heard from the honourable Camilla Belich that sensitive claims made up 65 percent of the proportion of people that will be under this amendment; and of those, also 70 percent were women.
explanation: Accurately relays the 65%/70% figures cited from the ACC sample.

text: we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
explanation: The census unoccupied-dwellings figure is real but conflates holiday homes, homes between tenancies, etc.; implying they are readily 'available' is misleading.

text: there is no Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause. There is no role for the 19 mana whenua of Tāmaki in the design, nor the implementation of the bill. There is no commitment to prioritising Māori housing, despite Māori facing the greatest need.
explanation: Specific, checkable claims about the bill's contents (no Tiriti clause, no mana whenua role); the 'greatest need' premise reflects established housing-disparity data.

text: Māori are underrepresented among homeowners precisely because of land loss, precisely because of discriminatory policy and economic exclusion.
explanation: Historical/causal claim about Maori homeownership; broadly supported by the historical record, stated with confidence.

text: There are 263,620 rangatahi aged between 16 and 19 here in Aotearoa. Around 92,000 are Māori, and a majority of those rangatahi Māori reside in my rohe of Tāmaki Makaurau.
explanation: Precise population figures; presented as data and plausible, though not independently confirmed in the text.

text: The latest Global Slavery Index estimates that 50 million people globally are trapped in modern slavery, and 8,000 of them are right here in Aotearoa.
explanation: Both figures match the Global Slavery Index 2023 estimates (~50m globally, ~8,000 in NZ); accurately attributed.

text: It's going bankrupt the country for the price of a Mount Vic extra tunnel. It's crazy, what's happening with this Government, fixated on their roads.
explanation: 'Bankrupting the country' for one tunnel is hyperbole.

text: They're needing a significant amount of money, in the hundreds of millions of dollars, and we know from what has been put in the media that DP World is looking around. They're having talks, but it's very, very secret, and I think we need a little bit more accountability and transparency for the people of Christchurch.
explanation: Attributed to media reports; the 'very secret' talks are characterised rather than confirmed.

text: Canterbury represents 13 percent of New Zealand's population. We contribute 15 percent of the vehicle kilometres travelled. But how much funding do we get in Canterbury? Just 5 percent—5 percent—of funding, basically, because all the funding is going to the North Island, especially Auckland.
explanation: Specific population/VKT/funding figures are presented as fact; directionally plausible but unverified and the 'all going to the North Island' framing overstates.

text: When they looked at the cost it would force on them, of around $63 million, their decision was "We're just going to change legislation so that we can get that money."
explanation: Cites a specific $63m figure but imputes a motive that the Government would dispute.

text: Close to 900 people making submissions; of those submissions, only two people—two submitters—supported this bill.
explanation: Submission count is broadly consistent with Belich's 860 figure; the 'only two supported' claim is specific and checkable.

text: Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won't get it twice.
explanation: The 'getting it twice' framing is the very double-dipping characterisation that White and Belich rebut as inaccurate.

text: I have visited the schools that were told they were going to get new classrooms, except there was never any money put aside for it.
explanation: Echoes the coalition's 'fiscal cliff' contention; plausible but a contested, unspecified claim.

text: There is no public transport in Levin.
explanation: Dismissive interjection; Levin/Horowhenua does have bus services, so the absolute claim is misleading.

text: Intent: "We're going to build 100,000 homes." Execution: "We built 1,000." It's great to have the intent, but we need the execution that can actually deliver it.
explanation: References KiwiBuild's 100,000 promise and large shortfall—broadly accurate, with rounded figures.

text: A big part of this Government's strategy is to double the value of exports, and we've seen tremendous growth. A key milestone... was the signing of the free-trade agreement with India only a couple of weeks ago, the one that Chris Hipkins said would never happen.
explanation: The FTA signing is real; the claim that Hipkins said it would 'never happen' is a contestable characterisation.

text: Twenty-five percent unemployment, and it’s all the parents’ fault!
explanation: The '25 percent' figure for youth unemployment is asserted without sourcing and is high relative to standard NZ youth unemployment measures.

text: I found out about a practice that’s been happening where people are watching child abuse, child rape on their webcams, and they do this internationally and they do it in countries of great vulnerability like the Philippines—500,000 children in the Philippines have had that experience.
explanation: Live-streamed child sexual abuse from the Philippines is well documented; the specific 500,000 figure is in the range of some estimates but is uncertain and not sourced here.

text: Do you know how much the median income is? It is, I think, $69,000
explanation: Cites a median income figure (~$69,000), in the plausible range for NZ individual/household measures; hedged with 'I think'.

text: What then happens is that MSD treat what she has got left as a windfall income, and they take everything that they have given that woman during that time away from her, including any rehab costs, including any of the energy costs that she has spent.
explanation: Consistent with the cross-bench account of how MSD recovers supplementary payments.

text: two people took cases to the court, and they actually had an eight-year process. Those people weren't alone in the way that they were being treated. They went through that process right to the Supreme Court.
explanation: Consistent with the long-running Fleming/Humphreys family-carer litigation culminating in the Supreme Court.

text: Some of its decisions included irresponsible tax cuts and tax breaks for tobacco companies and landlords.
explanation: References real policy changes but 'tax breaks for tobacco companies' is a contested framing of the excise freeze.

text: by its own regulatory impact statement, states that it has not had enough time to go through the detail of what the impacts would be, that there has been no robust analysis, that there has been no in-depth look at what the policy of this would be. The Ministry of Justice itself says that there is a risk through their work that it will create further division between Māori and Pākehā, between Māori and Crown relations.
explanation: Attributes specific warnings to official documents; plausible and well-sourced but unverified here.

text: I can point members to the exact clause, which is new section 8F(2), inserted by clause 5 of the bill, which says that if you breach a move-on order, you can go to prison.
explanation: Specific, falsifiable claim about the bill's content; plausible and checkable against the clause, though framed for maximum effect.

text: In October 2025, there was a successful court case that was taken by the Community Law Centres Aotearoa representing claimants who had had been made to pay their supplementary payments back when they had received ACC.
explanation: Specific, checkable account of the litigation and its outcome, consistent with other speakers.

text: We have the Government’s own Attorney-General stating that this bill is inconsistent with two important rights under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act: the freedom of expression and the freedom of movement.
explanation: Corroborated later in the debate by reference to a Section 7 report from the Attorney-General; names the specific rights affected.

text: They're under pressure because there's not enough staff: there's not enough doctors, there's not enough nurses, there's not enough allied professionals—there's not enough staff in general, and there's certainly not enough primary care upstream.
explanation: Workforce shortages are well documented, though stated without figures.

text: We saw that last time National tried this... people would suddenly get their cataracts fixed... but the knees and hips and all sorts of other things weren't being attended to because that particular DHB just needed to get those measures up and meet those targets.
explanation: Plausible and consistent with known gaming concerns, but presented without sourced data.

text: It explicitly adds an objective to work with private providers. It allows the Minister to hand-pick board members. It allows the director-general to actually sit in on board meetings... It scraps the audit requirements for the health plan, and it downgrades Māori leadership to advisory roles only.
explanation: Lists specific bill features; the characterisations are checkable against the bill text.

text: We received 47 submissions in all; 23 were in support and 23 opposed it.
explanation: Specific submission counts, though 23+23 does not reconcile to the stated 47 — a minor internal inconsistency.

text: That was an awful lot of exuberance for a Government bill that was mainly designed and drafted by the Auckland Council itself. But, nevertheless, you've got to take credit where you can get some, I suppose, if you're this Government.
explanation: Claim that the bill was mainly designed/drafted by Auckland Council; plausible given other speakers but not independently verifiable here.

text: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we've just heard and the scaremongering that's going on.
explanation: Bare 'more money' assertion with no figure; not substantiated in the text.

text: We're mandating health targets that ensure focus remains on what matters: reducing emergency wait times, improving cancer management, increasing childhood immunisations—that all went backwards under their Government.
explanation: The 'all went backwards under their Government' claim is a contestable comparison asserted without data.

text: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
explanation: Accurate that many of those jurisdictions have parody/satire copyright exceptions and NZ's 1994 Act lacks one — NZ is comparatively an outlier.

text: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
explanation: Recounts a plausible, specific sequence of prior attempts; consistent with the bill being a long-standing recurring proposal.

text: I also heard from the honourable Camilla Belich that sensitive claims made up 65 percent of the proportion of people that will be under this amendment; and of those, also 70 percent were women.
explanation: Precise figures attributed to a source.

text: the top 70 percent of income revenue in New Zealand comes from the 20 percent of those in the higher income brackets.
explanation: Cites concrete figures (top 20% paying ~70% of income tax).

text: employment was increasing, business confidence was improving, inflation had halved, the official cash rate had halved, mortgage rates nearly halved
explanation: Lists indicators with 'halved' framing but no actual numbers or dates.

text: New Zealand First is a nation-building party, building on our own resources, our own assets, our own wealth, our own businesses, our own globally competitive advantages in our own people, to make us great again.
explanation: Sweeping mission statement with no concrete policy or measure.

text: But one of the New Zealand First’s election promises was to set up a ministry for infrastructure, absorbing the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and other infrastructure aspects. This is about integrated and spatial planning.
explanation: Names the promise and the entities to be absorbed, though without timeframe or detail.

text: Tāmaki-makau-rau deserves a better transport system, one that does work, and Māori deserve a system that honours Te Tiriti. This bill is a foundation, but it is not the final word, and, on that basis, we commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Rhetorical framing ('foundation, not the final word') with little concrete content.

text: It assumes that if you threaten people with $2,000 fines and the rest—ha!—they'll simply disappear. But people don't disappear because Parliament tells them to; they move because they have somewhere safe to go.
explanation: References the $2,000 fine but the core is a general behavioural claim.

text: That's why we support making the minimum wage a living wage, that is why we support removing GST from kai so that whānau can afford to eat, and that is why we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
explanation: Names concrete policies (living wage, GST off food) though without figures or timelines.

text: Unlike the UK or Australian models, this bill introduces real teeth: director liability. This bill goes further by including penalties and liabilities for directors. If you profit from slave labour, the buck stops at the boardroom table.
explanation: Pinpoints the distinguishing feature (director liability) and contrasts it with overseas models.

text: There are 263,620 rangatahi aged between 16 and 19 here in Aotearoa. Around 92,000 are Māori, and a majority of those rangatahi Māori reside in my rohe of Tāmaki Makaurau.
explanation: Exact counts and a defined age band and region.

text: When they looked at the cost it would force on them, of around $63 million, their decision was "We're just going to change legislation so that we can get that money."
explanation: Concrete dollar figure attached to the claim.

text: Close to 900 people making submissions; of those submissions, only two people—two submitters—supported this bill.
explanation: Precise counts of submissions and supporters.

text: In Ōtautahi, we have over 54 percent of our emissions coming from land transport. No, it wasn't going to fix that.
explanation: Gives a concrete figure and locale.

text: Canterbury represents 13 percent of New Zealand's population. We contribute 15 percent of the vehicle kilometres travelled. But how much funding do we get in Canterbury? Just 5 percent—5 percent—of funding, basically, because all the funding is going to the North Island, especially Auckland.
explanation: Concrete percentages for population, vehicle kilometres, and funding share.

text: They're needing a significant amount of money, in the hundreds of millions of dollars, and we know from what has been put in the media that DP World is looking around. They're having talks, but it's very, very secret, and I think we need a little bit more accountability and transparency for the people of Christchurch.
explanation: Gives an order-of-magnitude cost and names DP World as a party in talks.

text: We have an amazing welfare system.
explanation: Vague boosterism with no detail or measure.

text: you go to the supermarket, everything’s on your phone; you go to a sports game, everything’s on your phone; checking in for a flight, everything’s on your phone—whatever we’re doing—so why couldn’t we have our driver’s licence on our phone? It’s a great step forward. A progressive step from a progressive Government. I commend the bill.
explanation: Identifies the concrete feature he values (digital driver's licences) but offers no detail on implementation or scope.

text: As much as I want to build a road to Levin—and I really want to build that road to Levin
explanation: Names a concrete project (a road to Levin) but gives no funding, timeframe, or plan.

text: A big part of this Government's strategy is to double the value of exports, and we've seen tremendous growth. A key milestone... was the signing of the free-trade agreement with India only a couple of weeks ago, the one that Chris Hipkins said would never happen.
explanation: Names the export-doubling goal and the India FTA milestone, but 'tremendous growth' is vague.

text: It's actually a publicly listed company that, if you're watching at home today, you could go and buy shares in... At what point do we say it's OK for publicly listed companies to then be subject to official information? ... Does that extend to power companies? I think of Genesis, Meridian, Mercury—they are, appropriately, not subject to the Official Information Act for those reasons.
explanation: Names concrete examples (Port of Tauranga, Genesis, Meridian, Mercury) to ground the point.

text: this law—it's another good reason to change the Government this November.
explanation: Slogan-like call with no policy content.

text: what happens when you have people with a conflict of interest in terms of determining what happens to a local street? For example, the local board member themselves might live in that street.
explanation: Gives a clear example but the question is exploratory rather than tied to figures or named provisions.

text: Do you know how much the median income is? It is, I think, $69,000
explanation: Provides a concrete figure, though hedged and without specifying which median measure.

text: two people took cases to the court, and they actually had an eight-year process. Those people weren't alone in the way that they were being treated. They went through that process right to the Supreme Court.
explanation: Names the number of claimants, the duration, and the appellate path.

text: if Tim Costley breaks his arm, then the accident compensation scheme kicks in without fault, and Tim Costley will receive 80 percent of his earnings; he will also receive household help because that will be helpful for him in his recovery; he will receive physio; he will receive taxis to and fro, as he needs them; there will be rehabilitation that he gets.
explanation: Itemises 80% earnings, household help, physio, transport, rehab.

text: And what is the Government's answer to this problem? Their answer is to sack almost 9,000 public servants. Now, this makes no sense.
explanation: Quantifies the cut but the critique itself is general here.

text: Governments are elected for a three-year term. They have that period of time to enact the legislation and curtailing normal parliamentary procedure that allows for the input from the public on something that is important... means that we should have at least four months, if not longer.
explanation: Specifies a minimum period (four months) but the surrounding argument is general.

text: the specific question I have in relation to clause 48 and 49, which is a consequential amendment to the Child Poverty Reduction Act, is will this particular clause and the change of section 52 to new section 11A maintain the same independence that is currently in section 52?
explanation: Precise clause-and-section references framing a focused question about preserving statutory independence.

text: we received 860 submissions, even though there were only 2½ days for people to actually put submissions in.
explanation: Exact figure and timeframe.

text: I can point members to the exact clause, which is new section 8F(2), inserted by clause 5 of the bill, which says that if you breach a move-on order, you can go to prison.
explanation: Cites the exact clause and section number and the precise consequence (imprisonment).

text: the bill mistakes measurement for improvement... No one disagrees with the fact that performance should be visible... but simply writing targets into law isn't going to do anything to create capacity.
explanation: States the conceptual flaw but not a fully detailed alternative.

text: We saw that last time National tried this... people would suddenly get their cataracts fixed... but the knees and hips and all sorts of other things weren't being attended to because that particular DHB just needed to get those measures up and meet those targets.
explanation: Concrete example (cataracts vs knees/hips) of how targets distort delivery.

text: It explicitly adds an objective to work with private providers. It allows the Minister to hand-pick board members. It allows the director-general to actually sit in on board meetings... It scraps the audit requirements for the health plan, and it downgrades Māori leadership to advisory roles only.
explanation: Itemises concrete provisions of the bill she objects to.

text: that's why we've prioritised three free GP visits for everybody every year through the Medicard
explanation: Concrete policy: three free annual GP visits via a named scheme.

text: We received 47 submissions in all; 23 were in support and 23 opposed it.
explanation: Concrete numbers on submissions for and against.

text: the Government agreed to extend the number of people who were excluded from having to repay under this bill. Initially, it was people who had filed formal claims, but now it's been extended to people who have raised complaints with MSD.
explanation: Labour secured a concrete, enacted change via the committee process — partial delivery on an opposition aim.

text: When we get elected at the end of this year, we will either repeal this or we will stop this work because we know that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is one of the founding documents of New Zealand.
explanation: A firm commitment to repeal/stop, but contingent on winning the election and therefore undelivered.

text: that's why we've prioritised three free GP visits for everybody every year through the Medicard
explanation: An opposition policy commitment, not a delivered programme — aspiration pending an election.

text: I'd just like to say I admire the thought and consideration of all parties on this bill. It's a shame that we were not able to reach consensus.
explanation: Inclusive, consensus-valuing tone that reaches across party lines.

text: The member from the member ACT Party was talking about how markets will take care of this; sometimes markets are not enough. Sometimes there is market failure, which is why we absolutely need a strong Commerce Commission and we absolutely need good governance in that respect as well.
explanation: Reasoned disagreement with an ally on substance rather than personal terms; engages the argument.

text: New Zealand First is a nation-building party, building on our own resources, our own assets, our own wealth, our own businesses, our own globally competitive advantages in our own people, to make us great again.
explanation: Aspirational identity rhetoric that appeals to supporters but offers no bridge to opponents.

text: Look, we know there were many submitters who were fearful and worried about the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, and fair enough—it is what we know. This is a bold change, and so we hear them.
explanation: Acknowledges and validates opponents'/submitters' concerns rather than dismissing them—bridge-building tone.

text: Our rangatahi need better rangatira than what we have in this Whare right now. I look you straight in the eye and I tell you that our people need to register to vote this year. That is the only way we can make a great impact right now. Vote this Government out.
explanation: Direct partisan call to vote the Government out; rallies her base rather than building consensus.

text: Then we heard the conservation Minister say that saving every species may simply be too expensive. Too expensive? Come on. Tell that to the kiwi—the actual kiwi; the bird. Tell that to the pekapeka. Tell that to the kōkako, whose call grows fainter every single year. What is the market value of extinction?
explanation: Stirring to sympathetic listeners but framed to indict opponents, not to persuade them.

text: That's why we support making the minimum wage a living wage, that is why we support removing GST from kai so that whānau can afford to eat, and that is why we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
explanation: Values-driven appeal that energises supporters but is pitched to her own side.

text: The accident compensation scheme was built on a simple promise, and that is: if you are injured, the State will stand beside you, not on top of you.
explanation: Memorable, principled framing of the no-fault ACC compact.

text: The bill is an attempt to restore balance and I do acknowledge that, and I acknowledge that these reforms do matter. They help to rebuild trust.
explanation: Bridge-building tone that credits the other side before raising disagreements.

text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in total opposition to this bill, a bill that will just cause more harm coming from a Government that clearly does not care about the most vulnerable in our society. This bill is absolutely a disgrace.
explanation: Condemnatory tone that rallies opponents of the bill rather than persuading the undecided.

text: I was very pleased when I heard the Associate Minister of Transport saying earlier that … they'd picked that up and that issue's going to be addressed. … I acknowledge that, because I think it's really important that when people come to talk to select committees and they actually come with a genuine concern that needs fixing, we don't just let it fall off the radar.
explanation: Credits a government minister across party lines and affirms the select-committee process.

text: I'd like to acknowledge Mike Butterick and the work he's done to progress this, and I also acknowledge the promotion that he's recently had.
explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement (Green MP crediting a National MP) that builds goodwill across the House.

text: I would have thought, with all the questions he has, he'd want this to go to a select committee so they could dive into it a little bit further and work out how it could be put forward in a better way for National to be able to support something that is actually quite a common-sense approach.
explanation: Invites an opponent to engage via select committee and frames a path for them to support it—consensus-seeking.

text: We're pretty sure that it'll get through this stage, because New Zealand First apparently—apparently—backs common sense, so we can count on them.
explanation: Light, semi-inclusive appeal to another party, but with a teasing edge.

text: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
explanation: An applause line aimed at his own side, not persuasion.

text: Virtue signalling over wellbeing doesn’t help pay the bills.
explanation: A dismissive applause line for his own side rather than persuasion.

text: you go to the supermarket, everything’s on your phone; you go to a sports game, everything’s on your phone; checking in for a flight, everything’s on your phone—whatever we’re doing—so why couldn’t we have our driver’s licence on our phone? It’s a great step forward. A progressive step from a progressive Government. I commend the bill.
explanation: Warm, relatable framing that praises the Government and commends the bill — positive and inclusive in tone.

text: My style of politics is anchored by the belief that that which is common to all of us is a powerful gravity—far greater than that or those who would seek to divide.
explanation: Consensus-seeking framing emphasising shared identity over division.

text: Community calls us to reach out to cross divides, to grow in empathy and understanding, not division and intolerance; to celebrate our differences, not try and eliminate them.
explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building language that explicitly seeks common ground and rejects us-vs-them framing.

text: this law—it's another good reason to change the Government this November.
explanation: Overt electioneering aimed at her own side.

text: Christmas Day is only a day, New Year is only a day, and election day is only a day. We should be making decisions which allow people to be involved in this process, and we should not rush just because it's a date that might be important to us in here
explanation: Memorable rhetorical framing arguing against rushing; persuasive but pitched to her own argument.

text: I absolutely respect Dr Webb's fear and hesitancy and the note of this Parliament that there are risks with that that we go too far, that we open things too wide and there are risks in that... I think, as he says, the balance is right here, and it can be looked at again if things go astray.
explanation: Acknowledges and builds on a colleague's concerns and incorporates them into her position; consensus-oriented.

text: I love the idea of local boards having more control over roads. I think it's a really sound one.
explanation: Endorses the Government's proposal across party lines before raising concerns — a bridge-building, common-ground opening.

text: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
explanation: Deliberately bipartisan, gave a platform to all parties — actively building cross-party consensus.

text: Well, how about thinking about all of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, not just the ones you know? Think about the ones you visited recently who are cut off and remain vulnerable every day
explanation: Confrontational toward the member opposite rather than bridge-building.

text: Labour is ready with a plan and ready to work with hapū, iwi, and whānau Māori.
explanation: Inclusive toward Māori communities but does not reach across the aisle; partisan reassurance.

text: something I think we could move forward as a Parliament, if we really want to have some benefit for Māori, is, perhaps, start looking closely at lending on things like multiply owned Māori land, especially when people have the means to service the mortgages and the loans for that.
explanation: Frames a proposal as something 'we could move forward as a Parliament' — inclusive, cross-party language inviting collaboration rather than attacking opponents.

text: I just want to do a big mihi to my colleagues, and colleagues across the House, who decided to protect the rights of consumers. That's a win for the people who matter, the people who put us here.
explanation: Acknowledges members across the House for protecting consumer rights — inclusive, consensus-affirming despite opposing the bill overall.

text: It's almost unsettling to hear the speeches opposite; I feel like they should be sitting on this side. I'm all for it—ka pai koutou; I'm really glad to hear that you are listening to the public of New Zealand.
explanation: Warmly acknowledges that opponents are listening to the public and finds common ground across the aisle rather than attacking.

text: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
explanation: Divisive partisan attack.

text: Sometimes, some decisions that we have to make are very hard decisions to make, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be made.
explanation: Acknowledges difficulty and the opponents' concern before defending the decision.

text: I would like to ask the House to imagine for a moment that—in a different country, in a different world—someone sold a teenager a lolly filled with poison. The teenager in this distant world reacts violently to the poison. The Government of this imaginary country pays the person—who sold the poisonous lolly to the youth—money to give the youth the antidote.
explanation: Vivid storytelling that engages the chamber, but designed to rally rather than persuade opponents.

text: lived experience is absolutely very important. But I’m not going to expect the lived experience of someone that is still living the life of a current, lifelong, very proud gang member.
explanation: Acknowledges the value of lived experience before qualifying it, softening an otherwise hard stance.

text: I want to make one thing extremely clear: this debate is not about whether addiction recovery matters; it does. I’m extremely proud of the fact that our Government is the first Government to ever have a Minister for Mental Health.
explanation: Pre-empts the obvious objection by conceding addiction recovery matters, broadening appeal beyond her own side.

text: we were able to negotiate with the Government—and I thank the Government for their good-faith interactions with us in this respect—to have a short select committee process of around a week.
explanation: Acknowledges cross-party cooperation, modelling constructive engagement.

text: the invitation to join us in this bill is still there.
explanation: Open, inclusive invitation for others to come on board rather than an adversarial framing.

text: This is a terrible bill. It goes much too far in addressing what everyone would acknowledge is sometimes a problem, which is, obviously, something that is very difficult within our cities, which is when we see antisocial behaviour.
explanation: Concedes opponents have identified a genuine problem, a partial bridge, before pivoting to opposition.

text: One of my proudest moments of being an Aucklander was when I went to the opening of Homeground. Those types of solutions that actually provide a community response to homelessness are what the Government should be investing in.
explanation: Offers a constructive, positive alternative rather than pure opposition.

text: the bill mistakes measurement for improvement... No one disagrees with the fact that performance should be visible... but simply writing targets into law isn't going to do anything to create capacity.
explanation: Acknowledges the opposing point ('no one disagrees') before rebutting.

text: Obviously, we are supporting this bill, and we enjoyed going through the process.
explanation: Constructive, cross-party tone supporting a Government bill and praising the process.

text: These were changes that were made by a previous National-Act Government in establishing Auckland Transport, but bringing these functions back now under elected members feels like the right thing to do. It strengthens, we believe, both voice and responsibility.
explanation: Endorses a current Government reform on its merits despite noting its origins, seeking common ground.

text: this is an example of one of those bills that is now more workable, accountable, and is a much more balanced piece of legislation from the collective efforts from all of those members from all of those different parties.
explanation: Credits all parties and the collaborative process; consensus-building and inclusive.

text: I would like to pick up on a comment made by the chair of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, Andy Foster, who has led a very good process, as he does on all of the bills that come to that select committee.
explanation: Builds goodwill across the House by acknowledging an opponent's good work.

text: Labour agrees, though, that the closing of a double-dipping loophole in welfare is important, because we, like everyone, know that Kiwis must feel confident in our welfare system
explanation: Concedes the principle while still opposing — a defensible, qualified position rather than a clean flip.

text: National was hugely supportive of the language—hugely supportive of the language—and I don't mind saying that I think there's a lot of good National people.
explanation: Acknowledges good faith on the other side even while attacking current policy, a consistent and fair-minded stance.

text: Māori are very much in support of the Palestinian people—always have been, always will be
explanation: Asserts a long-standing consistent position he traces to the Māori activist movement; broad claim, plausibly grounded but sweeping.

text: Almost 40,000 people have been unlawfully burdened with debts as a result of a practice that has carried on by both National and Labour Governments through decades.
explanation: Even-handedly blames Labour as well as National, consistent with the Greens' across-the-aisle critique.

text: I will be the first one to admit that some of these wellbeing objectives could have been implemented and reflected better in Government policies
explanation: Concedes a fault on his own side's preferred framework rather than defending it uncritically — a candid, self-consistent admission.

text: I heard from our colleagues that it's a targeted welfare system, no impacts on claimants, clients will not get less under this amendment, and we take them at their word.
explanation: Says NZ First want no claimant disadvantage yet accept assurances rather than test them, then vote for the bill.

text: New Zealand First do not want any undue hardship or material hardship as a result of these changes; however, we support this bill.
explanation: Tension: states a value against hardship while voting for the bill that submitters and the courts say causes that hardship.

text: I said no, I’m not writing another strategy, we’re forming an action plan with projects on it and we’re going to implement them, and we did.
explanation: Positions a stated preference for action over strategy as matched by his own record.

text: But one of the New Zealand First’s election promises was to set up a ministry for infrastructure, absorbing the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and other infrastructure aspects. This is about integrated and spatial planning.
explanation: Ties the current support to a stated NZ First election promise on integrated planning—words consistent with prior commitment.

text: the Labour Party started in a position of supporting this bill because of what it was told. It was just awake on the job. It found out what was going on. It found out that there was an injustice afoot and it wasn't prepared to tolerate it.
explanation: Openly acknowledges Labour's position change and frames it as evidence-driven rather than concealing the shift.

text: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
explanation: Words about non-partisanship matched by the action of co-hosting with National and including all parties.

text: Yes, it's a very important issue. We have to, otherwise we will not be doing justice to those who are going to be affected, because, as days go by, there will be more and more people—those who will be affected.
explanation: Responds to the 'rushed process' criticism by justifying speed, but only partially addresses the substance of the complaint.

text: this bill will deepen hardship for survivors of abuse, for survivors of sexual violence and abuse, and for those who suffer most in all of Aotearoa.
explanation: Prediction of worsened hardship; directionally supported by the affected cohort data, magnitude uncertain.

text: If people believe that decisions affecting their entitlements can be revisited years later, confidence in the system—confidence in the system—begins to erode.
explanation: Predicts erosion of public confidence from retrospective change; plausible but unmeasured.

text: Raising that threshold—the threshold rates—is going to raise hardship rates. It’s going to push whānau closer to arrears and foreclosures.
explanation: Predicts increased hardship, arrears and foreclosures from the threshold change; directionally plausible given reduced support, but magnitude uncertain and unquantified.

text: Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won't get it twice.
explanation: Predicts everyone 'will get' their entitlements; contested by the harm evidence raised.

text: We know that when people can't afford to see their GP, they delay their care, they get sicker and sicker, they end up in hospitals, and those emergency departments start to overflow.
explanation: Predictive claim about downstream ED pressure; directionally well-supported, magnitude unstated.

text: Of course New Zealanders remember managed isolation and quarantine, don't they? They remember what it was like trying to be able to see a loved one during the lockdowns... while that's back with a nationwide triage service under the three free doctors visits.
explanation: Emotive analogy equating a GP triage service with MIQ lockdown controls; weak logical link.

text: The Government is very focused on fixing the basics and building the future and growing an economy which ultimately grows jobs and opportunities, and unfortunately the politics and the agenda of the previous Government—which drove up inflation, drove up interest rates—ended up with high unemployment
explanation: Asserts a causal chain (previous Government → inflation → rates → unemployment) without evidence and to shift responsibility.

text: Labour’s pumped hydro scheme was a vanity project, and their intention to press ahead with it... was threatening the market-led investment needed to offer New Zealand the best chance of ensuring energy security.
explanation: Offers a plausible chilling-effect argument but asserts the 'vanity' framing without evidence.

text: At the start of this year, known remaining reserves of natural gas were 23 percent lower than at the same time last year... with 12 of the 17 gasfields that are currently operating expected to stop producing within the next 10 years, it is only going to continue to get more challenging without future gasfields being found.
explanation: Argument grounded in cited reserve data; conclusion about future challenge follows reasonably.

text: …in practical terms that means for every 100 kilometres travelled, these workers will receive an extra $19, which covers the current rise in fuel costs, which is around $8.50 for the average petrol vehicle and $11.80 for the average diesel vehicle.
explanation: Backs the rate with concrete cost figures showing the uplift exceeds the modelled fuel-cost rise; numbers support the conclusion.

text: Oh, this is the language specialist here from the Wairarapa. Ha, ha! He’s the expert on diction. The fact that he’s not even trained or educated properly or anything else but knows a bit about horse betting—it’s his only qualification—never stops him from saying something, though, does it?
explanation: Ad hominem directed at an interjector, with no argument.

text: So is the Minister's position that an Indian chef coming here under the Indian free-trade agreement (FTA) will have fewer rights than a Chinese chef coming in under the China - New Zealand FTA; in other words, that an Indian chef is worth less to the National Party than a Chinese chef?
explanation: Strawman/false equivalence: leaps from differing visa provisions to a claim about relative human worth.

text: if they're the Māori voice and they got only 3 percent of the vote most of the time, and yet they say the Māori people are 18 percent of the population, it means that one-sixth of the Māori people might support them and five-sixths don't. How can they call themselves the Māori voice?
explanation: Uses a numerical argument, but the inference conflates total party vote share with support among Māori specifically (many Māori vote for other parties), a flawed step.

text: What's the difference between Green MP Wade-Brown's accommodation or McAnulty from Labour's accommodation as opposed to yours? What is the difference? The answer is none.
explanation: Implicit tu quoque, but makes a fair consistency point about applying the same standard.

text: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
explanation: Makes a coherent point that NZ's careful wording differs from endorsement; the distinction is reasoned, if self-serving.

text: It is pure ideology and National members actually know it is wrong, and that's why they are quietly trying to go about it, because themselves even understand that that is a backward step.
explanation: Claims to know National members' private beliefs with no evidence — an unsupported assertion.

text: Instead—instead—what we got is a random, visionless, and harmful grab bag of laws that are more about politicians’ pet projects and petty grievances than they are about addressing the challenges we face right now.
explanation: Sweeping characterisation asserted without supporting evidence.

text: Why is he comfortable expanding defence partnerships with a country that has launched an illegal war with Iran, further destabilised the entire Middle East, and upended global fuel supply?
explanation: Loads several strong contested premises ('illegal war', 'destabilised') into a single question.

text: The thing about the age restriction is that it would require, in effect, a breaching of privacy and an exposure of privacy.
explanation: Identifies a plausible mechanism (age verification implies privacy intrusion), though asserted without detail on how.

text: A blanket ban on social media for under-16s may appear to be a way to keep our children safe—which we all want—but the reality is that, alone, a ban will not address the problem of online harm to children.
explanation: Concedes the ban's intent then argues its insufficiency, drawing on the Children's Convention Monitoring Group; reasoned if not heavily quantified.

text: We’re going to bring rigour and common sense to the hysteria surrounding climate change. Climate change policies in New Zealand have been driven by a tiny minority with loud voices who have no conception as to the consequences of their narrow, shallow ideas on the day-to-day functioning of the economy.
explanation: Dismisses climate policy as 'hysteria' driven by a 'tiny minority' — ad hominem and appeal to ridicule rather than evidence.

text: in 2022, when the Marsden Point refinery was closed down, with the approval of the then Labour Government—
explanation: Rests an argument on a contested attribution of agency.

text: I can tell you there’s one party over here who wants to ban mining on the Department of Conservation estate. They are never going to be up for the growth of revenue.
explanation: Treats opposition to one mining policy as proof a party opposes all revenue growth—a non-sequitur.

text: Sadly, there are some parts of the country, and members from Taranaki, who do not understand the vital importance of vanadium and other such ingredients. From time to time, the matua must excuse the words that come from Luddites. Virtually every modern accoutrement has critical minerals involved, whether it is computers, whether it is phones, whether it is other ordinary essentials.
explanation: Makes a reasonable point about minerals' ubiquity but wraps it in dismissive characterisation.

text: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
explanation: Links global supply facts to NZ's exposure to make a coherent point.

text: if New Zealanders are feeling powerless right now, it’s kind of by intent. That’s exactly the strategy and the plan of this Government, to have regular people switch off so that power and wealth gets concentrated in fewer and fewer hands.
explanation: Imputes a deliberate disempowerment strategy to the Government with no supporting evidence; speculative attribution of intent.

text: This Government says that they want to cut red tape—oh, but they mean it everywhere but the Epsom electorate.
explanation: Points to an apparent inconsistency (deregulation except where it affects certain electorates) with some basis.

text: means testing oftentimes ends up being a sham, and an administratively costly sham, because those that have the means are able to use their lawyers and accountants to put their means in a place that is difficult to look through.
explanation: Offers a causal mechanism (avoidance + admin cost) for opposing means testing, a reasoned point though without cited evidence.

text: Why is it socialism to invest in renewable energy but not socialism to actively invest hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer funds into fossil-fuel production?
explanation: Exposes an inconsistency in applying the 'socialism' label selectively to public investment.

text: "In effect, this reduces the requirement from approximately 2 million dwellings to approximately 1.4 million dwellings." That's a quote from the legislation that the Minister introduced.
explanation: Anchors her argument directly in the bill's own explanatory text — strong, verifiable evidence.

text: Yes, the Government acknowledges the impact of high electricity prices... the lines charge component of household electricity prices increased by 14 percent, while the energy and other component increased by 9 percent... We’ve reversed the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, which was the single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed in the first place.
explanation: 'Single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed' for the gas ban is a strong, contested causal attribution.

text: We’ve stopped work on the Lake Onslow boondoggle, which was having a chilling effect on our renewable generation. We now have the biggest renewable boom under way. We’re seeing lower power prices in the wholesale market and Australian Securities Exchange futures.
explanation: 'Biggest renewable boom' and 'lower wholesale prices' are selective, partly-supported claims presented without the qualifying detail.

text: Currently, around 70 percent of New Zealanders who live more than two hours from a main hospital live in this region.
explanation: A precise statistic presented as fact; striking enough that it warrants verification, so partial confidence.

text: only 64.7 percent of Māori children being fully immunised at two years of age when we came into Government ... it is now up to 71.5 percent— ... of children.
explanation: Specific official-style statistics presented as fact; plausible and checkable.

text: Under Labour, the number of public servants increased from 47,250 to 65,700.
explanation: Closely matches the documented rise in public service headcount 2017–2023.

text: That is a very challenging issue and it's something that we're working through. … An example of some of the things we've had to change is we had to take away a ute tax, there was going to be a fertiliser tax, a capital gains tax, a water tax, tax, tax, tax—
explanation: Lists a 'capital gains tax' among policies removed, though no such tax was enacted — misleading.

text: The bit that she forgot to say is that over six years, those poor people, the vulnerable she’s so worried about, are worse off today than they were six years ago.
explanation: Plausible for some measures (cost-of-living pressure) but contestable as a blanket claim across all vulnerable groups; mixed evidence.

text: Well, there's no direct evidence that farmers will be producing less. In fact, we produce enough food to feed 40 million people around the world. … There will always be enough food for New Zealanders to eat because we're not a population of 40 million people.
explanation: NZ's food-export-to-population framing is broadly accurate as a generalisation.

text: In the December quarter, meat exports increased by a significant 21.4 percent; dairy exports were up 10 percent, tourism... grew by 9.4 percent; transportation exports grew by 7.5 percent; and for our foresters, log exports were up by 3.7 percent.
explanation: Precise, checkable figures presented straightforwardly.

text: The Government has also contributed $10 million to address immediate humanitarian need.
explanation: Consistent with NZ's reported humanitarian contribution at the time; specific and checkable.

text: Yes, including that the last Labour Government made a reckless decision and approved the closure of Marsden Point.
explanation: Asserts the previous Government 'approved the closure'; the refinery's conversion was a private decision by its owner, making this misleading.

text: As night fell on the last Labour Government and as they fled from their Cabinet offices, there was a half-baked proposal—unfunded, incomplete—and in the interests of good constitutional Government, I couldn't take that forward in that incomplete state.
explanation: 'Unfunded, incomplete' is contradicted in the same session by claims of a legislated levy change and a Cabinet procurement decision.

text: Yes, especially when the Minister gave her consent for the decommissioning of the refinery.
explanation: Specific claim about Woods consenting to decommissioning; plausible but contested and unsupported in the text.

text: I shall be celebrating the arrival of the diesel storage, a recommissioned $100 million tank funded by a $1.2 billion fund negotiated by Winston Peters at the formation of the last Government.
explanation: Specific figures asserted as fact; plausible but unverified.

text: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
explanation: Figures align with commonly cited Strait of Hormuz and Asian refinery supply data.

text: this Government has chosen to spend billions of dollars in tax cuts that have been funded by debt, which produces precisely zero jobs.
explanation: 'Precisely zero jobs' is an absolute, unsupported claim; the funding-by-debt characterisation is itself contestable.

text: Is it fair that shareholders, including the Government, are collecting near record dividends from power companies while 200,000 New Zealanders cannot afford to heat their homes?
explanation: Embeds the checkable claims of ‘near record dividends’ and ‘200,000 cannot afford to heat their homes’, plausible but unsourced here.

text: So why did the Government decide to scrap the gas transition plan which had been due for publication at the end of 2023, after they came to Government, which would have meant that we would be at least 2½ years ahead of where we are now on gas transition?
