explanation: Embedded claim that a gas transition plan was due late 2023; plausible and specific but the '2½ years ahead' counterfactual is speculative.

text: they have made decisions to cut flood protection funding across this country by 41 percent compared to the former Government.
explanation: Specific 41% cut attributed to an OIA response from the Ministry for the Environment; sourced but unverified here.

text: "In effect, this reduces the requirement from approximately 2 million dwellings to approximately 1.4 million dwellings." That's a quote from the legislation that the Minister introduced.
explanation: Accurately quotes the legislation's first paragraph.

text: As I said, we are working through a process. Once that process is complete, decisions will be made and they'll be announced.
explanation: Contentless 'a process… decisions will be made' formulation.

text: A new hospital in South Auckland will mean better access to care closer to home. Drury was identified as a strong location due to its proximity to key transport corridors, including our roads of regional significance and planned public transport connections, making it easier for patients, staff, and visitors to access care. Over time, this will reduce pressure on existing hospitals, improve wait times, and ensure that Aucklanders can have confidence that high-quality healthcare will be there when they need it.
explanation: Names Drury and the locational rationale, but the benefits are stated without quantification or timing.

text: We provided tax relief in the 2024 Budget, for the first time in 14 years. We didn't put in place the 12c increase in tax on fuel which Labour would have done if they were elected in 2023. We axed the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax.
explanation: Names the budget year, the 12c figure, and a specific abolished tax.

text: The Government’s $604 million investment into new medicines delivered 33 new cancer treatments... Once fully implemented, the expansion will deliver 218 more chair days of treatment space each week... with each chair typically used by three to five patients per day.
explanation: Dollar figures, treatment counts, and operational detail (chair days, patients per chair).

text: They will be able to apply under the scheme for a loan to cover all or part of the cost of reducing their gas usage by at least 15 percent. The Government won’t be picking winners. Banks will be the lenders, retaining their usual commercial discipline. The Government will guarantee 80 percent of each loan under the scheme... The maximum value of any single loan will be $50 million, and the scheme will apply only to new loans, not refinancing. Up to $1.2 billion of loans could be written under this scheme.
explanation: Dense with concrete mechanisms and figures: 15% reduction, 80% guarantee, $50m cap, $1.2b total, new-loans-only.

text: Our seafood is better than theirs; Indians deserve to eat it.
explanation: A boosterish assertion with no measure or substantiation.

text: I'm informed that we have enough fertiliser now to get us through the winter. We're working very closely with fertiliser importers to make sure that spring will also be good.
explanation: Names a concrete near-term assurance (winter supply) but no costs, volumes or mechanisms.

text: we will judge the success of those missions not on the number of meetings they have but on how much more they will sell. We’re going to make more of the agreements we have in place and negotiate more, and I will be on a plane on Monday of next week going to India, the very first meeting.
explanation: Names a concrete metric (export sales not meetings), a named destination (India), and a precise time (Monday next week).

text: One of the things that we agreed with India is that, every year, 1,670 high-skilled workers... can come to New Zealand under a special visa that would be created. The visa will be for three years. At the end of that time, they would need to return home... It does not give them a right automatically to bring family members here, because that was not part of the negotiation.
explanation: Exact numbers (1,670), duration (three years), and the family-rights position.

text: Right now, apples face a 50 percent tariff into India; under this free-trade agreement, that tariff rate will reduce to 25 percent, with an initial quota of 32,500 tonnes that matches our current apple exports to India. This quota will grow to 45,000 tonnes, or 300 million apples every year, over the next six years.
explanation: Exact tariff change, quota tonnages, apple count, and timeframe.

text: But what we need is to be unshackled from this risk-averse, woke-riddled, doubt-riddled culture that we have inherited. If we do that, the world will be our oyster.
explanation: Slogan-level optimism with no mechanism.

text: I have received a number of reports, not the least of which is that the fuel import companies and the decision that they made to move New Zealand towards a just-in-time model is working as they contemplated. But, sadly, we are bereft of adequate storage. And I have received a report … a very threadbare proposal, unfunded, which … would have required us to raid the money that the Crown has put aside to meet the 50-day cushion internationally.
explanation: Identifies the just-in-time model, the storage shortfall, and the 50-day reserve constraint.

text: There is scope to rapidly develop the capacity for 90 million litres worth of storage in a matter of months. I suspect the person who made that stupid remark in the media was reading the Māori calendar or something like that.
explanation: Gives a concrete volume and timeframe for the Channel/Marsden Point capacity.

text: Our Government made a rapid decision, dedicated capital, and within eight weeks, New Zealand will have this additional fuel storage capacity either for an additional buffer or, in time, to be used by the fuel companies.
explanation: Names the site, capital ($20m-odd), capacity (up to 100 million litres), and timeframe.

text: when we spend 6 percent of GDP on capital projects, which basically means $27 billion—i.e., 50 percent of that is the Crown, the next 25 percent is local government, and the last 25 percent is private sector, including gentailers and other entities
explanation: Breaks the figure into a percentage-of-GDP, a dollar total, and a funding split.

text: you do not grow when you starve. That is the approach that this Government has taken to our economy.
explanation: Metaphorical framing with no figures or named measures.

text: It does enable the criminalisation—that is literally in the regulatory impact statement.
explanation: Pins the claim to a named document (the regulatory impact statement).

text: Is the Prime Minister comfortable with near-record power company profits and dividends being paid out to shareholders, helping to improve the look of the Government's books, while 65,000 more New Zealanders could not afford to heat their home adequately last winter?
explanation: Cites a concrete figure (65,000) and a clear comparison.

text: Why did his Government decide to cut flood protection funding at a time when extreme weather is becoming more frequent and severe, by approximately half compared to the former Government?
explanation: Puts a concrete magnitude (≈half, ~41%) on the alleged flood-protection funding cut against a named comparator.

text: they have made decisions to cut flood protection funding across this country by 41 percent compared to the former Government.
explanation: Precise percentage with a clear comparison baseline and a cited source.

text: On behalf of the Minister for Auckland, it seems to me important that we take a holistic approach to the question. As I've indicated, as the Government, we're taking a number of different approaches which will be beneficial to the people of Auckland as a city and as a region and also for all of New Zealand.
explanation: 'Holistic approach' and 'a number of different approaches' are vague platitudes with no mechanism, figure, or location.

text: within sort of the next two or three months at the latest, we would need to have progressed those and brought them forward.
explanation: Gives a rough timeframe (two to three months) though hedged.

text: it introduces an income tax exemption for income from a household sale of excess electricity back to the grid. From 1 April, individuals will not be required to file a return nor pay any tax in relation to this income.
explanation: Names the exact measure, who it affects, and the 1 April commencement.

text: It covers personnel from countries such as France and India in that campaign, along with civilians serving in medical units, members of the Merchant Navy during the world wars, and those who died while training for conflict. It also extends to post-Vietnam service, including veterans of Timor-Leste and Afghanistan, including the member herself
explanation: Lists concrete categories and named conflicts (France/India at Gallipoli, Merchant Navy, Timor-Leste, Afghanistan).

text: Just seven months after shovels hit the ground, I was delighted, yesterday, to celebrate the opening of 23 new homes for military families, including eight at the Linton Military Camp... five at RNZAF Base Ōhakea, and 10 at Burnham Military Camp.
explanation: Exact counts by location and a build timeframe.

text: I would have thought that member would have supported fast track, which is seeing... the biggest wind farm in New Zealand’s history... consented in the South Island... but no, he voted no to that. He’s voting no— to the very solutions that solve the problem he’s making.
explanation: Combative challenge rather than an attempt to bring the member along.

text: elections are meant to be a choice, a contest of ideas—a contest of ideas, not a contest of secrets. It seems like the Labour Party is wanting to have a contest of secrets.
explanation: Rhetorically tidy contrast aimed at his own side; not consensus-building.

text: Just last week, I had a young tradesman in his early 20s stop his ute, pull over and say to me, "Keep going. We need a National Government to keep building the future of this country."
explanation: Folksy, relatable story but speaks to the converted rather than persuading opponents.

text: As the Minister of Health, I want to see the focus go on the front line—more doctors, more nurses. I want to see more teachers and more police officers.
explanation: Appeals to broadly shared values (more frontline staff) but within a partisan frame.

text: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.
explanation: Inclusive, gracious acknowledgement reaching across affected groups rather than scoring points.

text: Well, I can tell you what: the Treaty has more principles than the Labour Party. It certainly has more transparency than the Labour Party.
explanation: Cheap-shot wordplay attacking the party's integrity rather than engaging substance.

text: Labour now has more leaks than Wellington Water. It's up to them to keep their house in order, but if my house was leaking as much as that, I'd be calling a plumber.
explanation: A jab at Labour's internal leaks; comedic point-scoring rather than substantive.

text: Well, we're working through a procurement process, but on this side of the House we are focused on affordable electricity prices, keeping the lights on, and protecting jobs, and the reality is, you can't run an electricity system on hope that it will rain. That's the Opposition's strategy—
explanation: The 'hope that it will rain' line caricatures the Opposition's position rather than engaging it.

text: I would have thought that member would have supported fast track, which is seeing... the biggest wind farm in New Zealand’s history... consented in the South Island... but no, he voted no to that. He’s voting no— to the very solutions that solve the problem he’s making.
explanation: Criticises the member's voting record — legitimate but accusatory ('the problem he's making').

text: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.
explanation: Respectful, dignified tone focused on those affected.

text: Oh, this is the language specialist here from the Wairarapa. Ha, ha! He’s the expert on diction. The fact that he’s not even trained or educated properly or anything else but knows a bit about horse betting—it’s his only qualification—never stops him from saying something, though, does it?
explanation: Pure personal mockery of a member's education and background; no policy content.

text: For the umpteenth time, and I’ll say it slowly... the person in charge of foreign policy is the Foreign Minister. That’s me, not the Prime Minister. Could the member get some updating—I know she had a lot of academic training but obviously no practical understanding of this game whatsoever.
explanation: Personal attack disparaging the member's competence ('no practical understanding').

text: If we'd not got back, these three parties, we were heading off to be Venezuela or Myanmar.
explanation: Sensationalist exaggeration aimed at opponents, though not a personal attack.

text: Well, we got trains back on track, and they’re working, unlike when you guys were there.
explanation: Pointed partisan dig but directed at the previous government's record rather than a personal insult.

text: and also congratulations to Chris Luxon and David Seymour in the formation of this Government, and their political parties
explanation: Courteous congratulation.

text: E hoki ki te kāinga, puhia ngā kurī, puhia i roto o Taranaki.
explanation: Translated as 'Go home, shoot the dogs, shoot them in Taranaki'; an inflammatory, off-topic remark that drew an objection and prompted an apology.

text: Yes, I can confirm there was some doodling left on the side of a Cabinet paper by the former Minister. There was, however, no budget, no proposal that I could credibly take forward to my colleagues. Consequently, we’ve taken the option of putting the acid on the oil companies to secure 28 days.
explanation: Belittles the predecessor's work as 'doodling on the side of a Cabinet paper', a personal/dismissive jab.

text: We are not going to meet the 2030 dreamy, fairy-tale, aspirational figures that we’ll be freeing ourselves of fossil fuels as a source of generating energy.
explanation: Derides the target as 'dreamy, fairy-tale' rather than engaging its feasibility on the merits.

text: Yes, including that the past Labour Government made a reckless decision in approving the closure of the Marsden Point refinery.
explanation: Opens an answer with an attack on the opposition's record.

text: Sir, it's a well-established tradition in the House that when moving from a general question to finicky pettifogging detail, you cannot expect the Prime Minister to have that detail. It's laid out in Speakers' rulings 197/2 and 197/4.
explanation: Dismisses opponents' questions as 'finicky pettifogging' but frames it as a procedural argument.

text: As I said, we are working through a process. Once that process is complete, decisions will be made and they'll be announced.
explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Simon Watts that without LNG there is no plan B for a dry year, he gives a pure process non-answer.

text: This Government is going through a procurement process... and the solution we provide won’t require waiting till 2037, costing $16 billion.
explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can have faith he hasn't pre-decided; repeats process talking points without addressing the concern.

text: The answer is that obligations sit in a number of places including, under the Privacy Act, on private companies, and, ultimately, the penalty regime in New Zealand is woeful, and it needs to be fixed. … It's all well and good for the former Minister on the other side of the House to sit there and complain, but we inherited a system from her, which we are now fixing.
explanation: Asked why he keeps deflecting blame when responsibilities lie with his Government; partly engages (obligations sit in multiple places) but again ends on blaming the former Minister.

text: Yes, those alternatives were considered. The member can find advice on the alternatives on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s website.
explanation: Direct yes plus a pointer to where the advice can be found.

text: This is a timely, temporary, and targeted response with the increase remaining in place for up to 12 months or until the price of 91 octane petrol falls below $3 per litre for four consecutive weeks. It will apply to home and community support workers who work for providers contracted by Health New Zealand, the Ministry of Social Development, and ACC.
explanation: Directly and completely answers how long the rate will remain.

text: the Government intends to invest up to $600 million in this programme through the Defence Capability Plan, with further homes planned through new builds and long-term leasing arrangements in locations that include Devonport, Trentham, and Whenuapai.
explanation: Largely future intent ('intends to invest', 'planned') beyond the already-delivered homes.

text: Dawn Aerospace, the University of Canterbury, and the University of Auckland were awarded a total of $1.48 million to support exciting projects, including flying a small satellite, biological microgravity experiments, and the CubeSat TPA-2 satellite hosting New Zealand's developed payloads.
explanation: An announced and awarded first round (action taken), though a pilot with outcomes still ahead.

text: These include specifically allowing for off-site construction to begin before a project information memorandum, or PIM, is issued by the local council. This will be a game-changer for the off-site manufacturing of minor dwellings. In addition, we are making changes to allow for more products to be used to construct granny flats, such as structural insulated panels with a CodeMark certificate.
explanation: Describes rule changes announced today; concrete but newly announced rather than long-implemented.

text: In response to the sustained impact of high fuel prices, we have increased by 50 percent the vehicle mileage reimbursement rates for eligible treatment-related travel... This targeted and temporary increase will remain in place while fuel prices stay elevated and is being kept under continual review with a clear threshold linked to petrol prices returning to more stable levels.
explanation: A concrete delivered measure ('we have increased'), not just a promise.

text: The Anzac Day Act has been modernised to acknowledge the service and sacrifice of all who have served New Zealand in times of war. Prior to the changes that we have made together, the Act failed to acknowledge conflicts and operations after 1966, meaning that many service personnel were technically excluded from official commemorations under the law.
explanation: Describes an enacted modernisation of the Anzac Day Act, a delivered legislative change he is responsible for.

text: the risk around the dry year has been costing New Zealand about $5 billion a year since 2017. Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I've said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.
explanation: Forecasts $265m/year savings and 2,000 jobs protected — a projected benefit whose accuracy is uncertain.

text: we have the City Rail Link project, we have major events funding coming, we have an Indian free-trade agreement coming on track. So we’ve got a lot of good things happening that will drive future growth and employment.
explanation: Predicts these will drive future growth and employment; plausible but vague and unquantified.

text: Now is not the time for a lecture to the member about the difference between criminal law and other, but I can only conclude she wasn't listening yesterday to the exchange across the House where I thought that was made tolerably clear.
explanation: A condescending jab ('she wasn't listening') aimed at the member rather than purely at the argument.

text: an “instrument of the Crown” is not a department but might otherwise describe—I’m trying not to use the word “entity”, because a Crown entity is different again. An example of the instrument of the Crown, I’m told, is PCO, the Parliamentary Counsel Office
explanation: Good-humoured, respectful follow-up to a colleague's query.

text: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
explanation: Disagrees on the substance respectfully.

text: The Government as a whole is responsible, but I would be remiss if I didn’t acknowledge the point that the member has prompted me to make, which is to say that New Zealand First has been very vociferous in the advocacy of the policy. I’ve been pleased to work alongside the Hon Shane Jones as well as Chris Bishop and, of course, the Government as a whole, and, I might add, we have been supported across the House in this endeavour.
explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of colleagues and opponents with no attack.

text: I think the member is a hard-working member of a hard-working committee—self-described but nevertheless, I’m sure exactly that.
explanation: Warm and respectful toward an opponent.

text: thinking about either malicious attacks or just mistakes or just data being lost: can I be reassured that there is some way that there will be paper? I’m not requiring any stone tablets to be produced by this Government or any other.
explanation: Good-humoured and non-adversarial.

text: While I was on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee and I generally support the direction, I just wanted to tease out some of what I would say were apparent inconsistencies.
explanation: Respectful framing focused on substance.

text: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.
explanation: Concedes merit across the aisle and signals openness to future work — consensus-building.

text: The Government as a whole is responsible, but I would be remiss if I didn’t acknowledge the point that the member has prompted me to make, which is to say that New Zealand First has been very vociferous in the advocacy of the policy. I’ve been pleased to work alongside the Hon Shane Jones as well as Chris Bishop and, of course, the Government as a whole, and, I might add, we have been supported across the House in this endeavour.
explanation: Generously shares credit across coalition partners and notes cross-House support; inclusive, bridge-building tone.

text: A number of veterans spoke to me throughout the day to express their appreciation for the recent changes passed by Parliament unanimously—thank you—in recognising the service of all of those who have served New Zealand... In the words of one gentleman at the Waimoku service... they no longer feel like second-class citizens on Anzac Day.
explanation: Acknowledges the unanimous cross-party support and thanks the House — inclusive and unifying.

text: I think the member is a hard-working member of a hard-working committee—self-described but nevertheless, I’m sure exactly that.
explanation: Good-humoured, gracious acknowledgement of an opposition member, lowering the temperature across the aisle.

text: I am urging, then, the select committee to go to Auckland Central and talk to the homeless whānau in Auckland Central. I am urging the select committee to go to Wellington Central, as well as the Rongotai, and talk to the constituents and talk to those people and our homeless whānau there.
explanation: Constructive call for the committee to engage directly with affected communities; inclusive but addressed to process rather than across party lines.

text: Noting that the dissolution of Parliament is on 1 October, I want to be balanced to say that even if we see a report-back date on 22 September, which grants an additional 2½ weeks on top of that... it still gives the current Government full ability to read this bill through all stages before the dissolution of Parliament.
explanation: Explicitly 'balanced', acknowledging the Government's legitimate interest in passing the bill before dissolution while still pressing for more time — a consensus-seeking framing.

text: will there be ways for us to be accessible from a disability lens, particularly when we’re looking at the ability for the new legislation website to have better ways for, I guess, speech transcription for those who are blind, in particular?
explanation: Advocates inclusion of an under-served group in a constructive way.

text: I do want to again acknowledge the Minister of Education for bringing this amendment to the House after hearing from the public.
explanation: Bridge-building tone that acknowledges an opponent's good action before pressing concerns.

text: I know that the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has a lot of questions around corporate tax, and I always learn a lot through her in a lot of these tax debates as a result, as well as the Minister, who, really, in the past has been incredibly helpful and informative in terms of our questions.
explanation: Warm, cross-party acknowledgement that builds goodwill.

text: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
explanation: Plausible interpretive argument that 'possible' would be read as 'reasonably possible'; some assertion rather than authority cited.

text: in the absence of any particular consequence being outlined for non-compliance with the particular requirements of new section 68A in terms of how law is to be published, I wouldn’t have thought there was any different outcome to that which would currently be the case.
explanation: Reasonable inference from the bill's silence on consequences, though no external authority cited.

text: Our prosperity and security depend on the sea. Recent events have shown how quickly disruptions to international shipping routes can affect supply chains. The oceans are a vital interest that must be actively secured.
explanation: Reasonable case linking maritime security to economic resilience, though stated at a general level without specifics.

text: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
explanation: Reasons by analogy from health-data breaches to a single-point-of-access legislation site; plausible but the analogy carries the argument.

text: thinking about either malicious attacks or just mistakes or just data being lost: can I be reassured that there is some way that there will be paper? I’m not requiring any stone tablets to be produced by this Government or any other.
explanation: Raises a legitimate redundancy/data-loss concern, but the case is made colourfully/rhetorically rather than with evidence.

text: when I actually look at the voting members, it has potential for a tie with no tiebreaker in that there are three appointed by the Minister, three appointed by the mayor—and we understand that already that power of the mayor is quite different from other councils around the country—and then they've got to agree on the chairperson.
explanation: Identifies a concrete structural deadlock risk by reasoning through the committee's composition.

text: they're not thrown out just because it was the other side that started them.
explanation: Sensible point about wasted spend, linked to the Infrastructure Commission report, though stated generally.

text: have some faith in our elected representatives to do the right thing because, ultimately, that's what we elect them for, and if we weren't all here to do the right thing, then we should probably walk out the door and go get another job.
explanation: Responds to a politicisation-of-appointments concern with an appeal to good faith rather than any safeguard or evidence.

text: I’m not convinced that that change would make a material difference. Of course, there are probably arguments that as soon as you’re accessing something online, through a device, you have actually downloaded that data, anyway, so there may well be some technical interpretation questions as to why you have “accessed… or downloaded” as being the option.
explanation: Plausible technical point that accessing online entails downloading, but somewhat asserted rather than established.

text: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
explanation: Reasoned point about reconciling cross-language interpretation, though asserted generally rather than evidenced.

text: the fact that the secondary legislation doesn't come into force until it's published kind of takes care of that. If the regulator wants the rule to be enforced or regulatable, they should publish it and bring it into force.
explanation: Reasoning is coherent: non-commencement-until-publication logically substitutes for a mandatory publication requirement.

text: If it was "must include", then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn't have to do it
explanation: Clean logical reasoning: a mandatory 'must include' would force reporting on a recommendation that may not exist.

text: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
explanation: Broad value statement with no mechanism or measure.

text: when I actually look at the voting members, it has potential for a tie with no tiebreaker in that there are three appointed by the Minister, three appointed by the mayor—and we understand that already that power of the mayor is quite different from other councils around the country—and then they've got to agree on the chairperson.
explanation: Spells out the exact membership numbers and the tie problem.

text: On behalf of the Minister for Auckland, it seems to me important that we take a holistic approach to the question. As I've indicated, as the Government, we're taking a number of different approaches which will be beneficial to the people of Auckland as a city and as a region and also for all of New Zealand.
explanation: Asked specifically why only 207 Housing First places for 940+ homeless and where they will go; answers with generalities and never engages the numbers.

text: As for the instrument of the Crown, I might benefit from some advice on that point and would look forward to coming back to him.
explanation: In response to Webb's direct question on what an 'instrument of the Crown' is, he honestly admits he cannot answer yet and defers.

text: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.
explanation: Gives a reason (more policy work/time) but stops short of fully resolving the drafting question.

text: the bill, we expect and hope, will come into force on 30 June of this year, with the powers to make secondary legislation as part of that and with the systems in place for the scheme to go live in August or September of this year.
explanation: Responds to Utikere's request for an indication of timeliness with concrete dates rather than deflecting.

text: It covers personnel from countries such as France and India in that campaign, along with civilians serving in medical units, members of the Merchant Navy during the world wars, and those who died while training for conflict. It also extends to post-Vietnam service, including veterans of Timor-Leste and Afghanistan, including the member herself
explanation: Directly answers the request for examples of who the new legislation covers.

text: By removing the need for a building and a resource consent, Kiwis will save up to $5,650 in direct costs and up to 14 weeks in paperwork.
explanation: 'Up to' framing flatters the figures, presenting a best case as the headline benefit.

text: Decades of underinvestment across successive Governments has meant that many military families were residing in homes that were no longer fit for modern family life—some dating back to the 1930s.
explanation: Claim of long-standing underinvestment and 1930s-era housing is plausible and broadly consistent with known defence estate issues.

text: Officials have told me that there have been some 94,000 views of the granny flat guidance web page and 52,000 downloads of the supporting resources.
explanation: Specific, checkable engagement figures attributed to officials; plausible, though web views are a weak proxy for the 'demand' claimed.

text: The Anzac Day Act has been modernised to acknowledge the service and sacrifice of all who have served New Zealand in times of war. Prior to the changes that we have made together, the Act failed to acknowledge conflicts and operations after 1966, meaning that many service personnel were technically excluded from official commemorations under the law.
explanation: Specific factual claim about the prior Act's 1966 cut-off; consistent with the described reform.

text: New Zealand law includes the Bill of Rights 1688, which is New Zealand law that predates New Zealand in terms of New Zealand
explanation: Accurate: the Bill of Rights 1688 is retained as part of New Zealand law (via the Imperial Laws Application Act 1988) and predates the modern NZ state.

text: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
explanation: Health-data systems including ManageMyHealth have been subject to security incidents; broadly accurate though stated generally.

text: When we’re seeing the wealth gap increasing by more than ever before in the history of Aotearoa
explanation: Superlative claim ('more than ever before in the history') is hyperbolic and unsupported; inequality trends do not clearly establish an all-time record.

text: One of the really important exercises that Auckland Council and Auckland Transport did a little while ago, under the advice of the seniors community group, was to get policymakers to, essentially, go from the Ferry Building in Britomart to, I believe, the Auckland War Memorial Museum without their smartphone and have to navigate public transport without that.
explanation: Specific factual recollection, appropriately hedged ('I believe'); plausible but not independently confirmed here.

text: the insertion of the definition around stored value instruments is a really important one, because... we do see more money-laundering happening by other avenues... It's really important in light of a drastic increase over the last decade of the use of cryptocurrency.
explanation: Cryptocurrency use has risen markedly over the decade; broadly accurate though 'drastic' is imprecise.

text: The one time that I can think of in recent history where it was actually successful in terms of getting the service put on when the service wasn’t supposed to be available actually wasn’t done by the Government or by the council but by FIFA, when they held the FIFA Women’s World Cup. FIFA actually managed to convince KiwiRail to actually put the service back on.
explanation: Plausible and consistent with the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup transport arrangements in Auckland; specific and checkable.

text: we are seeing, for example, in Canada, legislation is published in both English and French; and, for example, in Wales, legislation is published in both English and Welsh.
explanation: Accurate: Canadian federal legislation is bilingual (English/French) and Welsh legislation is published in English and Welsh.

text: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
explanation: Consistent with the Greens' stated accessibility/transparency positioning, but no action shown either way in the text.

text: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
explanation: Forecast that the regulations 'will require' machine-readable formats; plausible given the stated policy intent, but contingent on future regulations.

text: In terms of Air New Zealand, they have provided me with reassurances consistently that the changes they are making to their routes right now are temporary to address the current fuel crisis... maintaining regional connectivity is our number one priority.
explanation: Implicit prediction that route changes are temporary; depends on the fuel crisis easing, uncertain.

text: The cost-benefit analysis done by officials shows that these changes are expected to deliver between $2.6 billion and $4.1 billion in net benefits to Kiwis over 30 years through reduced inspection fees, less time spent on compliance, and fewer unnecessary repairs.
explanation: Projects $2.6–4.1bn benefits over 30 years; long-horizon official estimates of this kind are highly uncertain.

text: If we invest thousands in supporting the first thousand days of a child’s life, we can save millions in long-term costs that stem from poor health and poor education.
explanation: Conditional long-run prediction of fiscal savings; directionally supported by early-childhood evidence but magnitude and timeframe uncertain.

text: If we are sensible with the rules and the regulations that we put in place about who can work in our education and health systems, for example, by allowing those who train in CANZUK countries—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to work here as a right, we will save millions in costs associated with burnout and the constant under-resourcing of those sectors.
explanation: Predicts savings and reduced burnout; plausible but the 'save millions' outcome is asserted and depends on uptake and recognition standards.

text: It is the case that if a piece of secondary legislation is needing to be published, which provides a consolidation of all secondary legislation that incorporates all of the amendments made by every amending instrument—if it doesn't meet the requirements of publication, it is all repealed. So I have to correct that: it is all repealed.
explanation: Self-correction shows consistency between his stated aim of clarity and his conduct.

text: It’s not the State that saved my family; it was my mum. She took responsibility for our situation.
explanation: Consistent with the limited-government, individual-responsibility worldview he advances throughout; the personal account aligns with the stated value.

text: Yes, I am confident that my health and safety reforms focus on practical, common-sense changes that set businesses up for success in keeping people safe. The advice I received from my officials is that my reforms shift the focus towards managing critical risks and support the continued reduction in the incidence of serious workplace injuries and fatalities, thereby reducing the costs of these incidents for ACC.
explanation: Describes the direction (critical-risk focus) but without figures or specific provisions.

text: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market.
explanation: Names the commitment, timeframe (100 days) and intent to act before agreements finalise.

text: I'm advised that Fire and Emergency is taking a coordinated set of actions to manage the current fuel prices and potential supply pressures. They have established a Fuel Planning Group … classified as a 'critical customer' … working closely with their sector partners, including New Zealand Police and St John.
explanation: Names the Fuel Planning Group, the 'critical customer' classification, and the partner agencies.

text: It also means no more waiting for six months to access sick leave or 12 months to access annual leave.
explanation: Concrete timeframes (six months, 12 months) and a specific effect of the bill.

text: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
explanation: Precise figures (70%, 67%) tied to named groups.

text: I have been assured that no front-line firefighters or comms centre positions are proposed to be affected. However, on the other hand, I’m advised that savings will be reinvested in areas including those that support the safety of volunteers and paid firefighters, such as fleet, training and equipment.
explanation: Relayed assurances ('I have been assured'/'I'm advised') presented honestly as second-hand.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
explanation: Reframes 'cuts' as 'efficiencies' and cites a specific investment figure; the framing is contestable but the figure is concrete.

text: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
explanation: Presented as fact from the consultation; specific but unverifiable from the text.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand has inherited decades of under-investment in old trucks with the amalgamation of multiple services into one. They have a plan, and have had a plan for a number of years, to invest in new fleet and equipment. This year alone, they have a plan to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment.
explanation: Concrete, checkable budget figure presented as fact.

text: The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction.
explanation: Dates and the broad failure to complete Holidays Act reform are accurate to the public record.

text: The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction.
explanation: Criticism of the previous government's delay, but focused on the policy record rather than personal attack.

text: As I said, if this question had actually been about the fuel plan, I would've been able to come to the House with those relevant pieces of information. … I've had the exact same question in writing for pretty much month on month on month on end, and it's very difficult to know where she's going to go with the technical aspects of the question.
explanation: Mildly dismissive of the persistent questioner without a personal attack.

text: I’m not responsible for ACC itself, however the scale of ACC costs are not the sole indicator of whether or not the health and safety system is working well... I hear this constantly from the Opposition. It is clearly misleading.
explanation: Accuses the Opposition of being 'clearly misleading' — combative but about the argument, not the person.

text: Ah, she’s bit confused there, because the premise of the report was, actually, that for private counsellors, the cost was going up, resulting in delays for people going private, which is quite contrary to that question.
explanation: 'She's a bit confused' is a mild personal jab, though paired with a substantive point about the report's premise.

text: If the National Party had an off week last week, isn’t Labour having a terrible week this time? The emperor has no clothes.
explanation: Rhetorical jab at the opposing party rather than engagement with substance.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: 'Absolutely disgusting' is heated, but directed at spending decisions rather than a person.

text: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
explanation: Caricatures opponents' position rather than engaging specific objections.

text: food prices increased by over 12 percent in the year to March 2023. In the year to March 2026, food prices increased by 3.4 percent. It’s a much better improvement than that Government, when they sat on their hands.
explanation: ‘Sat on their hands’ is a dismissive jab attached to an otherwise factual comparison.

text: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
explanation: Partisan but framed around policy/funding decisions rather than personal attack.

text: I am proud of the significant progress made already, to have legislation ready and available for public feedback—a milestone that successive Ministers tried and failed to reach.
explanation: Claims progress, but the deliverable is legislation out for feedback, not yet enacted — intent with in-progress delivery.

text: Yesterday, I launched Anzac Stories with Archives New Zealand and the National Library. … The stories are of real people, places, animals, and items and are designed with the help of students from Belmont School in Lower Hutt and Adventure School in Porirua.
explanation: Describes a concrete initiative actually launched, not merely promised.

text: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market.
explanation: Stated commitment to repeal in progress; delivery announced but not yet completed.

text: I recently announced at the inaugural World Rural Health Conference in New Zealand that the Government would invest $1 million to train rural GPs to deliver planned-care services locally. This will increase access to support for people living in rural areas and reduce the need for hospital visits.
explanation: A funding announcement; delivery and uptake still to come.

text: For the first time, the Government’s target of 25 percent of the ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding has been invested in prevention and early intervention.
explanation: Claims a target met 'for the first time', suggesting actual delivery on a prevention commitment.

text: We’ve funded 74 clinical psychology interns, exceeding the 2025 target of 60... We’ve also seen a record uptake in psychiatry, with 48 first-year registrars entering training last year, up from 33 in 2024. That’s a 50 percent increase.
explanation: Shows targets met/exceeded on training intakes, evidencing follow-through.

text: Last month, I opened a new dedicated child mental health service in Counties Manukau. The service has been established to support young people, up to intermediate age, along with their families who are experiencing, or are at risk of developing, moderate to severe mental health challenges.
explanation: Reports a service actually opened last month.

text: The latest quarterly data shows we’ve exceeded our target for training 500 mental health and addiction workers a year, with 514 in training over the past year, up from 457 in the previous year... we’ve grown the front-line workforce by over 11 percent since coming to office.
explanation: Demonstrates delivery against a workforce target with year-on-year improvement.

text: That sort of question would have been quite helpful to have in writing as the primary question. That sort of detail can be sourced through a written parliamentary question.
explanation: Asked how many days of operational diesel reserves Fire and Emergency holds, she declines to answer and redirects to written questions.

text: I listened to small businesses and workers on my roadshows who told me that some health and safety professionals advised them to go to a lot of effort on ineffective paper-based compliance that does not reduce harm.
explanation: Reframes rather than directly engaging whether the experts calling it a 'regression' are correct.

text: I am not excluding psychosocial risk. If a psychosocial risk is likely to result in a death, notifiable injury, illness, or incident, then it must be managed as a critical risk. An example would be where stress could lead to serious accidents in the workplace.
explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of removal and explains the threshold, though doesn't address the 97 percent / 40 suicides figures specifically.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
explanation: Directly disputes the premise of the question and offers a counter-figure.

text: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market.
explanation: Clearly states Government policy in response to the question asked.

text: So I suggest that member look in the mirror.
explanation: Jackson asked whether she modelled the social/fiscal costs of hardship; she does not answer at all.

text: I accept that there are many families who are doing it tough right now. While it would be nice to have said that we had inherited a set of economic circumstances that made it easier for people and families to get ahead, that is not the case. In Budget 2024, our Government prioritised reducing the number of children in poverty with the measures that I outlined before to lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
explanation: Asked to commit to urgent pre-Budget actions for Te Tai Tokerau and, if not, why not; does not commit and points back to Budget 2024.

text: One was the Smithfield Alliance in Timaru, with about 700 affected workers, and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) worked very closely on the ground with those workers. The example that the member gave in Tokoroa, project phoenix, was stood up as a combination of work across Government agencies, council, and Toi Ohomai to work really closely with affected workers, and I'm really proud of what MSD have done on the ground.
explanation: Andersen asked how she is creating the conditions for jobs amid mass closures; the Minister answers with two redeployment examples within portfolio scope rather than the broader question.

text: If people have income from boarders, it should be counted against any housing or income support they receive from taxpayers. We want a fair, transparent, and equal system where those who require support get it if they don’t unnecessarily burden other taxpayers with support they shouldn’t have access to.
explanation: Engages the boarder-income policy but reframes around fairness rather than directly conceding people are left worse off.

text: Of the estimated 9,300 clients impacted by the entry threshold change, 6,400 are identified as families with children... the estimated average reduction in the entitlement will be $42 per week.
explanation: Directly answers both parts of the question — the number of families with children affected and the average weekly reduction.

text: What I can do is name a number of iwi leaders who are very disappointed with the performance of the spokesperson on Māori-Crown relations on that side of the House.
explanation: Asked to name one iwi/hapū supporting the review; names none and deflects into an attack on the questioner.

text: Again, I want to ensure that the maths from the Opposition member is accurate and credible, because, as we know, sometimes it isn’t.
explanation: Asked to admit more Māori went into unemployment than employment on his watch; deflects by questioning the asker's figures.

text: I respect the significant responsibility that Ngāi Tahu has in its takiwā and the ongoing relationships and partnerships that it has with the Department of Conservation... There is a wide variety of views, often with the same person, and we are absolutely focused that we build a better system for conservation—better for Kiwis, and better for all New Zealanders.
explanation: Does not directly say whether he agrees with the chair's characterisation.

text: we are not for the mandatory repayments considering the massive material impacts that would have on liquidity and other dynamics that would accrue to the retirement village operators ... particularly with the provision of aged care and the nature of the thin margins
explanation: Answers the retrospectivity question on mandatory repayments but does not address the fairness-to-residents core of Leary's question.

text: I am advised that since around June 2024, there has been a net reduction of 25.4 fulltime-equivalent staff at Te Puni Kōkiri.
explanation: Directly provides the specific staffing figure asked about.

text: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
explanation: Uses survey evidence to support the case for change rather than mere assertion.

text: I listened to small businesses and workers on my roadshows who told me that some health and safety professionals advised them to go to a lot of effort on ineffective paper-based compliance that does not reduce harm.
explanation: Rests on anecdotes from roadshows rather than the official advice cited against her reforms.

text: I agree with my statement, and I also agree with the recommendations from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s (MBIE’s) regulatory impact statement before the fair pay agreements legislation was passed, where MBIE recommended against introducing fair pay agreements.
explanation: Grounds her position in a specific official document (MBIE's regulatory impact statement) rather than assertion alone.

text: If any fair pay agreements were finalised, the increased costs would have greatly affected a range of businesses up and down the country, regardless of whether they could have afforded them. This would have increased prices for consumers and could cause business closures, which is worse for employees. I don’t consider that a blunt tool will help our labour markets for either employers or employees.
explanation: Coherent cost-to-prices-to-closures chain, but presented as certain without supporting data.

text: Horticulture New Zealand said, “This will be a burden on the Government to administer and compliance check yet another regulatory instrument being imposed on business. Most businesses will likely have to employ additional resource to administer the regime—where their margins are already very stretched.”
explanation: Supports her case by citing specific stakeholder submissions rather than bare assertion, though the sources are themselves opposed parties.

text: we have seen an increase in the number of special needs grants that have been granted for food for the month of March, which tells me the system is working.
explanation: Treats rising hardship-grant volume as evidence the system 'is working' — the conclusion does not follow from the premise.

text: Well, I accept that the immediate challenge that we're facing as a country due to the conflict in the Middle East that is completely outside any New Zealander's control is adding a layer of pressure to organisations at the front line.
explanation: Attributes hardship to the Middle East conflict without addressing the cited domestic data point.

text: despite it being challenging, in the last year, we saw 84,000 New Zealanders leave welfare into work. That's why I'm confident that what we are doing is working.
explanation: Cites a gross outflow figure as proof of success without addressing rising jobseeker numbers.

text: There were 60,000 people in case management, and there are now 70,000. Case management is the most effective programme that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) funds and delivers, and it is the significant increase in the number of people in case management that is a strong correlation to what we are seeing in terms of work exits.
explanation: Carefully says 'strong correlation' rather than causation, but uses it to imply the driver of work exits — correlation leaned on as evidence.

text: Well, there haven’t been any policy changes around advance payments, and MSD make decisions at the front line to assess an individual’s situation and their needs. Particularly with advanced payments, there is a caution because, obviously, when payments are made in advance, that means there are less in the following weeks for a beneficiary to look after their costs with.
explanation: Offers a coherent reason advances are treated cautiously (they reduce future weekly income).

text: what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector.
explanation: Implies an emerging recovery; directionally supported by cited filled-jobs data but uncertain as a forecast.

text: Well, I remain optimistic that our economic plan is working, and, as I said, business confidence is the highest it’s been since 2014. Will we get the target or not? We’ll get close
explanation: Predicts getting 'close' to the jobseeker reduction target, against Treasury advice of a large miss; optimistic vs current evidence.

text: 18- and 19-year-olds who currently go on to welfare are, on average, going to spend another 21 years on welfare.
explanation: An actuarial forward projection of welfare duration; model-based and plausible directionally but sensitive to assumptions and hard to verify.

text: If the National Party had an off week last week, isn’t Labour having a terrible week this time? The emperor has no clothes.
explanation: An applause line for his own side; combative rather than consensus-building.

text: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
explanation: Rallying his own side via a blanket characterisation of opponents.

text: Don’t let them gaslight you that the National Party voted for and supported their more than $60 billion spend-up. Yes, we supported the core and immediate health and wage support response, but, no, we never supported the billions of dollars in subsequent wastage
explanation: Defends the consistency of his party's voting record (backed core support, opposed later spending); plausible but unverified from the text.

text: with this anti -money-laundering third reading that it exactly exemplifies what this Government is all about: reducing business compliance costs, improving regulatory effectiveness and efficiency, continuing regulatory compliance with related international obligations, and providing sufficient funding for the regulatory system, and, of course, one single supervisor.
explanation: Ties the bill to the Government's consistent deregulatory agenda.

text: The economic landscape and consumer habits have evolved rapidly since the last revision of Fair Trading Act penalties, in 2014, under the last National Government.
explanation: Acknowledges it was his own party's previous government that last set the now-outdated penalties — an even-handed admission.

text: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
explanation: Predicts continued youth emigration to Australia absent policy change; directionally consistent with current net-migration trends but conditional and unquantified.

text: When Labour takes over in November this year, that’s exactly the Government New Zealand will have.
explanation: Predicts Labour wins the November 2026 election; a verifiable forecast but uncertain and self-interested, no polling cited.

text: in this Budget alone, 86,000 households will have their rent increased by $30, and 30,000 of those households are pensioners; the 8,700 public servants losing their jobs
explanation: Predicts rent rises of $30 for 86,000 households from Budget changes; directionally plausible but magnitude uncertain.

text: In 20 years, Māori will be over 25 percent of the population and the median age for Māori will be mid-30s, compared to early 40s for the rest of the population.
explanation: 20-year demographic projection consistent with StatsNZ population trends; demographic forecasts of this kind are relatively reliable.

text: The amendments proposed in this bill threaten that. They threaten kaitiakitanga, they threaten the value of consulting with kaitiaki and, therefore, the sustainability of our kāpata kai and, potentially, the sustainability of our commercial interests.
explanation: Predicts harm to sustainability of food sources and commercial interests if the bill proceeds — plausible but magnitude and timeframe uncertain.

text: by 2040, we’re going to hit 90 percent of debt-to-GDP, and by the 2060s, debt-to-GDP will balloon to 200 percent.
explanation: Long-range projection drawn from Treasury’s no-policy-change scenario; such scenarios are illustrative of trajectory, not forecasts, so high uncertainty over 15–40 years.

text: I say this because New Zealand has near on $200 billion of nominal debt and that has an interest attachment to that... Over the last few weeks that risk premium has gone up and we should expect it is going to make a difference to the Budget that is going to be announced in May.
explanation: Predicts the risk premium will affect the May Budget — plausible and near-term, though the size is unspecified.

text: I know that the next few months will be extremely tough for this country... but this too shall pass and I remain optimistic in this country. Brighter days will return, because this Government has a good plan.
explanation: Predicts tough months followed by recovery; directionally plausible but too vague on timeframe and magnitude to falsify precisely.

text: the cost of living crisis is what’s biting people more than ever before. And that’s going to get worse under this Government.
explanation: Predicts worsening cost of living under the current government; partisan and unquantified, evidence mixed.

text: I’m confident that this bill will fulfil its promise and protect the legacy of Charles Rooking Carter and continue to serve the Carterton community for at least another 130 years.
explanation: A 130-year forecast of community benefit—rhetorical and effectively unfalsifiable over that horizon, plausible in direction only.

text: Chanel plans to build on Lammermoor's organic status and achieve regenerative organic certification. That would make Lammermoor the world's first fine-wool producing farm with those credentials.
explanation: Forecasts a future certification and 'world's first' status — plausible but contingent on Chanel's plans.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Asserts profligacy by appeal to her own governance experience rather than evidence.

text: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
explanation: Reasonable argument (majority + inaction) but asserts they ‘didn’t address’ long-term issues without specifics here.

text: The reason that these are good is that they both reduce the burden of administration on businesses and those who are trying to legitimately raise capital or other financing, while still protecting and detecting criminal activities.
explanation: Identifies the balance the bill aims to strike; coherent but high-level.

text: Meta is not as transparent, although they will tell us, and they did tell us, that they are the most transparent. If you go to the transparency centre for Meta, however, what you will find is a step process that they go through and it gets to a point where it says, basically, in not so many words, “and then the algorithm does its magic”.
explanation: Supports the lack-of-transparency claim with a concrete example of Meta's own materials, contrasted with TikTok's researcher access.

text: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
explanation: Walks through the recommendation-engine mechanism to a clear conclusion about the attention/advertising incentive; logically connected and evidence-grounded.

text: how is that fair to existing residents when they're going to be worse off? ... if a vast number of New Zealanders see three months as a fairer repayment time, which is in my member's bill, would he consider reducing the repayment time, given that he seems to have arbitrarily chosen one year, which is what the operators want
explanation: Builds a fairness argument from concrete contract mechanics, though 'arbitrarily' and 'what operators want' are assertions.

text: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
explanation: Draws a pointed consistency argument — bipartisan harm-reduction talk alongside a bill she says expands a harmful market; specific, though the 'archaic definitions' claim is asserted.

text: There is no silver bullet, as has been expressed. A blanket ban sends a good signal and may have some help, but really, we need a multi-layered approach... We need education, we need prevention, we need peer support, we need accessible youth mental health care, and we need the platforms to take responsibility for the environments that they create.
explanation: Acknowledges a ban's limited utility and lays out a coherent multi-pronged response rather than a single fix.

text: One of them reports in its 2025 annual report that it has $600 million worth of undrawn debt capacity—in other words, that's the capacity of the retirement village residents' money—but also they have 27 percent of uncommitted arrays in stock and also 31 percent of a contract pipeline increase.
explanation: Uses operator financial disclosures to rebut the Minister's liquidity argument — evidence-based reasoning.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Holds competing truths together without false dichotomy—nuanced reasoning about a complicated legacy.

text: That is exactly what is being suggested. That is exactly—that's a slightly more efficient approach, but the Greens don't know what efficiency is.
explanation: Dismissive jab that strawmans the opposing position instead of rebutting the 'shut down the case' distinction.

text: because the largest item that they sold by turnover was Snapper—that is the Wellington public transport card—and it was slightly, slightly bigger—fractionally bigger—than the amount of food that they sold, we couldn't give them a liquor licence. They had a choice between either giving up the ability to sell public transport cards or not getting a liquor licence.
explanation: Uses a single anecdote to argue the law is arbitrary; persuasive but a generalisation from one case.

text: Yeah, the Auditor-General should have picked that up—absolutely. Lots of people should have picked that up, but we haven't, and that is one of the reasons we have an infrastructure deficit which looks as it does.
explanation: Links oversight failure to the infrastructure deficit, but the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

text: Two million, 1.6 million, 1.4 million—these are theoretical houses. They are the houses that conceivably could be built under a set of planning rules, but they are not the houses that will be built.
explanation: Draws a clear, valid distinction between zoning-enabled capacity and actual delivery.

text: We asked them that question: "What proportion of the costs of growth are paid for by that growth?" ... And they said, "Rough order of magnitude: 30 to 50 percent." That means that 50 to 70 percent is paid for by existing ratepayers, existing taxpayers, existing consumers. Growth is not paying for growth.
explanation: Evidence-based: cites the Infrastructure Commission's testimony and draws the arithmetic conclusion that follows.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Direction (orderly investment pipeline) but no amounts, named projects, or timing.

text: This bill is about reducing the compliance burden for making simple transactions and lending; for people to get on and get things done that they want. This is a practical and responsible bill, and I commend it to the House.
explanation: States the bill's general purpose (reducing compliance burden) but offers no figures, mechanisms, or named provisions.

text: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
explanation: Names a real mechanism (KiwiSaver default payments) but no rate, amount, or date.

text: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Identifies a precise mechanism (beneficial instruction changes auto-applied to pending residence applications).

text: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
explanation: Describes concrete mechanisms (data harvesting, amplification, attention-optimisation) rather than slogans.

text: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
explanation: Names a concrete idea (solar power, energy independence) but only as something to ‘explore’, no commitment or detail.

text: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
explanation: Names an alleged power but vaguely ('a heck of a lot of powers') without citing the clause.

text: Trumpism is well and truly here.
explanation: Vague slogan with no concrete content.

text: Here are the three steps we need to take: we need to overcome the political inertia to fix the broken electricity market... We need to support grid-scale renewables for households, communities, and iwi... And we need to beef up energy conservation
explanation: Lays out three named directions but without figures, mechanisms, or timeframes for delivery.

text: Everyone I've met with—everyone from the big end of town: the gentailers, the Major Electricity Users' Group, Electricity Networks Aotearoa, the Energy Trusts of New Zealand, the gas industry, to the smaller actors like the independent generators and retailers, the social retailers, the innovators, and those working at the bleeding edge of energy hardship, the Community Energy Network members—everyone has said that we need a national energy strategy.
explanation: Names many specific sector bodies and actors he consulted.

text: This Government has already cut $178 million of funding from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority, which provided funding for hot-water heating, low-cost energy-efficiency measures, an LED lighting scheme
explanation: Names the amount, the agency, and the affected programmes.

text: The latest stats are shocking. They're horrific: 44,000 more people could not pay their gas, electricity, or water bills on time; 65,000 more households couldn't afford to keep their homes affordably warm; 23,000 more households had a major problem with damp and mould.
explanation: Cites precise figures across three measures of energy hardship.

text: They want no congestion. They want to be able to use a good public transport system. Those things affect all of us. They affect all people, regardless of whether they are Māori or whether they are non-Māori.
explanation: General aspiration about wanting good transport, no mechanism or measure.

text: Now, Māori, actually, it doesn’t even say it’s in Auckland. Essentially, it could be one fifth of the entire population of New Zealand. In fact, it doesn’t even say you’ve got to be in New Zealand.
explanation: Concrete in scoping the term's potential breadth, but the consultation context he later concedes (public stage captures all Māori) qualifies it.

text: If we spend, in this case, $5.5 billion dollars on creating this CRL capacity, if you like, and we don’t develop around that, we are not fully recovering the value.
explanation: Names the CRL cost figure and ties it to a value-recovery argument.

text: the Infrastructure Commission has been very clear that growth is not paying for growth. At best, it’s paying for 50 percent of growth; at worst, 30 percent. The rest of that is falling on the taxpayer, the ratepayer, and whoever else it might be.
explanation: Cites a source and concrete percentage range.

text: Of the 11 major ports we’ve got, all of them are at least partially council owned; seven are fully council owned; three are partially privatised—Tauranga, Napier, and South Port—and one, Eastland, is owned by a community trust.
explanation: Precise figures and named ports for the ownership breakdown.

text: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
explanation: Accepts shared blame across parties rather than scoring points; builds common ground.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Explicit cross-party, consensus-seeking call for a bipartisan infrastructure pipeline.

text: This bill has had very wide support across the House, and I also add my support.
explanation: Notes cross-House agreement, but is a brief endorsement rather than an active attempt to build consensus.

text: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
explanation: Combative rallying of her own side; no attempt to persuade across the aisle.
