explanation: Names the institution, a dollar figure ($34.7m) and a named project, though 'subject to business case' leaves the timeline conditional.

text: the unique residential agricultural training facility Telford will be receiving $2.4 million to address deferred maintenance to ensure a fit for purpose, fully functioning agricultural campus.
explanation: Exact dollar figure, named facility and purpose (deferred maintenance).

text: We have learnt, from the past excesses of the COVID responses, that if the response is not targeted, timely, and temporary, the whole of New Zealand will suffer with increased inflation.
explanation: Asserts a causal link to COVID overspend and inflation without supporting evidence; an appeal to recent experience.

text: Based on the most recent figures published by Stats New Zealand, 48 percent of all children in material hardship—around 81,000—are in working households. Not all of these children will be in households eligible for the in-work tax credit, as some families in material hardship have incomes above the Working for Families threshold.
explanation: Cites the source data and notes the threshold qualification rather than overclaiming.

text: Labour were a party at the election who stood for nothing.
explanation: Unsupported absolute ('stood for nothing') functioning as a rhetorical slogan.

text: They are two entirely different visa categories that we treat completely differently. One is an Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV); one is an investor migrant programme. With everyone who comes in on an AEWV, we have a set level of English that is required for residence which has been set since the early 2000s and that this Government does not have any plans to change because it is important for settlement in New Zealand.
explanation: Draws a category distinction, though it sidesteps why outcomes (time in NZ) differ.

text: It's not university-level English, as the member is saying; it is literally the base level you need to be able to study at university. It is a long-held policy in this country, since the early 2000s, that a high level of English is required to settle well in New Zealand and to gain residence.
explanation: Distinguishes the actual standard from the member's characterisation, citing longstanding policy.

text: The 2024 ERO or Education Review Office report statistics speak for themselves: 70 percent of employers did not consider NCEA level 1 to be credible; 60 percent of teachers didn’t think it was a reliable measure of what students know and can do; half of parents and 40 percent of students don’t understand how the system works.
explanation: Grounds the policy rationale in cited survey evidence, though 'speak for themselves' leans on the data without further analysis.

text: A judicial review is more appropriate for evaluating decisions such as those that are to be made by a redress officer where the issue is about the reasonableness of the decision rather than the weight that it is right or wrong... and the right to seek a judicial review is enshrined in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Judicial Review Procedure Act.
explanation: Draws a clear distinction between appeal (findings of fact) and judicial review (reasonableness) and applies it to the redress officer's role.

text: Genuine consultation is about making sure you take time to get the detail right... Perhaps if this good process had been followed the last time NCEA was refreshed, it wouldn’t have been such an unmitigated disaster—take note.
explanation: Combative toward the Opposition rather than consensus-building.

text: What parents do like to talk to me about is the curriculum, and not only the New Zealand curriculum but the refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa, which is an amazing document that we have completely refreshed in under two years, and I would have expected questions around the work we have done on Te Marautanga o Aotearoa rather than a defence of their woeful education record in Government.
explanation: Rallies her own side and dismisses opponents; not consensus-building.

text: One retired teacher wrote to me to say, “I applaud your strategies and desire to elevate learning outcomes for students. I’m ashamed of the New Zealand Post Primary Teachers’ Association for wanting to choke your timely initiatives.”
explanation: Marshals supportive voices but in a one-sided way that does not engage critics' substance.

text: a vast majority of those are jobs that are on the green list, people that we need, like doctors, lawyers—sorry, not lawyers; we don’t need any more lawyers—nurses, teachers, engineers, and people who are in high-skilled roles that are in demand on the green list... they have to be labour market tested and there has to be a genuine job here in New Zealand for those roles.
explanation: The self-correcting lawyers joke lightens the exchange and reads as good-humoured.

text: new curriculum-aligned writing workbooks that are available to benefit up to 130,000 year 4 and 5 students... a funded digital writing tool benefiting more than 200,000 students in years 6 to 8 each year... it’s all going to be available in te reo Māori as well.
explanation: Responds to the te reo Māori heckle inclusively by confirming materials will be available in te reo, rather than dismissing it.

text: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
explanation: Names broad values (fairness, environment, community) but no concrete measures or mechanisms.

text: Pam from Aranui, who’s run a campaign to bring the bus back to Aranui. She’s taken her plea to the regional council this week, and the regional council have committed to bringing a bus back to Aranui.
explanation: Concrete local example with named place, actor, and a specific council commitment.

text: Agriculture, including horticulture, is the largest sector of New Zealand's tradable economy and represents about 80 percent of all merchandise exports.
explanation: Gives a concrete share (about 80 percent) and frames it precisely as merchandise exports.

text: at a time when youth unemployment is at 15 percent and, in some areas, NEET rates are over 40 percent
explanation: Gives precise percentages.

text: good people who are being forced out of vital work to pay for $3 billion of tax cuts for mega landlords and $300 million for big tobacco.
explanation: Names dollar amounts and the beneficiary groups.

text: the other side of the House believe in progressing an agenda that continues to leave people behind, but not as an unintended consequence of the agenda they’re pushing; it is, in fact, on purpose. And that is the very worst kind of politics.
explanation: Asserts intent to harm without evidence.

text: you need a plan, you need a strategy, and intention and hope is not a strategy.
explanation: A reasonable critique of governing without a plan, though stated as an aphorism rather than backed with specifics at this point.

text: this very bill—removes one of the key institutional reforms that was designed to and was successfully keeping pressure on the sector. The Grocery Commissioner was created because the supermarket duopoly was failing consumers, suppliers, and competitors.
explanation: Connects the institution's removal to weakened oversight, a coherent argument.

text: Reckons are a very dangerous thing when it comes to introducing new bills or changing laws. If we're just going to do that based on some reckons, we have to be very certain through the select committee process to establish that that's not the case and actually to follow a good process.
explanation: Argues for evidence-based law-making over impression ('reckons') and for verification via process — a sound methodological point, though colloquially put.

text: Just yesterday, One NZ came here to Parliament and released their second annual report into trust in AI... There were five major signals highlighted in this report that shape AI trust in New Zealand: (1) AI is becoming mainstream, but meaningful adoption remains shallow; (2) public sentiment is shifting from curiosity to scrutiny; (3) trust is being shaped by experience, not perception; (4) human oversight is becoming the baseline for trust... (5) AI's value case is narrowing as expectations of guard rails rise.
explanation: Marshals a named, dated report and its structured findings to argue that AI cannot simply replace public-service workers; evidence supports the conclusion.

text: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
explanation: Appeals to shared values, but framed as 'us vs that Government' rather than reaching across the aisle.

text: the other side of the House believe in progressing an agenda that continues to leave people behind, but not as an unintended consequence of the agenda they’re pushing; it is, in fact, on purpose. And that is the very worst kind of politics.
explanation: Pure us-vs-them framing that demonises the other side.

text: the other side of the House are worried about putting Robbie Williams into a stadium. That’s all you’ve got: Robbie Williams into a stadium.
explanation: Crowd-pleasing jibe aimed at his own side, not persuasion.

text: I actually would like to thank the Minister for the generosity of the answers and the engagement that she provided through that committee of the whole House process. It was a very good backwards and forwards exchange.
explanation: Builds goodwill by crediting an opponent's conduct.

text: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
explanation: Position is consistent with Labour's stated wellbeing-Budget framework he is defending.

text: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
explanation: An opposition commitment ('the Labour Party absolutely will') with no mechanism or delivered record attached — aspiration.

text: That's why we think three free GP visits is a good idea: because we know how to measure wellbeing.
explanation: A policy idea floated from opposition, not a delivered or in-progress commitment.

text: We clearly will be voting against this motion, and select committees should be respected and given the time that they need to make a good job.
explanation: A concrete commitment to vote against, but it is an opposition stance with no delivery dimension—intent rather than demonstrated result.

text: The other side of the House would rather just absolutely waste away your taxpayer money and borrow money to put us into significant debt.
explanation: Caricatures opponents as wanting to 'waste' money; partisan attack on motive rather than engagement with their position.

text: it has become a group of Wellington bureaucrats that are the taste police on content on the internet
explanation: Derisive 'taste police' framing of the BSA; aimed at an institution rather than a person, but sensationalised.

text: Under this bill, a company may not exploit a single human being, it could even be a model employer, but if it misses a paperwork deadline or files a deficient statement, it faces up to $200,000 in fines. This is not a policy brought on a cornerstone of freeing victims; it is built on filling in forms and ticking boxes.
explanation: Pointed but aimed at the bill's design, not the proponents personally.

text: Let me be absolutely clear: modern slavery is a moral abomination. The exploitation of human beings has no place here in New Zealand or around the world. There is not a single person in this House who is soft on slavery.
explanation: Explicitly credits all members, including opponents, as opposed to slavery before raising her disagreement.

text: I really do want to acknowledge all of the members and all of their views, because I do know that there are quite a lot of different views on this.
explanation: Respectful framing that validates differing positions.

text: at its heart, it’s not just a technical reform of the Commerce Commission; it’s a political choice. It’s a deliberate choice to weaken every watchdog that helps keep prices down for Kiwi families
explanation: Frames the reform as a deliberate choice to harm families; pointed attack on motive, though aimed at policy.

text: Reassurance is not a plan, talking points are not a plan, and rural New Zealand knows it.
explanation: Sharp critique of the Government's response as empty words — aimed at the substance of their approach rather than a personal attack.

text: At its heart, you know, this is modest, but it's an important piece of legislation. It's not trying to reinvent the wheel... It's about stewardship; it's about making sure a historical charitable arrangement continues to deliver real value to the Carterton community, and Labour supports that approach.
explanation: Measured, respectful, cross-party support framed around shared stewardship.

text: the Hon Dr Duncan Webb eloquently highlighted that illicit drugs, they are out of control in New Zealand, and any legislation that helps curb that is very important and also curbing the criminals—the white collar criminals—that sit at the top of some of this criminal architecture
explanation: Substantive, no personal attack; credits a colleague.

text: We're also keen to ensure that we do not disproportionately impact particular groups, including Māori, Pasifika, and prisoners with mental health needs, who are already overrepresented in the prison system.
explanation: Substantive, respectful concern for affected groups; no attack.

text: New Zealand is not the first country to run this experiment, and despite the ability to look at other jurisdictions, like Australia and like the United Kingdom, it seems we’d rather be a fast follower than a smart follower.
explanation: Names comparator jurisdictions but the 'fast vs smart follower' point is a slogan without a concrete alternative design.

text: In fact, we’re not borrowing a cent to provide this relief at all.
explanation: A concrete claim (no borrowing) but no figures or funding source given.

text: One of the safest places you could probably have a few beverages in is a licensed premise like one of our pubs, one of our restaurants.
explanation: Names the comparison (licensed premises vs elsewhere) but no figures.

text: do we really trust that a future Minister, with the stroke of a pen, won’t actually change that to $100,000 or $10,000? That in itself is really concerning.
explanation: Pinpoints a concrete drafting feature (ministerial discretion over the $100m threshold) as the locus of concern.

text: Under this bill, a company may not exploit a single human being, it could even be a model employer, but if it misses a paperwork deadline or files a deficient statement, it faces up to $200,000 in fines. This is not a policy brought on a cornerstone of freeing victims; it is built on filling in forms and ticking boxes.
explanation: Cites the concrete penalty figure and the precise compliance mechanism she objects to.

text: Anti-Semitism has gone through the roof in New Zealand in the past few months.
explanation: Vague magnitude with no figures or sources cited at this point.

text: people deserve some level of certainty—that’s what zoning is for. There are rules around the zone, how many storeys, what are the setbacks, what is the height in relation to boundary, what should I be allowed to build as of right.
explanation: Names specific planning controls (storeys, setbacks, height-to-boundary) without figures.

text: We had the $750 million walking and cycling bridge across Auckland Harbour, which, for that amount of money, didn't even include a bus lane.
explanation: Names a concrete project and dollar figure as evidence.

text: Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons.
explanation: Names location, building scale, current use, and reason for refusal.

text: We will repeal those two pieces of legislation—the Spatial Planning and the Natural Built Environment Acts—in the first 100 days.
explanation: Names the exact statutes and a concrete timeframe.

text: You can't shop around when you live an hour from town, you can't take public transport when there isn't any, and you can't just absorb rising costs where every litre of fuel underpins your livelihood, whether that's farming, forestry, tourism or simply trying to get your kids to school.
explanation: Names concrete circumstances and sectors, though without figures.

text: It expands the powers of the Department of Corrections, it creates new management categories, and it alters the balance between operational control and prisoners' rights.
explanation: Identifies concrete effects (new categories, rebalanced rights) though not the thresholds or numbers.

text: We approach this bill with three clear tests in mind: is it workable, is it properly resourced, and are the safeguards strong enough?
explanation: Sets out a concrete, named three-part evaluative framework.

text: With regard to clause 9, which replaces section 29 of the Act... It collapses the Ministry for the Environment into a single statutory office, with the Secretary for the Environment personally responsible to the Minister for all environmental functions... A ministry can push back. A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews and then their future roles, and so what we’re seeing here is a deliberate reduction in democratic oversight and accountability for our environment.
explanation: Cites clause 9/section 29 and the precise structural change.

text: Having this bill set out a minimum of 10 hours of meaningful human contact over 14 days, with an aspirational target of 14 hours a week, is a good move, and so, overall, despite some scrutiny at the select committee, we commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Cites precise figures and timeframes (10 hours/14 days; 14 hours/week aspiration).

text: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
explanation: Divisive ridicule of opponents rather than persuasion.

text: You are now sitting in the right place, according to most New Zealanders.
explanation: A partisan jab at the Opposition; rallying rather than bridge-building.

text: for every dollar that Government spends, that’s a dollar that a family doesn’t get to keep.
explanation: Relatable framing aimed at taxpayers, though it appeals to the existing fiscally-conservative base.

text: many of the people who are on our streets and who are regulars on our streets can be housed but sometimes with great difficulty because of their incredibly complex needs. We should never, ever resile from that. We know that this requires a great deal of effort from Government, local government, social agencies, and NGOs
explanation: Concedes a point opponents care about and points to shared responsibility across agencies.

text: Now, Phil to some of us is a hero. I probably shouldn’t be admitting that as an ACT MP, but the National Policy Statement on Urban Development, Mr Twyford, actually set the scene for why it’s important to build up around these expensive investments in transport, like the City Rail Link
explanation: Generous cross-party praise of a Labour MP, openly against partisan expectation, to build common ground.

text: The other side of the House would rather just absolutely waste away your taxpayer money and borrow money to put us into significant debt.

text: New Zealand is not the first country to run this experiment, and despite the ability to look at other jurisdictions, like Australia and like the United Kingdom, it seems we’d rather be a fast follower than a smart follower.
explanation: Reasonable call to learn from overseas evidence, but asserts NZ is copying uncritically rather than showing where the overseas evidence cuts against the bill.

explanation: Supports the 'we already have laws' argument with the existing legal framework, but uses it to imply new measures are redundant without engaging the supply-chain transparency gap the bill targets.

text: If you don't believe in free speech consistently—if you only believe in it for the views that you agree with—then you don't really believe in it at all.
explanation: A coherent principled argument about the consistency of free-speech commitments; logically sound though not evidence-based.

text: I know that Jamie Arbuckle mentioned that this is going to go into shop trading hours. These bars will be able to stay open all kinds of hours.
