text: Our regulatory system is well placed to support companies to meet any availability challenges because it is not prescriptive about packaging. The legislation is focused on outcomes and is flexible enough for food producers to pivot to alternative supplies without a whole lot of red tape.
explanation: Reasoning that outcome-based (non-prescriptive) rules permit substitution is coherent and follows from the premise.

text: For too long, Government sent the wrong message to farmers that if you do the right thing and invest in preserving or creating wetlands and native bush, you'll be punished with more controls on what you can do on your own land. This initiative flips the script from more regulation to incentives.
explanation: Asserts a 'wrong message' narrative without evidence, though the policy logic is stated.

text: More than 2 million hectares of New Zealand are affected by wilding pines and, left unchecked, the impact could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years. An independent assessment estimated the cost-benefit ratio at 30:1.
explanation: Cites independent assessment and a cost-benefit ratio to support the case for investment; evidence-based.

text: Well, thirsty wilding pines suck water out of the catchments. According to the Whakatipu Wilding Control Group, dense infestations could cut the flow into rivers by 30 percent to 40 percent, and they threaten four of our six biggest hydro catchments: Tongariro, Waitaki, Clutha, and Manapōuri.
explanation: Cites a source and names affected catchments to connect wildings to power prices; reasoning is mostly evidence-based.

text: They see more and more people lose their jobs and seek assistance, and then kick them while they're down.
explanation: 'Kick them while they're down' is an emotive, accusatory characterisation of the Government rather than engagement with the substance of its policy.

text: telling them to simply “Go and find a job.” when the member knows those jobs do not exist.
explanation: Criticises the policy and accuses the member of bad faith ('knows those jobs do not exist'); pointed and somewhat accusatory but aimed at the position rather than pure personal insult.

text: It has also cut funding to the Apprenticeship Boost, it has slashed Māori trades training, and it has recently broken yet another promise to young people by cutting the fees-free scheme.
explanation: Harsh framing ('broken yet another promise') but directed at policy decisions rather than personal character.

text: How can she claim that this is a new cost of living measure when this happens automatically every single year?
explanation: Direct challenge to the framing of the announcement, focused on substance not character.

text: significant resources are being put into the sanctions and obligations, and I want to know why the review is looking only at exits and not exits into work, and how do we know that the sanctions and the traffic light system are worth the amount of money that the Minister is spending on that?
explanation: Persistent but substantive challenge to the policy's value-for-money, no personal attack.

text: We know a Labour Government, if given the opportunity to be re-elected, will increase taxes, increase borrowing, increase spending, and it will be New Zealanders paying the bill
explanation: Predicts opponents' future fiscal behaviour; partisan assertion with no supporting evidence, uncertain.

text: New Zealanders know better, and that's why they'll re-elect National in November.
explanation: Predicts a National re-election in November; partisan and uncertain forecast.

text: Our next steps are to cut the red tape and to recognise the nature of the energy problem facing our country so that we can double renewable energy by 2050.
explanation: Forecasts doubling renewable energy by 2050; long horizon, plausible directionally but highly uncertain.

text: A new hospital in South Auckland will mean better access to care closer to home. Drury was identified as a strong location due to its proximity to key transport corridors, including our roads of regional significance and planned public transport connections, making it easier for patients, staff, and visitors to access care. Over time, this will reduce pressure on existing hospitals, improve wait times, and ensure that Aucklanders can have confidence that high-quality healthcare will be there when they need it.
explanation: Predicts reduced pressure and improved wait times 'over time'; plausible but contingent on a hospital still only at RFP stage.

text: At the start of this year, known remaining reserves of natural gas were 23 percent lower than at the same time last year... with 12 of the 17 gasfields that are currently operating expected to stop producing within the next 10 years, it is only going to continue to get more challenging without future gasfields being found.
explanation: Forecast that 12 of 17 gasfields stop producing within 10 years; directionally supported by declining-reserves trend, magnitude uncertain.

text: I've had a number of farmers contact me with concerns about the availability of both fuel and fertiliser. While I understand there have been some local challenges with getting diesel delivered, overall fuel supply remains sufficient, with good levels of fuel in the country and more on the way. I understand from the fertiliser industry that there is enough product both in New Zealand and ordered to meet demand until spring. I just want to say to farmers that at this stage, we just have to keep calm, plan ahead, work closely with suppliers, and make sensible business decisions about the use of inputs.
explanation: Reassuring, inclusive 'keep calm, plan ahead' message addressed to all farmers without partisan framing.

text: For too long, Government sent the wrong message to farmers that if you do the right thing and invest in preserving or creating wetlands and native bush, you'll be punished with more controls on what you can do on your own land. This initiative flips the script from more regulation to incentives.
explanation: Persuasive framing aimed at farmers; appeals to his own constituency rather than bridging.

text: I'm rather disappointed to hear my colleague Steve Abel there. I thought we almost had him in supporting, but never mind. Hopefully we can get him back.
explanation: Warm, bridge-building tone that frames the Green member as winnable rather than an adversary.

text: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
explanation: Expresses sentiment with no concrete content or commitment.

text: If you go to work and you’re on the minimum wage, you can earn up to about $950 a week—that’s a lot of money.
explanation: Gives a concrete weekly earnings figure, though qualified with 'about'.

text: The bill does not change existing services, funding allocations, or who can receive disability support services, and I think that's a very important point. It does not change any of that.
explanation: Enumerates the specific things claimed to be unchanged.

text: From 1 January 2027, Tai Poutini Polytechnic will operate within The Open Polytechnic of New Zealand. This will ensure that in-person, campus-based vocational education remains available on the West Coast.
explanation: As the Minister driving the vocational-education restructure she is describing a concrete structural change with a set start date, but it is an announcement of a future arrangement rather than completed delivery.

text: From 1 January, NorthTec will be reestablished as a stand-alone regional polytechnic. Among other financial supports to ensure its continued viability, I am delighted to announce the in-principle investment of $34.7 million for the development of a new Whangārei tertiary hub—subject to business case
explanation: An 'in-principle' investment 'subject to business case' is an announced intention, not yet delivered spending or built facilities.

text: the unique residential agricultural training facility Telford will be receiving $2.4 million to address deferred maintenance to ensure a fit for purpose, fully functioning agricultural campus.
explanation: A concrete committed allocation to an existing facility, slightly above mid because it is targeted maintenance funding rather than yet-delivered work.

text: This Government has put in place extra Youth Guarantee places, an extra 175 places this year, to a total of 8,400 young people who participated in Youth Guarantee schemes over 2025; Apprenticeship Boost, which subsidises employers—over $25 million was spent on Apprenticeship Boost through Vote Social Development.
explanation: Points to concrete funded programmes delivered, though modest in scale relative to the problem raised.

text: We will work through this disestablishment sensibly and calmly, working a process in consultation with staff, with students, with community, and with industry.
explanation: A stated commitment to a managed process, but at this point an intention rather than a delivered outcome.

text: My proposal was simple: that revenue from overseas betting should be ring-fenced, used only for animal welfare purposes, greyhound rehoming, or compensation for those affected.
explanation: Describes a tabled amendment he actually advanced, but it was not adopted, so it is action without delivered result.

text: She loves running. It's great.
explanation: Answering 'Do you want your dog to race?' he deflects to the dog enjoying running without addressing whether he wants it to race.

text: This Government has just committed to mining 40 percent of our conservation estate; the Minister was telling us about it at question time today. They have committed and redoubled on the bottom-trawling trashing of our oceans through the fisheries bill they’re passing.
explanation: ‘Mining 40 percent of our conservation estate’ is a sweeping characterisation that likely overstates the actual policy.

text: They have even started subsidising the fossil fuel industry again: $200 million for the fossil fuel industry.
explanation: Refers to a specific figure for fossil-fuel support; whether it constitutes a 'subsidy' is contested framing, so partly accurate at best.

text: Bird gel repellents are cruel substances that stick to wild birds and are designed to repel them from car parks and buildings and sports arenas and so forth. But in fact, they're aversive chemicals that cause irritation and harm to the birds, and there's ongoing incidents as birds are killed coming into contact with them.
explanation: Bird gel/repellent products do exist and animal-welfare groups have documented birds being harmed or trapped by them; the framing is one-sided but broadly supported.

text: The urgency meant only targeted engagement with stakeholders was possible and public consultation was not conducted. It also limited the ability to test final options with stakeholders.
explanation: Drawn directly from the bill's regulatory impact statement acknowledgements about limited consultation; presented faithfully.

text: the Supreme Court deliberated at length, whether he had a right under tort law to take those companies for negligence, and the fact that their pollution was impacting him and his family. The Supreme Court agreed there was a case to be heard.
explanation: Accurate account of the Supreme Court's decision in Smith v Fonterra to let the tort claim proceed to trial.

text: there's roughly, say, off his numbers, about 300,000 people who whakapapa Māori in Tāmaki-makau-rau, in Auckland.
explanation: Auckland's Māori-descent population is closer to ~210,000–250,000; 300,000 is on the high side, though he hedges that it is another member's figure.

text: the fast-track bill is the reason that the Port of Auckland has been able to extend so efficiently and quickly to make sure that the good people of Auckland have got capacity to bring goods into New Zealand.
explanation: Causal claim crediting fast-track legislation for Port of Auckland expansion; directionally plausible but a strong single-cause attribution that is hard to substantiate.

text: Lawful firearm owners were treated as criminals. This House passed legislation, unfairly taking their firearms, and, back then, ACT was the only party that stood up for them.
explanation: ACT did oppose the 2019 firearm reforms, making 'only party' broadly defensible, but 'treated as criminals' and 'unfairly taking' are loaded characterisations.

text: The Secretary for the Environment will now be required to report annually on the performance of their Environment Act functions, and that report will sit inside a new ministry, which will be created and will report to this House.
explanation: Consistent with the reporting amendment described by National members.

text: ACT was the only party that stood against the zero carbon Act while every other party in the House voted for it.
explanation: Broadly accurate — ACT (David Seymour) cast the sole vote against the Zero Carbon Act in 2019 while other parties supported it.

text: In 2023, it is estimated that alcohol-related harm cost New Zealand $9.1 billion.
explanation: Consistent with published NZ estimates of alcohol-related harm costs around this magnitude.

text: The Minister has been crystal clear that this bill's aim is about reducing "regulatory burden" and not about reducing harm.
explanation: Fairly characterises McKee's own framing of the bill as about removing red tape rather than harm reduction.

text: It was introduced on Monday night with no consultation with disabled people, and about 30 minutes before it was announced, there was a briefing for some disability groups. Now, just three days later, we are at the first reading
explanation: Specific procedural claims (Monday night introduction, 30-minute briefing, first reading three days later) presented as fact; plausible but unverified here.

text: if we set the precedent of compensating industries that have moved beyond the social licence of New Zealand, we set a dangerous precedent. There are other industries, if we are to deal, for example, with climate change, that we are likely to need to bring to an end as a Parliament, so we do not support the compensation.
explanation: Predicts Parliament will need to shut down other industries over climate change — directionally plausible but vague on which, when or how.

text: This Government, in their one term, will go down in history as the most environmentally destructive Government of New Zealand. I doubt that any Government will be as bad and as anti-environment as this one.
explanation: A prediction about future historical judgment; superlative ('most destructive ever') is speculative and hard to substantiate against past governments.

text: the environment that they disdain is what voters will be choosing to protect when they throw out the most destructive, anti-environmental Government in our history.
explanation: Predicts the government will be voted out; partisan and uncertain.

text: Even if it's too late for greyhounds, to somebody listening out there, they will eventually come for your industry, and I hope that there is someone left to speak for you.
explanation: A vague, fear-based prediction that unnamed 'industries' will be banned next; too unspecified and speculative to be well-supported.

text: I’d like to speak to the virtues of allowing overseas aircraft to be used in New Zealand in a sensible way—especially for the good people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, where they will now be able to get their produce to the world, jobs... the tourists will come in, there will be jobs, there will be improvements, all thanks to this Minister.
explanation: Predicts jobs, exports and tourism flowing from the measure; optimistic and unquantified.

text: Overall, this bill will increase the availability of alcohol in our communities, including at off-licences, which cause the most alcohol-related harm. We should be reducing harm from alcohol, not promoting it to obtain economic growth, which is stated is also the point of this law.
explanation: Predicts the bill will increase alcohol availability in communities — plausible directionally but the net effect is contested given the bill's tightening provisions.

text: We've got a space cadet coming in from outer space to tell us all about how we rely on the environment.
explanation: Direct personal mockery ('space cadet') of the preceding Green speaker.

text: Lawful firearm owners were treated as criminals. This House passed legislation, unfairly taking their firearms, and, back then, ACT was the only party that stood up for them.
explanation: Criticises a legislative process but uses charged framing ('treated as criminals') that edges toward sensationalism.

text: the answer from the previous Minister in the chair, the Hon James Meager, leaves a lot to be desired.
explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the answer rather than attacking Meager personally — pointed but legitimate.

text: I’m very concerned, based on the answers that we’ve received in this committee stage, that that is left undefined. Therefore—I shudder to even mention this—but is this creating a separation in legislation between people if we’re going to allow such a term to remain undefined in this important part of the committee stage?
explanation: Raises a charged 'separation' implication but frames it as a question and flags reluctance ('I shudder'); not a personal attack, though leaning toward insinuation.

text: saying there was no use of “agree to disagree” when the bill was introduced and so it must be fine is not really, in a parliamentary process, a suitable answer when members from parties across this House are raising legitimate questions for Aucklanders engaged in the process of a 30-year transport plan that has been through a select committee, had issues identified, and had them flagged in the select committee report
explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the Minister's procedural answer, not the Minister personally; engages the substance of the process.

text: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
explanation: Gracious, conciliatory and free of personal attacks despite a contentious bill.

text: What I think that the Opposition has forgotten in debating this bill is that there’s a thing called the student allowance and there’s a thing called training and there is a thing called responsibility and accountability.
explanation: The repetitive 'there’s a thing called' construction is condescending toward the Opposition, implying they've forgotten basics.

text: To those who have concerns: back the bill to select committee. Give it proper scrutiny and suggest improvements. That is how Parliament is supposed to work. As with all my bills, my door is open to any MP who would like to better understand the changes that are being made.
explanation: Respectful, process-focused and explicitly open to other MPs.

text: Some parties in this House may support freeing criminals and punishing success, but this Government has flipped the script, and we’re freeing New Zealanders to succeed and making sure the criminals get punished.
explanation: Strawmans opponents as supporting 'freeing criminals and punishing success' — a deliberate misrepresentation.

text: Youth crime was completely out of control. There was no encouragement, there was no oversight, there were no kids even going to school. The previous Government left it in the too-hard basket.
explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the prior government, though about policy neglect.

text: We reject the soft-on-crime ideology of the Opposition. We defunded the taxpayer money pit for section 27 cultural reports, but we will never defund the Police.
explanation: 'Soft-on-crime ideology' and 'money pit' are loaded labels for opponents' positions.

text: The Minister has been crystal clear that this bill's aim is about reducing "regulatory burden" and not about reducing harm.
explanation: Critical but engages the Minister's stated rationale rather than attacking her personally.

text: The reporting is talking about the number of applicants, and the number of applicants declined, but that doesn't really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied.
explanation: Probing but respectful, focused on the clause and the departmental report's stated aims.

text: It was introduced on Monday night with no consultation with disabled people, and about 30 minutes before it was announced, there was a briefing for some disability groups. Now, just three days later, we are at the first reading
explanation: Critical of process but focused on the conduct of the legislative process rather than personal attack.

text: There is a pattern that has emerged from the current Government: when working New Zealanders win workers' rights cases through the courts, like pay equity, like Uber drivers, and like this case where parents who became full-time carers for their disabled children have been awarded by the court that they are employees of the Government... the Government's response... is to change the law. That is a political choice.
explanation: Sharp critique of government conduct that engages with specific actions rather than character.

text: This Minister has been consistent in targeting disabled people and the systemic erosion of disabled people's rights.
explanation: Imputes deliberate malign intent ('targeting disabled people') to the Minister personally rather than critiquing a policy.

text: this industry was not built in Wellington by MPs in this House or by fancy suits in the Beehive. This industry was built by hard-working New Zealanders—Kiwis with rough hands
explanation: Populist rural rallying that draws an us-vs-Wellington line rather than seeking common ground.

text: Even if it's too late for greyhounds, to somebody listening out there, they will eventually come for your industry, and I hope that there is someone left to speak for you.
explanation: Rallies sympathisers via threat rather than persuading the unconvinced.

text: We believe that you can protect the environment while also making space for the beautiful humans of New Zealand that live within the environment. We need space for everybody.
explanation: Inclusive, warm framing ('space for everybody') seeking to reconcile development and protection.

text: We need to be allowing port companies to trade, to find the most efficient way to get our goods to the world and the most efficient way for New Zealanders to get the stuff they need from around the world into our country, so that when a painter or a tradie goes out to buy a length of wood or a pail of paint, they’re not paying more
explanation: Relatable framing (painter, tradie, grocery shopper) to bring ordinary voters along, but rallies only the deregulation side.

text: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
explanation: Acknowledges the difficulty for all sides and extends goodwill, though it does not actively bridge across positions.

text: To those who have concerns: back the bill to select committee. Give it proper scrutiny and suggest improvements. That is how Parliament is supposed to work. As with all my bills, my door is open to any MP who would like to better understand the changes that are being made.
explanation: Inclusive, invites opponents into the process and offers engagement rather than dismissing concerns.

text: Some parties in this House may support freeing criminals and punishing success, but this Government has flipped the script, and we’re freeing New Zealanders to succeed and making sure the criminals get punished.
explanation: Us-vs-them framing that shuts down rather than builds consensus.

text: ACT was the only party that stood against the zero carbon Act while every other party in the House voted for it.
explanation: Consistent with ACT's long-held contrarian positioning; cites its own voting record to establish consistency.

text: The Green Party have always and will always support sensible, evidence-based drug harm minimisation and this place, Parliament, needs to have the courage to do that.
explanation: Consistent with the Greens' long-standing, on-record harm-reduction stance; words align with the party's established position.

text: It's very clear to me, from the speeches that we've heard from members opposite, that what they see in leadership is seeking the limelight in the theatrette, rather than quiet work in the background to secure fuel supply.
explanation: Characterises opponents as limelight-seekers rather than engaging their actual arguments — a dismissive imputation of motive.

text: I'm really buoyed by the fact that there was complete agreeance that the area within this bill about the protection or the care for the grave of Mr Carter would be maintained and cared for regardless of it being legislated.
explanation: Warm, good-faith acknowledgement of cross-House agreement.

text: I am so pleased that most of this House is on board with the direction of travel, and I really support the work that Minister Erica Stanford is doing already, and I really look forward to seeing where we get to with this.
explanation: Respectful and constructive; credits a Minister's work, no attacks.

text: It is unjust to prioritise the niceties of urban Wellington and Auckland when the locals of Tiniroto and Ruakituri are still taking a two-hour detour because the roads have been closed for nearly 10 months.
explanation: Pointed criticism of governmental priorities framed as injustice, but aimed at policy/allocation rather than personal attack.

text: So Te Tai Tonga has a simple message for the Minister: leave some fish for the mokos, Shane—leave some fish for the mokos. That's the message from Te Tai Tonga: be a good kaitiaki—be a good kaitiaki.
explanation: Direct, pointed appeal to the Minister by name, but framed as a values plea rather than a personal insult.

text: Ricardo Menéndez March from the Green Party is going to heckle, to apologise on behalf of the gangs, to say, “It’s not their fault, don’t pick on them. They’re nice people, they do good things in our community.”
explanation: Puts fabricated words in an opponent's mouth and mocks him; deliberate misrepresentation and ridicule.

text: That is the Green Party of 2026, that is the Green Party of today, and that’s the people the Labour Party want to be mates with, and I think that’s disgraceful.
explanation: Guilt-by-association attack on two parties' character rather than their arguments.

text: Oh, Reuben Davidson doesn't like this change. We'll remember that. People in Christchurch East will remember that. He wants you to have a different price at the till then you do on the shelf. He just said it across the House.
explanation: Mischaracterises Davidson as wanting price discrepancies — a strawman attributed to him personally.

text: The National Party, on this side, has a variety of views. We are a broad church. You've heard from me in favour of the legislation, you'll hear from colleagues opposed to it, but, ultimately, I think that's what makes politics really, really important in this place.
explanation: Respectfully recognises colleagues who hold the opposite view as part of a healthy debate.

text: So why has the upkeep of Mr Carter's grave not been included in the legislation, and can the member confirm that the grave ultimately will still be maintained?
explanation: Respectful, substance-focused scrutiny of the bill, engaging directly with the select committee's report.

text: We are not going to be driven by Green Luddites or ill-informed people about energy security.
explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side by denigrating opponents; makes no attempt to persuade or build common ground.

text: Within eight weeks, New Zealand—eight weeks—I've achieved, on behalf of the Government, what the last regime could not do for 1,000 weeks; simply dedicated a small amount of money, relatively speaking, to upgrade 100 million litres' worth of storage; recommissioned a crude tank, to the best of my knowledge, for the purposes of holding additional diesel.
explanation: Self-promoting and combative contrast with opponents; rallies own side rather than seeking common ground.

text: Being very interested in clean, green outcomes, I think it's very important that we join with the different stakeholders in our community and explore the role that hydrogen can play boosting our fuel resilience, our energy resilience ... It is important, however, that when people apply for innocuous prospecting permits, they are not pilloried, they are not cancelled, and they are not harassed by opponents to mining when they are legally entitled to go and get an innocuous permit.
explanation: Opens with 'join with the different stakeholders' but pivots to defending miners against 'opponents', appealing to his own side.

text: It could very well be that critical minerals are needed for hearing aids, and I rather fear that hearing aids are needed for the member from Western Māori sitting to my right.
explanation: Alienating ridicule of an opponent, the opposite of consensus-building.

text: But what we need is to be unshackled from this risk-averse, woke-riddled, doubt-riddled culture that we have inherited. If we do that, the world will be our oyster.
explanation: Rousing but us-vs-them framing ('woke-riddled... culture') that rallies rather than unifies.

text: It's very clear to me, from the speeches that we've heard from members opposite, that what they see in leadership is seeking the limelight in the theatrette, rather than quiet work in the background to secure fuel supply.
explanation: Combative contrast drawn to denigrate the other side; no attempt at common ground.

text: I'm really buoyed by the fact that there was complete agreeance that the area within this bill about the protection or the care for the grave of Mr Carter would be maintained and cared for regardless of it being legislated.
explanation: Highlights common ground and shared goodwill rather than division.

text: The world wants me to think it’s a toy so that I play with it all the time, so it makes me more accessible, and they make it look fun and all colourful and there are things to do and interesting things to see. But it’s a trap.
explanation: Relatable parenting analogy that builds common ground, though it appeals to shared sentiment rather than persuading opponents.

text: One thing that we have all agreed on is our position against and on migrant exploitation. We’ve followed that really closely when we review Immigration New Zealand and where that’s going and the work that we’re doing around that.
explanation: Emphasises cross-committee agreement and constructive collaboration.

text: I am here today as the representative of the Napier electorate. For Napier City and Matawai, for rural and urban, for employer and employee, for landlord and tenant—for every person, no matter how they cast their vote.
explanation: Deliberately inclusive — pairs opposing groups and commits to represent all constituents regardless of vote; strongly consensus-building.

text: So Te Tai Tonga has a simple message for the Minister: leave some fish for the mokos, Shane—leave some fish for the mokos. That's the message from Te Tai Tonga: be a good kaitiaki—be a good kaitiaki.
explanation: Memorable, values-based refrain ('leave some fish for the mokos'), though addressed in opposition to the Minister rather than building consensus.

text: Reassurance is not a plan, talking points are not a plan, and rural New Zealand knows it.
explanation: Crisp rhetorical line, but combative and addressed to his own side.

text: We approach this bill with three clear tests in mind: is it workable, is it properly resourced, and are the safeguards strong enough?
explanation: Measured and constructive but speaks for one party's stance rather than seeking cross-party common ground.

text: At its heart, you know, this is modest, but it's an important piece of legislation. It's not trying to reinvent the wheel... It's about stewardship; it's about making sure a historical charitable arrangement continues to deliver real value to the Carterton community, and Labour supports that approach.
explanation: Inclusive framing that backs a Government MP's bill on its merits.

text: The National Party, on this side, has a variety of views. We are a broad church. You've heard from me in favour of the legislation, you'll hear from colleagues opposed to it, but, ultimately, I think that's what makes politics really, really important in this place.
explanation: Acknowledges legitimate internal disagreement and frames conscience debate as valuable — open and inclusive in tone.

text: That is the Green Party of 2026, that is the Green Party of today, and that’s the people the Labour Party want to be mates with, and I think that’s disgraceful.
explanation: Pure us-vs-them demonisation that shuts down cross-party dialogue.

text: So why has the upkeep of Mr Carter's grave not been included in the legislation, and can the member confirm that the grave ultimately will still be maintained?
explanation: Asks a precise, well-targeted question citing section 7(a) and the specific grave-upkeep obligation.

text: It is a really pragmatic change that the Minister has outlined as to why we are bringing this about, and, therefore, I commend it to the House.
explanation: Endorses the change in general terms ('pragmatic') without describing any mechanism or detail.

text: It’s going to insert a new clause 73A into the Public Finance Act which will, “(1) Except as expressly authorised by any Act, the Crown must not pay money (directly or indirectly) to a gang.”.
explanation: Cites the exact new clause (73A) and quotes the precise statutory wording the bill would insert.

text: The maximum penalty for breaching the Fair Trading Act is going from $600,000 up to potentially $5 million. We're going to hold these people to account.
explanation: States the current and proposed maximum penalties precisely.

text: If we think about our deep-sea species like hoki and orange roughy, they have almost been pushed to the brink of extinction.
explanation: Orange roughy has been heavily depleted, but hoki is generally regarded as relatively well-managed; lumping them as near-extinction overstates the case.

text: Yet here we are, giving more fish to commercial interests, making it easier for them to catch more with less oversight, blocking camera footage on boats, legalising the dumping of fish.
explanation: A pointed, contestable characterisation of the reforms ('legalising dumping') that frames provisions in their least favourable light.

text: We've established a ministerial oversight group that is getting briefings twice daily—twice daily—from a talented group of people that are monitoring the situation.
explanation: Describes a concrete monitoring mechanism actually stood up, though delivery of outcomes is still in progress.

text: We've announced some targeted, timely, and temporary support for 143,000 middle working class New Zealanders out there.
explanation: An announcement of support — stated action without demonstrated follow-through.

text: The first is the Conduct of Financial Institutions regime, which we brought into place in March 2025. That requires, of course, all financial institutions to operate fairly and transparently towards consumers in the products they offer. Next, we do have the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, which is before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment.
explanation: Claims credit for the CoFI regime as enacted ('brought into place in March 2025') — a delivered measure — though its relevance to remittance costs is asserted rather than demonstrated.

text: After 16 long years, it restores democracy by ensuring that elected people are accountable for transport decisions. It ensures accountability by making sure that council is in charge of transport and that the council-controlled organisation is in charge of delivering public transport. It ensures local responsiveness by empowering local boards to make better and greater decisions on transport-related matters
explanation: Describes what the bill does on enactment; concrete structural change but outcomes not yet delivered.

text: If we think about our deep-sea species like hoki and orange roughy, they have almost been pushed to the brink of extinction.
explanation: Implies continued collapse of these stocks; directionally arguable for orange roughy but overstated and not clearly forecast.

text: I'm not privileged to that information. What I can say is that all overseas applications must go through a benefit to New Zealand test, and they will be assessed on their merits.
explanation: Asked specifically why Ministers overrode the OIO on the Clydevale farms; declines, citing lack of knowledge, and gives a generic answer.

text: Look, it's not in this specific bit of legislation, so it's not something that I've considered per se. That's speculative in terms of what changes there may be, but this bill doesn't speak to those as well.
explanation: Declines to answer the retirement-villages question, but legitimately on the grounds it is outside the bill's scope, and says so plainly rather than pivoting to talking points.

text: it is simply about that: giving the trust the necessary time to complete those final accounts and to make the distributions and wind up the trust in an orderly manner. The rest of the bill, including the immediate repeal of the outdated ministerial powers, can commence straight away.
explanation: Answers directly why a staggered commencement was chosen — to allow time for final accounts and orderly wind-up.

text: residents will see no negative impact. Fees for contracted long-time residential care are actually already set nationally under the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018. So removing the outdated ministerial power in section 12 does not change what the residents may pay.
explanation: Directly addresses the question about fees and services for care-home residents with a clear 'no negative impact' and reasoning.

text: Yes, I can confirm that the grave will still be maintained. It's a very good question... So the Carter Society has already given a formal undertaking to continue maintaining the grave. The select committee was satisfied with that assurance.
explanation: Directly answers the question asked (will the grave be maintained?) with an unequivocal yes and the supporting basis.

text: What immediate actions is the Minister taking to stop the escalation of the 170,000 tamariki experiencing child poverty and hardship, particularly for Māori, who make up a quarter of this number across Aotearoa?
explanation: Frames the question with concrete figures: 170,000 children and Māori as a quarter of that number.

text: Does the Minister agree that increasing rents for social housing tenants is fair, when, in the Far North alone, 2,241 Māori are experiencing severe housing deprivation?
explanation: Cites a precise figure (2,241) for severe housing deprivation in the Far North.

text: What does the Minister say to the more than 12,000 Māori in the Far North and Whangārei receiving main benefits who will hear her describe the welfare system as a "safety net" while their housing costs increase?
explanation: Names a concrete figure and regions for benefit recipients affected.

text: In relation to gang members, yep, you're right: there's three more gang members in New Zealand than there are police officers. But the good news is this: help is on its way. Next Thursday, 59 police officers will graduate, and there'll be 56 more police officers than gang members.
explanation: Exact numbers and date: three more gang members now, 59 graduating next Thursday, 56 net more officers.

text: Let me give you some of the numbers: in 2025, there were over 100,000 police foot patrols—that is nearly double on 2023. This number here—that wasn't reported on 1News, but is a very important figure—is there are 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime and there is a 22 percent reduction in serious repeat offenders. Ram raids have also dropped by 85 percent.
explanation: Dense with concrete figures: 100,000+ foot patrols, 49,000 fewer victims, 22% fewer serious repeat offenders, 85% fewer ram raids.

text: We had our heroes step up to do the work but they didn't really know where the information was coming from, where they could feed it, or where they were going to get it from. We fixed that with a lot of work with the current bill that is going through the House
explanation: Identifies the concrete gap and the legislative response, though without detail of the mechanism.

text: the Prime Minister... recognised the importance of being able to actually make it much easier for marae to replenish supplies and has removed a lot of the red tape and compliance and went to a high-trust model so that we can do that. That has made a fundamental difference.
explanation: Names the change (red-tape removal, high-trust model) and beneficiary (marae) but no figures.

text: What immediate actions is the Minister taking to stop the escalation of the 170,000 tamariki experiencing child poverty and hardship, particularly for Māori, who make up a quarter of this number across Aotearoa?
explanation: Cites a specific hardship figure and Māori share; broadly consistent with poverty statistics, though the exact basis is unstated.

text: Does the Minister agree that increasing rents for social housing tenants is fair, when, in the Far North alone, 2,241 Māori are experiencing severe housing deprivation?
explanation: Specific statistic presented as fact within a question; plausible and checkable.

text: What does the Minister say to the more than 12,000 Māori in the Far North and Whangārei receiving main benefits who will hear her describe the welfare system as a "safety net" while their housing costs increase?
explanation: Specific factual claim embedded in the question; plausible though unverified here.

text: Those who like to live in this fantasy world and think we don't know what it's like out there; I live in South Auckland. I know exactly the situations we're trying to deal with.
explanation: Appeal to personal experience ('I live in South Auckland') to dismiss opposing views.

text: I am actively working on the regulatory environment with officials. … There is currently a tougher regime for vapes than there is for cigarettes, and we have seen the adverse effects manifest in Australia, where illicit tobacco is the largest part of the market. The wrong settings can and will create unintended outcomes, and we will fix it.
explanation: Uses the Australian illicit-tobacco experience as cautionary evidence; a relevant comparison, though presented as a single analogy.

text: in the serious organised-crime space, we have had repeated occurrences of these prisoners continuing to operate criminal activity from this space.
explanation: Empirical premise used to justify the bill, but offered as assertion without cited evidence.

text: otherwise we will end up with perverse outcomes where we would be choosing to not see it rather than see it, report it, and therefore risk being held accountable for it being in your supply chain.
explanation: Sound incentive analysis: warns that punishing disclosure of slavery found in good faith could discourage looking — a coherent unintended-consequences argument.

text: Currently, superannuation costs New Zealand 5 percent of GDP; that is lower than the OECD average of 8 percent, and significantly lower than some other of the OECD countries who are at 15 percent and 16 percent of the GDP.
explanation: Uses comparative data to rebut the affordability claim; conclusion follows from the evidence cited.

text: In relation to gang members, yep, you're right: there's three more gang members in New Zealand than there are police officers. But the good news is this: help is on its way. Next Thursday, 59 police officers will graduate, and there'll be 56 more police officers than gang members.
explanation: Predicts that after next Thursday's graduation there will be 56 more police officers than gang members; near-term and concrete, likely accurate barring offsetting changes.

text: As we've stipulated repeatedly, hypothetical discussions around what will or will not happen in future settings is not helpful to the public, or reassuring.
explanation: Asked whether the Police Eagle helicopter could operate under level 3/4; refuses to answer by labelling the question unhelpful.

text: As the Hon Chris Penk well outlined on behalf of the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery yesterday, work is ongoing and well under way to consider any hypothetical future shortages. Any future settings in this area will be developed. … I'm not sure it's helpful to presuppose any changes in settings at this point.
explanation: Asked whether 'critical customer' status guarantees enough fuel for police; deflects to 'work is ongoing' and declines to engage the question.

text: I cannot be responsible for what was delivered in 2023. I can refer to what has occurred in 2025 and assure the member that since that period of late 2025, we are ahead of targets and delivering positive outcomes
explanation: Asked why fewer first specialist appointments were delivered in 2025 than 2023; declines to engage the comparison and redirects to recent performance.

text: Planning is ongoing and continuing. We have a fuel plan in place. … this Government is supporting that by ensuring supply is maintained, as according to the announcements that we've made around increasing storage that was secured by Minister Jones and announced by Minister Jones this morning.
explanation: Asked how police can plan with no operational detail; rebuts the premise and points to a concrete storage announcement but gives no operational detail.

text: No. I've been advised that the Health New Zealand detox service for Northland reported today that it only has a six-week wait time. However, I understand that more work needs to be done to support those in the Far North and across New Zealand struggling with methamphetamine addiction.
explanation: Gives a clear 'No' to whether the region faces a meth crisis as framed, with a direct factual basis, while conceding more work is needed.

text: That is a very challenging issue and it's something that we're working through. … An example of some of the things we've had to change is we had to take away a ute tax, there was going to be a fertiliser tax, a capital gains tax, a water tax, tax, tax, tax—
explanation: Asked for a jobs-lost estimate from named plant closures; gives no number and pivots to attacking previous-government taxes.

text: Well, I don't think there is a massive chasm, but its election year and there's always going to be a bit of kicking and screaming in New Zealand.
explanation: Asked to explain the gap between Indian and NZ accounts of the deal; dismisses it as election-year noise rather than addressing the substance.

text: I'm informed that we have enough fertiliser now to get us through the winter. We're working very closely with fertiliser importers to make sure that spring will also be good.
explanation: Partially answers how he'll support farmers on input costs — addresses supply but not the cost question directly.

text: Well, that's because that language is in many agreements, including the UAE agreement and the EU agreement that that member's party voted for during this term of Parliament.
explanation: Directly answers Peters' challenge about the Māori clause by pointing to precedent in other agreements.

text: One of the things that we agreed with India is that, every year, 1,670 high-skilled workers... can come to New Zealand under a special visa that would be created. The visa will be for three years. At the end of that time, they would need to return home... It does not give them a right automatically to bring family members here, because that was not part of the negotiation.
explanation: Directly answers Peters' question about family entry rights: no automatic right, and explains why.

text: I acknowledge that there have been people who are concerned about this disestablishment, and that hasn't been helped by perhaps some of the misinformation about it. If we keep coming back to what is actually happening, there are no substantive changes to the functions under the Environment Act…
explanation: Attempts a reassuring tone but frames dissent as misinformed rather than inviting it in.

text: given the right support and the right encouragement, how people from our disabled sector who are living with a disability can be involved in employment and self-employment, and the wonderful experience that that brings for our disabled people should not be diminished in any way.
explanation: Positive, inclusive framing using a relatable individual story to bring people along.

text: every one of us, regardless of what we do and where we live, impacts on the environment, and therefore every single one of us has a responsibility to improve the lot of the environment.
explanation: Inclusive, unifying call to shared responsibility that explicitly resists pitting groups against each other.

text: I think it is incredibly important that we get away from pointing the finger at different parts of our economy, at different parts of our communities. We have to be joined up on taking responsibility for improving our environment.
explanation: Explicit appeal to stop sectional blame and act collectively; consensus-seeking.

text: With that in mind, it didn’t take very long for nasty Labour to come back, did it? Carmel Sepuloni was on her feet, talking—making up, actually, some text message of fake news somebody happened to send her with such intricate detail from the Koru lounge, from a drunk person. What absolute rubbish!
explanation: 'Nasty Labour', 'absolute rubbish', accusing a named member of 'making up' a message — personal attack and motive impugning.

text: Well, what I have on my paper, it says "It looks like a tax, it smells like a tax, it's a tax."
explanation: Flippant response to a point of order; a slogan rather than substantive engagement.

text: not just put out press releases about houses that nobody can live in or under, not just put up roading cones around the country, but to do the hard work and deliver for Kiwis
explanation: Mocking jab at the prior government's housing (KiwiBuild) and roadworks record; tied to policy but dismissive.

text: Yes, I do. I thank the member for asking that question. Indeed, it's the first question she's asked me in 2½ years on agriculture. … farmers being worth $60 billion worth of exports and up to 360,000 jobs in the economy.
explanation: The '2½ years' jab is a mild dig at the questioner rather than a personal attack.

text: I reject not only the characterisation of that question but its intent and its meaning.
explanation: Firmly rebuts a loaded, accusatory question without resorting to a personal insult of his own.

text: I acknowledge that there have been people who are concerned about this disestablishment, and that hasn't been helped by perhaps some of the misinformation about it. If we keep coming back to what is actually happening, there are no substantive changes to the functions under the Environment Act…
explanation: Acknowledges concern but attributes it partly to 'misinformation', implicitly faulting critics rather than only addressing substance.

text: given the right support and the right encouragement, how people from our disabled sector who are living with a disability can be involved in employment and self-employment, and the wonderful experience that that brings for our disabled people should not be diminished in any way.
explanation: Constructive, respectful and people-focused with no attack.

text: every one of us, regardless of what we do and where we live, impacts on the environment, and therefore every single one of us has a responsibility to improve the lot of the environment.
explanation: Respectful, common-ground framing.

text: there have been no enduring benefits for the over $200 million that has been wasted by the previous Government on this failed experiment.
explanation: Harsh but aimed at a policy/programme outcome rather than a person.

text: The way to actually allow New Zealanders to do more is not to tax them more; it's to allow them to create businesses to sell more, to do well overseas, to meet their ambition, and for the Government to go and join them.
explanation: An ideological assertion about growth-over-tax; coherent but offered as self-evident with no evidence linking the export approach to broad prosperity.

text: The bit that she forgot to say is that over six years, those poor people, the vulnerable she’s so worried about, are worse off today than they were six years ago.
explanation: Broad outcome claim asserted without data or which metrics are meant.

text: not just put out press releases about houses that nobody can live in or under, not just put up roading cones around the country, but to do the hard work and deliver for Kiwis
explanation: Caricatures opponents' delivery rather than arguing from specifics.

text: Well, no, that's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is our commitment is to promote. It is very clear in the advice the Government's received and in the text of the agreement: New Zealand must promote investment. That is the obligation that the Government has taken on.
explanation: Distinguishes a commitment to 'promote' from a commitment to 'invest', citing the text and advice.

text: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination on 95 percent of New Zealand's forestry and wood exports on day one. Australian forestry exports, under their free-trade agreement, increased by 120 percent under their FTA in the first 12 months, while our exports during that period fell.
explanation: Uses the Australian FTA comparison to argue for the benefit, though it implies causation from a single comparison.

text: I don’t think we’ve got much, sort of, hope with the lack of progress with “roads of National Party’s significance”, that they’re going to have to shut any of them down, because hardly any of them are built in terms of that space. Unfunded, no revenue, wanting to toll them, all of those sorts of things.
explanation: Mocking partisan jab ('roads of National Party's significance') aimed at the opponent's programme rather than engaging the bill's substance.

text: It’s a failure of this Government of public transport.
explanation: Blunt criticism of the Government's record; directed at policy/performance rather than a person, but a sweeping assertion.

text: It may have been perhaps that, you know, the inability of the Government to progress its legislative agenda has meant that we’ve passed that particular date. If the Government saw this as a priority, it could’ve scheduled this a little bit earlier.
explanation: A pointed dig at the Government's legislative management, but about process rather than personal.

text: But to hear from the Minister that judicial review is the option that's available to people as a form of accountability, that is extremely concerning.
explanation: Pointed criticism, but directed at the substance of the Minister's answer rather than at him personally.

text: does the Minister have any sort of indication as to timeliness to address some of the issues that have been raised in this report by the committee, particularly related to the commentary on page 4 of the report?
explanation: Polite, substantive request for clarity on timing.

text: the Green Party puts forward a plan that is evidence based, where we show everybody the money for how we would fix the tax system, which currently sees those in the top—
explanation: Claims the party publishes fully-costed plans, consistent with the Greens' practice of releasing alternative fiscal plans.

text: You will see an unrelenting focus—a focus that New Zealand has never seen before—from this Government on growing exports by value. We’re going to double that over 10 years.
explanation: Sweeping target with little concrete mechanism stated; aspiration at this stage.

text: Labour closed that city down. We're rebuilding it but giving them more options.
explanation: 'We're rebuilding it' claims credit for action but is vague — no mechanism, figure, or delivered result cited.

text: We’ve made commitments to close down those homeless motels that people were being dumped in from all around the country and they were languishing; it was harming them, it harmed the reputation of our city.
explanation: Restates a commitment to end emergency motel housing; stated intent without delivery shown here.

text: Right now, New Zealand seafood exporters face tariffs of 33 percent in India but under the FTA, 90 percent of our exports in seafood will move to a zero tariff rate, phased in over seven years. We've also, for the first time, had a commitment from India ... that perishable goods will cross their border and be cleared within 24 hours.
explanation: Describes a concrete, signed agreement delivering specified market-access gains, though benefits are prospective and phased.

text: New Zealand has secured tariff-free access for lamb, wool, coal, leather, forestry, most industrial products, infant formula, and seafood; and reductions of duty rates for our wine, as an example, from 150 percent to as low as 25 percent. For the first time in any India FTA, New Zealand has secured preferential access for apples, mānuka honey, and a tariff-free quota for kiwifruit, almost four times what we currently sell them.
explanation: Describes a concluded/secured agreement with concrete terms, not just an aspiration.

text: Since becoming the Minister for Children, in November 2023, I'm proud to say I have visited all 72 front-line Oranga Tamariki offices and secure residences, as well as a number of Oranga Tamariki - and community-run supervised group homes and remand homes.
explanation: Stated commitment to front-line engagement is matched by the described action of visiting all offices.

text: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
explanation: The proportionality entitlement claim is checkable against Standing Orders; presented confidently and plausibly but disputed by Webb.

text: manufacturing accounts for 230,000 people employed in this economy—230,000 people; about 10 percent of the economy. It underpins about two-thirds of the value of all our exports.
explanation: Manufacturing employment ~230k and a large share of exports are broadly in line with known figures; 'two-thirds of exports' is on the high side and depends on definition.

text: We want to restore national unity, and that's probably going to be the hardest thing to do, with all the division we've got. And we're going to boost social cohesiveness
explanation: Aspirational language about unity and cohesion with no mechanism.

text: investment should be balanced, which means you should have a mixture of rail and good roading networks. We are having to spend $500 million extra on fixing up some of the potholes—won't fix it all.
explanation: Names a concrete spend ($500m on potholes) and a balanced rail/road principle, though without a fuller plan.

text: We're going to have an inquiry into the banking competition. We're going to expand the role of the Grocery Commissioner. We're going to rewrite that dreadful credit contracts and consumer finance Act
explanation: Lists named, concrete commerce actions (banking inquiry, Grocery Commissioner, CCCFA rewrite) though without detail on how or when.

text: We're going to repeal that dreadful proposal, the fair pay agreement, by Christmas.
explanation: Names the policy and a concrete deadline (by Christmas).

text: manufacturing accounts for 230,000 people employed in this economy—230,000 people; about 10 percent of the economy. It underpins about two-thirds of the value of all our exports.
explanation: Precise employment count and economic-share figures.

text: By convention, a six-week call for submission corresponds to a six-month report back, or four weeks for a four-month report back. The clerk of the committee originally understood it to be a six-month report back and so issued a submission for the six-week period. However, shortly after the Easter break, it came to his attention that the report back was, in fact, only a four-month report back, and... I instructed him to call for submissions proportional to the report-back date, which, in effect, is the four weeks.
explanation: Directly and fully explains why the submission period changed from six to four weeks, including the clerk's error and the proportionality convention.

text: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
explanation: Directly rebuts the claim that he breached ruling 117/1, asserting the proportionality exception applies.

text: By convention, a six-week call for submission corresponds to a six-month report back, or four weeks for a four-month report back. The clerk of the committee originally understood it to be a six-month report back and so issued a submission for the six-week period. However, shortly after the Easter break, it came to his attention that the report back was, in fact, only a four-month report back, and... I instructed him to call for submissions proportional to the report-back date, which, in effect, is the four weeks.
explanation: Lays out a logical chain (report-back length → proportional submission window) to justify the decision.

text: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
explanation: Grounds the rebuttal in the Speaker's rulings and the clerk's consultation with the Speaker, though without quoting the specific provision.

text: maybe she should come up to Franklin, just south of Auckland, and try and get on the motorway and drive to work at 6.30 in the morning... because it's absolutely congested, that they are ignorant fools, because I'm not sure that they're going to agree with you
explanation: Rebuts the induced-demand claim with a single congested-commute anecdote rather than counter-evidence; appeal to anecdote.

text: investment should be balanced, which means you should have a mixture of rail and good roading networks. We are having to spend $500 million extra on fixing up some of the potholes—won't fix it all.
explanation: Reasonable balanced-investment point grounded in a stated figure.

text: that Labour Government over there, for the last six years, just saw them as a cash tool and they imposed heaps of regulation on them without properly considering the nature and the cost and the burden of that regulation on small businesses
explanation: Asserts regulatory over-burden without specific evidence; plausible but unsubstantiated generalisation.

text: We will champion our farmers and growers, we will respect our farmers and growers, and we will see them as the solution, and not the problem.
explanation: Rhetorical affirmation with no mechanism or measure.

text: a major announcement was publicised this morning in turning Southland's lignite reserve, I believe it's something like 9 billion tonnes, into urea, and also electricity generation from the hydrogen.
explanation: Names the resource (Southland lignite), a figure (9 billion tonnes) and the outputs (urea, hydrogen electricity), though hedged with 'something like'.

text: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
explanation: Cites an export figure and names RMA reform.

text: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand's merchandise export trade.
explanation: Multiple concrete figures quantifying the sector's economic role.

text: Our agricultural sector, our horticultural sector, our primary sector, is $63 billion—some 82 percent of our merchandise exports.
explanation: Concrete dollar value and percentage share quantifying the sector's economic weight.

text: In the final 10 seconds that I have, moving forward, we need to include young people in the conversation and the design of the solutions to address this issue, which is all about them.
explanation: States a principle (include young people) without a mechanism for how.

text: Fifteen jobs were advertised on online
explanation: Gives a concrete figure (fifteen jobs) sourced to reporting, though context (location, timeframe) is partial.

text: We've got organisations like the Kindness Collective, who do an incredible job serving children and whānau in need, who have experienced a 336 percent increase in demand for their services
explanation: Names the organisation and a precise percentage increase.

text: with that particular proposal, which, again, is going to impact 9,300 households from 1 April 2027, targeted consultation was only done within the—basically, the Government talking to itself; not talking to any external stakeholders about how it will impact on those people.
explanation: Precise figure (9,300 households), commencement date, and scope of consultation.

text: 68 percent of people who reported food insecurity said they were experiencing it for the first time; 48 percent of low-income respondents have experienced it, but so have 29 percent of medium-income families, and even 12 percent of high-income families.
explanation: Multiple precise figures broken down by cohort.

text: our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
explanation: Cherry-picks one IMF growth-ranking snapshot and juxtaposes with Equatorial Guinea to imply NZ is near-failed-state; misleading framing of a narrow metric.

text: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
explanation: 'Funding hasn't been cut, just reallocated' is contested by the example of jobs falling from 30 to 12.

text: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
explanation: The ~$60 billion primary export figure is roughly accurate; the causal attribution to policy is his inference.

text: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand's merchandise export trade.
explanation: Primary-sector export earnings, employment and ~80%+ share of goods exports are broadly consistent with official figures.

text: I know of the dicyandiamide issue that Fonterra had with what was a compound additive to fertiliser; it ended up in the food chain, and it was incredibly disruptive to our markets in Asia in particular—those critical markets.
explanation: Accurate reference to the 2013 DCD (dicyandiamide) residue scare that disrupted NZ dairy trade and prompted withdrawal of the product.

text: Yes, we are disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment, but for very good reason... This merger is simply about reducing bloated bureaucracy. We saw, under the previous Government, something like 16,000 extra bureaucrats were appointed.
explanation: 'Bloated bureaucracy' is a partisan jab, though attached to a policy rationale.

text: after six years in the wilderness, after six years of directionless ambling around, directionless travel, economic hard times, we are back.
explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the prior government; rhetorical rather than substantive.

text: we are not getting rid of the Ministry for the Environment's functions. Its role has always been advisory. We're simply moving these functions to the newly appointed Secretary for the Environment, who I understand—not yet met—is an exceptional operator. I encourage that side of the committee to have some faith in the officials and their expertise.
explanation: Reassuring tone and an invitation to the other side to trust the officials, mildly bridge-building.

text: The 190 cancers already detected through this expansion show exactly why this Government backed it. These are mothers, daughters, wives, and friends who will now be able to spend more time with their loved ones.
explanation: Emotionally resonant and broadly relatable, but framed to credit the government rather than build cross-party consensus.

text: after six years in the wilderness, after six years of directionless ambling around, directionless travel, economic hard times, we are back.
explanation: Rallies one side with triumphal language; not aimed at persuading opponents.

text: we are not getting rid of the Ministry for the Environment's functions. Its role has always been advisory. We're simply moving these functions to the newly appointed Secretary for the Environment, who I understand—not yet met—is an exceptional operator. I encourage that side of the committee to have some faith in the officials and their expertise.
explanation: Directly addresses Brooking's concern that environmental functions will be lost, stating they are being shifted, not removed.

text: They see more and more people lose their jobs and seek assistance, and then kick them while they're down.
explanation: Rhetorical assertion of bad intent; no evidence linking specific policy to the claimed harm.

text: as we heard today in the House, the fewer jobs that we have since this Government came into office—you know, many leaving their regions and leaving for Australia.
explanation: Cites a trend as evidence but the link is asserted with 'you know' rather than substantiated.

text: significant resources are being put into the sanctions and obligations, and I want to know why the review is looking only at exits and not exits into work, and how do we know that the sanctions and the traffic light system are worth the amount of money that the Minister is spending on that?
explanation: Frames a cost-effectiveness question linking spending to a measurable outcome, though without supplying its own figures.

text: the evaluation only looks at exits, and not exits into work. How does she know that it's not the case management system or job coaching that is actually achieving work exits and that it is nothing to do with the sanctions? Why did the review not include that?
explanation: Identifies a confounding/attribution problem — exits may be driven by case management rather than sanctions — a valid methodological critique.

text: the regulatory impact statement says—this was not their preferred option. What they recommended the Government do is actually invest in more programmes around employment, around education, around training
explanation: Grounds the argument in officials' advice in the regulatory impact statement; evidence-based reasoning that the government acted against its own officials.

text: Yes, we are disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment, but for very good reason... This merger is simply about reducing bloated bureaucracy. We saw, under the previous Government, something like 16,000 extra bureaucrats were appointed.
explanation: Asserts the merger reduces bureaucracy without showing the merger itself cuts headcount; the staffing figure is context, not proof of the claim.

text: The 190 cancers already detected through this expansion show exactly why this Government backed it. These are mothers, daughters, wives, and friends who will now be able to spend more time with their loved ones.
explanation: Pairs a real figure with a strong appeal to emotion ('mothers, daughters, wives') to carry the argument.

text: new section 61AA says, “(1) The Agency may—(a) stop, divert, or otherwise control traffic on a State highway; or (b) close a State highway (or any part of it) to traffic.” It also goes on to say, “(2) The Agency may only exercise the power under subsection (1) if the Agency considers it appropriate to do so for the protection and safety of the public.”
explanation: Quotes the exact clause and subsections of the new section 61AA, giving precise legislative detail.

text: This Government has failed on public transport and we need to do better, not only for this generation but future generations, and to change the way we think about how we transit and transport ourselves around our cities, our towns, and our communities.
explanation: A broad verdict and aspirational call with no concrete measures, figures, or mechanisms.

text: We look at things like the electrification of our public transport network, of our personal vehicles, and of our business vehicles and we know that we’ve gone backwards.
explanation: Lists the areas (public transport, personal and business vehicles) but gives no figures or measure of the claimed regression.

text: New Zealand is one of the worst countries in the world when it comes to our biodiversity and what is being done.
explanation: Strong claim with no figures or metric attached.

text: We cannot support this bill. It is yet again an attack on our environment. It is an attack on us.
explanation: States a position with no supporting detail.

text: new section 61AA says, “(1) The Agency may—(a) stop, divert, or otherwise control traffic on a State highway; or (b) close a State highway (or any part of it) to traffic.” It also goes on to say, “(2) The Agency may only exercise the power under subsection (1) if the Agency considers it appropriate to do so for the protection and safety of the public.”
explanation: Direct, verbatim citation of the bill's text; a verifiable and accurate description of the provision.

text: We look at things like the electrification of our public transport network, of our personal vehicles, and of our business vehicles and we know that we’ve gone backwards.
explanation: 'gone backwards' on electrification is a directional, partly verifiable claim but stated without data, so its accuracy is uncertain.

text: New Zealand is one of the worst countries in the world when it comes to our biodiversity and what is being done.
explanation: Broadly supported: NZ has one of the highest proportions of threatened indigenous species; the loose 'one of the worst' phrasing is defensible but imprecise.

text: This is where I throw someone under the bus, because it wasn’t me who parked my car at the time; it was somebody else who had been using my car, and I will not mention his name.
explanation: Light, self-effacing anecdote with no attack on others; declines to name the actual driver.

text: This Government has failed on public transport and we need to do better, not only for this generation but future generations, and to change the way we think about how we transit and transport ourselves around our cities, our towns, and our communities.
explanation: Critical of the Government's record but framed around policy and a call to 'do better' rather than personal attack.

text: We cannot support this bill. It is yet again an attack on our environment. It is an attack on us.
explanation: Escalating 'attack on us' framing; emotive characterisation of a structural bill.

text: This Government has failed on public transport and we need to do better, not only for this generation but future generations, and to change the way we think about how we transit and transport ourselves around our cities, our towns, and our communities.
explanation: Generational, inclusive framing ('this generation and future generations') but opens with a partisan failure charge that appeals mainly to his own side.

text: This is where I throw someone under the bus, because it wasn’t me who parked my car at the time; it was somebody else who had been using my car, and I will not mention his name.
explanation: Candidly admits the infringement wasn't his doing yet declines to name the other person, consistent with the responsibility he then takes.

text: I take full responsibility.
explanation: Accepts responsibility for the infringement despite having just noted it was someone else driving his car — words match an accountable posture.

text: I wasn’t part of the committee and I haven’t been over all the details of this legislation, but I looked through and we can say, yes, we are going to support this today, but we also leave the coalition Government coalition with the challenge of, what are they doing?
explanation: Frank admission of the limits of his own knowledge of the bill before stating his position — candour rather than overclaiming expertise.

text: I look opposite me and I see tobacco lobbyists, I see gun lobbyists, I see Hobson's Pledge lobbyists, I see absolute profiteers, landlords, conspirators, and climate change deniers.
explanation: A string of pejorative labels applied to opponents personally rather than addressing their arguments.

text: This Government has taken us back 60 years—60 years.
explanation: Hyperbolic condemnation rather than substantive critique.

text: I want to mihi and thank the Government made up of parties funded and supported by the hyper-rich, the 2 percenters who own more than 50 percent of the wealth
