explanation: Sarcastic 'thank you' framing characterising opponents as captured by the rich; rhetorical jab.

text: Do not be hateful or angry, whānau mā. Do not be hateful or angry at this new Government's treatment and disrespect. Be inspired. Be motivated to be more ourselves.
explanation: Counsels against hatefulness, a relatively constructive note amid an adversarial speech.

text: It doesn't matter whether you have indigenously arrived here or just arrived last week.
explanation: Respectful, unifying tone.

text: we had a rise in crime, mainly driven by their culture of excuses—it wasn't your fault if you bashed somebody over the head; it was society's fault.
explanation: Caricatures opponents' views — deliberate misrepresentation.

text: I think it's 877, according to Copilot. We're nearly up to three years in Government.
explanation: Mild corrective dig at the previous speaker, more cheeky than abusive.

text: If you get a conviction and the consequence is a bit of time on the couch playing PlayStation, well that doesn't send a clear message that society denounces the act.
explanation: Colourful but aimed at the policy outcome, not a person.

text: Now, the fact that somebody, a party that was involved with that litigation, contacted people in the officials of the Government two years before, I would not think would be a disqualifying matter for actually progressing that legislative change... It is absolutely regrettable that there was no record kept of that meeting from 2024 or the information that was sent through... we take that on the chin and that’s absolutely right—we should have.
explanation: Measured tone, acknowledges fault ('we take that on the chin') without attacking opponents.

text: This is a broad church, this Parliament, but we all desire to improve the lot of our fellow New Zealanders.
explanation: Respectful, generous framing of political opponents.

text: From the river to the sea, Palestine must be free.
explanation: A rallying slogan for one side; contested and polarising rather than consensus-building.

text: It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
explanation: Reframes the debate inclusively ('and, and' rather than 'either/or'), inviting a both-ways approach.

text: There should be an inquiry into this, but if not for anyone, for the Government's own sake.
explanation: Frames the demand as being in the Government's own interest, an attempt to persuade rather than purely attack.

text: Do not be hateful or angry, whānau mā. Do not be hateful or angry at this new Government's treatment and disrespect. Be inspired. Be motivated to be more ourselves.
explanation: Urges supporters away from anger toward positive motivation; constructive in tone though still aimed at her own base.

text: It doesn't matter whether you have indigenously arrived here or just arrived last week.
explanation: Inclusive framing extending kaitiakitanga to all New Zealanders regardless of origin; invites others in.

text: There are two things that I believe this Parliament should always be united on. One is national security and the other one is emergency management.
explanation: Explicit appeal to cross-party unity on shared priorities.

text: Camilla Belich, who just spoke, who in my view has been an outstanding Opposition spokesperson for emergency management, and she has recently been promoted into the justice spokesperson role. You've been outstanding working with me.
explanation: Generously acknowledges an Opposition MP and credits cross-party collaboration.

text: Violence breeds violence and violence emboldens violence.
explanation: Aphorism with no concrete content.

text: We want to end poverty. We want to have a tax policy where we would have 2.2 million people living better.
explanation: Attaches a figure (2.2 million people) to a tax aim but gives no rates, thresholds, or mechanism.

text: We wanted to see GST off kai. We wanted to see an end to duopolies in supermarkets. We wanted to see the end to seabed mining
explanation: Lists concrete, named policy positions (remove GST on food, break supermarket duopoly, end seabed mining).

text: I am proud as heck that we showed those who paid $440,000 to get a single MP in that our little $17,000 per candidate goes a long way.
explanation: Cites concrete dollar figures contrasting campaign spend per MP.

text: Māori miss their first specialist appointments at 15.2 percent, compared to 4.7 percent for non-Māori. ... ambulatory sensitive hospitalisation (ASH) rates for tamariki Māori aged zero to four are at 8,510 per 100,000, versus 5,400 for non-Māori.
explanation: Multiple precise comparative statistics with rates and denominators, sourced to the report.

text: There is no silver bullet, as has been expressed. A blanket ban sends a good signal and may have some help, but really, we need a multi-layered approach... We need education, we need prevention, we need peer support, we need accessible youth mental health care, and we need the platforms to take responsibility for the environments that they create.
explanation: Names several distinct levers (education, prevention, peer support, mental health care, platform responsibility) but without detail on how each is delivered.

text: food prices are up around 9 percent since this Government took office.
explanation: Gives a percentage and a reference period.

text: Many of the seniors got as much as $2.15 a week in the Government's tax package.
explanation: Names a precise dollar amount and group affected.

text: under the "Procedure for making determination", clause 20C(1)(b), it talks about making submissions, and then in subclause (2), it says "the redress officer may determine their own procedures for making a determination."... I'm keen to understand her expectation of how that will be delivered and the duty of care on the redress officer to ensure that the format of the submissions are the most appropriate to determine a fair—to achieve justice, really.
explanation: Cites the exact clause and subclause and the precise wording at issue.

text: One of them reports in its 2025 annual report that it has $600 million worth of undrawn debt capacity—in other words, that's the capacity of the retirement village residents' money—but also they have 27 percent of uncommitted arrays in stock and also 31 percent of a contract pipeline increase.
explanation: Cites the annual report, dollar figure, and two percentage metrics.

text: This Government has taken us back 60 years—60 years.
explanation: Sweeping hyperbole presented as fact; not a precise, verifiable claim.

text: Can he tell this House where the radioactive waste, which remains hazardous for tens of thousands of years, from nuclear vision will be stored, and has he consulted with any iwi on whose w’enua it might sit?
explanation: The claim that nuclear waste stays hazardous for tens of thousands of years is broadly accurate for some isotopes.

text: does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable, and why is the Government relying on statistics that exclude industries such as transport?
explanation: It is broadly accurate that headline renewable-electricity figures exclude transport and total energy.

text: Māori miss their first specialist appointments at 15.2 percent, compared to 4.7 percent for non-Māori. ... ambulatory sensitive hospitalisation (ASH) rates for tamariki Māori aged zero to four are at 8,510 per 100,000, versus 5,400 for non-Māori.
explanation: Detailed figures attributed to the Minister's own report; checkable and presented accurately.

text: What is stopping the Government right now from introducing an Israeli sanctions bill to Parliament, just as we did in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine
explanation: Accurate reference to the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 as precedent.

text: I look opposite me and I see tobacco lobbyists, I see gun lobbyists, I see Hobson's Pledge lobbyists, I see absolute profiteers, landlords, conspirators, and climate change deniers.
explanation: Ad hominem characterisation in place of evidenced argument.

text: It opens up the door for corporate exploiters. It makes sure there are no winners here. The only winners are those investors who this Government is well reputed for protecting. The loser here is the taiao. We do not support what the Government is intending to do with this bill. Shame on you.
explanation: Attributes motive and predicts outcomes without supporting evidence in the passage.

text: Every year, this Government will refuse to tax the rich, the super-rich made wealthy on that model of capitalism. Every year, they'll protect capital gains, protect inheritance, protect the hoarding of land and assets by those who already hold them by compounding on the original theft—interest on injustice.
explanation: Asserts a sweeping causal narrative with strong rhetoric but little specific evidence.

text: if kaupapa Māori models were actually delivering results, why has the Government not mandated more investment towards taking these approaches to address this pile of poor statistics
explanation: Conditional argument linking effective models to the case for more investment, though it assumes the premise it asserts.

text: does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable, and why is the Government relying on statistics that exclude industries such as transport?
explanation: Draws a valid distinction between renewable electricity share and total energy use, a substantive analytical point.

text: We had our heroes step up to do the work but they didn't really know where the information was coming from, where they could feed it, or where they were going to get it from. We fixed that with a lot of work with the current bill that is going through the House
explanation: Diagnoses a specific identified problem (lack of command and control) and links the fix to it.

text: the India free-trade agreement that our good friend Todd McClay's going to be signing in the next few days—five million people trading with 1.4 billion
explanation: Predicts the India FTA will be signed within days; near-term and corroborated elsewhere in the debate, so fairly likely.

text: They get the new tax in and then they just keep on expanding and expanding and expanding... If you give the Labour Party half a chance, they'll be coming after your tax in a big way.
explanation: Predicts open-ended tax expansion under a future Labour government; speculative and not evidenced.

text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is already being used across the public sector, and by the end of September 2026, an AI assistant for Government New Zealand will enable users to find answers quickly and easily across Government services.
explanation: A dated forecast (AI assistant live by end September 2026); plausible but delivery and capability are uncertain.

text: When we get elected at the end of this year, we will either repeal this or we will stop this work because we know that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is one of the founding documents of New Zealand.
explanation: Embeds a prediction that Labour will be elected at year's end; uncertain partisan forecast.

text: We saw, in the John Key Government, moves towards reducing the Public Service. In the end, that was unsuccessful; and I have to say, this is likely to go the same way too.
explanation: Predicts these cuts will fail like the Key-era effort; reasoned by historical analogy but uncertain.

text: It's a plan that's destined to fail, and the people who will pay the price are everyday New Zealanders who either rely on public services or are public servants or have public servants in their families.
explanation: Predicts the plan will fail and harm services; asserted with certainty but not evidenced.

text: the New Zealand - India free-trade agreement is going to be signed on Monday.
explanation: Specific near-term prediction of the FTA signing, corroborated by other speakers, so fairly likely.

text: Within 24 hours, the internet has named the Minister of Health "Dr Cigareti" and named the finance Minister "Nicotine Willis". ... Ordinary people up and down the country are laughing at you because of the ridiculousness of funding your tax cuts by making more people smoke.
explanation: Amplifies mocking nicknames and 'laughing at you' ridicule of named ministers — personal derision rather than substantive critique.

text: Does the Minister realise that people across the Wellington region, including the Hutt Valley, will be directly affected by 8,700 job cuts to the public sector, and does he understand that if someone says “Hope so.” to job losses, this makes the lives of families struggling under the cost of living even harder?
explanation: Uses a quoted 'Hope so.' to characterise the Minister as cavalier; pointed but tied to an actual remark.

text: They are responsible for the lives they will harm—for the amputations, for the strokes, for the heart attacks, for the health costs, for the congested hospitals.
explanation: Vivid harm-attribution; emotive but tied to a policy consequence rather than a personal insult.

text: reference to the Government's talking points of strong and stable Government while actually being the most unstable Government arrangement ever agreed under MMP
explanation: Attacks the Government's self-description; legitimate political point but framed for maximum contrast.

text: Which targets have the milestone for the year under review been met and which have or will be met in the current financial year?
explanation: Neutral, procedurally framed question with no attack.

text: its commitments of matching the Labour Party's health funding promises at the election. I am deeply worried about the concern that those promises will not be met because of the Government's unfunded tax plans
explanation: Identifies the funding-matching commitment but no figures.

text: Which targets have the milestone for the year under review been met and which have or will be met in the current financial year?
explanation: A precise, answerable accountability question framed around milestones and the review year.

text: Why did his Government deliver fewer first specialist appointments in 2025 than in 2023, a year in which there were also health unions?
explanation: Specific year-on-year comparison with a named confounder controlled for.

text: surveys released yesterday showed over 70 percent of young people are happy with the changes that are proposed ... I can also reassure him that 70 percent of smokers also want to quit.
explanation: Gives concrete percentages tied to specific groups.

text: available medicines being delivered by pharmacies, as we have done by removing the $5 co-payment across the country. That type of access to medicines needs to be maintained.
explanation: Names the specific mechanism and amount ($5 co-payment, nationwide).

text: That's great when you're in question time and you're promoting your faux indignation performance, but outside of this Chamber, "Oh, yes, we'll have a look at that superannuation thing that's getting in the way."
explanation: Accuses opponents of staging a 'faux indignation performance' — an attack on their sincerity rather than their argument.

text: Yet again, they are the target of quick, easy economic virtue signalling. It is so predictable that when we want to score some kind of political traction, the catch cry of superannuation affordability rings out.
explanation: Dismisses opponents' position as 'virtue signalling' and traction-seeking, attacking motive but staying on the policy topic.

text: I am not going to be performative and decry that this is a homeless bill. That is not what this bill is about. This bill is about providing powers to intervene to prevent a certain type of conduct and behaviour.
explanation: Implies opponents are being 'performative', a mild jab, but mostly redirects to substance.

text: I do acknowledge the ACT member for talking about being judged by the outcomes of our legislation, and not just that we have legislation, but I think it has been traversed clearly in this House that this is the starting point that we need.
explanation: Engages the opposing party's substantive point (judge by outcomes) and concedes its validity before answering it.

text: I'd also like to acknowledge my colleague Camilla Belich's approach in this legislation.
explanation: Praises an opponent's considered contribution; the antithesis of a personal attack.

text: Regarding Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the bill fails to recognise that the Crown must take positive steps to protect Māori, and it does not meet the Crown's obligation of active protection.
explanation: Sharp criticism aimed squarely at the bill's substance, not at individuals.

text: Opening these conversations and listening to Chlöe Swarbrick and all the politicians across the board tonight—it’s been extremely eye opening to hear that come to a common ground on some of these issues.
explanation: Respectful, collaborative tone toward members across the House.

text: How can he justify scrapping Aotearoa’s world-leading smoke-free laws, sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy?
explanation: Loaded, emotive framing ('sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy') rather than a neutral policy question.

text: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti.
explanation: Sweeping 'attacked my whole world from every corner' is sensationalist hyperbole rather than engagement with specific policies, though aimed at the Government's programme rather than an individual.

text: I'd also like to acknowledge my colleague Camilla Belich's approach in this legislation.
explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit an opposition member's approach — consensus-building rather than combative.

text: I’m old enough to know when we first introduced health and safety legislation and we fundamentally started with a reporting mechanism and a policy development. Over time, that legislation grew teeth, it grew strength, and it grew, most importantly, accountability for those who do wrong.
explanation: Reframes ACT's 'weak bill' critique constructively, building a case that a modest start is legitimate without attacking opponents.

text: I do acknowledge the ACT member for talking about being judged by the outcomes of our legislation, and not just that we have legislation, but I think it has been traversed clearly in this House that this is the starting point that we need.
explanation: Acknowledges an opponent's valid argument and folds it into a case for the bill — consensus-seeking.

text: It is returning our streets to the communities that own them, not allowing us to be intimidated and to be frightened just for being in our own cities.
explanation: Emotive 'reclaim our streets' framing that rallies supporters but does not seek common ground.

text: at its core, New Zealand First supports this bill because it is firmly rooted in our foundational belief that we need to protect community and country.
explanation: Stated rationale is consistent with NZ First's long-standing law-and-order positioning; words align with the party's record, though not independently verified here.

text: New Zealand First stood in our coalition agreement to defend the superannuation age of entitlement at 65, and we will continue to protect that position.
explanation: Defending super at 65 is a long-standing, consistently held NZ First position, matching the party's record.

text: Māori make up a disproportionate amount of prisoners in the current prison system.
explanation: States direction (disproportionate) without a figure or proportion.

text: See you at Tūrangawaewae on the 20th.
explanation: Names a concrete place and date, but as a brief sign-off it commits to little beyond an appearance.

text: Māori experience disability at higher rates than non-Māori, and face compounded barriers across education, health, employment, housing, and incomes.
explanation: Names the relevant domains but gives no figures.

text: despite clear evidence and advocacy by justice experts since the He Whaipaanga Hou report in 1988.
explanation: Names a specific report and date anchoring the claim, though the 'clear evidence' is not itemised.

text: The bill makes additional amendments to the Corrections Act 2004, which was recently amended in 2025 to remove explicit references to Te Tiriti.
explanation: Names the statute, the year, and the precise nature of the prior amendment.

text: This follows the same pattern as the Employment Relations Amendment Bill, where the Government ensured that Uber drivers and other contractors can be recognised as employees. This was the result of direct lobbying from Uber.
explanation: Mischaracterises the coalition's contractor changes, which tightened (not eased) the path for contractors to be deemed employees; the 'direct lobbying from Uber' causal claim is unsupported.

text: There are 40 people with family care - related cases filed with the Employment Relations Authority. This bill will ensure that they do not receive employment benefits for their mahi.
explanation: The case count is a specific factual assertion (plausible but unverifiable here); the second clause is her interpretation of the bill's effect.

text: The bill makes additional amendments to the Corrections Act 2004, which was recently amended in 2025 to remove explicit references to Te Tiriti.
explanation: Accurate factual claim about the legislative history and the 2025 removal of Treaty references.

text: despite clear evidence and advocacy by justice experts since the He Whaipaanga Hou report in 1988.
explanation: Accurately references a real, influential 1988 report (Moana Jackson's He Whaipaanga Hou) on Māori and the justice system.

text: Māori make up a disproportionate amount of prisoners in the current prison system.
explanation: Well-established statistical fact — Māori are heavily overrepresented in NZ's prison population.

text: There were 7,000 traffic incidents concerning heavy vehicle parking in the Wiri Business Association's district alone, including two fatalities last year.
explanation: Specific statistics presented as fact; plausible but not independently verifiable from the text, so credited cautiously.

text: I'll refer him to Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004, which is the rule which most of these bylaws and other rules are made under, that confers ministerial power to set rules by regulation, and then local authorities are the bodies which are delegated to, within that, to make the rules.
explanation: Accurate characterisation of how the Land Transport (Road User) Rule and local-authority rule-making interact.

text: Would he not consider then, if those objectives are going to be imposed on Aucklanders, the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read "reducing congestion" as one of the objectives of that plan, given that most Aucklanders tell pollsters and local politicians alike that congestion is their number one problem in Auckland's transport system
explanation: Claim that congestion is Aucklanders' number-one transport problem is commonly cited and plausible but unsourced here.

text: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti.
explanation: An emotive list-based appeal asserting attack across many domains without evidence or argument linking the policies to the claimed harm.

text: How can he justify scrapping Aotearoa’s world-leading smoke-free laws, sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy?
explanation: Asserts a causal link between repeal and funding tax cuts as established fact without laying out the evidence.

text: It’s not the phone’s fault, and it’s not the tools’ fault; it’s how we use them, and how humans engage with that behaviour, and the algorithms that are being sent from God knows where.
explanation: Reasonable point distinguishing tools from use, but ‘algorithms sent from God knows where’ is vague rather than evidenced.

text: Te Pāti Māori sees all work as valuable. If a person is taking on the responsibility of the Government, they should receive the same benefit as a Government employee.
explanation: A values-based equity argument; coherent but rests on a contestable equivalence between family carers and state employees.

text: the use of the new powers proposed under this bill is likely to have a disproportionate effect on Māori within the prison system and their whānau on the outside, who may also be subject to what are otherwise internal decisions made by managers from within prisons.
explanation: Conclusion follows reasonably from the cited overrepresentation premise, though the causal link to the new powers is assumed.

text: Would he not consider then, if those objectives are going to be imposed on Aucklanders, the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read "reducing congestion" as one of the objectives of that plan, given that most Aucklanders tell pollsters and local politicians alike that congestion is their number one problem in Auckland's transport system
explanation: Backs the proposal with public-opinion evidence, but partly an appeal to popularity.

text: how should Aucklanders expect to see this council-controlled organisation (CCO) developing? Is it a public transport CCO or is it something else?
explanation: Identifies a logical inconsistency in the bill's definition of the CCO's scope and asks the Minister to resolve it.

text: How do we guarantee the democratic accountability and a way and a mechanism for local people to have some oversight over the provision of local public transport services, like they do in other transport services
