text: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
explanation: General claim with no mechanism for how development and protection coexist.

text: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
explanation: Names the new ministry and a list of domains, but the 'will support' claims have no mechanism or evidence.

text: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
explanation: Concrete on scale and age but general on the change itself.

text: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
explanation: Gives a concrete figure and timeframe.

text: we are streamlining the Public Service—less duplication, more efficiency. By merging environmental management, planning, and development, it makes sense. This is about fixing the basics and building the future. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Relies on slogans ('fixing the basics and building the future') with no mechanism, figures, or detail.

text: They have stripped $1 billion from a focus on the environment.
explanation: Names a figure but not the programmes or timeframe behind it.

text: I will point to the submission by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (PCE), Simon Upton... there is a “real risk with this ‘mega-ministry’ that the trade-offs will [now] be resolved within the organisation” by officials, whereas they should have been and should be elevated to ministerial decision-making where the accountability for those trade-offs will sit.
explanation: Names the PCE and the specific concern about internal vs ministerial resolution of trade-offs.

text: the main cornerstone of their economic policy appears to be cutting spending on things like Auckland light rail, axing Industry Transformation Plans, the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme, the Income Insurance Scheme
explanation: Names several concrete, identifiable policies and programmes being cut.

text: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
explanation: Exact introduction/reading/submission dates, submission window, hearing time and submission count.

text: submissions were called with a closing date of 20 February, so one day for people to submit on the fact that this Government has decided to disestablish the Ministry for the Environment... We received and considered submissions from 588 interested individuals and organisations, we heard oral evidence from 22 submitters—that was under three hours of hearings—and, then, the committee deliberated for 40 minutes on this bill.
explanation: Dense with concrete dates, submitter counts, and durations.

text: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
explanation: Argues the case without attacking opponents.

text: Last weekend, on Sunday, on the way back from the dairy awards evening in Rotorua, I dropped into the Maungatautari sanctuary and had a look round. It’s just an amazing, amazing thing that’s happened there; the locals have done a lot of great work.
explanation: Warm, generous acknowledgement of community conservation work; no conflict.

text: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement across party lines.

text: Why don’t they go and prune kiwifruit?
explanation: Dismissive interjection implying unemployed youth simply aren't trying; flippant rather than engaging the substance of job availability.

text: It’s called working hard.
explanation: Interjection reframing extended sitting hours as 'working hard'; a partisan jab rather than engagement with the scrutiny concern raised.

text: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
explanation: Largely substance-focused, though the 'wine bars in pristine areas' framing edges toward caricature.

text: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
explanation: Critical but focused on process facts rather than personal attack.

text: This is an absolute travesty for New Zealand, and this Government should be absolutely ashamed of themselves.
explanation: Hyperbolic condemnation ('absolute travesty', 'should be ashamed') aimed at the Government collectively.

text: delivering tax cuts for their rich mates. That is the cornerstone of their economic policy.
explanation: "Rich mates" is a derisive, sensationalising characterisation rather than substantive policy critique.

text: They frame nature as an obstacle to growth, and that is lazy politics. That is lazy economics and lazier governance from that side of the House.
explanation: Repeated 'lazy' characterisation of opponents' approach; harsh but aimed at their politics rather than personal traits.

text: All this Government has done is to pretend that we have a decision to make between economic growth and environmental protections. That is absolutely a false dichotomy.
explanation: Criticises the government's framing ('pretend') with an edge but stays on the argument.

text: At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense.
explanation: Sharp but argues against the policy and the chair's process, not her character.

text: I don't think any of us on either side of the House would disagree with us wanting to achieve all of that, but the devil is in the detail, or the proof is in the pudding, as they say.
explanation: Concedes the opponents' stated aims are shared, engaging with substance rather than attacking.

text: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
explanation: Has a clear means-ends logic (revenue funds facilities) but leans on a vivid anecdotal contrast rather than data.

text: It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill.
explanation: Minimising interjection; asserts simplicity as a reason to dismiss concerns without supporting it.

text: After all, we accept common-sense protections around risks for children in the physical world: think about things like how we require seat belts in cars, we fence swimming pools, and we regulate harmful products like alcohol. The online environment should not be exempt from the same common-sense thinking simply because it is digital.
explanation: Argument by analogy to existing safety regulation; intuitively appealing but leans on the analogy rather than evidence that online regulation works comparably.

text: Why don’t they go and prune kiwifruit?
explanation: Asserts seasonal horticultural work as a solution without addressing the availability or location argument; an unsupported retort.

text: You can do it by putting it at the heart of the planning for our roads and for our urban development and our housing—put it at the heart of that and make it a more efficient system so the decisions have to be made in consideration with the environment.
explanation: Offers a reasoned rationale (embedding environmental consideration in integrated planning) but without evidence it will work.

text: The bill will enable the department to use and develop “to the greatest extent”—what does that mean? It is very ambiguous.
explanation: Legitimately flags vague statutory wording, though stops at raising the question rather than analysing it.

text: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
explanation: The causal 'because they would not be in Government' is an unfalsifiable counterfactual presented as fact.

text: only one person supported this, compared to 587 submitters made up of academics, iwi and hapū, experts, community groups, and environmental stewards from across the country, who were saying, "This is a terrible idea. Do not do this to the country."
explanation: Cites submission weight as evidence; an appeal to volume of opinion rather than to the merits, but grounded in the record.

text: it was literally two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings. Then it came to select committee, and within 40 minutes, we had just decided that "Do you know what? We're just going to rubber-stamp this."
explanation: Uses specific procedural facts to support the 'inadequate process' argument.

text: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
explanation: Grounds the claim in a named evidence source (MfE's own reporting) and the conclusion follows.

text: Bronwyn Hayward from University of Canterbury has pointed out that the assurances in the Cabinet paper that say that stakeholders may fear environmental priorities will be diluted and these concerns are unfounded because other countries successfully integrate similar functions—she could find “no evidence of other countries that have successfully integrated such diverse oversight as Environment” with development and economic objectives. The only ones she could find were the Maldives and Kosovo, which have really unfortunate and concerning conflict of interest issues.
explanation: Cites a named academic and a specific evidentiary finding to rebut the Cabinet paper's claim.

text: The 80s called and they want their trickle-down economics back.
explanation: Catchy analogy/appeal rather than evidence; functions as a dismissal.

text: There is no economy with polluted rivers. There is no productivity on eroded land. There is no growth on a warming planet. The environment is the economy
explanation: Rhetorical tricolon making a coherent environment-underpins-economy argument; persuasive structure but evidence is implied, not cited.

text: All this Government has done is to pretend that we have a decision to make between economic growth and environmental protections. That is absolutely a false dichotomy.
explanation: Correctly names the growth-vs-environment framing as a false dichotomy; an analytical point, though asserted rather than demonstrated.

text: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
explanation: Backs the strong conclusion ('appalling track record') by enumerating specific concrete actions as evidence rather than mere assertion.

text: submissions were called with a closing date of 20 February, so one day for people to submit on the fact that this Government has decided to disestablish the Ministry for the Environment... We received and considered submissions from 588 interested individuals and organisations, we heard oral evidence from 22 submitters—that was under three hours of hearings—and, then, the committee deliberated for 40 minutes on this bill.
explanation: Builds the 'rushed process' case directly from documented procedural facts.

text: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
explanation: Offers a both-things framing but mostly asserts her side's position rather than reaching across.

text: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
explanation: Confident and resonant framing, though it appeals chiefly to those already sympathetic.

text: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
explanation: Frames the issue as above partisanship and welcomes cross-party work — unifying.

text: The Prime Minister promised all New Zealanders that he would fix the cost of living, but nothing is getting better.
explanation: 'Nothing is getting better' is an absolute, unsupported characterisation; cost-of-living indicators are mixed, not uniformly static.

text: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
explanation: Characterises the bill as letting the Minister sell land 'as he sees fit', an overstatement of the discretionary powers as described.

text: only one person supported this, compared to 587 submitters made up of academics, iwi and hapū, experts, community groups, and environmental stewards from across the country, who were saying, "This is a terrible idea. Do not do this to the country."
explanation: Numbers broadly cohere with the 588-submitter figure cited later; the '587 opposed / one supporter' split is a strong but not independently verified characterisation.

text: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
explanation: The factual core—no party campaigned on disestablishing the ministry—is plausible and unrebutted, though hard to verify exhaustively.

text: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
explanation: MfE environmental reporting does document declines across several domains, broadly supporting the claim.

text: it was literally two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings. Then it came to select committee, and within 40 minutes, we had just decided that "Do you know what? We're just going to rubber-stamp this."
explanation: Concrete, checkable process claims that align with Radhakrishnan's later account (under three hours, 40-minute deliberation).

text: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
explanation: Precise process figures consistent with Radhakrishnan's 'less than three hours of hearings' account.

text: Wealth doesn't trickle down. All that happens is that the inequality gap widens, public services decline, housing is privatised, public transport is privatised, education is privatised, public transport declines, roads increase, and unemployment increases.
explanation: Directionally supported on inequality, but the chain of privatisations/unemployment is overstated and presented as certainty.

text: They have stripped $1 billion from a focus on the environment.
explanation: Specific dollar claim asserted without sourcing; plausible but unverified in the text.

text: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
explanation: The $1.3bn healthcare-saving figure tracks modelling associated with the legislation; plausible but contested.

text: The last 50 years has seen a dramatic decline in taxes on the rich across advanced democracies.
explanation: Broadly accurate: top marginal and capital tax rates have fallen across OECD democracies since the 1970s-80s, though "dramatic" generalises.

text: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
explanation: Precise dates and figures consistent with other members' accounts of the truncated process.

text: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
explanation: Points to a long, consistent 15-year personal record of opposing seabed mining—words backed by a documented track record.

text: as a descendant of Parihaka, I must, and always will, use my sphere of influence to stand for peace
explanation: Ties her stance to her heritage and a consistent peace position; self-consistent values statement.

text: I will speak to my experience when Labour was in Government and established the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, elevating it from an office that sat within the Department of Internal Affairs... so that independent policy advice pertaining to those matters would actually see the light of day and would not be subsumed in a mega-ministry. This bill is taking us in the opposite direction.
explanation: Draws on her own party's consistent prior action (elevating Ethnic Communities to a ministry) to ground today's opposition.

text: We will indeed be opposing this, and when we get back into Government, we’ll fix this righteous mess they have made.
explanation: Vague future commitment to 'fix' contingent on returning to government, with no mechanism or detail.

text: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
explanation: Broad promise that one structural change will deliver across many areas, asserted rather than demonstrated.

text: Last year, with support of our National Party caucus and our Prime Minister and education Minister, I introduced my member’s bill to ban social media for under-16s. It’s great to stand here today and see this work progressed.
explanation: Concrete action taken (introduced a member's bill) now reflected in committee work; delivery in progress rather than fully enacted.

text: I have received no official advice on the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. That sits under the auspices of the Minister for Social Development and Employment.
explanation: Direct, clear answer to what advice he has received.

text: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
explanation: Disputes the premise of a cut and answers partly, then redirects to the wider programme.

text: I can assure the member that I'm a staunch advocate for the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. I have a peripheral involvement with the Clutha District in the Jobbortunities initiative there; I do know that it works.
explanation: Affirms support but again pivots to the fast-track jobs argument rather than concrete steps.

text: Te Pāti Māori's support for changes to section 4 is conditional on broad support by te iwi Māori on proposed changes made with iwi Māori, while acknowledging the independent voices of whānau, hapū, and iwi, who may take different positions.
explanation: States a clear, conditional party position.

text: —in the disposals and swap process, and they are not unilateral, Priyanca Radhakrishnan... there is a process which is set out there and it's quite an extensive process... Labour is not interested in the submissions—it's already made its mind up—but I'm looking forward to the submissions and seeing what New Zealanders have to say.
explanation: Addresses the unilateral-disposal concern directly.

text: We are going to be cautiously supporting this to go to select committee, but that’s as far as we’ve gone at this stage. We want to hear from people as to what they’ve got to say about this.
explanation: Clear statement of NZ First's position (qualified support to select committee) without evasion.

text: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
explanation: DOC manages roughly a third of NZ's land and the Act dates to 1987—both broadly accurate.

text: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
explanation: Cites a specific figure on Australia's ban and asserts success; the number is plausible but unsourced and 'successful' is an early, contestable judgement.

text: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
explanation: Argues 'reallocation not cut' but mostly reframes rather than addressing the Kaikōura-specific reduction cited.

text: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
explanation: Attributes the confidence surge to Government policy ('probably') without isolating causes.

text: I know of the dicyandiamide issue that Fonterra had with what was a compound additive to fertiliser; it ended up in the food chain, and it was incredibly disruptive to our markets in Asia in particular—those critical markets.
explanation: Uses a real historical case as evidence that streamlining must retain rigour, supporting his cautionary conclusion with a relevant precedent.

text: our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
explanation: Relies on a single ranking plus a guilt-by-association analogy rather than balanced evidence.

text: Everywhere else in the world, you pay to see the sights, you pay to see the attractions, and you should do the same here in New Zealand so that we can use that money and put it back into improving and protecting our environment and biodiversity.
explanation: 'Everywhere else in the world' is an overgeneralised appeal to analogy supporting the charging policy.

text: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
explanation: Argument by analogy to age-gated activities; rhetorically tidy but relies on the analogy rather than evidence the analogy holds online.

text: I was recently in Australia and saw the successful, positive impact of their ban for under-16s on social media.
explanation: Relies on personal anecdote ('I saw') to assert a policy's success rather than outcome data.

text: we are streamlining the Public Service—less duplication, more efficiency. By merging environmental management, planning, and development, it makes sense. This is about fixing the basics and building the future. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Assertions of efficiency without evidence; 'it makes sense' substitutes for an argument.

text: I can assure the member that I'm a staunch advocate for the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. I have a peripheral involvement with the Clutha District in the Jobbortunities initiative there; I do know that it works.
explanation: Professes to be a 'staunch advocate' while accepting funding has been reoriented and saying it isn't his portfolio—words sit in some tension with the described changes.

text: We will be scrutinising this, and we hope there will be a full select committee process, because this is a very important bill but we don't want this to be a stalking horse for doing some other things that it's not necessarily intended to do.
explanation: A coalition partner publicly flagging it will scrutinise its own Government's bill; a stated commitment to oversight with no visible action yet to confirm it.

text: This month, we are conducting a major foot-and-mouth disease preparedness exercise in Taranaki: operation “Farm Gate”... New Zealand has never had a case of foot-and-mouth disease, but if we did, it would cost this country around $15 billion in lost exports... and in destroyed herds and flocks.
explanation: Describes an active readiness exercise underway, building on a signed industry agreement.

text: We have the toughest biosecurity border protection in the world. But risk can never be zero... well-established readiness and response plans have helped us to eradicate four separate incursions of fruit fly during this term of Government.
explanation: Points to four eradications delivered this term as evidence of capability.

text: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
explanation: Reports concrete progress on a funded eradication effort.

text: This bill is a great example of how Government is making real regulatory change that will benefit farming businesses and the wider primary sector. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Claims delivery of 'real regulatory change' for a bill only at first reading and not yet enacted; intent and announcement rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: On Sunday, the Government announced an extra $79 million over three years to escalate the fight against wilding pines. This takes the total to $109 million. This additional spending will mean Biosecurity New Zealand can back the crews, contractors, and landowners already doing the hard yards... That’s this coalition Government: fixing what matters.
explanation: Announced funding with a delivery plan, but the announcement itself is recent and outcomes are prospective.

text: Our forces are working hard towards becoming an increasingly integrated combat capable Anzac force, integrated by 2035.
explanation: Forecasts an integrated Anzac force by 2035; a plausible long-term goal but a decade out and dependent on policy continuity.

text: the bill, we expect and hope, will come into force on 30 June of this year, with the powers to make secondary legislation as part of that and with the systems in place for the scheme to go live in August or September of this year.
explanation: Forecast of commencement and go-live timing ('expect and hope'); plausible and partly within his control, but contingent on Cabinet and the Governor-General.

text: within sort of the next two or three months at the latest, we would need to have progressed those and brought them forward.
explanation: Plausible projection of the regulation timetable, working back from the stated go-live date.

text: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
explanation: Implicitly forecasts likely eradication success ('looking promising'); cautiously hedged with 'fingers crossed'.

text: More than 2 million hectares of New Zealand are affected by wilding pines and, left unchecked, the impact could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years. An independent assessment estimated the cost-benefit ratio at 30:1.
explanation: 'Left unchecked... could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years' is a long-horizon projection; directional but highly uncertain.

text: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
explanation: Credits an Opposition member by name and praises a cohesive cross-party process — bridge-building.

text: You can do it by putting it at the heart of the planning for our roads and for our urban development and our housing—put it at the heart of that and make it a more efficient system so the decisions have to be made in consideration with the environment.
explanation: Constructive framing of the government case, but addresses sceptics only superficially.

text: In the final 10 seconds that I have, moving forward, we need to include young people in the conversation and the design of the solutions to address this issue, which is all about them.
explanation: Inclusive call to bring affected young people into solution design; unifying though general.

text: If we can't convince the Government to go with the default six months, then we would support the member's amendment to at least extend it out to four months for all the reasons that he gave.
explanation: Cross-party gesture endorsing a Green member's compromise amendment, seeking common ground on a fallback position.

text: this Government continues to kick them while they are struggling, instead of looking at things to support families in a cost of living crisis.
explanation: Rallies sympathy for struggling families but frames the government as wilfully harmful, appealing to its own side rather than persuading opponents.

text: I believe that we need to have a little bit of faith in our youth sometimes. They are actually smart and they understand the potential harm online, and they have the resilience to navigate those challenges. I think we just need to give them a little bit of guidance and education.
explanation: Inclusive, optimistic framing that brings young people in rather than positioning them only as victims.

text: Maybe it is time for all of us to reflect on our own habits. Maybe it is time for us to put down our cell phones a little bit more often, spend more time with our children, listen to them... no technology will replace the guidance, love, and people of our family.
explanation: Universal, self-including appeal to shared family values; unifying but soft.

text: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
explanation: Praises a Government measure from the Opposition benches — credits the other side where she agrees.

text: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
explanation: Collegial and respectful, no opponents targeted.

text: we are streamlining the Public Service—less duplication, more efficiency. By merging environmental management, planning, and development, it makes sense. This is about fixing the basics and building the future. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Brief and on-policy, no attacks.

text: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
explanation: Criticises the bill's scope and the Government's choice on policy grounds, no personal attack.

text: MSD advised that the Government should be investing in education, training, and employment for young people, and those members were like “Nah, don’t think so—not today.”
explanation: The mock quote ('Nah, don’t think so—not today') caricatures the government members, though the underlying point about ignoring MSD advice is substantive.

text: The Hon David Seymour has repeatedly attacked other Government agencies for wasteful spending and bureaucratic bloat, but his own ministry ignored official advice to choose the cheapest structure, grew far beyond its stated size, and relied on expensive temporary staff rather than hiring permanently—the exact behaviours he criticises in others.
explanation: Pointed and personalised to Seymour, but anchored in his record and policy conduct rather than character insult.

text: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
explanation: Identifies the specific power and its trigger (weather/road risk) though stays at description level.

text: Young people not in employment, education, or training is up to 60 percent.
explanation: Gives a figure, but 'up to 60 percent' is loosely bounded and undefined as to the population it covers.

text: The bill allows infringement notices and reminders to be served electronically... It also enables electronic warrants of fitness, certificates of fitness, and certificates of loading.
explanation: Lists specific mechanisms the bill enables, naming the document types affected.

text: There are 40,000 fewer people employed than when Luxon took office.
explanation: Concrete figure (40,000) with a clear reference point.

text: The Productivity Commission had about 22 staff and it cost around $6.5 million a year. Today, the Ministry for Regulation has grown to around 93 staff, more than four times the size of the agency it was set up to replace, and its costs are sitting at about $16.6 million a year.
explanation: Concrete figures for staff counts and annual costs of both agencies.

text: The bill is a modernisation bill. It is bringing us to a digitalised driver’s licence, which I look forward to. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Identifies the bill's core purpose (digital licence) but offers little detail beyond it.

text: We needed to look outwards and strengthen those relationships following a period of lacklustre representation and advocacy on the international stage.
explanation: Vague characterisation with no concrete examples.

text: We now come to a New Zealand and India free-trade agreement that was initially considered an impossible task, but it is something that we have achieved... It is an agreement that will open up relationships for our exporters and that will draw attention to New Zealand from India.
explanation: Names the agreement but benefits are described generally.

text: In addition to that, we have the Singapore - New Zealand essential supplies agreement. What that does is bring to New Zealanders... the stability of supply.
explanation: Names a specific agreement and its purpose, but no detail on scope or terms.

text: I believe that having a bill or a piece of legislation that simply introduces an age limit is not going far enough, not doing enough to actually address the real harms that many have spoken to us about.
explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated preference for a multi-recommendation approach over a single age limit.

text: If we can't convince the Government to go with the default six months, then we would support the member's amendment to at least extend it out to four months for all the reasons that he gave.
explanation: Stated willingness to compromise is consistent with her party's argued preference for a longer committee period.

text: Last year, with support of our National Party caucus and our Prime Minister and education Minister, I introduced my member’s bill to ban social media for under-16s. It’s great to stand here today and see this work progressed.
explanation: Her advocacy today is consistent with the bill she introduced — words and record align.

text: I think there’s a lot assumption that parents know. I would hold the view that a lot of parents don’t know. They’ve never grown up with the technology. They’ve never had the ability to use the technology.
explanation: Reasonable generational point supporting the case for parent education, but rests on personal observation rather than data (though it echoes the 92.9% survey cited earlier).

text: We went through a tunnel in the Kaimais that hasn’t had a passenger rail train go through it in 14 years... We’re connecting Auckland, Hamilton, and Tauranga, the “golden triangle”, with public transport options. At a time when fuel prices are increasing, now is the time to make that change and to invest in more public transport.
explanation: Links rising fuel prices to a public-transport case; reasonable but leans on an anecdotal train trip rather than data.

text: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
explanation: Identifies specific omitted areas (affordability, emissions, accessibility), a substantive critique, though it doesn't evidence the impact of the omission.

text: The Government was given a range of options—five policy options, in fact—to address how they could assist young people into work, and they chose to go with the cheapest option.
explanation: Anchors criticism in the existence of alternative official options, supporting the claim of a cost-driven choice.

text: The Hon David Seymour has repeatedly attacked other Government agencies for wasteful spending and bureaucratic bloat, but his own ministry ignored official advice to choose the cheapest structure, grew far beyond its stated size, and relied on expensive temporary staff rather than hiring permanently—the exact behaviours he criticises in others.
explanation: Hypocrisy argument supported by the specific cost/staffing facts she previously laid out; logically connected.

text: The Productivity Commission had about 22 staff and it cost around $6.5 million a year. Today, the Ministry for Regulation has grown to around 93 staff, more than four times the size of the agency it was set up to replace, and its costs are sitting at about $16.6 million a year.
explanation: Uses like-for-like comparison data to support the claim of bloat; conclusion follows from the figures.

text: One statistic they shared was particularly striking: 92.9 percent of parents surveyed said they had little to no idea how to keep their children safe online.
explanation: Cites a specific survey figure from Our Kids Online; plausible and precisely stated, but the underlying survey's representativeness is unverified.

text: Young people not in employment, education, or training is up to 60 percent.
explanation: A 60 percent NEET rate is implausibly high versus standard NZ youth NEET statistics (typically in the low double digits); likely overstated or mis-stated.

text: MSD advised that the Government should be investing in education, training, and employment for young people, and those members were like “Nah, don’t think so—not today.”
explanation: The claim that MSD advised investment over the chosen option is consistent with the RIS references made by multiple speakers.

text: Most of the burden of this cost will fall on 4,300 young people and their families, who will no longer be eligible for support.
explanation: Precise figure presented as fact from the bill's analysis; plausible and specific though not confirmed in text.

text: We know that even Treasury advised against this expensive project—advised against setting up a stand-alone department—saying that a smaller unit within an existing agency would be cheaper and easier to establish. That advice was ignored in favour of the most expensive option
explanation: Specific factual claim about Treasury advice; plausible and consistent with reporting, presented concretely.

text: The bill allows infringement notices and reminders to be served electronically... It also enables electronic warrants of fitness, certificates of fitness, and certificates of loading.
explanation: Accurate, checkable description of the bill's digitisation provisions.

text: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
explanation: Describes a concrete, delivered action (bringing the exhibit to Parliament and hosting a cross-party event), not just an aspiration.

text: I'm rather disappointed to hear my colleague Steve Abel there. I thought we almost had him in supporting, but never mind. Hopefully we can get him back.
explanation: Good-humoured and respectful toward an opponent — expresses disappointment without any personal attack and keeps the door open.

text: This bill cuts unnecessary bureaucracy and red tape. Trusting credible overseas regulators like Australia, the UK, Canada, and the US is smart. It's about delivering for our farmers and growers. We are fixing the basics and building the future for our rock star primary producers.
explanation: Assertions that the approach is 'smart' with no supporting evidence or reasoning offered.

text: I take the Minister's point that there's no massive change—or “any change”, I think, is what the Minister said—to risk thresholds per se. But in trying to speed up the process, if the checks and balances aren't there to ensure the appropriate management of these substances and new organisms, then there is a risk there.
explanation: Acknowledges and fairly restates the Minister's point before registering her own concern — engages rather than dismisses.

text: There is no economy with polluted rivers. There is no productivity on eroded land. There is no growth on a warming planet. The environment is the economy
explanation: Memorable, well-constructed framing, though it speaks to her own side's premises.

text: I don't think any of us on either side of the House would disagree with us wanting to achieve all of that, but the devil is in the detail, or the proof is in the pudding, as they say.
explanation: Acknowledges common ground across the House before pivoting to critique — a mildly inclusive framing.

text: delivering tax cuts for their rich mates. That is the cornerstone of their economic policy.
explanation: Us-vs-them framing that demonises opponents' supporters; not consensus-building.

text: This is a Government that is an absolute shambles. This is a Government that will take us backwards. It's a regressive Government
explanation: Rallying condemnation that alienates rather than persuades the undecided.

text: OK, have a look at this external consultation list. I just read it out to you. The SPCA wasn't on it, and no veterinary organisation was on that list. Given it's veterinary medicines, it seems a strange omission.
explanation: Directly answers Miles Anderson's challenge ('It is a consultation, isn't it, Steve?') by pointing to the actual consultation list and identifying who is missing.

text: This is all about fixing the basics so that build a future for Kiwi families, Kiwi families that could be moving into their own house today but have been stopped by rules that are onerous and put unnecessary obligations particularly on lenders.
explanation: Aspirational framing about enabling families to build homes; states intent behind the bill but describes no delivered outcome, so it is announcement/aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: Intent: "We're going to build 100,000 homes." Execution: "We built 1,000." It's great to have the intent, but we need the execution that can actually deliver it.
explanation: Describes a prior government's grand promise that was not delivered—a low-strength record.

text: A big part of this Government's strategy is to double the value of exports, and we've seen tremendous growth. A key milestone... was the signing of the free-trade agreement with India only a couple of weeks ago, the one that Chris Hipkins said would never happen.
explanation: Points to a concluded FTA as delivery against the export strategy.

text: As much as I want to build a road to Levin—and I really want to build that road to Levin
explanation: An aspiration stated in a maiden speech with no commitment, mechanism, or delivery behind it.

text: We are not producing enough babies in this country to ensure that we have a stable or even growing population. We are going to rely on migration... We will have a declining population if it isn’t for smart, skilled immigration
explanation: Predicts a declining population absent migration — directionally supported by current fertility/demographic data.

text: The move to a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs will mean clearer accountability, faster guidance, and more reliable support for businesses who are trying to comply with the law. The transition is on track to go live on 1 July 2026
explanation: Forecasts the transition will go live on schedule and improve accountability — plausible but a prediction about delivery.

text: I am concerned that this is going to backfire completely and that for the more serious criminal cases, those people will have no real redress.
explanation: Prediction that the eligibility framework will backfire and leave serious-offence survivors without real redress; plausible concern but speculative and contested by the Minister's response.

text: if they choose the other pathway, they're very likely to become the cases that we hear about where large awards are made because there is no causal connection between their behaviour later in terms of that and the liability of the State for what is abuse.
explanation: Predicts survivors diverting to litigation and winning large awards; directionally reasoned from the incentive structure but uncertain in magnitude.

text: My understanding of this piece of law is that it will extinguish their rights. It does affect a lot of people.
explanation: Prediction about the bill's legal effect on pending claimants; directionally plausible but hedged ('my understanding') and uncertain.

text: We clearly will be voting against this motion, and select committees should be respected and given the time that they need to make a good job.
explanation: Stated voting position is consistent with the argument he has just made for full select committee time; words and intended action align within the text.

text: when the House is sitting, I would like to be in the House doing the work of this House in these debates. This is the premier institution of Parliament. It is the House of Representatives, and I take my role of representing my constituents in this House, in this seat, very seriously.
explanation: States a parliamentary value (prioritising House attendance) consistent with the very point he is arguing; a stated principle with no visible contradiction.

text: It’s nothing like KiwiBuild. KiwiBuild might not have built enough houses, but it didn’t send people to their graves.
explanation: Candidly concedes his own party's KiwiBuild shortfall rather than defending it, showing consistency between word and the known record.

text: I move, That the motion be amended to replace the words "20 August 2026" with "20 September 2026".
explanation: Takes concrete procedural action (moving a formal amendment) rather than only asserting a view, though delivery depends on the House.

text: What I think that the Opposition has forgotten in debating this bill is that there’s a thing called the student allowance and there’s a thing called training and there is a thing called responsibility and accountability.
explanation: Points to alternative supports (student allowance, training) as a counter, but bundles them with 'responsibility' as rhetoric rather than detailed argument.

text: If you go to work and you’re on the minimum wage, you can earn up to about $950 a week—that’s a lot of money.
explanation: Roughly consistent with full-time minimum-wage gross weekly pay, but 'a lot of money' is a value judgement and the figure omits tax and hours assumptions.

text: The bill does not change existing services, funding allocations, or who can receive disability support services, and I think that's a very important point. It does not change any of that.
explanation: Restates the Government's reassurance; contested by opposition speakers who argue the bill extinguishes accrued rights of family carers.

text: if the Minister had signalled that this was going to come well in advance, she could have introduced this bill earlier and allowed it to have adequate select committee scrutiny.
explanation: Directly addresses and answers the Minister's stated reason for the truncated timeline rather than evading it.

text: we have a top-line, as our leader says—a top-line for superannuation at 65. It’s something that is non-negotiable. It’s a bedrock for our policy, so keeping that superannuation at 65 in a policy like this, that’s written in legislation, is really important
explanation: Restates a long-standing, consistently held NZ First position on super at 65; consistent with the party's known record, though self-asserted.

text: When I was a young 17-year-old looking at who I was going to vote for... I came from a hard background, no money sometimes, no food sometimes... I knew, from my background, that the Government doesn’t help poor people. I needed every cent I could get to try to get out of that.
explanation: Links his stated small-government values to a consistent lifelong voting choice; the self-account is internally consistent though unverifiable.

text: This Government has moved quickly to reduce barriers to entry into the grocery sector, including creating an express lane for new supermarkets and strengthening penalties for misleading or deceptive pricing. Grocery prices are influenced by a range of factors, including global commodity prices, transport costs, energy prices, weather events, and wider inflation pressures.
explanation: Asked whether increased competition has brought prices down; lists reforms and price-driver caveats but never says prices fell.

text: If this member was so interested in all these issues, they would not have sat on their hands for six years.
explanation: Asked whether predatory pricing is acceptable; entirely dodges to attack the questioner's record.

text: I ask the member to put that question to the young and dynamic Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, because that is the Minister who gets the monthly update from the Companies Office
explanation: Asked how many of 188 liquidations were small businesses; redirects to another Minister rather than answering.

text: That is why businesses and manufacturers are going to back this Government for its re-election, and it’s exactly why they will not return the last lot
explanation: Asked what immediate support is being provided to struggling businesses; pivots to campaign messaging without specifics.

text: Research shows that by improving mental health in the workplace, productivity can increase by around 6 percent to 10 percent. There is strong economic evidence for investing in better mental health in the workplace, with returns of around $5 for every $1 invested into initiatives such as employee assistance programmes. That’s why today I have launched a business mental health tool kit that delivers free and confidential mental health support in a way that works best for the workplace.
explanation: Cites productivity and ROI evidence to justify the initiative; conclusion follows from the premises.

text: Opening these conversations and listening to Chlöe Swarbrick and all the politicians across the board tonight—it’s been extremely eye opening to hear that come to a common ground on some of these issues.
explanation: Explicitly acknowledges cross-party common ground and values the contributions of others.

text: if there’s small alterations in legislation that we can see today and that we can alter to criminalise rangatahi being affected by the internet and being affected by breaches of their privacy, I think that’s what we should be doing as politicians.
explanation: Frames support for another member's bill in cooperative, solution-oriented terms.

text: any concerns around how this bill will operate, that can be teased out at select committee. That is the purpose of a select committee, and I want to acknowledge New Zealand First for pointing out some of the things they believe need to be addressed at a select committee.
explanation: Reasonable procedural argument that operational concerns are properly resolved at select committee.

text: there are reasons, under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act—just like there are under the Official Information Act—to withhold information. You can write that into legislation very easily to actually address those times when it would be inappropriate to release the information.
explanation: Directly rebuts the commercial-sensitivity objection by pointing to existing withholding provisions; logically responsive.

text: a truncated select committee process of three months, instead of the usual six, does not meet a threshold for consultation for this community. If, as my colleague pointed out, it is a shortened time frame for submissions—three weeks for people with disabilities to put submissions in—it is not enough time for genuine consultation
explanation: Reasoned argument tying the compressed timeline to inadequate consultation, with concrete comparison.

text: Parliament does not accept email submissions. I don't believe Parliament accepts an email with a voice-type submission. There are a whole series of barriers for people to actually submit to our Parliament. Our Office of the Clerk are under-resourced.
explanation: Builds a concrete accessibility argument and proposes alternatives (email, video submissions).

text: when food companies, for example, have to do LGOIMA or Official Information Act kind of thing, when they incur costs, guess who actually pays for it! It’s actually the customers who have to pay, because they’ve incurred costs.
explanation: Cost-pass-through point drawn from personal import/export anecdote; intuitive but anecdotal and conflates private firms with the publicly-owned ports at issue.

text: I'm thinking of Farzana Yaqubi, a 21-year-old law student, resident of West Auckland. She was walking home, and she was stabbed to death. That is after eight weeks prior when she had complained to police about a stalker... perhaps if that murderer was caught when he was stalking Farzana, she may still be here.
explanation: A powerful case to motivate the policy, but a single anecdote rather than systemic evidence of the law's effect.

text: We have 49,000 fewer victims because National is focused on making sure that we deliver on our promises.
explanation: Attributes the fall directly to Government focus without isolating other factors.

text: you’ve got some big ports who are very successful, then you’ve got those who are really struggling, specifically around their job and workforce investment strategies. Then the port companies spend a large amount of money in terms of investment but don’t attract the vessels that should be coming, so is there a better way to do that within New Zealand?
explanation: Lays out a real coordination problem (mismatched investment and vessel attraction) to justify the bill, though without supporting figures.

text: if we’re giving money to criminals, regardless of whether the programmes that they deliver are good or not, it means that, actually, we can’t spend money on something else: can’t spend money on health; can’t spend money on education.
explanation: Valid opportunity-cost argument that funds spent here cannot be spent elsewhere; sound but stated in absolute terms.

text: this Government actually inherited, I think, an unsustainable situation in the disability sector. It inherited a ministry out of control and not able to control its own spending.
explanation: Asserts unsustainability and loss of spending control without citing figures or evidence.

text: remember what Kahurangi Carter said? “Who would you be more afraid of seeing down an alleyway; would it be a police officer or patched gang member?” Which one would it be? They’ve chosen to choose the side of the gang members. What a disgrace.
explanation: Strawman and false dichotomy—infers opponents support gangs from an unrelated rhetorical question.

text: Ricardo Menéndez March from the Green Party is going to heckle, to apologise on behalf of the gangs, to say, “It’s not their fault, don’t pick on them. They’re nice people, they do good things in our community.”
explanation: Pure strawman—invents the Green MP's position rather than engaging anything he actually said.

text: Oh, Reuben Davidson doesn't like this change. We'll remember that. People in Christchurch East will remember that. He wants you to have a different price at the till then you do on the shelf. He just said it across the House.
explanation: Distorts the opponent's position rather than engaging it (strawman).

text: I encourage National and ACT to rethink their position. Send this bill to the select committee so that those conversations can be teased out through official advice at select committee. It’s the place to have that conversation so that we can say, “Yes, we support transparency. Here are the areas where we would need to have carve-outs
explanation: Respectful appeal to opposing parties focused on process and substance.

text: this Government has a pattern of behaviour. They are repeatedly putting these types of truncated processes in place, and then what happens is the committee goes, "Oh look, we don't have enough time to do this."
explanation: Critical of Government process and procedure, mildly mocking ('Funny that!') but not a personal attack.

text: people of all faiths—Jewish, Muslim, and Christian people; people of other faiths or no faith; people from all backgrounds, all ethnicities, and all walks of life—may live together in equality, freedom, peace, and safety
explanation: Respectful and conciliatory, focused on shared humanity.

text: I’d like to start off by congratulating my colleague across the House Lemauga Lydia Sosene, who I serve with on the Governance and Administration Committee.
explanation: Respectful toward a political opponent.

text: I think that this is an overreach and it is a solution looking for a problem. But I actually wish my colleague best of luck at select committee.
explanation: Firm criticism of the bill but gracious toward the member.

text: I'm thinking of Farzana Yaqubi, a 21-year-old law student, resident of West Auckland. She was walking home, and she was stabbed to death. That is after eight weeks prior when she had complained to police about a stalker... perhaps if that murderer was caught when he was stalking Farzana, she may still be here.
explanation: A respectful, substantive account used to justify the stalking law; no personal attack on opponents.

text: what I’m asking for, through this bill, is transparency and the ability to look at a possible national port strategy that would have a more complementary strategy for ports within New Zealand.
explanation: Names the goal (transparency, national port strategy) but the mechanism for 'complementary' strategy stays general.

text: you’ve got some big ports who are very successful, then you’ve got those who are really struggling, specifically around their job and workforce investment strategies. Then the port companies spend a large amount of money in terms of investment but don’t attract the vessels that should be coming, so is there a better way to do that within New Zealand?
explanation: Identifies concrete weaknesses (workforce investment, investment that fails to attract vessels) but no named ports or numbers.

text: there are reasons, under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act—just like there are under the Official Information Act—to withhold information. You can write that into legislation very easily to actually address those times when it would be inappropriate to release the information.
explanation: Accurate that both LGOIMA and the OIA already contain grounds for withholding information.

text: Parliament does not accept email submissions. I don't believe Parliament accepts an email with a voice-type submission. There are a whole series of barriers for people to actually submit to our Parliament. Our Office of the Clerk are under-resourced.
explanation: Broadly reflects real friction in the parliamentary submission process, though 'does not accept email submissions' is stated more absolutely than is strictly accurate, and is partly hedged ('I don't believe').

text: this Government has a pattern of behaviour. They are repeatedly putting these types of truncated processes in place, and then what happens is the committee goes, "Oh look, we don't have enough time to do this."
explanation: The coalition's frequent use of urgency and shortened committee timelines is well documented, supporting the 'pattern' claim.

text: The latest reports have 1,200 people killed as a result of Hamas’ attack on Israel on 7 October, while at least 16,000 Palestinians have been killed since then, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
explanation: Figures align with reported tolls and are properly attributed to their source.

text: More children have been killed in Gaza than in all the world’s conflicts combined in each of the past three years.
explanation: Echoes a Save the Children comparison that was circulating; broadly supported but a striking framing that is hard to fully verify.

text: as a company—and often these port companies, some of them are local government entities, as in council-controlled organisations. But some of them are actually, like Port of Tauranga is, you know, it’s a private company. I remember—and a lot of them are listed in the Stock Exchange.
explanation: Misleading: Port of Tauranga is majority council-owned (via Bay of Plenty Regional Council) though NZX-listed, so calling it 'a private company' and saying 'a lot of them' are listed overstates private ownership.

text: It has only been one sleep since that stalking law has actually come into law—it's only been one sleep, and already a 39-year-old man has been charged with stalking; allegedly stalking and harassing a woman getting off the bus. That's already working.
explanation: Specific, checkable claim about a charge under the new law; carefully says 'allegedly'.

text: ram raids are virtually every night going back to the last election, everyone was complaining about ram raids. It's down 85 percent.
explanation: Ram raids did fall sharply, but an 85% figure presented without timeframe/baseline risks overstatement.

text: We have 49,000 fewer victims because National is focused on making sure that we deliver on our promises.
explanation: References a victimisation figure tied to the Government's target; the specific number is plausible but unverified and causation is asserted.

text: Increased patrol of police, 40 percent.
explanation: Stated as fact but unsourced and ambiguous as to what is measured.

text: this Government actually inherited, I think, an unsustainable situation in the disability sector. It inherited a ministry out of control and not able to control its own spending.
explanation: Whaikaha/disability funding did face widely-reported budget overruns in 2024, so directionally supported, but 'out of control' overstates it.

text: If I look across at the Tasman, at the national disability support service there, a wonderfully set-up scheme to actually try and help people has got out of control and is becoming unsustainable.
explanation: Australia's NDIS cost-sustainability concerns are real and widely reported, but 'out of control' is hyperbolic.

text: Down my way, in Central Otago, we also had the excellent announcement of $180 million to go into the Southern Lakes area—some of it for operational funding over four years, and some of it for capital funding.
explanation: An announced funding figure presented as fact.

text: We know that $135 million is going to go into supporting our ambulance services across the country. We had the excellent announcement of around $15.5 million for specialist palliative care for children
explanation: Specific pre-Budget figures presented as announced commitments.

text: That’s why we have reintroduced things like three strikes, the gang patch ban, etc.
explanation: Accurate: the coalition reinstated three strikes and legislated a public gang patch ban.

text: any concerns around how this bill will operate, that can be teased out at select committee. That is the purpose of a select committee, and I want to acknowledge New Zealand First for pointing out some of the things they believe need to be addressed at a select committee.
explanation: Acknowledges NZ First's concerns and invites cross-party engagement through the committee process.

text: I encourage National and ACT to rethink their position. Send this bill to the select committee so that those conversations can be teased out through official advice at select committee. It’s the place to have that conversation so that we can say, “Yes, we support transparency. Here are the areas where we would need to have carve-outs
explanation: Explicitly invites opponents in and offers a compromise frame (support transparency plus agreed carve-outs).

text: That six-month process is a fundamental element of the democratic process of this House. This is the people's House; it is not our House
explanation: Appeals to a shared democratic value ('the people's House') to make a unifying case for process.

text: people of all faiths—Jewish, Muslim, and Christian people; people of other faiths or no faith; people from all backgrounds, all ethnicities, and all walks of life—may live together in equality, freedom, peace, and safety
explanation: Inclusive, unifying language that reaches across communities rather than rallying one side.

text: I’d like to start off by congratulating my colleague across the House Lemauga Lydia Sosene, who I serve with on the Governance and Administration Committee.
explanation: Cordial cross-party acknowledgement of the bill's sponsor despite opposing the bill.

text: I do want to acknowledge and I am pleased that the different members have provided a contribution because it’s always good to be able to test the thinking in different political contributions, but I do stand behind the reason for this bill
explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of opposing contributions while holding her position; inclusive tone.

text: I rise on behalf of the Labour Party and want to be very clear that we are supporting this bill going to select committee. I want to place that on Hansard, because the contributions of late would seem to indicate that that is not the position that the Labour Party is taking.
explanation: Unambiguously states Labour's position on the gangs bill and corrects the record directly.

text: I think that this is an overreach and it is a solution looking for a problem. But I actually wish my colleague best of luck at select committee.
explanation: States National's opposition plainly while still extending goodwill.

text: what I’m asking for, through this bill, is transparency and the ability to look at a possible national port strategy that would have a more complementary strategy for ports within New Zealand.
explanation: Directly answers the repeated 'what's the problem' challenge by stating her aim of transparency and a national port strategy.

text: We absolutely are going to support it in ACT, and I want to acknowledge Labour for supporting it as well.
explanation: States ACT's position clearly and credits Labour's support without hedging.

text: I am absolutely shameless when it comes to my constituency of Palmerston North, I’ll give the member that.
explanation: Self-aware, candid admission of constituency advocacy; words match an openly-held priority.

text: the political lineage of the exclusions in the 2002 Act was actually brought to the House in December 2001 by Labour MP Sandra Lee under a Labour Government. It was then passed over to Chris Carter, who took it through its third reading in December 2002. So it’s actually come from within the team; they thought that the exclusion was important, and I think it is too.
explanation: Turns the consistency lens on Labour—arguing the exclusion they now want to remove was their own creation; this is a point about the proponents, not Reti's own record.

text: I do want to acknowledge and I am pleased that the different members have provided a contribution because it’s always good to be able to test the thinking in different political contributions, but I do stand behind the reason for this bill
explanation: Consistently restates the same transparency rationale she opened with, holding position under criticism.

text: New Zealand should rightfully expect that we will be a strong Opposition, that we will hold the Government to account for working in the best interests of all New Zealanders, and that we will hold the Government to account for the promises they made.
explanation: States the Opposition role in general terms without naming particular issues or mechanisms.

text: The only growth that we've seen is the growth in unemployment, the growth in business liquidations, and the growth in the number of Kiwis leaving for Australia and other countries because the opportunities are simply not here.
explanation: Names categories of negative trends but no figures or timeframes.

text: What advice has he received or requested regarding Auckland's skyrocketing level of unemployment, now twice what it was three years ago, and the correlation between job losses in Auckland and homelessness?
explanation: Quantifies the change ('twice') and names a concrete linkage, though without a base figure.

text: What I remember very clearly was in the early 1990s when both my parents lost their jobs in a community where the vast majority of people lost jobs, because of the closure of things like the freezing works. These were people that had always worked... but the jobs simply weren't there.
explanation: Concrete personal account anchored in a real historical event (freezing works closures).

text: Will he guarantee that the Budget will provide real relief for Aucklanders, given, on his watch, Auckland’s unemployment rate is almost double what it was three years ago, the number of people on a benefit is up 40 percent, and the number of young people out of work and/or training is up almost 60 percent?

text: It commits to the roads of national significance along TNL2, Taureka Northern Link 2, State Highway 29, and State Highway 29A.

text: In housing and urban growth, over 10 years, we expect to see 12,000 more greenfield houses and 3,000 more infill projects.
explanation: Concrete numbers and a 10-year horizon.

text: Since 2000, we have had population growth of 76 percent, compared to the national average of 38 percent. We have seen GDP growth since 2000 of 148 percent, compared to the national average of 87 percent.
explanation: Precise comparative growth statistics over a defined period.

text: Since 2000, we have had population growth of 76 percent, compared to the national average of 38 percent. We have seen GDP growth since 2000 of 148 percent, compared to the national average of 87 percent.
explanation: Bay of Plenty did grow well above average; the exact figures are plausible but unverified here.

text: National will take six weeks to sort coalition. Willis is”—a derogatory word—“and can’t do simple sums.
explanation: Ad hominem; an unverifiable anonymous message used to impugn the Finance Minister.

text: Many people have been saying outside this House—and I’m going to add my voice to it—that this Government is looking like the most backward, regressive, divisive Government that we have ever seen as a country. I absolutely agree with that.
explanation: Appeal to popularity ('many people are saying') plus an unsubstantiated superlative.

text: What I remember very clearly was in the early 1990s when both my parents lost their jobs in a community where the vast majority of people lost jobs, because of the closure of things like the freezing works. These were people that had always worked... but the jobs simply weren't there.
explanation: Persuasive personal anecdote used as an analogy to today; emotionally effective but evidentially limited.

text: The only growth that we've seen is the growth in unemployment, the growth in business liquidations, and the growth in the number of Kiwis leaving for Australia and other countries because the opportunities are simply not here.
explanation: Cites real trends but asserts causation rhetorically.

text: Why should Aucklanders support the move-on orders when the Ministry of Justice has said there is no evidence that move-on orders would reduce crime, Police have opposed criminalising rough sleeping, and Treasury have said that the costs would outweigh the benefits?
explanation: Marshals three named institutional sources (Justice, Police, Treasury) as evidence against the policy; relies on appeal to authority but cites concrete positions.

text: We needed to look outwards and strengthen those relationships following a period of lacklustre representation and advocacy on the international stage.
explanation: Criticises the previous government's diplomacy as 'lacklustre' without personal attack.

text: It's in the bedrooms, and these children will have lifelong illness. They will not only suffer lifelong illness; they will cost our health system even more.
explanation: Predicts lifelong illness and higher health costs from mould exposure; directionally supported but stated with overcertainty for all cases.

text: They've flogged off Fonterra, they've flogged off Alliance meats, and they've flogged off Silver Ferns Farms, one after the other. Well, ladies and gentlemen, on 7 November, all that's going to stop.
explanation: Predicts asset sell-offs will stop after the 7 November election—contingent on an uncertain electoral and policy outcome.

text: If we'd not got back, these three parties, we were heading off to be Venezuela or Myanmar.
explanation: Counterfactual prediction of national collapse; implausible and unsupported.

text: and the Green Party is never going to make it back at all, and nor is Te Pāti Māori.
explanation: Predicts permanent decline of both parties — contradicted by their continued presence; implausible as an absolute claim.

text: This is the high point. It’s going down now... I know a bunch of losers when I see them. Any money you like—you’re going that way
explanation: Predicts the Greens'/Te Pāti Māori's decline from here — a confident but unsubstantiated forecast.

text: We now come to a New Zealand and India free-trade agreement that was initially considered an impossible task, but it is something that we have achieved... It is an agreement that will open up relationships for our exporters and that will draw attention to New Zealand from India.

text: In housing and urban growth, over 10 years, we expect to see 12,000 more greenfield houses and 3,000 more infill projects.

text: can I acknowledge the new Speaker of the House and all of the presiding officers. We hope for only one thing: that there will be fairness and clarity in the rulings that are undertaken here.
explanation: Conciliatory and institution-respecting; offers reciprocal respect across the chamber.

text: Many people have been saying outside this House—and I’m going to add my voice to it—that this Government is looking like the most backward, regressive, divisive Government that we have ever seen as a country. I absolutely agree with that.
explanation: Strongly partisan condemnation that appeals to her own side rather than persuading the undecided.

text: We were very fortunate to have the three councils, the local MPs, all of the key businesses, and the community all aligned on what the most important things were for our region.

text: It commits to the roads of national significance along TNL2, Taureka Northern Link 2, State Highway 29, and State Highway 29A.
