text: sailings cancelled due to mechanical faults have dropped from 70 percent of all sailings in 2021 to 1 percent in 2025: from 70 percent down to 1 percent. text: Last year, we completely overhauled the Marsden Point process with KiwiRail, opened the design data to the market, who put forward their own designs at their cost to identify cheaper ways of building. text: Who settled the central North Island Tribes' 14-iwi settlement? Who settled that? The Māori Wardens—who gave them their start? text: I don’t have that exact figure at the moment, but of course, it varies. What we inherited of course was a wide variety of arrangements in place across many Government departments

text: Unless there’s significant investment and outreach, food banks, and social housing, for every homeless person the police move along, two more—
explanation: Predicts that without investment two more homeless people will appear for each one moved on; directionally plausible but the specific magnitude is rhetorical and unverifiable.

text: I said very clearly about three weeks ago that Māori would revolt in the streets. I said there would be civil disobedience—not my choice. I said you'll get protests worse than the Springbok Tour.
explanation: Predicts street protests exceeding the 1981 Springbok Tour; large hīkoi did follow, but 'worse than the Springbok Tour' overshoots what eventuated.

text: this Government actually inherited, I think, an unsustainable situation in the disability sector. It inherited a ministry out of control and not able to control its own spending.
explanation: Criticism aimed at a ministry and prior settings rather than a person, but 'out of control' is loaded and somewhat sensational.

text: let's actually just engage in this debate in good faith, actually recognise that the Government is actually trying to do something to actually provide certainty to the disability sector and community.
explanation: Constructive, respectful tone urging engagement over conflict.

text: I think we actually have a responsibility in this House to debate and discuss these issues with respect, with facts, and actually not with rhetoric and create scaremongering or other things that could cause distress.
explanation: Explicitly calls for respectful, fact-based debate and against scaremongering.

text: We will affirm the Minister's view that policy setting for public funding belongs in Parliament, not in courtrooms.
explanation: A principled framing that rallies the governing side without inviting opponents in.

text: a truncated select committee process of three months, instead of the usual six, does not meet a threshold for consultation for this community. explanation: Names exact timeframes: three months vs the usual six, and three weeks for submissions.

explanation: Precise figures with clear sourcing and dates.

explanation: Prediction that demand will grow with an ageing population; well-supported by demographic evidence.

text: Te Pāti Māori sees all work as valuable. If a person is taking on the responsibility of the Government, they should receive the same benefit as a Government employee.
explanation: Consistent with the party's stated position on valuing all work; a value statement with no contradicting action visible.

text: We do not own these seats; we are kaitiaki for our people.
explanation: A stated value of stewardship/accountability to constituents; consistent in tone with her professed kaupapa but no action shown either way within the text.

text: There is a real solution sitting right here in this Parliament, it is called the Youth Homelessness Prevention Bill. explanation: Her advocacy against this bill is backed by her own prior action proposing an alternative — words match deeds.

text: That's why we support making the minimum wage a living wage, that is why we support removing GST from kai so that whānau can afford to eat, and that is why we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
explanation: Stated values matched to consistent, on-record Te Pāti Māori policy positions.

text: this suggests, in my view, that the Government may be looking at limiting the information that's available to the media, the information that's available to the public.
explanation: An inference/forecast about the Government's intent to limit information access; plausible directionally but speculative and not yet evidenced.

text: We will repeal the Regulatory Standards Act when we are in Government, and I know that's the same commitment the Labour Party and the Green Party have made also.
explanation: A clear future commitment to repeal, but it is aspiration pending an election with no delivery, and depends on forming a government.

text: That is why Te Pāti Māori will implement a wealth tax. Under our policy, 98 percent of Aotearoa will pay less tax.
explanation: An aspiration conditional on winning office; no delivery.

text: We will continue to do that, and we hope that with your support you will allow tangata whenua to freely express themselves in our cultural identity here in Aotearoa.
explanation: States intent to 'continue' but is a soft commitment dependent on the Speaker's goodwill, with no concrete action specified.

text: section 7(3) provides that a notice can only be issued and take effect after it has been approved by the House of Representatives. text: I want to begin by thanking the Regulations Review Committee, chaired most ably by my colleague Arena Williams. It is also a committee where we usually agree on most things.

explanation: Cites community-commissioned research and points to a substitute (manufactured sand); a reasoned case, though the evidence is asserted not shown.

explanation: Points to a delivered law already producing an enforcement action; concrete follow-through, though one case is early evidence.

text: that's exactly why they will not continue to be in power post this election, because they just don't get it.

explanation: Claims credit for delivered results in protracted campaigns; several are genuine achievements, though credit is shared across iwi and others.

text: Te Pāti Māori will tax the rich. It's horrible to hear and listen to it over here: it is not an "if"; it is a "when".
explanation: Emphatic commitment but aspirational, with no mechanism or delivery shown.

text: We want to end poverty. We want to have a tax policy where we would have 2.2 million people living better.

text: I see the role very much as protection of members’ rights to speak freely in this House, and to go about their business across the country unimpeded.

text: I think that that is, unfortunately, the lot of a Speaker, but I’ll do my best to be fair and even across the House.

text: Firstly, can I say that our Standing Orders really are just a guide for how this House works. They’re important and they give us a framework, but they’re not absolute.

text: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.

text: 13,000 new public homes under our Government since 2017.

text: 1,800 extra police on the beat under our Government
explanation: Claims delivery on a recruitment commitment; figure roughly matches the term's net police increase.

explanation: A forecast about a long-term future outcome (truck journeys removed, emissions cut) attributed to projections; plausible and directionally supported for an inland port, but long-range and uncertain.

text: I am so pleased we are proposing a national infrastructure agency that will have a long-term and evidence-based approach to what investments we need to make to take New Zealand forward, to support productivity, livability, and employment, not driven by ideology with unintended consequences and unmanaged financial waste.
explanation: Describes a proposal ('we are proposing'), i.e. an announcement, not a delivered policy; no implementation demonstrated.

text: I have chaired Te Whare Korowai, Hamilton Christian Nightshelter, and turned a non-existent business with a $2,000 start-up loan from my dad into a million-dollar enterprise.
explanation: Claims concrete personal follow-through — building a business from a small loan to a million-dollar enterprise — i.e. delivered results rather than aspiration, though it is a self-report.

text: To all the small-business owners out there, I am one too. I can relate. You are the backbone of the New Zealand economy. Help is coming.

text: I understand the challenges of local government and I have seen how central government has disrespected local government for the last six years with disingenuous engagement and how we must do it differently and work together to achieve good and sustainable outcomes.

text: I believe in less government, personal choice, and responsibility—a Government that sets up the right macro policy settings that enables success, and then gets out of the way.

text: Yes, we do appreciate the farmers—50 percent increase in export revenue in the primary sector when we were in office, through COVID and many other challenges.

explanation: Names the institution and the exact bailout figure.

text: There can be no prosperity without peace
explanation: General aphorism with no figures, mechanism, or concrete content.

text: It's not so nice that it took the deaths of 7,000 children—that we know of—to do it. ... every 10 minutes in Gaza a child is murdered.
explanation: Uses concrete figures and a rate, though sourcing is informal.

text: In the first four weeks, we surpassed the death toll of children that we'd seen in Ukraine in almost a year.
explanation: Concrete time windows and a comparative metric.

text: We're not a wee, little, small, insignificant nation. We do punch above our weight in international forums and on the global stage. We are looked to as a moral, principled voice
explanation: Stirring but general — no concrete action, mechanism, or figure.

text: calling for immediate, permanent, unconditional ceasefire—calling on our friends, on our allies, on our trading partners, on our Five Eyes network, on the family of nations in the Commonwealth, and on our Pasifika neighbourhood to do the same.
explanation: Names a precise demand (immediate, permanent, unconditional ceasefire) and the specific channels to pursue it, though without mechanism for delivery.

text: We want to restore national unity, and that's probably going to be the hardest thing to do, with all the division we've got. And we're going to boost social cohesiveness
explanation: Invokes unity and cohesion, but pairs it with blaming 'the division we've got' on the prior government, limiting its inclusiveness.

text: So I think, as Peeni Henare said, we can disagree without being disagreeable, and I think that is something we should remember.
explanation: Explicitly endorses respectful cross-party debate and approvingly cites an opponent — genuinely consensus-building.

text: The Hon Julie Anne Genter—you've got to admire her passion ... Calling people fools is not a way to win an argument. Just because they disagree with you does not mean they don't have a valid point of view
explanation: Models reciprocity and openness to others' viewpoints rather than scoring partisan points.

text: Our solutions are different, but that time is over now. It's over because every 10 minutes in Gaza a child is murdered. So our solutions have to be united. We have to stand together. We have to stand strong
explanation: Appeals across the House to shared human values and common cause, explicitly inviting unity rather than scoring partisan points.

text: We're not a wee, little, small, insignificant nation. We do punch above our weight in international forums and on the global stage. We are looked to as a moral, principled voice
explanation: Uplifting, inclusive national framing intended to rally collective pride and resolve.

text: It was a National Government that stood up for Palestine in the General Assembly of the United Nations and gave Palestine official status in that forum.
explanation: Credits an opponent party's past principled stance to build cross-party common ground on the issue.

text: each one of those children would have had their favourite toy, their favourite subject at school. They might have been a little bit loud, or a little bit quiet, or naughty. They would have been somebody’s everything, that they’re not just numbers
explanation: Emotionally resonant and humanising, effective rhetoric, but primarily moves those already sympathetic rather than persuading opponents.

text: maybe she should come up to Franklin, just south of Auckland, and try and get on the motorway and drive to work at 6.30 in the morning... because it's absolutely congested, that they are ignorant fools, because I'm not sure that they're going to agree with you
explanation: Turns Genter's own 'ignorant fools' line back on her by invoking constituents; combative but not itself a personal insult.

text: that Labour Government over there, for the last six years, just saw them as a cash tool and they imposed heaps of regulation on them without properly considering the nature and the cost and the burden of that regulation on small businesses
explanation: Sharp criticism of the prior government's treatment of small business; targets policy/record rather than persons, but uses loaded framing ('cash tool').

text: So I think, as Peeni Henare said, we can disagree without being disagreeable, and I think that is something we should remember.
explanation: Calls for disagreement without disrespect, crediting an opponent's framing.

text: The Hon Julie Anne Genter—you've got to admire her passion ... Calling people fools is not a way to win an argument. Just because they disagree with you does not mean they don't have a valid point of view
explanation: Rebukes the 'fools' insult while acknowledging the opponent's passion and granting opponents may have valid views — measured and respectful.

text: We rushed through, after the terrible event in Christchurch a few years ago, some firearms legislation, which was well intentioned but has had far-reaching and adverse effects ... he's had to go out and go through a very expensive process to set up a legal range on his property. ... it's needless, it's pointless, it's wasteful
explanation: Criticises the regulation while repeatedly conceding it was 'well intentioned'; engages substance respectfully.

text: without the farmers—they literally carry us on their back—and without the income that they earn through their exports, this country would be a much poorer place than it is today.
explanation: Praise for farmers; the implied 'public enemy number one' jab at the prior government is mild.

text: reference to the Government's talking points of strong and stable Government while actually being the most unstable Government arrangement ever agreed under MMP
explanation: Characterising a three-party coalition as 'the most unstable ever under MMP' is an opinionated superlative not borne out at formation; rhetorical overstatement.

text: surveys released yesterday showed over 70 percent of young people are happy with the changes that are proposed ... I can also reassure him that 70 percent of smokers also want to quit.
explanation: Both figures are plausible and in line with public-health survey ranges, but cited loosely without a named source.

text: I was shocked, like many New Zealanders, to hear that the Government proposed to repeal these laws in order to fund their tax cuts.
explanation: The repeal's fiscal contribution toward tax-cut funding was a contested framing; partly grounded (the revenue was counted) but presents motive as established fact.

text: In his first day in the job—in fact, before he even got the job—Dr Reti has managed to mobilise the entire health sector against him.
explanation: 'The entire health sector' is hyperbole; broad opposition existed but the universal claim is overstated.

text: Yes, we do appreciate the farmers—50 percent increase in export revenue in the primary sector when we were in office, through COVID and many other challenges.
explanation: Primary-sector export revenue did rise substantially over Labour's term; '50 percent' is plausibly in range but rounded and unsourced.

text: the previous National Government had increased the weight of trucks and had a sweat-the-assets campaign that resulted in underfunding and a degradation of our roading network that continues today
explanation: References real policies (higher truck mass limits, road-maintenance constraint) but the causal claim about lasting degradation is contestable and one-sided.

text: When we came in, actually, Tai Poutini Polytech on the West Coast was broke. We had to step up. We wrote out a cheque for $35 million just to keep them afloat
explanation: Specific, checkable claim about a $35m rescue of Tai Poutini; plausible and concrete though unverified here.

text: you can look at the Prime Minister of Israel, who's been under suspicion of corruption and bribery since 2019
explanation: Netanyahu was indicted on corruption/bribery charges in 2019; accurate, though 'suspicion' understates the formal indictment.

text: It's not so nice that it took the deaths of 7,000 children—that we know of—to do it. ... every 10 minutes in Gaza a child is murdered.
explanation: Casualty figures cite contested wartime tallies; the '7,000 children' and 'every 10 minutes' framings echo reported estimates but are uncertain and emotively rounded.

text: In the first four weeks, we surpassed the death toll of children that we'd seen in Ukraine in almost a year.
explanation: A specific comparative claim that is broadly consistent with reported child-casualty disparities, but the exact comparison is hard to verify and depends on contested counts.

text: a Government in Aotearoa New Zealand quite unexpectedly recognised Palestine's right to self-determination and Statehood. ... I hate to point this out, but the Labour Government didn't do it for six years, and they did vote down my motion on Statehood
explanation: The claim that Labour did not previously recognise Palestinian statehood and voted down her motion is a specific, checkable assertion presented plausibly.

text: Does he acknowledge the deaths of over 16,000 Palestinians, more than 7,000 of whom are children, and that the disproportionate targeting of civilians can never constitute an exercise of the right to self-defence?
explanation: The casualty figures align broadly with Gaza health-ministry tolls reported by early December 2023, though such figures were contested and unverified at the time.

text: It matters that until now, both the caretaker Government and our incoming Prime Minister have failed to call for a lasting ceasefire.
explanation: Accurate that neither had called for a permanent ceasefire before this; 'failed' is an evaluative gloss on the factual record.

text: I think it's because those three parties can agree on very little, and that's why their agenda is not one that is framed in the positive of common aspirations, but one framed in the negative; one that will take us backwards.
explanation: Predicts the agenda 'will take us backwards' — vague and partisan, hard to falsify.

text: They are responsible for the lives they will harm—for the amputations, for the strokes, for the heart attacks, for the health costs, for the congested hospitals.
explanation: Predicts increased smoking-related harm from the repeal; directionally supported by public-health evidence but magnitude and attribution uncertain.

text: its commitments of matching the Labour Party's health funding promises at the election. I am deeply worried about the concern that those promises will not be met because of the Government's unfunded tax plans
explanation: Predicts health-funding shortfall driven by 'unfunded tax plans'; plausible partisan forecast, contingent and unproven.

text: What's been forgotten is it was going to cost $15.7 billion. ... $15.7 billion will be roughly $30 billion by the time it's built. And it wouldn't be built until the middle of next year.
explanation: Extrapolates a doubling to ~$30bn from the 98% overrun average; a defensible projection but applying an average as a forecast is uncertain.

text: We are going to commit to moderate rises in minimum wage. ... we used to do roughly about 50c when we were last in Government every year.
explanation: Backs the stated approach with the party's prior record of ~50c annual rises, lending consistency.

text: a Government in Aotearoa New Zealand quite unexpectedly recognised Palestine's right to self-determination and Statehood. ... I hate to point this out, but the Labour Government didn't do it for six years, and they did vote down my motion on Statehood
explanation: Frames Labour as inconsistent (sharing the value yet voting down her Statehood motion for six years) — a hypocrisy charge aimed at others, not a self-consistency signal.

text: We're going to repeal that dreadful proposal, the fair pay agreement, by Christmas.
explanation: Firm commitment with a timeframe; FPA repeal was in fact legislated, supporting follow-through, though stated here as intent.

text: We're going to have an inquiry into the banking competition. We're going to expand the role of the Grocery Commissioner. We're going to rewrite that dreadful credit contracts and consumer finance Act
explanation: Announced agenda items at the start of a term — intent stated, delivery not yet demonstrated.

text: available medicines being delivered by pharmacies, as we have done by removing the $5 co-payment across the country. That type of access to medicines needs to be maintained.
explanation: Claims credit for a concrete, delivered measure (removing the $5 prescription co-payment nationally), which Labour did implement.

text: Yes, we do appreciate the farmers—50 percent increase in export revenue in the primary sector when we were in office, through COVID and many other challenges.
explanation: Claims credit for a concrete delivered outcome (export revenue growth) achieved while in office, though external factors also drove it.

text: When we came in, actually, Tai Poutini Polytech on the West Coast was broke. We had to step up. We wrote out a cheque for $35 million just to keep them afloat
explanation: Defends the Te Pūkenga reform as a delivered intervention, though concedes it is 'only just starting' and imperfect.

text: calling for immediate, permanent, unconditional ceasefire—calling on our friends, on our allies, on our trading partners, on our Five Eyes network, on the family of nations in the Commonwealth, and on our Pasifika neighbourhood to do the same.
explanation: A clear stated position and call to action, but from Opposition with no power to deliver it — aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: Well, I’ve got news for Christopher Luxon: your circus, your clowns.
explanation: Derisive 'circus/clowns' framing of the governing parties — a cheap shot, not substantive critique.

text: Now, they’re going backwards to different places... Nicola Willis wants to go backwards to 1993... Winston Peters wants to go back to 1983... I suspect David Seymour... wants to go back to 1963.
explanation: Rhetorical device mocking opponents as wanting to return to past decades; pointed but aimed at their politics.

text: this is a three-way Government that will be the most extreme, the most right-wing Government I think since at least the early 1990s in New Zealand.
explanation: Charged label ('most extreme') but directed at the Government's politics rather than persons.

text: Sir Robert Muldoon, who ran riot as both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and put New Zealand in a position where we almost went broke, where the Reserve Bank was required to make sure that it went to ambassadors overseas and asked them to draw down foreign currency on their credit cards because New Zealand's foreign reserves had been drawn down so badly.
explanation: 'Ran riot' is a sharp characterisation of a former PM, but it critiques his governance record rather than launching a personal slur on a present member.

text: How is it that we have found ourselves as a country where we’re discussing te reo Māori as if it’s a bad thing?... te reo Māori is an official language, and we should be proud of it.
explanation: Passionate but engages the substance of language policy rather than attacking persons.

text: in the Waikato we will be in our first 100 days signing a memorandum of understanding with the University of Waikato about establishing a third medical school.
explanation: A signed MOU is an early step, not delivery of the medical school itself; commitment newly stated.

text: that’s why we’re seeing the first piece of legislation coming through next week helping to get the Reserve Bank back, focused on that core mandate, so that we can get the economy back under control, get that cost of living under control.
explanation: Imminent legislation indicates follow-through is beginning, but delivery not yet achieved.

text: we’ve discovered in the last week or so that he can’t tell the difference between the number one and the number 35. Chris Bishop seems to think that the outcome of the previous Government’s smoke-free changes was that there would be one outlet in all of Northland selling cigarettes, when in actual fact the publicly available number was 35.
explanation: Asserts the publicly available figure was 35 outlets rather than one; a specific factual correction presented as established.

text: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent.
explanation: The peak figures cited are broadly accurate (NZ ~7.3%, UK ~11.1%); minor imprecision in giving two NZ numbers.

text: When we made the change to go the other way, we had a full public consultation process run by an independent panel and then we came back and then we put it through the House and put it through a select committee.
explanation: Accurately describes the previous Government's process for the 2018 Reserve Bank reform, which did involve an independent review and select committee scrutiny.

text: Sir Robert Muldoon, who ran riot as both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and put New Zealand in a position where we almost went broke, where the Reserve Bank was required to make sure that it went to ambassadors overseas and asked them to draw down foreign currency on their credit cards because New Zealand's foreign reserves had been drawn down so badly.
explanation: Muldoon did hold both PM and Finance roles and NZ faced a severe foreign-exchange/constitutional crisis in 1984; 'almost went broke' and the credit-card anecdote are colourful and partly hyperbolic.

text: this is a three-way Government that will be the most extreme, the most right-wing Government I think since at least the early 1990s in New Zealand.
explanation: A sweeping characterisation offered as judgement ('I think') without supporting evidence.

text: Now, they’re going backwards to different places... Nicola Willis wants to go backwards to 1993... Winston Peters wants to go back to 1983... I suspect David Seymour... wants to go back to 1963.
explanation: Caricatures each opponent's views via decade labels rather than engaging their actual positions.

text: Climate change remains the single most important issue for New Zealand, not only from an environmental perspective but also from an economic perspective. If New Zealand wants to sell its goods into the world, we have to be doing the right thing by our planet.
explanation: Links climate action to export market access — a coherent economic argument, though asserted rather than evidenced.

text: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent.
explanation: Uses two or three country data points to argue no relationship between mandate and inflation — a weak inference from a tiny sample, as the next speaker points out.

text: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market.
explanation: Position is consistent across time: opposed FPAs when introduced, campaigned to repeal, now repealing — words match record.

text: I don’t believe in tolerating diversity; it sounds like you’re putting up with it. Actually, we embrace it and we celebrate it, and we’re a much, much better country for doing that.
explanation: Stated value consistent with Labour's positioning, though a value statement with no specific action attached here.

text: When we made the change to go the other way, we had a full public consultation process run by an independent panel and then we came back and then we put it through the House and put it through a select committee.
explanation: His call for select-committee scrutiny is consistent with the process his own Government followed for the reverse change, lending the position credibility.

text: If any fair pay agreements were finalised, the increased costs would have greatly affected a range of businesses up and down the country, regardless of whether they could have afforded them. This would have increased prices for consumers and could cause business closures, which is worse for employees. I don’t consider that a blunt tool will help our labour markets for either employers or employees.
explanation: Predicts price rises and business closures from FPAs; directionally plausible but counterfactual and contested, magnitude uncertain.

text: How is it that we have found ourselves as a country where we’re discussing te reo Māori as if it’s a bad thing?... te reo Māori is an official language, and we should be proud of it.
explanation: Appeals to shared national pride in te reo as common ground, though framed against the Government.

text: I don’t believe in tolerating diversity; it sounds like you’re putting up with it. Actually, we embrace it and we celebrate it, and we’re a much, much better country for doing that.
explanation: Articulates an inclusive, affirming vision; aimed at rallying support for diversity, persuasive within its frame.

text: Climate change remains the single most important issue for New Zealand, not only from an environmental perspective but also from an economic perspective. If New Zealand wants to sell its goods into the world, we have to be doing the right thing by our planet.
explanation: Frames climate action in terms appealing beyond his base (exporters, the economy).

text: We will champion our farmers and growers, we will respect our farmers and growers, and we will see them as the solution, and not the problem.
explanation: Rallies the rural base warmly but appeals only to one constituency.

text: our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
explanation: Designed to ridicule the prior government via a loaded comparison.

text: when the Labour Party announced that they were prepared to sacrifice 21 percent of the sheep and beef sector at the altar of the climate change policy
explanation: Emotive "at the altar" framing attacks motive rather than the policy detail.

text: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
explanation: Prediction about repealing smokefree law; consistent with public-health modelling cited at the time, though magnitudes are uncertain and long-term.

text: We are going to meet our carbon zero 2050 goals. We are on track to meet those targets
explanation: A long-horizon prediction of meeting 2050 net-zero; asserted confidently but emissions trajectories make it uncertain.

text: we delivered over 13,000 public homes in our term in office
explanation: Claims credit for a concrete delivered programme of public housing, largely borne out by the build record.

text: wool will be back in Government buildings. It is my favourite part of the coalition agreement.
explanation: A stated commitment from the coalition agreement; delivery still ahead at this point.

text: I believe in limited government; that, actually, we all hold solutions to many of the problems we face; that we are at our best when the community response can lead the Government response.
explanation: A stated value consistent with his National Party affiliation, but no action shown to test it.

text: This is an unnecessary, short-sighted bill. It is not evidence based. It won't do the things that the National Party are telling New Zealanders it will do.
explanation: Strong assertions ('not evidence based', 'won't do the things') without, at this point, the specifics to substantiate them.

text: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
explanation: The ~$0.5bn value is a contested industry estimate presented as settled fact.

text: For six years—perhaps more—rural New Zealand had been in a state of emotional decline. Many had suffered the left’s farming illiteracy.
explanation: 'The left’s farming illiteracy' is a dismissive characterisation of opponents, though aimed at competence on policy.

text: Whilst I absolutely refuse to politicise mental illness, while I absolutely refuse to politicise suicide, the terrible havoc and loss it leaves on rural communities is enormous. It is felt especially by those in small, tight-knit communities.
explanation: Respectful, serious acknowledgement of rural mental health harm without partisan attack.

text: For six years—perhaps more—rural New Zealand had been in a state of emotional decline. Many had suffered the left’s farming illiteracy.
explanation: Asserts a six-year 'emotional decline' caused by opponents without evidence; relies on the 'illiteracy' jibe.

text: He had travelled ill with cancer for four hours from Kaitāia to be part of that day. He battled on with his condition; he battled on with his post-cyclone recovery, and yet he still managed the time to be there for himself, for his community.
explanation: Emotive single anecdote used to characterise rural resilience — appeal to emotion rather than evidence.

text: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
explanation: Names the policy and attaches a figure ('half a billion dollars') but no timeframe or detail on safeguards.

text: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
explanation: States a coalition commitment to reverse the live export ban; intent, not yet delivered.

text: Whilst I absolutely refuse to politicise mental illness, while I absolutely refuse to politicise suicide, the terrible havoc and loss it leaves on rural communities is enormous. It is felt especially by those in small, tight-knit communities.
explanation: Sincere, empathetic appeal that could resonate across the chamber, though framed within his own caucus's pitch.

text: He had travelled ill with cancer for four hours from Kaitāia to be part of that day. He battled on with his condition; he battled on with his post-cyclone recovery, and yet he still managed the time to be there for himself, for his community.
explanation: Storytelling that honours a community; warm but addressed to shared rural sentiment.

text: New Zealand should rightfully expect that we will be a strong Opposition, that we will hold the Government to account for working in the best interests of all New Zealanders, and that we will hold the Government to account for the promises they made.
explanation: A stated commitment to a recognised constitutional role; consistent with being in opposition but no action yet to test it.

text: we should be judged on what we deliver, not “I think I can, I think I can, I hope I can.”
explanation: Invites accountability against delivery, consistent with a results-focused stance; sets a standard he accepts being held to.
